int U_i U_j d_i d_j a, which has no known sign (integral-estimate analysis F37, A1896-A1897, A1899-A1902; these are statements about the
method, not about profiles; A1898 and A1901 REFUTED two intermediate steps of the first version, both repaired).
Other weight families, spatial ones included, are not exhausted (A1728, A1903, A1986), and no bound on sup abs(W) has been derived from decay alone
(A1791, A1895 OPEN).

(b) (integral-estimate analysis C55, A1524-A1525.) Let 2/5 < c < 1; here U, P in C^1 suffice. If
int (1 + abs(y)^2)^(1/c - 3/2) abs(W)^2 dy < infinity, then U = 0. In particular abs(W) <= C(1 + abs(y))^(-gamma)
with gamma > 1/c suffices, as does abs(W) <= C abs(y)^(-1/c) (log abs(y))^(-beta) for abs(y) >= 2 with beta > 1/2;
1/c is the decay rate of the vorticity of a nonzero homogeneous tail (degree -p-1 = -1/c).

(c) (A093, A1535.) Let c > 0. If lambda_max(S(y)) < 1 for every abs(y) <= sup abs(U)/c, then U = 0.

(d) (the literature audit LIT362, A3044-A3045.) Let 0 < c < 2/3; here U, P in C^1 suffice. Write
q = tr((DU)^2) = abs(S)^2 - abs(W)^2/2, so that -Laplacian P = q. If q >= 0 everywhere or q <= 0 everywhere, then
U = 0. If 0 < c < 1, U -> 0 uniformly and (q(. + a) = q for some a != 0, or q(. + a_n) -> q in D' along some sequence
with abs(a_n) -> infinity), then U = 0; both alternatives assume 0 < c < 1 and uniform decay (A3068). More generally,
for 0 < c < 1 one sign of q forces U = 0 for every uniformly sublinear U with E(R) = o(R^2).

(e) (The auditor's spherical-source criterion, A3056-A3057.) Let 0 < c < 1/2; here U, P in C^1 suffice. For r >= 0 let
Q(r) be the integral of q(r theta) over theta in the unit sphere S^2. If Q(r) >= 0 for every r, or Q(r) <= 0 for every
r, then U = 0. The same holds if the mean q_0(rho, z) of q over the circles about the rotation axis has one sign,
since Q(r) = 2pi int_{-1}^{1} q_0(r sqrt(1 - u^2), r u) du. A nonzero profile therefore has Q and q_0 of both strict
signs. The underlying statement is kinematic and uses no equation: a C^1 divergence-free field U with E(R) = o(R) and
one sign of Q is zero. The shear U = (0, 0, g(x1, x2)) with g = (1 - x1^2 - x2^2)^2 on the unit disc and g = 0 outside
it is C^1 and divergence-free and has Q = 0 and E(R) = (2pi/5)R + O(R^(-1)), so o(R) cannot be replaced by O(R) in the
kinematic statement; this field does not decay, and for 2/5 < c < 1/2 it does not solve (E). On 0 < c < 1/2, (e)
contains the sign statement of (d); (d) also covers 1/2 <= c < 2/3 (A3057).

(f) (The cumulative-source criterion, the literature audit LIT367, A3063-A3064.) Let 2/5 < c < 1/2; here U, P in C^1 suffice. For
r > 0 let G(r) be the integral of q over the ball abs(y) < r, so that G(r) = int_0^r s^2 Q(s) ds, let N(r) be the
integral of (U.y)^2/r^2 over the sphere abs(y) = r, let K(r) = int_0^r s G(s) ds, and let Pbar(r) be the mean of P
over that sphere (the source and the review write S and A for G and K). Then G(r) = -4pi r^2 Pbar'(r) and
K(r) = rN(r) - E(r). If K(r) >= -C for all sufficiently large r and some constant C, then U = 0. In particular U = 0
if G(r) >= 0 for all sufficiently large r, or if Pbar is nonincreasing for all sufficiently large r; this contains the
case Q >= 0 of (e) on 2/5 < c < 1/2, since G(r) = int_0^r s^2 Q(s) ds. A nonzero profile therefore has G < 0 and
Pbar' > 0 at arbitrarily large radii, liminf K(r) = -infinity and limsup int_0^r s^3 Pbar'(s) ds = +infinity; with its
energy law E(r) = L r^beta + O(r^(beta-1)), beta = 5 - 2/c, the set of r in [R, 2R] with K(r) <= -(k/2)L R^beta has
measure at least k 2^(-beta-2) R for all large R, where k = (2^(beta+1) - 1)(1 - beta)/(1 + beta) > 0. The underlying
statement is kinematic and uses no equation: a C^1 divergence-free field with E(r) = o(r) and K(r) >= -C for all large
r has int abs(U)^2 <= C, and if G(r) >= 0 for every r it is zero; a field of finite energy has liminf
K(r) = -int abs(U)^2. Two controls bound it. U = (0, 0, f(x1, x2)) with f smooth, compactly supported and nonzero has
q = G = K = 0 and E(r) = 2r int f^2 + O(r^(-1)), so o(r) cannot be replaced by O(r); it does not decay, and for f = 1
near the origin it does not solve (E). U = (1 + abs(y)^2)^(-(a+1)/2) Jy with 1 < a < 3/2 is smooth, divergence-free,
decaying and tangent to every sphere, so N = 0, K = -E and G(r) = -T(r)/r < 0, with T(r) the integral of abs(U)^2 over
the sphere abs(y) = r, and its energy, of order r^(3-2a), is infinite; so G <= 0 at large radii does not give finite
energy. This field does not solve (E) for any c and omega. The endpoints c = 2/5 and c = 1/2 are not covered (A3063).

(g) (The exterior-source criterion, the literature audit LIT369, A3072-A3073.) Let 0 < c < 1/2; here U, P in C^1 suffice. For a
point a and r > 0 let Q_a(r) be the integral of q(a + r theta) over theta in S^2, so that Q_0 = Q. If, for some center
a and some b >= 0, Q_a(r) <= 0 for every r > b, then U = 0. A nonzero profile therefore has, about every center a,
radii r1 < r2 with Q_a(r1) < 0 < Q_a(r2), and a radius r > b with Q_a(r) > 0 for every b; in particular q does not
have compact support. This includes c = 2/5, where Theorem 1 also gives E(R) = o(R); there it is a conditional
statement, not nonexistence. With Pbar_a(r) the mean of P over the sphere abs(y - a) = r,
(r^2 Pbar_a')' = -r^2 Q_a/(4pi), so the excluded condition is that r^2 Pbar_a' be nondecreasing for all large r, which
differs from the condition on Pbar in (f). The underlying statements are kinematic apart from one step: a nonzero C^1
divergence-free field with E(R) = o(R) has, about every center a, radii r1 < r2 with Q_a(r1) < 0 < Q_a(r2), and if
Q_a(r) <= 0 for every r > b it vanishes where abs(y - a) > b; the equation enters only through the statement that, for
every real c != 0 and every omega, a compactly supported C^1 solution U, P of (E) is zero. The field U = (0, 0, f(x1,
x2)) of (f) has q = 0, is not compactly supported and has E(r) = 2r int f^2 + O(r^(-1)), so o(R) cannot be replaced by
O(R) in the kinematic statement. On 0 < c < 1/2, (g) contains the case Q <= 0 of (e). Negative means at arbitrarily
large radii are not asserted, and no such sign condition is derived from decay (A3074 OPEN).

(h) (The positive-moment criterion, the literature audit LIT366, A3075-A3076.) Let 2/5 < c < 1/2; here U, P in C^1 suffice. Let
q_+ = max(q, 0), q_- = max(-q, 0), M_+ = int abs(y)^2 q_+ and M_- = int abs(y)^2 q_-. If M_+ < infinity, then U = 0. A
nonzero profile therefore has M_+ = infinity; in particular int (1 + abs(y))^2 abs(q) = infinity. The underlying
statement is kinematic and uses no equation: a C^1 divergence-free field with E(R) = o(R) and M_+ < infinity has
finite energy, M_- <= M_+ and 2 int abs(U)^2 = M_+ - M_- = int_0^infinity r^4 Q(r) dr, the last integral converging
absolutely. For bounded U, P in C^1 and (E), finite energy then gives U = 0 for every real c != 2/5 and every omega,
by the energy identity (2 - 5c) int abs(U)^2 = 0; on 2/5 < c < 1/2 this step is also contained in Theorem 1, and no
novelty is claimed for it (A3076). At c = 2/5 only the identity is obtained, and c = 1/2 is not covered. The field
U = (0, 0, f(x1, x2)) of (f) has q = M_+ = 0 and E(r) = 2r int f^2 + O(r^(-1)), so o(R) cannot be replaced by O(R).
Decay and E(R) = o(R) do not make M_+ finite for divergence-free fields: the swirl U = (1 + abs(y)^2)^(-(a+1)/2) Jy
of (f), 1 < a < 3/2, has M_+ = infinity, and it does not solve (E) for any c and omega. Whether decay makes M_+ finite
for profiles is not known (A3077 OPEN).

(i) (The work-sign criterion, the literature audit LIT371, A3079-A3080, and its spherical-mean form, spectral analysis, A3106.) Let 0 < c < 1/2;
here U, P in C^1 suffice. Write (E) as the forced Euler equation (U.grad)U + grad P = Phi with
Phi = -(1 - c)U - ((Ay).grad)U - omega JU, and let w = U.Phi = U.grad(P + e) = -2(1 - c)e - (Ay).grad e, with
e = abs(U)^2/2, be the work of this force (D in LIT371). If w >= 0 everywhere or w <= 0 everywhere, then U = 0. A
nonzero profile therefore has points where w > 0 and points where w < 0; that both signs occur at arbitrarily large
radii is not asserted. This includes c = 2/5, where Theorem 1 gives finite energy. The integral of w over the ball
abs(y) < r is the flux F(r) of (2.2.2) with p = 0, and the proof uses the rate abs(R^(-alpha) E(R) - L) <= C/R of
Theorem 1, not only E(R) ~ L R^alpha. Two further statements need neither U bounded nor U(R.) -> 0. For every
0 < c < 1 and every omega, a C^1 profile with w = 0 everywhere is zero, with no growth or decay condition. More
generally (A3106; spectral analysis, as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, entry of 2026-11-04T08:29:36Z; review
the accompanying artifacts), let ebar(r) and wbar(r) be the means of e and w over
the sphere abs(y) = r. The term omega d_phi e of w = -2(1 - c)e - c y.grad e + omega d_phi e has zero spherical mean,
so wbar = -c r^(1-k)(r^k ebar)' with k = 2(1 - c)/c, and r^k ebar(r) -> 0 as r -> 0. Hence for every 0 < c < 1 and
every omega a C^1 profile with wbar(r) >= 0 for all r > 0, in particular one with w >= 0 everywhere, is zero, with no
growth or decay condition. In the bounded Hb class with 0 < c < 1/2, a nonzero profile has radii r1, r2 > 0 with
wbar(r1) < 0 < wbar(r2), so w and its mean over circles about the rotation axis take both strict signs on those
spheres; for 2/5 < c < 1/2 the proof uses the remainder of Theorem 1, and at c = 2/5 the finite energy. These means
are taken about the origin; the statement is not transferred to another center, and that both signs occur at
arbitrarily large radii is not asserted (A3107 OPEN). For a C^1 divergence-free field v on R^N, N >= 2, and H in C^1
with v.grad H of one sign, v.grad H = 0 if v is in L^s for some 1 <= s <= N/(N-1), with no condition on H, or if v is
in L^s and int abs(H)^(s/2) < infinity for some finite s > N/(N-1). This extends Theorem 1.1 of D. Chae,
Liouville-type theorems for the forced Euler equations and the Navier-Stokes equations, arXiv:1306.5839v1, 2013, which
assumes 3N/(N-1) < s < infinity, abs(v)^2 + abs(p) in L^(s/2) and a work of one sign vanishing exactly where v does;
no novelty is claimed for the extension. So for every 0 < c < 1 a C^1 profile with w of one sign is zero if U is in
L^s for some 1 <= s <= 3/2, or if U is in L^s and P - p0 is in L^(s/2) for some finite s > 3/2 and some constant p0;
in the bounded Hb class with 0 < c < 1/2 and c != 2/5, the cases s <= 2 already follow from finite energy (A3080). The
constant profile U = a != 0, P = -((1 - c)a + omega Ja).y has w = -(1 - c)abs(a)^2 < 0 and is uniformly sublinear; it
fails decay, Hb and every finite L^s condition, so these hypotheses cannot simply be dropped when w <= 0. No sign of w
is derived from decay or from (E) (A3081, A3107 OPEN).

(j) (Positive-density source returns, the literature audit LIT368, A3084-A3085.) Let 0 < c < 1/2; here U, P in C^1 suffice. Fix
a != 0, a test function phi supported in the ball abs(y) < r0, and let I_n be the pairing of q(. + na) with phi. If
q(. + na) -> q in D' as n -> infinity along a set D of positive integers of positive upper density, then U = 0;
uniform decay, assumed in the return statement of (d), is not needed. More precisely, the number of n <= N with
abs(I_n) >= epsilon is at most C E(N abs(a) + r0)/epsilon, so for a nonzero profile with 2/5 < c < 1/2 and a test phi
with I_0 != 0, a return set D has O(N^beta) elements below N, with beta = 5 - 2/c (A3085). The underlying statement is
kinematic and uses no equation: a C^1 divergence-free field v with E_v(R) = o(R) whose source q_v = tr((Dv)^2) returns
in this sense along a set of positive upper density is zero; for a = e3 it suffices that the average of q_v over the
rotations about the vertical axis returns (A3085). In a kinematic argument, E(R) = o(R) cannot replace the uniform
decay of (d): with V0 a smooth divergence-free field supported in abs(y) < 1/4 and equal to -Jy near 0, the field U,
the sum of V0(y - m e3) over the integers m = sum epsilon_j 10^j with finitely many digits epsilon_j in {-1, 0, 1}, is
smooth with bounded derivatives, has E(R) = O(R^d), d = log 3/log 10, infinite energy, U(R.) -> 0 in D' and no uniform
decay, and satisfies U(. + 10^k e3) = U on every compact set for all large k. Near 0 it equals -Jy, the terms of (E)
other than grad P have curl -2e3 there, and it solves (E) for no c and omega. Whether a sparse return excludes bounded
Hb profiles, or whether positive density is optimal for them, is not known (A3086 OPEN).

(k) (Radii of negative cumulative source, the literature audit LIT370, A3087-A3088.) Let 2/5 < c < 1/2; here U, P in C^1 suffice.
Let U be nonzero, with N, K and Pbar as in (f) and beta = 5 - 2/c. For every lambda > 1 and 0 < kappa < 1 - beta there
is a constant C such that, for all large R, the set of r in [R, lambda R] with K(r) <= -kappa E(r) has logarithmic
measure, the integral of dr/r over it, at least [1 - beta/(1 - kappa)] log lambda - C/R, and Lebesgue measure at least
[1 - beta/(1 - kappa) - C/R](lambda - 1)R; at these radii int_0^r s^3 Pbar'(s) ds >= kappa E(r)/(4pi). This is an
inequality for an accumulated integral, not a sign of Pbar' or of Q at these radii. The underlying statement is
kinematic and uses no equation: it holds for every C^1 divergence-free field with E(r) = L r^beta + O(r^(beta-1)),
L > 0 and 0 < beta < 1, and no derivative of the error term is taken. The energy law alone gives no limit and no
eventual sign of K: for every L > 0 and 0 < beta < 1 there is a smooth divergence-free field that tends uniformly to
0, has E(r) = L r^beta + O(r^(beta-1)) and K(10^n) = L 10^(n beta) + O(10^(n(beta-1))) -> +infinity, and has K = -E on
other arbitrarily large radii. It is a swirl f(abs(y))Jy with thin poloidal shells of high spherical-harmonic degree
at the radii 10^n, whose energy is subtracted from the swirl just outside each shell; it has
E'(10^n) = (beta + 2)L 10^(n(beta-1)), so the derivative law E' ~ beta L r^(beta-1) fails along 10^n, and it solves
(E) for no c and omega. An eventual sign of K for profiles, a pointwise limit stronger than liminf K = -infinity, and
an optimal density constant are not known (A3089 OPEN).

(l) (The critical positive-source weight, the literature audit LIT373 and LIT374, A3094-A3095, A3098-A3099.) Let 2/5 < c < 1/2; here
U, P in C^1 suffice. Let beta = 5 - 2/c as in (k), so that 2 - beta = 2/c - 3 lies in (1, 2). For a center a let
Q_a(r) = int_{S^2} q(a + r theta) dtheta, the integral of q over the unit sphere scaled to radius r about a, and let
Pbar_a(r) be the mean of P over the sphere abs(y - a) = r. If, for one center a, int
(1 + abs(y - a))^(2/c-3) max(q, 0) dy < infinity, or int_1^infinity r^(2/c-1) max(Q_a(r), 0) dr < infinity, then
U = 0. Since (r^2 Pbar_a')' = -r^2 Q_a/(4pi), the second integral equals 4pi int_1^infinity
r^(2/c-3) max(-(r^2 Pbar_a')', 0) dr, a weighted amount of decrease of r^2 Pbar_a', not a pointwise sign. Since
abs(q) <= abs(DU)^2 (Frobenius norm), it also suffices that int (1 + abs(y - a))^(2/c-3) abs(DU)^2 dy < infinity, for
instance that abs(DU) <= C abs(y)^(-1/c)(log abs(y))^(-1/2-epsilon) for some epsilon > 0 and all large abs(y). The
first criterion contains (h), whose weight 2 is larger, and the second contains (g) in this range of c. The natural
rate abs(DU) <= C(1 + abs(y))^(-1/c), which a decaying C^2 profile has as soon as DU = O(abs(y)^(1/2)) (A476-A477,
A492, A498), bounds the integral of the weighted derivative integrand over the sphere abs(y) = r only by C/r, whose
integral diverges, so it decides neither convergence nor divergence (A3096). The underlying statement is kinematic and
uses no equation: for a C^1 divergence-free field with E(R)/(L R^beta) -> 1, L > 0 and 0 < beta < 1, there are
c_beta > 0, depending only on beta and a fixed cutoff, and C such that int_{abs(y) < R}
abs(y)^2 max(q, 0) dy >= c_beta L R^beta and int_{1 < abs(y) < R}
abs(y)^(2-beta) max(q, 0) dy >= beta c_beta L log R - C for all large R, about every fixed center, and the same bounds
hold with abs(y)^2 max(q, 0) dy replaced by r^4 max(Q_a(r), 0) dr; two-sided bounds a0 R^beta <= E(R) <= A0 R^beta
give the same conclusions with another positive coefficient. The logarithmic bound holds with the explicit coefficient
k_beta = beta(2 - beta)(1 - beta) in place of beta c_beta, and k_beta > 4 beta c_beta for every 0 < beta < 1
(the literature audit LIT374, A3098-A3099; review in the accompanying artifacts; the integral-estimate analysis comparison
as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, saved at 2026-11-04T08:18Z, A3099): with H_a(R) = int_{abs(y - a) < R}
abs(y - a)^(2-beta) max(q, 0) dy, the energy ratio gives liminf_{R -> infinity} H_a(R)/log R >= k_beta L, and
E(R) = L R^beta + O(R^(beta-1)) gives H_a(R) >= k_beta L log R - C for all large R, about every fixed center; both
hold with H_a(R) replaced by int_0^R r^(4-beta) max(Q_a(r), 0) dr, and E(R) = L R^beta + O(R^(beta-1)) also gives that
the compact signed pairing int q(y) abs(y)^(2-beta) chi(y/R) dy lies between k_beta L log R - C and
beta(2 - beta)L log R + C. Under the energy ratio alone the same two coefficients hold with errors o(log R) in place
of C, and an additive upper error O(1) fails in general: a smooth tangential swirl f(abs(y))Jy with
E(R) = L R^beta(1 + (log R)^(-1/2)) + O(1) satisfies the ratio hypothesis, and its signed pairing is
beta(2 - beta)L log R + 2beta(2 - beta)L (log R)^(1/2) + O(1) (A3116-A3117;
the accompanying artifacts, Sections 3 and 5). A logarithmic lower bound alone does not
imply the power lower bound for int_{abs(y) < R} abs(y)^2 max(q, 0) dy, so the two statements are separate (A3099).
For a profile, k_beta = (5 - 2/c)(2/c - 3)(2/c - 4), independent of omega. For a nonzero profile Theorem 1 gives the
energy ratio (A3053). The power 2 - beta cannot be lowered in this kinematic statement: for every L > 0 and
0 < beta < 1 a smooth swirl U0 = f0(abs(y))Jy that tends uniformly to 0 and has E(R) = L R^beta for R >= 2 has
int_{abs(y) < R} abs(y)^2 max(q, 0) = L h_beta R^beta + O(1), h_beta = (3 - beta)^(3/2)/sqrt(5 - beta),
int_{1 < abs(y) < R} abs(y)^(2-beta) max(q, 0) = beta L h_beta log R + O(1), and int (1 + abs(y))^gamma
max(q, 0) < infinity for every gamma < 2 - beta; its radial moment int_0^R r^4 max(Q_0(r), 0) dr is
(2 - beta)L R^beta + O(1), its radial critical moment int_1^R r^(4-beta) max(Q_0(r), 0) dr is
beta(2 - beta)L log R + O(1), the upper coefficient of the signed pairing (A3099), its signed moment int_{abs(y) < R}
abs(y)^2 q is (2 - beta)L R^beta for R > 2, and the moment of max(-q, 0) is [h_beta - (2 - beta)]L R^beta + O(1), with
h_beta > 2 - beta. On abs(y) > 2 it is b abs(y)^((beta-5)/2) Jy; the azimuthal component of (E) forces
1 + c(beta - 5)/2 = 0, which holds exactly when beta = 5 - 2/c, and then the required pressure gradient
b^2 abs(y)^(beta-5)(y1, y2, 0) has nonzero curl, so U0 solves (E) for no c and omega. Whether the critical moment of a
bounded Hb or decaying profile is finite is not known (A3097, A3100 OPEN); c_beta is not asserted optimal, and the
endpoints c = 2/5 and c = 1/2 are not covered. The coefficient k_beta cannot be raised in the kinematic statement
(the literature audit LIT377, A3118-A3119; review in the accompanying artifacts; the spectral analysis
comparison as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, entry of 2026-11-04T08:58:26Z): for every epsilon > 0 there is a smooth
uniformly decaying divergence-free field with E(R) = L R^beta for R >= 2, E_a(R) = L R^beta + O_a(R^(beta-2)) about
every fixed center and a smooth Poisson pressure, for which H_a(R)/(L log R) tends to a limit smaller than
k_beta + epsilon about every fixed center, the positive part of q being taken pointwise before any angular
integration. Each of these fields has a compact swirl core whose momentum residual has nonzero curl for every c and
omega, so none solves (E). One smooth field attains k_beta (the literature audit LIT380, A3139-A3140; source
as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, sha256 2056b6a9 as reviewed, revised to
6fde407a in its status paragraph and in one sentence that makes the active-block index explicit (A3142); review
the accompanying artifacts; the integral-estimate analysis comparison as summarized in the accompanying artifacts,
retained in the review as summarized in the accompanying artifacts; its revision 524dd668 is CONFIRMED except one sentence
inferring a vanishing toroidal share from an upper bound alone, which is REFUTED, A3142-A3143; the revision b13f5a14
replaces that sentence, CONFIRMED, A3144): for every L > 0 and 0 < beta < 1 there is a C-infinity divergence-free
field, odd under y -> -y, with E(R) = L R^beta for R >= 2, E_a(R) = L R^beta + O_(a,epsilon)(R^(beta-2+epsilon)) for
every epsilon > 0, every derivative D^h U of order h >= 0 bounded by C_(h,epsilon) abs(y)^((beta-3)/2-h+epsilon) at
large abs(y), so that U and all its derivatives tend uniformly to 0, and a smooth Poisson pressure, for which
H_a(R)/log R and int_1^R r^(4-beta) max(Q_a(r), 0) dr/log R both tend to k_beta L, int_{2 < abs(y - a) < R}
abs(y - a)^(-beta)abs(U_tan)^2 dy = o(log R), with U_tan as below, and G_a(R)/log R -> infinity, with G_a as in (m),
about every fixed center; G_a(R) = o(R^p) for every p > 0, and abs(y)^((5-beta)/2) abs(DU) is unbounded. Its core has
a momentum residual with nonzero curl for every c and omega, so it solves (E) for no c and omega (A3139). For every
C^1 divergence-free field with the energy ratio, H_a(R)/log R -> k_beta L at a center forces G_a(R)/log R -> infinity
at that center (A3140; see (n)). If limsup_{R -> infinity} H_a(R)/(L log R) <= k_beta + epsilon, then the component of
U tangential to the spheres about a carries, in the limit superior as R -> infinity, at most the fraction
epsilon/[beta^2(2 - beta)] of int_{2 < abs(y - a) < R} abs(y - a)^(-beta)abs(U)^2 (A3119). The radial form behaves in
the same way, with the tangential energy retained (the literature audit LIT376, A3121-A3122; review
the accompanying artifacts; the integral-estimate analysis comparison
as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, revised at 2026-11-04T09:07Z after A3123 REFUTED a closing sentence of its first version
that called k_beta not optimal for the pointwise form; the revision is CONFIRMED, A3128). With max(Q_a(r), 0) taken
after the spherical integration, U_tan the component of U tangential to the spheres about a and
F_tan,a(R) = int_{2 < abs(y - a) < R} abs(y - a)^(-beta)abs(U_tan)^2, E(R) = L R^beta + O(R^(beta-1)) gives
int_1^R r^(4-beta) max(Q_a(r), 0) dr >= k_beta L log R + beta(2 - beta)F_tan,a(R) - C for all large R, and the energy
ratio gives the corresponding liminf bound; if moreover int_2^infinity r^(4-beta) max(-Q_a(r), 0) dr is finite, then
under E(R) = L R^beta + O(R^(beta-1)) the two sides differ by O(1), and under the energy ratio alone by o(log R)
(A3122, A3138). The coefficient k_beta cannot be raised for this form either: for every epsilon > 0 a smooth uniformly
decaying divergence-free field with E(R) = L R^beta for R >= 2, E_a(R) = L R^beta + O_a(R^(beta-2)) and a smooth
Poisson pressure has int_1^R r^(4-beta) max(Q_a(r), 0) dr/(L log R) tending to a limit smaller than k_beta + epsilon
about every fixed center, and it solves (E) for no c and omega (A3121). For each tau in (0, 1], among fields with this
energy law and F_tan,0(R)/(beta L log R) -> tau, the least possible value of the liminf of
int_1^R r^(4-beta) max(Q_0(r), 0) dr/(L log R) is beta(2 - beta)(1 - beta + beta tau), and a smooth field attains it
as a limit about every fixed center (A3122). The field of LIT380 attains k_beta at tau = 0 (A3139). Whether k_beta is
optimal for profiles in either form is not known (A3120, A3124, A3141 OPEN).

(m) (The critical gradient weight, the literature audit LIT378, A3125-A3126.) Let 2/5 < c < 1/2; here U, P in C^1 suffice. If
DU = o(abs(y)^(-1/c)) as abs(y) -> infinity, then U = 0. More precisely, with abs(DU) the Frobenius norm,
alpha = 5 - 2/c and H = (1 - 1/c)^2((3 - 1/c)^2 + 4)/((3 - 1/c)^2 + 2), every nonzero profile in this class satisfies
int_{1 < abs(y - a) < R} abs(y - a)^(2/c-3) abs(DU)^2 dy >= alpha H L log R - C_a for all large R about every center a
and limsup_{abs(y) -> infinity} abs(y)^(1/c) abs(DU(y)) >= (alpha H L/(4pi))^(1/2) > 0, with L > 0 the energy constant
of Theorem 1, for every finite omega (Theorem 3(n)). This is a limit superior over distant points, not a lower bound
on every sphere or in every direction. If moreover U is C^2 and DU = o(abs(y)^(1/2)), then
abs(DU) <= C(1 + abs(y))^(-1/c) (A3102, see the paragraph after Theorem 1), so for a nonzero such profile this limit
superior is finite and positive (A3126). The underlying statement is kinematic and uses no equation (the literature audit LIT378,
A3125; source as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, sha256 10135e94 as reviewed,
revised to 67682265 in its status paragraph only (A3136); review
the accompanying artifacts; the synthesis comparison as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, whose
remark W2 is the bound on the limit superior, A3126): for a C^1 divergence-free field with
E(R) = L R^beta + O(R^(beta-1)), L > 0 and 0 < beta < 1, let t = (beta - 3)/2, k = (beta + 1)/2,
H_beta = t^2(k^2 + 4)/(k^2 + 2) and G_a(R) = int_{1 < abs(y - a) < R} abs(y - a)^(2-beta) abs(DU)^2 dy; then
G_a(R) >= beta H_beta L log R - C_a for R >= 2 about every fixed center a, and the energy ratio gives
liminf_{R -> infinity} G_a(R)/log R >= beta H_beta L, hence limsup_{abs(y) -> infinity} abs(y)^((5-beta)/2)
abs(DU(y)) >= (beta H_beta L/(4pi))^(1/2). At beta = alpha, H_beta = H. H_beta is the sharp constant C_(3,gamma) of
the Hardy-Leray inequality for solenoidal fields with a finite weighted norm (Hamamoto, arXiv:2305.12177v1,
Theorem 1.1) at gamma = 1 - beta/2, and it is also the sharp constant in the earlier classes of compactly supported
fields, axisymmetric (Costin and Maz'ya, arXiv:math/0703116v2), with swirl independent of the azimuth (Hamamoto and
Takahashi, arXiv:1904.01338v1) and without symmetry (Hamamoto, Nonlinear Analysis, DOI 10.1016/j.na.2019.111634), on
the theorem pages checked (A3129; the full papers and their final versions are not certified, A3130 OPEN); the
weighted norm of U is infinite, and the proof localizes the inequality instead of applying these theorems. Since
H_beta - (2 - beta)(1 - beta) >= 11/12, beta H_beta > k_beta, so this bound is stronger than the one that (l) gives
through max(q, 0) <= abs(DU)^2 (A3126). The coefficient is attained: one smooth uniformly decaying divergence-free
field with E(R) = L R^beta for R >= 2, E_a(R) = L R^beta + O_a(R^(beta-2)) and a smooth Poisson pressure has
G_a(R) = beta H_beta L log R + O_a(1) about every fixed center; its compact swirl core has a momentum residual with
nonzero curl for every c and omega, so it solves (E) for no c and omega (A3125). Whether the coefficient is optimal
for profiles, and whether the decay of U controls DU, is not known (A3127 OPEN).

(n) (The source-gradient tradeoff, the literature audit LIT379, A3132-A3133.) Let 2/5 < c < 1/2; here U, P in C^1 suffice. A finite
logarithmic rate for the critical gradient moment of (m) forces a strict surplus in the critical positive-source
moments of (l). The underlying statement is kinematic and uses no equation (source
as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, sha256 74ab8bf0 as reviewed, revised to 764ee00a in its
status paragraph only (A3142); review in the accompanying artifacts; the spectral analysis
comparison as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, entry of 2026-11-04T09:12:21Z, retained in the review as
as summarized in the accompanying artifacts): let U be a C^1 divergence-free field with E(R)/(L R^beta) -> 1, L > 0 and
0 < beta < 1, let t = (beta - 3)/2, k = (beta + 1)/2 and m = 2 - beta, so that k_beta = beta m(1 - beta), and about a
fixed center a let F_a(R) = int_{1 < abs(y - a) < R} abs(y - a)^(-beta)abs(U)^2 dy, T_a(R) the same integral of
abs(U_tan)^2, with U_tan the component of U tangential to the spheres about a, G_a(R) as in (m),
I_a(R) = int_{1 < abs(y - a) < R} abs(y - a)^(2-beta) max(q, 0) dy and J_a(R) = int_1^R r^(4-beta) max(Q_a(r), 0) dr.
Then F_a(R)/log R -> beta L, k F_a <= (G_a T_a)^(1/2) + (k + 1)T_a + C and J_a >= m[(1 - beta)F_a + beta T_a] - C for
all large R, and 0 <= J_a <= I_a <= G_a. If limsup_{R -> infinity} G_a(R)/(beta L log R) <= M < infinity, then
M >= t^2, liminf_{R -> infinity} T_a(R)/(beta L log R) >= d_beta(M - t^2), and the liminf of J_a(R)/log R and of
I_a(R)/log R is at least k_beta L + m beta^2 L d_beta(M - t^2), where

No helicity or symmetry condition is imposed. Each part retains its stated additional hypotheses; in particular part
(m) uses derivative decay for its nonexistence criterion, and parts (m) and (n) use the C^2 premises and
DU = o(abs(y)^(1/2)) of A3102 for their finite-amplitude consequences (A3137). Proof outline. (a) Theorem 1 gives
E(2R) = O(R^(5-2/c)) with 5 - 2/c < 2, hence the shell bound sup_{R >= 1} R^(-2) int_{R <= abs(y) < 2R} abs(U)^2 <
infinity, and int (1 + abs(y)^2)^(-(m+2)/2) abs(U)^2 dy < infinity for every m > 3 - 2/c (synthesis CO59(a), integral-estimate analysis C56,
A1530-A1531; as summarized in the accompanying artifacts). An energy identity for the vorticity equation with a radial cutoff
then gives W and DU in L^2, U in L^6 and the exact identities int abs(S)^2 = (1/2) int abs(W)^2 and
(1 - 3c/2) int abs(W)^2 = int W.SW (A1433-A1434). For trace-free S, W.SW <= sqrt(2/3) abs(S) abs(W)^2, so
(1 - 3c/2) int abs(W)^2 <= (sup abs(W)/sqrt(3)) int abs(W)^2, hence W = 0 and U = 0 (A1435). The constant t* comes
from the nonlinear version (integral-estimate analysis C57): with t = abs(W)^2 and a C^1 weight g, g(0) = 0, g' >= 0, the transport identity
W.SW = t + B.grad(t)/2 gives int phi_R [2 g' W.SW - 2 g' t + 3c g] = -int g B.grad(phi_R) >= 0 for radial cutoffs
phi_R, which combined with int phi_R (abs(S)^2 - t/2) -> 0 and the trace-free bound leaves a pointwise density bounded
below by a square plus h(t) = 2 g't - 3c g - t/2 - (2/3) g'^2 t^2; for g = t + (21/20) t^2 and 0 < c <= 1/2,
h(t) >= t^2 (47/24 - (14/5) t - (147/50) t^2) > 0 on (0, t*), an exact polynomial statement (A1584-A1585). For the
rows of Corollary NW.2, h/t is a cubic with rational coefficients that has no root on [0, T_k^2] (exact Sturm counts,
integral-estimate analysis check N6, A1635). The strain forms use the
Betchov identity int W.SW = -(4/3) int tr(S^3) with abs(tr(S^3)) <= abs(S)^3/sqrt(6) and
-tr(S^3) <= (-lambda_min(S)) abs(S)^2/2; with W bounded, as assumed in (a), bounded S makes DU bounded, so
W = O(1/abs(y)) (A492) and the far-field condition holds automatically (A1534). Without the bound on W the same
identity is used with a cutoff: the energy bound of Theorem 1 and bounded S give int_{B_R} abs(DU)^2 = O(R^3), and
the resulting inequality, applied finitely often, lowers the exponent to 2, 1 and 0 and then gives DU = 0 (integral-estimate analysis C62,
A2004-A2005). (b) Locally bounded W with finite weighted L^2 mass at the exponent
3 - 2/c in (-2, 1) gives int_{B_R} abs(BS(W))^2 = o(R^(5-2/c)) for the Biot-Savart integral BS(W); U(R.) -> 0 in D'
removes the harmonic remainder, so U = BS(W) and E(R) = o(R^(5-2/c)), against the positive energy constant of
Theorem 1 (A1524-A1525). Conversely every nonzero profile in this class has limsup_k b_k^2 >= L/C4^2 > 0 for the
normalized shell norms b_k = 2^(-k(3-2/c)/2) norm(W)_{L^2(2^(k-1) <= abs(y) < 2^k)}, with L the energy constant and
C4 explicit (A1526). (c) Backward orbits of B = (cI - omega J)y + U enter a slightly larger ball, which is backward
invariant, and on it abs(W)^2 decays exponentially along the flow; boundedness of W on that compact ball (automatic
for U in C^1) forces W = 0, U is constant, and
U(R.) -> 0 makes it zero (A093, A1535). (d) For divergence-free C^1 U, q = d_i d_j(U_i U_j) in D', so
abs(int q chi(./R)) <= K R^(-2) E(2R) for a fixed cutoff chi; Theorem 1 gives E(R) = o(R^2) because 5 - 2/c < 2, so
one sign of q forces q = 0. Under uniform decay the translated identity gives int q(. + a_n) phi -> 0 for every test
function phi, so a period or a return forces q = 0. Then P is harmonic, the rescaled equation and the radial mean
value of grad P (as in Lemma 2.2) give grad P = 0, and the dot product of (E) with U gives
B.grad abs(U)^2 = -2(1-c)abs(U)^2 along backward orbits that stay in compact balls, so U = 0 (A3044; review
the accompanying artifacts; the integral-estimate analysis comparison A113 and the spectral analysis comparison,
A3045). E(R) = O(R^2), which is what Theorem 1 gives at c = 2/3, would not suffice, and no statement is made there
(A3046). (e) Theorem 1 gives E(R) = o(R) for 0 < c < 1/2, since 5 - 2/c < 1 (rechecked in A3053), and the cutoff bound
of (d) makes one sign of Q force Q = 0. With f = sqrt(1 + abs(y)^2), whose Hessian has the positive eigenvalues
(1 + abs(y)^2)^(-1/2) and (1 + abs(y)^2)^(-3/2), the radial test f chi(./R) then gives int chi(./R) U.(D^2
f)U = -int U.H_R U, where H_R is supported in R <= abs(y) <= 2R and abs(int U.H_R U) <= C E(2R)/R; hence
(1 + L^2)^(-3/2) E(L) <= C E(2R)/R -> 0 for every L, and U = 0. For Q <= 0 the convex test alone suffices (A3056;
review in the accompanying artifacts; the spectral analysis comparison of 2026-11-04T07:15:46Z and the
integral-estimate analysis comparison A117, A3057). (f) For divergence-free C^1 U, q = div((U.grad)U) after local mollification, so G(r) is
the flux of (U.grad)U through the sphere abs(y) = r; in polar form this flux equals N' - (T - N)/r, where T(r) = E'(r)
is the integral of abs(U)^2 over the sphere and 0 <= N <= T, so rG = (rN - E)' and K = rN - E, with no constant since
E and rN are O(r^3) at 0. If K >= -C for r >= r_0, then rE' >= rN = E + K >= E - C, so (E - C)/r is nondecreasing on
[r_0, infinity); it tends to 0 since E = o(r), so E <= C. For a nonzero profile with 2/5 < c < 1/2, Theorem 1 gives
E(r) = L r^beta + O(r^(beta-1)) with L > 0 and 0 < beta < 1, which is infinite energy, so U = 0. The divergence of (E)
gives -Laplacian P = q in D', and the divergence theorem, again by mollification, gives G = -4pi r^2 Pbar'. For finite
energy, int_1^infinity N <= int_1^infinity E' < infinity gives radii r_j -> infinity with r_j N(r_j) -> 0, hence the
liminf. The measure bound follows from K <= rE' - E averaged over [R, 2R], which gives (1/R) int_R^(2R)
K <= -k L R^beta + O(R^(beta-1)), together with K >= -E(2R) (A3063; review
the accompanying artifacts; the spectral analysis comparison of 2026-11-04T07:31:27Z, A3064). (g) The
convex tests of (e), centered at a, give the ordered signs: otherwise Q_a >= 0 below some r_0 and Q_a <= 0 above it,
and Q_a(r)(f(r) - f(r_0)) <= 0 with f(r) = sqrt(1 + r^2), together with the cutoff bound of (d), gives E = 0. If
Q_a <= 0 beyond b, a radial test h(abs(y - a)) with h = 0 on [0, rho], 0 <= h' <= 1, 0 <= h(r) <= r and h', h'' > 0
beyond rho has positive definite Hessian where abs(y - a) > rho, and the cutoff error is O(E(2R + abs(a))/R), so
U = 0 where abs(y - a) > rho, for every rho > b. A compactly supported C^1 profile has a complete carrier flow Phi_t
with det DPhi_t = exp(3ct), and alpha = U.dy satisfies Phi_t^* d alpha = exp((2c - 1)t) d alpha, so the bounded open
set where curl U != 0 is invariant while its volume is multiplied by exp(3ct); for c != 0 it is empty, U is harmonic
with compact support, and U = 0. This is the invariant-volume argument of A067; for c != 2/5 the energy identity
(1 - 5c/2) int abs(U)^2 = 0 already suffices, and the circulation argument also covers c = 2/5 (A3072; review
the accompanying artifacts; the integral-estimate analysis comparison A120, A3073). (h) With
f_R(y) = abs(y)^2 for abs(y) <= R and 2R abs(y) - R^2 beyond, a convex C^(1,1) test with D^2 f_R = 2I on the ball and
0 <= D^2 f_R <= 2I, the identity int q chi(./L) f_R = int chi(./L) U.(D^2 f_R)U + O((R/L)E(2L)), the limit
L -> infinity at fixed R and then R -> infinity give 2E(R) <= M_+, finite energy, finite M_- and the identity, with no
difference of infinite quantities. For a profile, P differs by a constant from the Riesz-transform pressure P0 in L^2,
by the rescaled equation and the mean value property of the harmonic difference, and the cutoff energy identity gives
(2 - 5c) int abs(U)^2 = 0 (A3075; review in the accompanying artifacts; the integral-estimate analysis
comparison A121, A3076). (i) With a cutoff chi_R and phi(t) = t/(1 + t) when s <= N/(N-1), or phi(t) = t^m with
m = (sN - s - N)/(2N) when s > N/(N-1), replaced by (t + eps)^m - eps^m with eps fixed when 0 < m < 1, the Lipschitz
chain rule gives int_{H>0} chi_R phi'(H) v.grad H = -int phi(max(H, 0)) v.grad chi_R and the analogue on {H < 0}, with
no contribution from {H = 0}; the right sides tend to 0 by Holder's inequality, with exponents s/(2m), s and N in the
second case, and the one sign of v.grad H with Fatou's lemma gives v.grad H = 0 on {H != 0}, hence everywhere by
continuity. For a profile with w = 0, (Ay).grad e = -2(1 - c)e, so e(exp(tau A)y0) = exp(-2(1 - c)tau) e(y0) for real
tau, while exp(tau A)y0 -> 0 as tau -> -infinity; boundedness of e near 0 gives e(y0) = 0. In the Hb class, if w has
one sign and is not identically zero, then F has a fixed sign and abs(F) >= d > 0 for large r. For 2/5 < c < 1/2,
(2.2.3) gives abs(R^(-alpha) E(R) - L) >= (2d/(c alpha)) R^(-alpha), against the bound C/R of Theorem 1, since
alpha < 1; the remainder is not differentiated. At c = 2/5, (2.2.2) gives F = -(cr/2)E' <= 0, so w >= 0 gives w = 0,
and w <= 0 with w not identically zero gives E' >= 2d/(cr) at large r, against finite energy; below 2/5, U = 0 by
Theorem 1. The same identities give int_R^infinity F(r) r^(-1-alpha) dr = (c/2)(R^(-alpha) E(R) - L) = O(1/R) as a
signed improper integral, and int_1^infinity abs(F)/r = (c/2)(E(infinity) - E(1)) at c = 2/5 (A3079; review
the accompanying artifacts; the integral-estimate analysis comparison A123, A3080). (j) For C^1
divergence-free v, q_v = d_i d_j(v_i v_j) in D', so I_n = int v_i v_j (d_i d_j phi)(y - na) dy; the balls of radius r0
about the points na have bounded overlap and lie in abs(y) < N abs(a) + r0 for n <= N, so the sum of abs(I_n) over
n <= N is at most C E_v(N abs(a) + r0) = o(N). This gives the counting bound and, against abs(I_n) >= abs(I_0)/2 on a
set of positive upper density, gives I_0 = 0; then q_v = 0, and the convex test sqrt(1 + abs(y)^2) of (e), with cutoff
error C E_v(2R)/R, gives v = 0; for profiles Theorem 1 gives E(R) = o(R). In the control, distinct digit strings give
distinct integers, at most 3(9R/8)^d of them lie in [-R, R], and for every M and all large k an integer m with
abs(m) <= M has such an expansion if and only if 10^k + m has one, which gives the exact local return (A3084; review
the accompanying artifacts; the spectral analysis comparison of 2026-11-04T07:58:02Z, A3085).
(k) Outside the set, rN/E > 1 - kappa and N <= T = E', so (1 - kappa) times the logarithmic measure of the complement
is at most log(E(lambda R)/E(R)) = beta log lambda + O(1/R), taken from the energy law without differentiating its
error; integrating rE'/E by parts gives the Lebesgue version (A3088). In the control, the shells Z_n = (Lambda_n
h_n/r^2)Y_n e_r + (h_n'/r) grad_{S^2} Y_n, with Y_n zonal of degree ell_n = ceiling(10^n/delta),
Lambda_n = ell_n(ell_n + 1) and h_n supported in abs(r - 10^n) < delta, are divergence-free and orthogonal to the
swirl; the subtraction keeps E equal to L r^beta outside [10^n - delta, 10^n + 3] and within C 10^(n(beta-1)) of it
there; N(10^n) = 2L 10^(n(beta-1)) gives K(10^n) = rN - E; the sup bounds for spherical harmonics give uniform decay;
and on an untouched annulus U = b r^p Jy with p = (beta - 5)/2, where the azimuthal component of (E) forces 1 + cp = 0
and then a pressure gradient with nonzero curl (A3087; review
the accompanying artifacts; the spectral analysis comparison of 2026-11-04T07:58:02Z, A3088).
(l) For C^1 divergence-free U, q = d_i d_j(U_i U_j) in D' (by mollification), so int q psi = int U.(D^2 psi)U for
compactly supported C^(1,1) tests psi. The test phi_rho(y)chi(y/T), with phi_rho = abs(y)^2 for abs(y) <= rho and
2 rho abs(y) - rho^2 beyond, whose Hessian is 2I inside and (2 rho/abs(y))(I - e_r e_r^T), positive semidefinite,
outside, and chi = 1 on abs(y) <= 1 and 0 outside abs(y) <= 2, gives 2E(rho) <= M_+(2T) + C_chi(rho/T)E(2T), with
M_+(R) = int_{abs(y) < R} abs(y)^2 max(q, 0), C_chi = 4(sup abs(grad chi) + sup abs(D^2 chi)) and both radii finite;
T = t_beta rho with t_beta = max(2, (2^(beta+2) C_chi)^(1/(1-beta))) absorbs the last term and gives
M_+(R) >= c_beta L R^beta with c_beta = 1/(2(2 t_beta)^beta) for all large R, and integration by parts on a finite
interval [r_0, R] gives the logarithmic bound. The coefficient k_beta comes from the localized test abs(y)^(2-beta)
chi(y/R). The uncut weight abs(y)^(2-beta) is convex, C^1 and locally in W^(2,1), with Hessian
(2 - beta)abs(y)^(-beta)(I - beta e_r e_r^T) >= (2 - beta)(1 - beta)abs(y)^(-beta) I. The localized test is not
convex, since a convex function on R^3 with compact support is zero; the terms of its Hessian that contain derivatives
of chi(y/R) are supported in R < abs(y) < 2R, have norm at most C R^(-beta) there, and contribute at most
C R^(-beta)E(2R) (A3116). Hence the pairing is at least (2 - beta)(1 - beta) int_{abs(y) < R}
abs(y)^(-beta)abs(U)^2 - C R^(-beta)E(2R), and integration by parts on a finite interval gives int_{abs(y) < R}
abs(y)^(-beta)abs(U)^2 = R^(-beta)E(R) + beta int_0^R t^(-beta-1)E(t) dt, which is beta L log R + o(log R), and
beta L log R + O(1) under the remainder, which is why the additive two-sided bounds for the signed pairing are stated
under the remainder (A3116); on abs(y) > 2 the uncut Hessian gives
U.(D^2 abs(y)^(2-beta))U = (2 - beta)abs(y)^(-beta)[(1 - beta)abs(U)^2 + beta abs(U_tan)^2], with U_tan the component
tangential to the spheres, and the retained term beta(2 - beta) int abs(y)^(-beta)abs(U_tan)^2 gives the tangential
fraction (A3119); with t = beta/(1 - beta), k_beta/(beta c_beta) >= 2(t + 2)2^(5t)/(t + 1)^2 > 4 (A3098-A3099; review
the accompanying artifacts). For a fixed center a,
E(R - abs(a)) <= E_a(R) <= E(R + abs(a)) transfers the energy ratio. With a radial chi the pairing involves only Q_a,
which gives the radial form, and the Poisson equation for the spherical mean of P gives the pressure form. For the
control, q0 = b^2 abs(y)^(beta-5)[(3 - beta) - (5 - beta)y3^2/abs(y)^2] on abs(y) > 2, with b^2 = 3 beta L/(8pi), the
integral of the positive part of the bracket over S^2 is (8pi/3)(3 - beta)^(3/2)/sqrt(5 - beta), and
q0 = div((U0.grad)U0) with the divergence theorem gives the signed moment 2E(R) - (8pi/3)f0(R)^2
R^5 = (2 - beta)L R^beta (A3094-A3095; review in the accompanying artifacts; the
integral-estimate analysis comparison as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, revised at 2026-11-04T08:15Z; A3096 refuted two statements of its
superseded first version, both corrected in the revision).
(m) Write r = abs(y), z = log r and U(r theta) = r^t v(z, theta); then int r^(-beta) abs(U)^2 dy = int abs(v)^2
dz dtheta and int r^(2-beta) abs(DU)^2 dy = int (abs(v_z + t v)^2 + abs(grad_S v)^2) dz dtheta. Zero flux through
every sphere gives v.e_r zero spherical mean, so there is no radial mode of degree zero. In the expansion
v = f Y e_r + g grad_S Y + h e_r x grad_S Y over real spherical harmonics Y of degree ell >= 1, Lambda = ell(ell + 1),
divergence freedom gives g = (f' + k f)/Lambda, different modes and the poloidal and toroidal parts are orthogonal,
and for a compactly supported weight eta(z) an exact integration by parts writes the integral of eta times the
gradient density minus H_beta times the energy density of each mode as a sum of nonnegative terms, whose coefficients
are smallest at Lambda = 2, plus terms bounded by C(beta) int (abs(eta') + abs(eta''))abs(v)^2, uniformly in Lambda.
With eta = 1 on [log 2, log R] and fixed transitions on (0, log 2) and (log R, log 2R), the outer error is at most
C R^(-beta)E(2R) = O(1), so G_0(2R) >= H_beta int_{2 < abs(y) < R}
abs(y)^(-beta)abs(U)^2 - C = beta H_beta L log R - C as in (l), and ball inclusions transfer the energy law to every
center. The control is the degree-one poloidal field with f = b r^t outside B_2, b^2 = beta L/(1 + k^2/2), whose
spherical integral of abs(DU)^2 is beta H_beta L r^(beta-5), filled to the energy L 2^beta in B_2 by a compact swirl
term; near 0 it equals d e3 + a0 Jy with a0 > 0, and its momentum residual (1 - c)d e3 + (M + M^2)y, M = a0 J, has
curl 2a0 e3 (A3125). A bound abs(DU) <= D0 abs(y)^(-(5-beta)/2) at large abs(y) gives G_0(R) <= C + 4pi D0^2 log R, so
4pi D0^2 >= beta H_beta L, and D0 decreasing to the limit superior gives the stated bound;
H_beta - (2 - beta)(1 - beta) = 3(3 - beta)(beta + 1)/4 - 16 beta/(beta^2 + 2 beta + 9) >= 9/4 - 4/3 = 11/12 (A3126).
(n) In the variables of (m), with f = v.e_r and w the tangential part of v, divergence freedom reads
partial_z f + k f + div_S w = 0, and abs(grad_S f) <= abs(grad_S v) + abs(w) pointwise. Multiplying by eta_R f, with
eta_R a cutoff in z = log r whose derivative is bounded and supported in two strips of width log 2, and integrating by
parts on the sphere gives k(F_a - T_a) = int eta_R grad_S f.w + O(1), the O(1) bounded by the energy on the strips,
and Cauchy-Schwarz gives the first inequality; the second is the radial bound of (l) with the tangential energy
retained (A3122). Solving the first for T_a/F_a under G_a <= (M + o(1))beta L log R gives d_beta(M), and retaining the
radial part of the derivative energy gives d_beta(M - t^2) (A3132-A3133). For the envelope d_opt, each spherical
degree is treated separately: for consecutive degrees lambda_j and lambda_(j+1) the sphere identities give G_a - A_j
F_a + B_j T_a >= -C with constants A_j and B_j > 0 such that the line M = A_j - B_j x passes through (M_j, x_j) and
(M_(j+1), x_(j+1)); the main term is nonnegative because (nu - lambda_j)(nu - lambda_(j+1)) >= 0 at every eigenvalue
nu = i(i + 1), and d_opt(M) is the largest of the values (A_j - M)/B_j (A3152). (o) Under the endpoint hypothesis the
localized spectral gap forces DU, in logarithmic variables, to be close in the mean to a homogeneous degree-one matrix
field M0(a(z), n) with a slowly varying vector a(z); the three source limits are the sphere integrals of tr(M0^2) and
of its positive and negative parts, and comparing a finite D with the Frobenius norm of M0 on two polar caps about
a(z) gives D >= D_* (A3149). The explicit gap of LIT385 makes the same cap comparison under the budget H_beta + delta,
with the mean square error (10 delta/beta) beta L log R of (p) and the caps abs(n.a(z))/abs(a(z)) >= 2^(-1/2), of
total area 4pi(1 - 2^(-1/2)), on which the norm of M0 is least at the cap edge; this forces delta >= epsilon_beta
(A3179). (p) Under the budget H_beta + delta the identity of (m) bounds the mean square distance of DU, in logarithmic
variables, from the frozen degree-one matrix field of (o) by (10 delta/beta) beta L log R and the degree-one energy
from below by (1 - delta/beta) beta L log R, up to o(log R); the frozen field has the exact source integrals C_s, C_p
and C_n, abs(tr A^2 - tr B^2) <= abs(A - B)(abs(A) + abs(B)) and Cauchy-Schwarz give the error e_beta(delta), and two
families of cutoffs give the lower and upper bounds without a gradient estimate on the cutoff strips (A3161).
These smallness, integrability, sign, lower-bound, moment and return conditions are not known to follow from decay
(A1436, A1529, A1536, A1569, A3038, A3046, A3058, A3065, A3074, A3077, A3081, A3086, A3097, A3100, A3107, A3120,
A3124, A3127, A3135, A3141, A3148, A3151, A3155, A3159, A3163, A3168, A3175, A3178, A3180, A3183, A3187, A3190, A3196,
A3205, A3217, A3225 OPEN). Parts (a)-(c) were rechecked independently (A3036; review
the accompanying artifacts; the integral-estimate analysis comparison A110, A3037). The recheck proves
the closed bound sup abs(W) <= sqrt(3)(1 - 3c/2) in (a) with no additional condition on the vorticity at infinity
(U bounded and U(R.) -> 0 in D' are still assumed, A3068); this also follows from the closed endpoint
sup abs(W) <= T*(c) above, since T*(c) > sqrt(3)(1 - 3c/2) (integral-estimate analysis A110, A3037).

**Choice for item 1.** Theorem 5 is the strongest nonexistence theorem obtained in the target range: it holds for every
omega and every c in [2/5, 1/2), with no symmetry, smallness, decay rate, finite energy or derivative decay. Its
regularity class is C-infinity, stronger than the report's C^2 baseline, and its one extra hypothesis is the helicity
sign condition, so it is CONDITIONAL in the sense of the labels, with a complete proof. Theorem 1 is the strongest statement with no extra hypothesis (PROVED). Section 2 proves both in full, together with the coverage theorem that Theorem 5 uses. Theorem 8 needs no
helicity or tail condition; its extra hypothesis is a smallness or integrability condition on curl U or on the strain,
or a sign or translation condition on q = tr((DU)^2), or a sign of its means over the spheres abs(y) = r, a
lower bound for its cumulative radial integral K(r) (Theorem 8(f)), a nonpositive sign of its means over the spheres
about one center beyond some radius (Theorem 8(g)), or a finite moment int abs(y)^2 max(q, 0) (Theorem 8(h)) or its
form int (1 + abs(y))^(2/c-3) max(q, 0) with the smaller critical weight (Theorem 8(l)), or one sign of the work
U.grad(P + abs(U)^2/2) (Theorem 8(i)), none of which is known to follow from decay.

This section proves item 1a in full. The accompanying artifacts record the underlying analysis (sections 2.0-2.9),

and of both pressure normalizations found no new gap, A385). Exception: the proof of Theorem W
is not reproduced; it is summarized in the accompanying artifacts (CONFIRMED A176, A177). The dynamical structure theorem of

### 2A. The energy law

### 2.0 Setting, hypotheses, and where the Euler structure enters

Fix c > 0 and omega in R. Let J be the matrix with J y = (-y_2, y_1, 0), A = cI - omega J and B(y) = Ay + U(y).
The profile equation is

    (1-c) U + (B.grad) U + omega J U + grad P = 0,      div U = 0.                                       (2.0.1)

Since tr J = 0, div(Ay) = 3c and div B = 3c.

Notation.
- q = |U|^2/2, E(R) = int_{|y|<R} |U|^2 dy, A_R = {R < |y| < 2R}, |A_R| = (28 pi/3) R^3.
- alpha = 5 - 2/c, g(R) = R^{-alpha} E(R).
- M_0 = sup|U|, eps(R) = sup_{|y| >= R} |U(y)|.
- I(R) = int_{|z| >= 4R} |z|^{-4} |U(z)|^2 dz.
- p* = 3c/(1-c) (for 0 < c < 1), so that 3(1 - 2/p*) = alpha.
- T_ij = R_i R_j, the Fourier multiplier -xi_i xi_j/|xi|^2, bounded and self-adjoint on L^2(R^3).
- K_ij(w) = (3 w_i w_j - delta_ij |w|^2)/(4 pi |w|^5) for w != 0.
- Gamma(w) = 1/(4 pi |w|).
For 2/5 < c < 1 one has 0 < alpha < 3 and p* > 2. For 2/5 < c < 1/2, 0 < alpha < 1 and 2 < p* < 3.

Hypotheses.
- H0(C^1): U in C^1(R^3; R^3), P in C^1(R^3), and (2.0.1) holds pointwise.
- Hb: U is bounded, and U(R .) -> 0 in D'(R^3) as R -> infinity.
Hb is implied by U -> 0 uniformly at infinity (dominated convergence), and by boundedness together with U in L^p for
some p < infinity. No hypothesis is made on P beyond H0(C^1): no decay, no limit at infinity, no normalization. No
symmetry, smallness, integrability, decay rate or derivative decay is assumed.

Constants. The constants called C in the conclusions of Theorem A depend only on c, M_0 and E(4); the intermediate
bounds of Lemmas 2.4-2.5 depend on the inputs K and mu, as displayed there. None depends on omega. In the
energy estimates the rotation enters only through three exact cancellations: U.JU = 0, (Jy).y = 0 and div(Jy) = 0;
the pressure normalization (Lemma 2.2, Step 1) also uses the cancellation of the omega terms under the divergence,
and Corollary A.5 uses that exp(t omega J) is orthogonal.

Where the Euler structure enters. (1) The local energy equality (2.2.1), obtained by taking the dot product of
(2.0.1) with U. (2) The pressure, only through its Poisson equation and the normalization Lemma 2.2. Lemma 2.2 is
derived from the equation in divergence form and Hb; no normalization of P is assumed. (3) In Corollary A.4(iv)
only, Omega = curl U, through the Biot-Savart law. The vorticity equation is not used anywhere in this section.

### 2.1 Statements

**Theorem A.** Assume H0(C^1) and Hb, 0 < c < 1, omega in R.
(i) If 0 < c < 2/5, then U = 0 and P is constant.
(ii) If c = 2/5, then U is in L^2(R^3), and int_{|y|>R} |U|^2 <= C R^{-1} for R >= 2. More precisely,
     int_{|y|>R} |U|^2 = O(R^{-5}) as R -> infinity (Proposition 2.7).
(iii) If 2/5 < c < 1, then the limit L = lim_{R -> infinity} R^{-alpha} E(R) exists in [0, infinity), and

         | R^{-alpha} E(R) - L | <= C R^{-1}        for all R >= 2.                                       (2.1.1)

     Moreover L > 0 unless U = 0. If in addition U -> 0 uniformly at infinity, the right side of (2.1.1) can be
     replaced by C (eps(R/2) R^{-1} + R^{(alpha-5)/2}), which is o(R^{-1}).

**Corollary A.1 (vanishing renormalized energy).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem A(iii) with 2/5 < c < 1/2,
E(R) = L R^{5-2/c} + O(R^{4-2/c}) and 4 - 2/c < 0. So E(R) - L R^alpha -> 0.

**Corollary A.2.** Assume H0(C^1), Hb and 2/5 < c < 1. Each of (a), (b) forces U = 0.
(a) liminf_{R -> infinity} R^{-alpha} E(R) = 0. In particular this holds if |U(y)| = o(|y|^{-(1-c)/c}) as
    |y| -> infinity.
(b) U is in L^p(R^3) for some 0 < p <= p*.
(d) (Pointwise lower bound.) If U is not identically 0, then sup_{R<|y|<2R} |U| >= c_1 R^{-(1-c)/c} for all
    R >= R_1, where c_1 = (3 (2^alpha - 1) L/(56 pi))^{1/2} > 0 and R_1 depends on the solution.

Lorentz spaces. lambda_f(s) = |{|f| > s}|, f*(t) = inf{s > 0 : lambda_f(s) <= t},
||f||_{p,q} = (int_0^infinity (t^{1/p} f*(t))^q dt/t)^{1/q} for 0 < q < infinity, and
||f||_{p,infinity} = sup_{t>0} t^{1/p} f*(t) = sup_{s>0} s lambda_f(s)^{1/p}. L^{p,p} = L^p.

**Corollary A.4 (endpoint Liouville theorems).** Assume H0(C^1), Hb, 2/5 < c < 1, omega in R. Each of the
following forces U = 0.
(i) (Shells.) liminf_{R -> infinity} R^{-alpha} int_{R<|y|<2R} |U|^2 dy = 0.
(i') (Weak-type shells.) liminf_{R -> infinity} ||U 1_{R<|y|<2R}||_{p*,infinity} = 0.
(ii) (Borderline weight.) int_{|y|>1} |U(y)|^2 |y|^{-alpha} dy < infinity.
(iii) (Lorentz.) U is in L^{p*,q}(R^3) for some 0 < q < infinity.
(iv) (Vorticity.) Omega = curl U is in L^{3c,q}(R^3) for some 1 <= q < infinity.

Sharpness. (a) Every such profile has E(R) <= C R^alpha, so int_{|y|>1} |U|^2 |y|^{-alpha-e} dy < infinity for every
e > 0. A nonzero profile has int_{1<|y|<R} |U|^2 |y|^{-alpha} dy = alpha L log R + O(1). So the weight in (ii) is
the exact borderline. (b) The model tails |y|^{-(1-c)/c} and |y|^{-1/c} (restricted to |y| > 1) lie in
L^{p*,infinity} and L^{3c,infinity} respectively, and in no L^{p*,q}, L^{3c,q} with q < infinity (proof in 2.8).
(c) (iii) contains (b) of Corollary A.2 at p = p* and is strictly stronger, because L^{p*} is a proper subspace of
L^{p*,q} for q > p*.

**Theorem W (weak profiles; statement).** Assume:
(HW) U in L^infinity(R^3; R^3), div U = 0 in D', P in D'(R^3), and
         (1-4c) U + omega J U + div(U (x) Ay + U (x) U) + grad P = 0   in D'(R^3),
     where div(V (x) W)_k = d_j(W_j V_k). (For U in C^1 this is (2.0.1), because
     ((Ay).grad U)_k = d_j((Ay)_j U_k) - 3c U_k.)
Assume also Hb, 0 < c < 1 and omega in R. Convention for weak fields: M_0 and eps(R) are essential suprema, all
equalities between velocity fields hold almost everywhere, and in Corollary A.4(iv) curl U is the distributional
curl, assumed represented by a function in L^{3c,q}; "U -> 0 uniformly" means eps(R) -> 0. Under (HW) and Hb the pressure normalization and the annular
decomposition (Lemmas 2.2, 2.3 below) hold, with the proofs read in D': they use only the equation in divergence
form, boundedness of U and Hb (integral-estimate analysis, as summarized in the accompanying artifacts section 0). So P is in L^2_loc. Define the energy defect

    D[U] = (5c/2 - 1) |U|^2 - div(q B + P U)      in D'(R^3).

D[U] = 0 for every H0(C^1) solution (Lemma 2.1). The profile is called dissipative if D[U] >= 0.
(W.1) Put tau = -t in (0, 1), s = -log tau, Q_s = e^{omega s J}, u(x, t) = tau^{c-1} Q_s U(tau^{-c} Q_s^T x) and
      p(x, t) = tau^{2c-2} P(tau^{-c} Q_s^T x). Then (u, p) is a weak solution of the Euler equations on
      R^3 x (-1, 0), and its Duchon-Robert energy defect D(u) satisfies
      < D(u), phi > = int_{-1}^0 tau^{5c-3} < D[U], phi(tau^c Q_s . , t) > dt. Hence D(u) >= 0 iff D[U] >= 0, and
      D(u) = 0 iff D[U] = 0. If for every compact K, sup_{|z| <= h} int_K |U(y+z) - U(y)|^3 dy = o(h) as h -> 0
      (for example U in C^{0,theta}_loc with theta > 1/3), then D[U] = 0.
(a) If D[U] = 0, then Theorem A (i)-(iii) (including (2.1.1), the positivity of L and the refinement under uniform
    decay), Corollary A.2 (a), (b), (d) (with ess sup in place of sup) and Corollary A.4 (i)-(iv) hold verbatim, with
    the same constants.
(b) If D[U] >= 0 and 0 < c < 2/5, then U = 0 a.e.
(c) If D[U] >= 0 and c = 2/5, then U is in L^2, int_{|y|>R} |U|^2 <= C R^{-1} for R >= 2, and D[U] = 0. (The
    auditor adds, A177, that the exterior energy is then O(R^{-5}), as in Proposition 2.7.)
(d) If D[U] >= 0 and 2/5 < c < 1, then L = lim R^{-alpha} E(R) exists in [0, infinity). With Dm(r) = `D[U](B_r)` and
    delta(R) = (2/c) int_R^infinity r^{-1-alpha} Dm(r) dr (finite),
        -C R^{-1} <= R^{-alpha} E(R) - L <= C R^{-1} + delta(R)      for R >= 2.
    If L = 0, then |R^{-alpha} E(R) - delta(R)| <= C R^{-1} for R >= 2. U is in L^2 if and only if L = 0 and
    `D[U](R^3)` < infinity, and then `D[U](R^3)` = (5c/2 - 1) ||U||_2^2.
The proof of Theorem W is in integral-estimate analysis, as summarized in the accompanying artifacts (CONFIRMED A176, A177). It runs the proof of 2.2-2.5 below with
the identity of Lemma 2.1 replaced by its distributional form with the defect term (radial identity (2.2.2) with
the extra term -`D[U](B_R)`, valid for a.e. R). Consequence for the method: for 2/5 < c < 1 the positivity of L, and
with it every Liouville statement above, rests on zero defect. It is not claimed that zero defect is necessary for
a Liouville theorem, and no nonzero dissipative weak profile is known.

### 2.2 The energy identity

**Lemma 2.0 (Hb with moving test functions).** Let U be bounded with U(R .) -> 0 in D'(R^3). Then
int U(Rz) psi(z) dz -> 0 for every psi in L^1(R^3). Consequently, if psi_R -> psi in L^1(R^3) as R -> infinity, then
int U(Rz) psi_R(z) dz -> 0.

*Proof.* C_c^infinity is dense in L^1, and |int U(Rz) (psi - phi)(z) dz| <= M_0 ||psi - phi||_1. For the second
claim, |int U(Rz)(psi_R - psi)(z) dz| <= M_0 ||psi_R - psi||_1. []

**Lemma 2.1.** Under H0(C^1), pointwise,

    (1 - 5c/2) |U|^2 + div(q B + P U) = 0.                                                                (2.2.1)

Hence E is C^1, and for every R > 0 and every constant p,

    (cR/2) E'(R) + (1 - 5c/2) E(R) = -F(R),      F(R) = int_{|y|=R} (q + P - p) U.n dS.                    (2.2.2)

Equivalently, for 0 < R_1 < R_2,

    g(R_2) - g(R_1) = -(2/c) int_{R_1<|y|<R_2} |y|^{-1-alpha} (q + P - p) U.(y/|y|) dy.                     (2.2.3)

The constant p may be chosen independently on each annulus.

*Proof.* The dot product of (2.0.1) with U, together with U.JU = 0, gives (1-c)|U|^2 + B.grad q + U.grad P = 0.
Since div B = 3c and div U = 0, B.grad q = div(qB) - 3c q and U.grad P = div(PU), which gives (2.2.1). The field
qB + PU is C^1, so the divergence theorem on B_R applies. On |y| = R, B.n = cR - omega (Jy).n + U.n with (Jy).n = 0.
So int_{S_R} q B.n dS = (cR/2) E'(R) + int_{S_R} q U.n dS, because E'(R) = int_{S_R} |U|^2 dS for continuous U.
Any constant p may be inserted in F because int_{S_R} U.n dS = 0. For (2.2.3), the definition of alpha gives
(cR/2) E' + (1 - 5c/2) E = (c/2) R^{1+alpha} g'(R). Integrate g' = -(2/c) R^{-1-alpha} F(R) over [R_1, R_2] and use
polar coordinates. []

### 2.3 The pressure

Two standard facts about T_ij are used.
(F1) For f in L^2(R^3) with compact support, T_ij f = d_i d_j (Gamma * f) in D'(R^3), and on the open set
     {x : dist(x, supp f) > 0}, T_ij f is the smooth function int K_ij(x - z) f(z) dz. Proof: f is in L^1 with
     compact support, Gamma * f is in L^1_loc and tempered, and (Gamma * f)^ = f^/|xi|^2. Applying d_i d_j gives the
     multiplier -xi_i xi_j/|xi|^2. Off supp f, Gamma * f is smooth and its second derivatives are (d_i d_j Gamma) * f,
     and d_i d_j Gamma = K_ij on R^3 \ {0}.
(F2) For phi in C_c^infinity(R^3) with supp phi in B_rho, the function T_ij d_k phi is in L^1(R^3). Proof: it is in
     L^2, hence in L^1(B_{2 rho}). For |x| >= 2 rho, by (F1) and an integration by parts,
     T_ij d_k phi(x) = int (d_k K_ij)(x - z) phi(z) dz, and |grad K_ij(w)| <= C |w|^{-4}, so
     |T_ij d_k phi(x)| <= C |x|^{-4} ||phi||_1. T_ij commutes with translations, and T_ij[f(./R)] = (T_ij f)(./R).
Put F_ij = U_i U_j, which is bounded. By (F2) the formula

    < G_k, phi > = - sum_ij int F_ij (T_ij d_k phi) dx,      phi in C_c^infinity(R^3),                    (2.3.1)

defines a distribution G_k (the canonical pressure gradient); continuity in phi follows from the two bounds in the
proof of (F2).

**Lemma 2.2 (pressure normalization).** Assume H0(C^1) and Hb. Then d_k P = G_k in D'(R^3), k = 1, 2, 3.

*Proof.* Step 1 (Poisson equation). Taking the divergence of (2.0.1) in D', with div U = 0, gives
-Delta P = d_i d_j F_ij. The omega-terms cancel: div((Ay.grad) U) = c div U - omega J_ji d_j U_i and
div(omega J U) = omega J_ji d_j U_i. Also (U.grad)U = div(U (x) U) in D' since div U = 0.
Step 2 (the remainder is harmonic). For psi in C_c^infinity, T_ij(Delta psi) = -d_i d_j psi (multipliers). Hence
< Delta G_k, phi > = < G_k, Delta phi > = sum_ij int F_ij d_i d_j d_k phi dx, and
< Delta d_k P, phi > = -< Delta P, d_k phi > = sum_ij int F_ij d_i d_j d_k phi dx. So h_k = d_k P - G_k is a harmonic
distribution, hence (Weyl's lemma) a smooth harmonic function.
Step 3 (dilations). Write U_R(z) = U(Rz). At y = Rz, (2.0.1) reads

    (grad P)(Rz) = -(1-c) U_R - omega J U_R - (Az.grad_z) U_R - R^{-1} div_z(U_R (x) U_R).

Pairing with psi in C_c^infinity and integrating by parts gives
int (d_k P)(Rz) psi(z) dz = int U_R . (Lambda_k psi) dz + R^{-1} sum_j int U_{R,k} U_{R,j} d_j psi dz, where
Lambda_k psi = (4c - 1) psi e_k - omega psi J^T e_k + (Az.grad psi) e_k (from div(Az psi) = 3c psi + Az.grad psi).
For the canonical gradient, the definition and the commutation of T_ij with dilations give

    R^{-3} < G_k, psi(./R) > = -R^{-1} sum_ij int F_ij(Rz) (T_ij d_k psi)(z) dz,                          (2.3.2)

whose absolute value is at most R^{-1} M_0^2 sum_ij ||T_ij d_k psi||_1.
Step 4 (h_k = 0). Fix x and a radial phi in C_c^infinity with int phi = 1. By the mean-value property,
h_k(x) = int h_k(x + Rz) phi(z) dz = int h_k(Rw) psi_R(w) dw with psi_R = phi(. - x/R). By Steps 2-3,
h_k(x) = int U_R . Lambda_k psi_R dw + R^{-1} sum_j int U_{R,k} U_{R,j} d_j psi_R dw + R^{-1} sum_ij int F_ij(Rw)
(T_ij d_k psi_R)(w) dw. As R -> infinity, Lambda_k psi_R -> Lambda_k phi in L^1, so the first term tends to 0 by
Lemma 2.0. The second term is at most R^{-1} M_0^2 ||grad phi||_1. The third is at most
R^{-1} M_0^2 sum_ij ||T_ij d_k phi||_1, by translation invariance of T_ij. So h_k(x) = 0. []

Consequence. Assume H0(C^1) and Hb. If U is in L^2 and c != 2/5, then U = 0 (A031 section 3). For 0 < c < 1
this also follows from Theorem A: by Theorem A(i) if c < 2/5, and if 2/5 < c < 1 because U in L^2 gives L = 0.

**Lemma 2.3 (pressure on an annulus).** Assume H0(C^1) and Hb, and let R > 0. Write F = F^1 + F^2 + F^3, the
restrictions of F to {R/2 <= |z| < 4R}, {|z| < R/2} and {|z| >= 4R}. Put

    Pi_1 = sum_ij T_ij F^1_ij,   Pi_2 = sum_ij T_ij F^2_ij   (both in L^2),
    Pi_3(x) = int_{|z| >= 4R} sum_ij [K_ij(x - z) - K_ij(-z)] F_ij(z) dz      (|x| < 2R).

Then there is a constant p_R with P = p_R + Pi_1 + Pi_2 + Pi_3 a.e. in B_{2R}, and

    ||Pi_1||_{L^2(R^3)} <= ( int_{R/2 <= |z| < 4R} |U|^4 )^{1/2} <= eps(R/2) E(4R)^{1/2},                  (2.3.3)
    |Pi_2(x)| <= (4/pi) R^{-3} E(R/2)                  for R <= |x| < 2R,                                  (2.3.4)
    |Pi_3(x)| <= (192/pi) R I(R)                       for |x| < 2R,                                       (2.3.5)
    I(R) <= 4 int_{4R}^infinity r^{-5} E(r) dr.                                                            (2.3.6)

*Proof.* Let phi be in C_c^infinity(B_{2R}). By Lemma 2.2, < d_k P, phi > = < G_k, phi >. Split (2.3.1) according to
F = F^1 + F^2 + F^3. F^1 + F^2 is bounded with compact support, so it is in L^2, and since T_ij is self-adjoint
its contribution is < d_k(Pi_1 + Pi_2), phi >. For |z| >= 4R, (F1) and an integration by parts give
(T_ij d_k phi)(z) = int (d_k K_ij)(z - x) phi(x) dx. The double integral converges absolutely (integrand at most
C M_0^2 |z|^{-4} |phi(x)|), and d_k K_ij is odd, so the F^3 contribution is int phi d_k Pi_3 dx, where
differentiation under the integral sign is justified by the same bound. So grad(P - Pi_1 - Pi_2 - Pi_3) = 0 in
D'(B_{2R}), and B_{2R} is connected.
(2.3.3): by Plancherel and Cauchy-Schwarz, |sum_ij xi_i xi_j |xi|^{-2} F^1_ij^(xi)| <= (sum_ij |F^1_ij^(xi)|^2)^{1/2},
and sum_ij U_i^2 U_j^2 = |U|^4.
(2.3.4): for R <= |x| < 2R, x is at distance >= R/2 from supp F^2, so by (F1)
Pi_2(x) = int sum_ij K_ij(x - z) F_ij(z) dz. For a vector u, |sum_ij K_ij(w) u_i u_j| = |3 (w.u)^2 |w|^{-2} - |u|^2|
/(4 pi |w|^3) <= |u|^2/(2 pi |w|^3), and |x - z| >= R/2.
(2.3.5): k_u(w) = sum_ij K_ij(w) u_i u_j satisfies |grad k_u(w)| <= (6/pi) |u|^2 |w|^{-4} (differentiate; the three
terms have coefficients 6, 15, 3). For |x| < 2R, |z| >= 4R and t in [0, 1], |tx - z| >= |z|/2, so
|k_u(x - z) - k_u(-z)| <= |x| (6/pi) 16 |u|^2 |z|^{-4} <= (192/pi) R |u|^2 |z|^{-4}.
(2.3.6): I(R) = int_{4R}^infinity r^{-4} E'(r) dr. Integrate by parts, use r^{-4} E(r) <= (4 pi/3) M_0^2 r^{-1} -> 0,
and drop the boundary term at 4R, which is negative. []

### 2.4 Flux bound and the dyadic step

Let Phi(R) = int_{A_R} |q + P - p_R| |U| dy, with p_R from Lemma 2.3.

**Lemma 2.4.** Assume H0(C^1) and Hb. For R > 0,

    Phi(R) <= (1/2) eps(R) E(2R) + eps(R/2) E(4R)
              + (28 pi/3)^{1/2} R^{3/2} E(2R)^{1/2} [ (4/pi) R^{-3} E(R/2) + (192/pi) R I(R) ].              (2.4.1)

If moreover E(r) <= K r^mu for all r >= 1, with 0 <= mu <= 3, then for R >= 2,

    Phi(R) <= C_1 (M_0 K + K^{3/2}) R^mu,      C_1 an absolute constant.                                    (2.4.2)

*Proof.* On A_R, q + P - p_R = q + Pi_1 + Pi_2 + Pi_3. The q term contributes at most (1/2) eps(R) E(2R). The Pi_1
term contributes at most ||Pi_1||_2 ||U||_{L^2(A_R)} <= eps(R/2) E(4R). The Pi_2 and Pi_3 terms contribute at most
their supremum on A_R times ||U||_{L^1(A_R)} <= |A_R|^{1/2} E(2R)^{1/2}. This is (2.4.1). For (2.4.2) use eps <= M_0,
E(R/2) <= K R^mu, E(2R) <= 8 K R^mu, E(4R) <= 64 K R^mu (R/2 >= 1, mu <= 3) and, from (2.3.6),
I(R) <= 4K (4R)^{mu-4}/(4 - mu) <= K R^{mu-4}. The Pi_2 and Pi_3 terms are then at most C K^{3/2} R^{(3 mu - 3)/2},
and R^{(3 mu - 3)/2} <= R^mu since mu <= 3. []

**Lemma 2.5 (dyadic step).** Assume H0(C^1), Hb, 0 < c < 1, and E(r) <= K r^mu for r >= 1 with 0 <= mu <= 3. Put
beta = mu - 1 - alpha.
1. For R >= 2 and R <= R_1 < R_2 <= 2R, |g(R_2) - g(R_1)| <= C_2 R^beta, with
   C_2 = (2/c) max(1, 2^{-1-alpha}) C_1 (M_0 K + K^{3/2}).
2. If beta > 0, then E(R) <= C R^{mu-1} for R >= 2.
3. If beta = 0, then E(R) <= C R^{mu-1} (1 + log R) for R >= 2.
4. If beta < 0, then L = lim_{R -> infinity} g(R) exists and |g(R) - L| <= C R^beta for R >= 2.

*Proof.* 1: apply (2.2.3) on R_1 < |y| < R_2 with p = p_R, bound |y|^{-1-alpha} on A_R by
max(1, 2^{-1-alpha}) R^{-1-alpha}, and use (2.4.2). 2: given R >= 2, choose k >= 0 with R/2^k in [2, 4). Summing 1
over the chain R/2^k, ..., R gives g(R) <= max_{[2,4]} g + C_2 R^beta/(2^beta - 1); multiply by R^alpha and use
R^alpha <= R^{mu-1}. 3: the same sum has k = O(log R) terms, each at most C_2. 4: for 2 <= R <= R', write
R' = 2^j R t with t in [1, 2). Then |g(R') - g(R)| <= sum_{i<j} C_2 (2^i R)^beta + C_2 (2^j R)^beta <= C R^beta, so g
is Cauchy at infinity; let R' -> infinity. []

### 2.5 Proof of Theorem A

Start from E(r) <= (4 pi/3) M_0^2 r^3, that is mu = 3. Each application of Lemma 2.5 items 2-3 yields a bound
E(r) <= K' r^{mu'} for all r >= 1 (on [1, 2] use E(r) <= E(2)).

(i) 0 < c < 2/5, so alpha < 0. While mu >= 1, beta = mu - 1 - alpha > 0, and item 2 lowers mu by 1. After the steps
3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 0 we have E(r) <= K r^0 for r >= 1, and beta = -1 - alpha. If beta > 0, item 2 gives
E(R) <= C R^{-1} -> 0. If beta = 0, item 3 gives E(R) <= C R^{-1} (1 + log R) -> 0. If beta < 0, item 4 shows that
g is bounded, and E(R) = R^alpha g(R) -> 0. E is nonnegative and nondecreasing, so E = 0. Hence U = 0, and (2.0.1)
gives grad P = 0.

(iii) 2/5 < c < 1, so 0 < alpha < 3. While mu - 1 > alpha, item 2 lowers mu by 1. If mu - 1 = alpha is reached,
item 3 gives E(R) <= C R^alpha (1 + log R) <= C' R^{mu - 3/4}, and we set mu' = mu - 3/4, so mu' - 1 < alpha. All
exponents used stay in [alpha, 3]. When mu - 1 < alpha, item 4 gives the limit L. Then E(r) <= K' r^alpha for
r >= 1, and item 4 with mu = alpha (beta = -1) gives (2.1.1).
Positivity of L. Suppose L = 0. Then (2.1.1) gives E(R) <= C R^{alpha - 1}. Inductively, if E(r) <= K_j r^{alpha - j}
for r >= 1 with alpha - j >= 0, item 4 with mu = alpha - j (beta = -j - 1) gives |g(R) - L| <= C R^{-j-1}, with the
same limit L = 0, that is E(R) <= C R^{alpha - j - 1}. After finitely many steps the exponent is negative, so
E(R) -> 0 and U = 0.
Refinement when U -> 0 uniformly. Once E(r) <= K' r^alpha, (2.4.1) gives Phi(R) <= C eps(R/2) R^alpha +
C R^{(3 alpha - 3)/2}, so by (2.2.3) each dyadic increment of g on [R, 2R] is O(eps(R/2) R^{-1} + R^{(alpha-5)/2}).
Summing over R, 2R, 4R, ... (eps is nonincreasing and the sums are geometric) gives the improved bound; it is
o(R^{-1}) because eps -> 0 and alpha < 3.

(ii) c = 2/5, so alpha = 0 and g = E. The exponents go 3 -> 2 -> 1 by item 2. At mu = 1, beta = 0, and item 3 gives
E(R) <= C (1 + log R) <= C' R^{1/4}. Item 4 with mu = 1/4 shows that E converges, so U is in L^2. Item 4 with mu = 0
gives |E(R) - E(infinity)| <= C R^{-1}. []

**Proposition 2.7 (c = 2/5: refined tail).** Under H0(C^1) and Hb with c = 2/5, Tl(R) = int_{|y|>R} |U|^2 is
O(R^{-5}).

*Proof.* By Theorem A(ii), Tl(R) -> 0 as R -> infinity, and (2.2.3) with alpha = 0 (g = E) gives
Tl(R) = -(2/c) sum_{k >= 0} int_{A_{2^k R}} |y|^{-1} (q + P - p_{2^k R}) U.(y/|y|) dy, the series converging absolutely
by the bounds below. Rerun (2.4.1) with the tail in place of E. The q and Pi_1 terms are at most (3/2) M_0 Tl(R/2),
since int_{R/2 <= |z| < 4R} |U|^2 <= Tl(R/2). The Pi_2 term is at most C R^{-3/2} ||U||_2^2 Tl(R)^{1/2}. The Pi_3 term
is at most C R^{-3/2} ||U||_2^2 Tl(R)^{1/2}, since R I(R) <= R (4R)^{-4} Tl(4R). Hence
Phi(R) <= C (Tl(R/2) + R^{-3/2} Tl(R)^{1/2}). Since Tl is nonincreasing and the dyadic sums are geometric,

    Tl(R) <= C R^{-1} Tl(R/2) + C R^{-5/2} Tl(R)^{1/2}.

So Tl = O(R^{-tau}) implies Tl = O(R^{-tau'}) with tau' = min(tau + 1, (5 + tau)/2). From tau = 0 this reaches
tau = 4 in four steps. Then the first term is O(R^{-5}), and Young's inequality bounds the second by
(1/2) Tl(R) + C R^{-5}. Absorbing gives Tl(R) = O(R^{-5}). []

### 2.6 Proofs of Corollaries A.1 and A.2

A.1: multiply (2.1.1) by R^alpha; alpha - 1 = 4 - 2/c < 0 for c < 1/2.
A.2(a): by (2.1.1), g(R) -> L, so the liminf hypothesis gives L = 0, and Theorem A(iii) gives U = 0. If
|U(y)| <= d(|y|) |y|^{-(1-c)/c} with d -> 0, then E(R) = o(int_1^R r^{2 - 2(1-c)/c} dr) + O(1) = o(R^alpha), since
3 - 2(1-c)/c = alpha > 0.
A.2(b): if p < 2, |U|^2 <= M_0^{2-p} |U|^p, so E is bounded and R^{-alpha} E(R) -> 0. If 2 <= p <= p*, Hoelder's
inequality on R_0 < |y| < R gives R^{-alpha} E(R) <= R^{-alpha} E(R_0) + C R^{3 - 6/p - alpha}
||U||^2_{L^p(|y| > R_0)}, and 3 - 6/p - alpha <= 0 exactly when p <= p*. So limsup R^{-alpha} E(R) <=
C ||U||^2_{L^p(|y| > R_0)} for every R_0, which tends to 0. Apply (a).
A.2(d): by (2.1.1), E(2R) - E(R) = (2^alpha - 1) L R^alpha + O(R^{alpha - 1}). The left side is at most
|A_R| sup_{A_R} |U|^2, and R^{alpha - 3} = R^{-2(1-c)/c}. []

### 2.7 The Biot-Savart law under weak-type vorticity bounds

T f(x) = (4 pi)^{-1} int f(z) x (x - z) |x - z|^{-3} dz denotes the Biot-Savart operator; for f in C_c^infinity,
T f = curl(Gamma * f).

**Lemma 2.6.** Let U be in C^1(R^3; R^3) with div U = 0, U bounded, U(R .) -> 0 in D'(R^3), and assume
Omega = curl U is in L^{3c,infinity}(R^3) for some 1/3 < c < 1. Then U = T Omega.

*Proof.* Choose 1 < p_1 < 3c < p_2 < 3 and split Omega = Omega 1_{|Omega| > 1} + Omega 1_{|Omega| <= 1}
= Omega_1 + Omega_2. From lambda_Omega(s) <= K s^{-3c}, int |Omega_1|^{p_1} <= lambda_Omega(1) + int_1^infinity
p_1 s^{p_1 - 1} K s^{-3c} ds < infinity and int |Omega_2|^{p_2} <= int_0^1 p_2 s^{p_2 - 1} K s^{-3c} ds < infinity.
For f in L^p, 1 < p < 3, |T f| <= (4 pi)^{-1} |.|^{-2} * |f|, so T f is in L^{3p/(3-p)} by the Hardy-Littlewood-
Sobolev inequality (Stein, Singular Integrals, chapter V, section 1). For f in C_c^infinity, -Delta T f =
curl(-Delta Gamma * f) = curl f; both sides are continuous from L^p to D' (the left by HLS), so
-Delta T f = curl f in D' for all f in L^p. Since div U = 0, -Delta U = curl Omega in D'. Hence
h = U - T Omega_1 - T Omega_2 is harmonic, hence smooth. Fix x and a radial phi in C_c^infinity with int phi = 1.
For every R > 0, h(x) = int h(x + Rz) phi(z) dz. With q_i = 3 p_i/(3 - p_i), Hoelder gives
|int (T Omega_i)(x + Rz) phi(z) dz| <= R^{-3/q_i} ||T Omega_i||_{q_i} ||phi||_{q_i'} -> 0. The U term is
int U(Rw) phi(w - x/R) dw -> 0 by Lemma 2.0. So h(x) = 0. []

### 2.8 Proof of Corollary A.4

Facts on Lorentz spaces (standard; Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, section 1.4; Bennett-Sharpley,
Interpolation of Operators, chapters 2-4).
(L1) For q < infinity, ||f||_{p,infinity} <= (q/p)^{1/q} ||f||_{p,q}. Proof: f* is nonincreasing, so
     int_0^t (s^{1/p} f*(s))^q ds/s >= f*(t)^q int_0^t s^{q/p - 1} ds = (p/q) (t^{1/p} f*(t))^q.
(L2) For a set E of finite measure and 0 < r < p, int_E |f|^r <= (p/(p - r)) |E|^{1 - r/p} ||f||_{p,infinity}^r.
     Proof: with N = ||f||_{p,infinity}, int_E |f|^r = int_0^infinity r s^{r-1} |{y in E : |f| > s}| ds
     <= int_0^infinity r s^{r-1} min(|E|, N^p s^{-p}) ds; split at s_0 = N |E|^{-1/p}.
(L3) For q < infinity and f in L^{p,q}, ||f 1_{|y| > R}||_{p,q} -> 0 as R -> infinity. Proof: f_R = f 1_{|y| > R}
     has lambda_{f_R} <= lambda_f < infinity, and lambda_{f_R}(s) decreases to 0 for each s > 0. Hence f_R* <= f*
     and f_R*(t) -> 0 for every t > 0; apply dominated convergence to int (t^{1/p} f_R*(t))^q dt/t.

(i) By (2.1.1), R^{-alpha}(E(2R) - E(R)) -> (2^alpha - 1) L. The hypothesis gives L = 0 because alpha > 0, and
Theorem A(iii) gives U = 0.
(i') (L2) with r = 2 < p*, E = {R < |y| < 2R}, |E| = (28 pi/3) R^3 and 3(1 - 2/p*) = alpha gives
int_E |U|^2 <= (p*/(p* - 2)) (28 pi/3)^{1 - 2/p*} R^alpha ||U 1_E||_{p*,infinity}^2. Apply (i).
(ii) Write I_w(R) = int_{1<|y|<R} |U|^2 |y|^{-alpha} dy = int_1^R r^{-alpha} dE(r). Integration by parts gives
I_w(R) = R^{-alpha} E(R) - E(1) + alpha int_1^R r^{-alpha-1} E(r) dr. By (2.1.1), r^{-alpha} E(r) = L + O(1/r), so
I_w(R) = alpha L log R + O(1). If L > 0 the integral in (ii) diverges. So L = 0 and U = 0. (The same computation
with the weight r^{-alpha-e} gives a finite limit for every profile: Sharpness (a).)
(iii) By (L3) and (L1), ||U 1_{|y| > R}||_{p*,infinity} -> 0, which gives (i').
(iv) By (L1), Omega is in L^{3c,infinity}, and 1 < 3c < 3. By Lemma 2.6, U = T Omega, so
|U| <= (4 pi)^{-1} |.|^{-2} * |Omega|. The function |.|^{-2} is in L^{3/2,infinity}(R^3). By O'Neil's convolution
inequality (R. O'Neil, Duke Math. J. 30 (1963) 129-142: L^{p,q} * L^{3/2,infinity} is contained in L^{s,q} with
1/s = 1/p - 1/3, for 1 < p < 3 and 1 <= q <= infinity, in R^3) with p = 3c, and 1/(3c) - 1/3 = 1/p*, U is in
L^{p*,q}. Apply (iii). (An alternative route, only sketched here and using further standard inputs, gives a worse
but finite second index: Hedberg's pointwise bound for the Riesz potential I_1 together with the boundedness of the
maximal function on L^{p,s}, p > 1, gives U in L^{p*, q/(1-c)}.) []

Sharpness (b). For f = |y|^{-k} on {|y| > 1} and p = 3/k, lambda_f(s) = (4 pi/3)(s^{-p} - 1) for s < 1, so
f*(t) = (1 + 3t/(4 pi))^{-1/p}, and t^{1/p} f*(t) increases to (4 pi/3)^{1/p} as t -> infinity. Hence f is in
L^{p,infinity}, and, since int^infinity dt/t diverges, in no L^{p,q} with q < infinity. With k = (1-c)/c this is
p = p*; with k = 1/c it is p = 3c.

Remarks 2.8. (1) Only Theorem A(iii) enters (i)-(iii). (2) (iv) uses Omega = curl U only through Lemma 2.6, and holds
on all of 2/5 < c < 1. If Omega 1_{|y| > R_0} is in L^{3c,q} for some R_0, the same conclusion holds, since Omega is
bounded on B_{R_0}. (3) (iv) contains the pointwise criterion |Omega(y)| <= C (1 + |y|)^{-gamma} with gamma > 1/c,
because then Omega is in L^{3c}; this improves Corollary A.2(c) of the source (gamma > max(1/c, 2)) for
1/2 < c < 1. Pointwise little-o decay (Corollary A.2(a)) implies the shell criteria (i) and (i'), since
||U 1_{R<|y|<2R}||_{p*,infinity} <= ((28 pi/3) R^3)^{1/p*} sup_{R<|y|<2R} |U|, but it neither implies nor follows
from the global Lorentz criterion (iii).
This incomparability, and the proper embeddings in Sharpness (c), are statements about function spaces; they are
not evidence for or against the existence of profiles.

### 2.9 Relation to the literature, contribution, and limits

Known parts.
- Theorem A(i) is not new. It is Chae-Shvydkoy (arXiv:1201.6009, ARMA 209 (2013)) Theorem 3.2 with p = infinity, and
  Chae-Tsai (MRL 2014) Theorem 3.2 in the rotating form, once the pressure normalization (Lemma 2.2) is supplied.
  The proof here is independent.
- The upper bound E(R) <= C R^alpha is Chae-Shvydkoy Corollary 3.4 (stated there for v in L^p, p >= 3).
  These attributions require translating the similarity parameter (theirs is 1/c - 1), the pressure convention
  (their associated pressure; here Lemma 2.2), and, for Chae-Tsai, the rotating form.
- Chae-Shvydkoy Theorem 3.2 (v in L^p, 3 <= p <= infinity, with similarity parameter at most 3/p) contains the part
  3 <= p <= p* of Corollary A.2(b) for omega = 0 (this range is nonempty only for c >= 1/2). Chae-Tsai (MRL 21 (2014)
  437-447) Theorem 3.2 (time-periodic solutions of the self-similar system, V in L^p(R^3 x [0, S_0]), 3 <= p <= infinity,
  canonical pressure assumed) contains the same range in the rotating form, once Lemma 2.2 is supplied. Its literal
  bounded endpoint p = infinity, alpha = 0 (c = 1) fails as printed: V = v0 constant with P = -abs(v0)^2/3 satisfies the
  periodic equation and the associated pressure (A1768-A1770); the range used here is unaffected.
- Xue (arXiv:1408.6619v2) treats the same time-periodic self-similar system. For 2/5 < c < 1/2 its similarity
  parameter 1/c - 1 lies in (1, 3/2), so its Theorem 1.1(1) (V in L^3_s L^p_y with 3 <= p < infinity, C^1 in s and
  locally C^3 in y, normalized pressure) is in its energy-growth alternative and gives no vanishing conclusion in this
  range. An audit of proof steps of that version (the literature audit LIT392; source
  as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, sha256 be741aa4 as reviewed, current 1d589056, status
  paragraph only, A3212; review in the accompanying artifacts, sha256 3b4fb703; the integral-estimate analysis
  comparison as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, sha256 82ec163c, retained in the review as
  as summarized in the accompanying artifacts) found that the ball-energy lower bounds of its displays (5.2) and (5.16), in the
