  proof of Theorem 1.2 on nondecaying profiles, do not follow from the pointwise growth of sup_s abs(V(y, s)) with
  smoothness, periodicity and solenoidality alone, since smooth periodic divergence-free fields, which solve no
  periodic Euler system, have that growth and a smaller maximal ball energy (A3197; A3198 REFUTED as an inference);
  that its pressure lemma needs finite physical energy and the normalized pressure (A3200 REFUTED for the unrestricted
  forms); and that at the critical value 3/2 of the parameter, the endpoint c = 2/5, the premises of Theorem 1.1(2)
  give finite constant energy at every time and the fixed-time pressure estimate (A3199). No theorem of Xue is
  refuted, the whole proof is not certified (A3201 OPEN), and no result here uses it.
- Chae-Shvydkoy section 2.2 already names the local energy equality as the operative requirement of the energy
  method, so the principle of Theorem W(a) is not new; W(b)-(d) have no known exact precedent.
- Lower bound. Bronzi-Shvydkoy (arXiv:1310.8611, Theorem 1.1) prove, for omega = 0, a C^3 profile of a locally
  self-similar blowup of a finite-energy H^s solution, with the associated pressure and the growth condition
  int_{|y|~L} |v|^p <~ L^gamma for some p >= 3, gamma < p - 2 (bounded profiles satisfy it with any p > 5), that
  either v = 0 or R^alpha <~ E(R) <~ R^alpha. The upper bound there comes from the ambient energy, the lower bound
  from a bootstrap of the local energy inequality, the same mechanism as 2.5 here. Corollaries A.2(a), (b) and
  A.4(ii), (iii), (iv) use only a lower bound E(R) >= c_0 R^alpha for large R, so in that setting they follow from
  Bronzi-Shvydkoy Theorem 1.1 (with Holder's inequality for A.2(b) when p < 3, and O'Neil's inequality for A.4(iv)).
- Near c = 2/5. Bronzi-Shvydkoy Remark 1.5 recalls from Shvydkoy (Nonlinearity 26 (2013) 425-436) that at the
  energy-conservative exponent (c = 2/5 here), under v in L^2 and |v(y)| <~ |y|^{1-delta}, the shell energy is
  O(L^{-5+delta'}) for every delta' > 0. Proposition 2.7 gives the exterior energy O(R^{-5}) under Hb and boundedness.
  The c = 2/5 result of table B with bounded gradient uses Chae-Wolf (arXiv:1706.02020v2) Theorem 3.1 (A103, A109). An
  audit of that version (the literature audit LIT395; source as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, sha256
  3e5cbb0b as reviewed, current 00ccf454, status paragraph only, A3219; review
  the accompanying artifacts, sha256 ae475db7; the integral-estimate analysis comparison
  as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, sha256 12d3a443, retained in the review as summarized in the accompanying artifacts) found
  that its projected local energy inequality (2.11), the backwards identity (2.12), a square expansion on page 12, the
  radius comparison in (4.9) and the final chain on page 31 are false as printed, as explicit smooth local Euler
  fields show, which do not decay and contradict none of its theorems (A3208 REFUTED as displays); that the corrected
  projected balance holds (A3207) and gives a classical local criterion for the absence of a terminal energy atom
  under a uniform local L^2 bound, a finite sup_r r^(-1) int_{Q_r} abs(v)^3 and a vanishing lower limit of r^(-1)
  int_{Q_r} abs(v)^3 (A3209); and that the application A103 uses Theorem 3.1 and a directly computed terminal trace,
  not these displays, so it is unaffected (A3210). The general weak-solution passage of that paper is not certified,
  and the criterion is not known to apply to decaying profiles for 2/5 < c < 1/2 (A3211 OPEN).
Not known to us in the literature (beyond the sources named; not verified exhaustively): the existence of the limit
L with the rate (2.1.1), and Corollary A.1; the lower bound L > 0 in the rotating case omega != 0, and for every
omega under boundedness and Hb alone, with no ambient solution and with the pressure normalization derived rather
than assumed (approach3 item 6 had the dichotomy under the decay hypothesis |U| <= C(1 + |y|)^{-(1-c)/c});
Corollaries A.2(d) and A.4(i), (i'), which use the limit in (2.1.1); Proposition 2.7 with the exact exponent; and
Corollaries A.2 and A.4 in exactly the present form and hypotheses.

Contribution to the central problem. For 2/5 < c < 1 and every omega, a nonzero profile has
E(R) = L R^alpha + O(R^{alpha-1}) with L > 0; in the target interval 2/5 < c < 1/2, E(R) - L R^alpha tends to zero
(Corollary A.1). The natural rate |y|^{-(1-c)/c} cannot be beaten on any dyadic shell (Corollary A.2(d)). In the
Lorentz scale the stated criteria exclude every profile with U in L^{p*,q} for some 0 < q < infinity or Omega in
L^{3c,q} for some 1 <= q < infinity, below the weak-type level of the model tails (L^{p*,infinity} for U, L^{3c,infinity} for Omega). The
stated criteria do not exclude critical weak-space membership alone. (Corollary A.4(i') excludes weak-type shells
whose L^{p*,infinity} quasi-norm tends to 0 along a sequence of radii; it does not exclude global membership in
L^{p*,infinity}.)

Limits of the method. Put k = (1-c)/c, a = omega/c and R_beta = e^{beta J}. A twisted-homogeneous natural tail is
U_0(r theta) = r^{-k} R_{-a log r} F(R_{a log r} theta) (r > 0, |theta| = 1), with F in C^1(S^2), not identically 0.
These are exactly the fields with U_0(e^{sA} z) = e^{-(1-c)s} e^{-omega s J} U_0(z) for all s, and they solve the
linear part (1-c) U + (Ay.grad) U + omega J U = 0 of (2.0.1). They are divergence free only for suitable F, and no
claim is made that such a tail belongs to a profile. Let A_F = int_{S^2} |F|^2 > 0. A bounded field equal to U_0 on
{|y| > R_0} has E(R) = (A_F/alpha) R^alpha + C_0 for R >= R_0, with C_0 = E(R_0) - (A_F/alpha) R_0^alpha. If such a
field were a profile, (2.1.1) would give L = A_F/alpha > 0. Moreover the refinement of Theorem A under uniform decay
gives E(R) - L R^alpha = O(R^{5-3/c}), which tends to 0 for c < 3/5 (for 2/5 < c < 1/2 this is also Corollary
A.1). So for 2/5 < c < 3/5 (in particular on the target range) C_0 = 0 would be forced: the interior energy must match, E(R_0) = (A_F/alpha) R_0^alpha. Such a tail is
consistent with Corollary A.2(d), and it lies in L^{p*,infinity} but in no L^{p*,q} with q < infinity. This shows
only that the leading far-field rate is compatible with the identities checked here, subject to the matching
condition C_0 = 0 (for c < 3/5). These estimates do not exclude a nonzero profile with the natural energy growth. The
thresholds of Corollaries A.2 and A.4 are attained by tails that solve the linear part of (2.0.1), not by known
exact profiles. Whether exact nonzero profiles exist for 2/5 < c < 1/2 is the open problem. It is not claimed that
every nonzero profile lies in L^{p*,infinity} or has a power-law asymptotic form.

### 2.10 Bounded profiles without the dilation hypothesis (Corollary A.5)

Proposed by the auditor (the accompanying artifacts), reviewed by the literature audit and by the synthesis
(as summarized in the accompanying artifacts), CONFIRMED A406-A407. Write A = cI - omega J and M = (1-c)I + omega J, so the
profile equation is MU + (Ay + U).grad U + grad P = 0.

**Corollary A.5.** Let 0 < c < 1 and omega be real, and let U in C^1 be bounded and P in C^1 solve the profile
equation with div U = 0. No decay and no dilation limit is assumed. Then there is a unique b in R^3 with U(R.) -> b
in distributions and weak star in L^infinity as R -> infinity, and grad P = G[U] - Mb, where G[U] is the canonical
double-Riesz pressure gradient of section 2.3. With z0 = -A^{-1} b, the pair W(y) = U(y + z0) - b,
P~(y) = P(y + z0) + (Mb).y solves the same equation and satisfies Hb. Hence Theorem A applies to W: for
0 < c < 2/5, U = b is constant and P = -(Mb).y + constant; at c = 2/5, W is in L^2 with exterior energy O(R^{-5});
for 2/5 < c < 1, int_{|y|<R} |W|^2 = L R^{5-2/c} + O(R^{4-2/c}) with L > 0 unless U is constant.

*Proof.* (1) The pressure. The Poisson equation -Delta P = d_i d_j(U_i U_j) and the definition of G[U] make each
component of grad P - G[U] a tempered harmonic distribution (all terms are tempered since U is bounded, by the
divergence form d_k P = -(1-4c)U_k - omega(JU)_k - d_j((Ay)_j U_k + U_j U_k)), hence a polynomial H. Rescaling
the equation, (grad P)(Rz) = -MU_R - (Az.grad)U_R - R^{-1} div(U_R tensor U_R) with U_R(z) = U(Rz), which is
bounded on each fixed test uniformly in R >= 1, while `G[U](R.)` is O(R^{-1}) on each fixed test. So H(R.) is
bounded on each test, and a positive-degree component of H would give a pairing growing like a positive power of R.
Thus H = g is constant.

(2) The background. Along any R_n -> infinity a subsequence of U_{R_n} converges weak star to some bounded v, and
passing to the limit in the rescaled equation (the quadratic term carries the factor R^{-1}) gives
Mv + (Az.grad)v + g = 0. M is invertible since 1 - c > 0; put b = -M^{-1} g and w = v - b, so (Az.grad)w = -Mw.
Differentiating t -> <e^{tM} w(e^{tA}.), phi> on transformed tests shows w(e^{tA}z) = e^{-tM} w(z) almost
everywhere. Since z -> e^{tA}z preserves the essential supremum and e^{-tM} = e^{-(1-c)t} e^{-omega t J} with J skew,
||w||_infinity = e^{-(1-c)t} ||w||_infinity, so w = 0 for any t > 0. Every subsequential limit is b, which gives
full convergence, uniqueness of b and grad P = G[U] - Mb.

(3) Centering. Since A z0 = -b, the carrier at y + z0 is Ay + W(y), and the equation at y + z0 becomes
MW + (Ay + W).grad W + grad P(y + z0) + Mb = 0, which is the equation for (W, P~). Testing U(Rz + z0) against an
L^1 function and translating the test by z0/R shows W(R.) -> 0, which is Hb. Theorem A now applies to W. In the
constant case the equation gives P = -(Mb).y + constant. If U decays, then b = 0 and nothing changes for the target
problem. The constants in the energy law may depend on b and z0. QED.

### 2B. The dynamical structure theorem (item 1b)

The text of this subsection is dynamical analysis's as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, sections D0-D6, version of 2026-11-02 22:45Z, CONFIRMED
by the auditor for D0-D6 (A248, after the repairs requested in A230-A232 and A241), folded in at 23:01Z. The synthesis
applied the three qualifications that A248 lists as remaining, and changed nothing else: the omega != 0 condition in D1
Remark (iii); the exact A155 statement and passage law |g'(r)| = exp((1-2c)T(r)) in D6 Remark (iv); and the replacement of
the sentence calling regular kinematic realizability open (D5 Remarks (ii)), which A242, A243 and A246 supersede. At 23:15Z the next sentence, on case (beta), was
updated with A252 and A253, as in dynamical analysis's own revision of 23:10Z. A248 also
notes that the claim of being self-contained is too strong where standard external theorems are invoked or full proofs are
deferred; read it in that sense. References of the form as summarized in the accompanying artifacts... are to the auditor.

Provenance. Every result below is CONFIRMED in its source form; the audit entry numbers are given in brackets. Where the audited
proof is the auditor's (A122, A111), its argument is reproduced, not cited. The text is self-contained: no working file is needed
to follow it. Nothing is stronger than its confirmed source.

#### D0. Setting, hypotheses, notation

Fix c in (0, 1/2) and omega in R (the range of c used is stated in each part; several parts hold for all c > 0). J is the matrix
with J y = (-y_2, y_1, 0), so J v = e_3 x v, J^T = -J. Put A := cI - omega J and

    B(y) := A y + U(y),     X(y) := c y + U(y) = B(y) + omega J y,     Omega := curl U,     S := (DU + DU^T)/2.

The profile equation is

    (1-c) U + (B.grad) U + omega J U + grad P = 0,        div U = 0.                                          (D0.1)

Hypotheses.
- H0: U in C^2(R^3; R^3), P in C^1(R^3), (D0.1) holds pointwise (then P is C^2, since grad P is C^1 by (D0.1)).
- H1': U(y) = o(|y|) uniformly as |y| -> infinity. (The mandatory decay U -> 0 implies H1'.)
No symmetry, smallness, integrability, decay rate or restriction on omega is assumed anywhere in Section D.

Notation. phi_s is the flow of B ("forward" time s); psi_t := phi_{-t} the backward flow; Z := {Omega != 0} (vortical set);
N := {B = 0}; alpha(a) := the backward limit set of a (limit points of psi_t(a), t -> infinity); vol = dy_1 dy_2 dy_3;
sigma := i_Omega vol, the vorticity flux 2-form, sigma(v, w) = Omega.(v x w); for a vector field F, F^flat := F.dy is the
associated 1-form; H := P + |X|^2/2 + c(c-1)|y|^2/2 - omega (Jy).X (Bernoulli function). Since X = U + c y and (Jy).y = 0,
this H equals P + |U|^2/2 + (Ay).U - c(1-2c)|y|^2/2: it differs by -c(1-2c)|y|^2/2 from the function H = P + |U|^2/2 + (Ay).U
used elsewhere in this report. Only the H defined here is used in Section 2B.

Convention. In Section 2B only, Z := {Omega != 0} denotes the vortical set; the front notation and Sections 2C and
2D write O = {Omega != 0} and use Z for the complement {Omega = 0} (integral-estimate analysis Note A80; A2676).

Facts used throughout (all for every omega; [A001-A005, A019, A082]).
(F1) div B = 3c, so det Dphi_s = e^{3cs}.
(F2) Bernoulli form of (D0.1): (1-2c) X + Omega x B + grad H = 0, hence B.grad H = -(1-2c) X.B with X.B = |X|^2 - omega (Jy).U.
(F3) Vorticity equation: curl of (D0.1) gives (B.grad) Omega = (DU - I - omega J) Omega, equivalently the Lie bracket
     [B, Omega] := (B.grad)Omega - (Omega.grad)B = -(1+c) Omega.
(F4) Cauchy formula: Dphi_s(a) Omega(a) = e^{(1+c)s} Omega(phi_s a) for all a, s. Proof: both sides solve dM/ds = DB(phi_s a) M,
     M(0) = Omega(a) (for the right side use (F3) and DB = A + DU); uniqueness of solutions of this linear ODE.
(F5) Trapping. By H1' there is R_0 with |U(y)| <= c|y|/2 for |y| >= R_0; then B.y = c|y|^2 + U.y >= c|y|^2/2 there, so
     d|Y|^2/ds >= c|Y|^2 outside the ball D := {|y| <= R_0}: forward orbits that leave D never return, every backward orbit
     enters D in finite time and stays in it (psi_t(D) is contained in D for t >= 0). B is C^1 with |B(y)| <= C(1+|y|), so phi_s
     is a complete C^1 flow of C^1 diffeomorphisms. Every alpha(a) is a nonempty compact connected invariant subset of D, and
     the compact invariant set Lambda := intersection of psi_t(D), t >= 0, is Lebesgue-null by (F1) [A006].
(F6) Transport of the velocity 1-form [A004]: L_B U^flat = -(1-2c) U^flat + d(|U|^2/2 - P), where L_B is the Lie derivative.
     Proof: (L_B U^flat)_i = B_j d_j U_i + U_j d_i B_j; D B^T U = c U + omega J U + grad(|U|^2/2) (as DB^T = cI + omega J + DU^T),
     and (B.grad)U + omega J U = -(1-c) U - grad P by (D0.1). Applying d: L_B sigma = -(1-2c) sigma, i.e. phi_s^* sigma =
     e^{(2c-1)s} sigma (also a direct consequence of (F3), (F1): L_B(i_Omega vol) = i_{[B,Omega]} vol + (div B) i_Omega vol).

#### D1. Circulation law, periodic orbits, and the lower bound on periods

Theorem D1 (every c > 0 in (a), (b); c != 1/2 in (c), (d); every omega). Assume H0.
(a) (Kelvin law in similarity variables [A004].) For every closed C^1 curve C and every s for which the flow image
    C(s) := phi_s(C) exists (all real s under H1', since then the flow is complete; periodic orbits have complete flow
    regardless),
        oint_{C(s)} U.dl = e^{(2c-1)s} oint_C U.dl.
    The same holds with X in place of U (X^flat - U^flat = d(c|y|^2/2) is exact).
(b) (Multipliers of vortical periodic orbits [A028].) Let gamma be a periodic orbit of B of period T on which Omega != 0. Then
    the monodromy Dphi_T(y), y in gamma, has eigenvalues 1 (on B(y)), e^{(1+c)T} (on Omega(y)) and e^{(2c-1)T}; for c < 1/2,
    gamma is a hyperbolic saddle with a 2-dimensional unstable manifold (tangent to B, Omega) and a 2-dimensional stable
    manifold. For c < 1/2 and the backward flow the direction Omega is the unique contracting direction (rate 1+c) and the
    third direction expands at rate 1-2c.
(c) (Zero circulation [A004].) For c != 1/2 and every periodic orbit gamma (any period, vortical or not), oint_gamma U.dl = 0.
(d) (Period bound [A030].) Assume moreover H1' and omega != 0. Every nonstationary periodic orbit gamma of B, of period T,
    satisfies
        integral_0^T |B(gamma(s))|^2 ds = -2 omega A_xy(gamma),      T >= 2 pi/|omega|,
    where A_xy(gamma) := (1/2) oint_gamma (y_1 dy_2 - y_2 dy_1) is the signed area of the projection of gamma on the
    (y_1, y_2)-plane traversed in the direction of the flow. In particular A_xy(gamma) has sign opposite to omega (the projected
    loop is retrograde in this signed-area sense; pointwise monotone rotation is not claimed), and equality T = 2 pi/|omega| forces the projection to be a circle traversed uniformly.
    For omega = 0 there are no nonstationary periodic orbits (c != 1/2).

Proof. (a) d/ds oint_{C(s)} U.dl = oint_{C(s)} L_B U^flat = -(1-2c) oint_{C(s)} U.dl by (F6), the exact form integrating to zero
over a closed curve; integrate the linear ODE in s.
(b) Dphi_T(y) B(y) = B(phi_T y) = B(y) (the flow commutes with itself). By (F4) with s = T, Dphi_T(y) Omega(y) = e^{(1+c)T}
Omega(phi_T y) = e^{(1+c)T} Omega(y). The product of the three eigenvalues is det Dphi_T = e^{3cT} by (F1), so the third is
e^{3cT - (1+c)T} = e^{(2c-1)T}. For c < 1/2 the three moduli 1, e^{(1+c)T} > 1, e^{(2c-1)T} < 1 are distinct: gamma is
hyperbolic with the stated dimensions. Reading time backward exchanges the roles.
(c) Apply (a) with C = gamma and s = T: phi_T(gamma) = gamma as a set with the same orientation, so oint_gamma U.dl =
e^{(2c-1)T} oint_gamma U.dl, and e^{(2c-1)T} != 1 for c != 1/2.
(d) Write U = B - A y = B - c y + omega J y along gamma, parametrized by s with dy = B ds:
    0 = oint_gamma U.dl = integral_0^T |B|^2 ds - c oint_gamma y.dy + omega oint_gamma (Jy).dy.
The middle term is oint d(|y|^2/2) = 0; (Jy).dy = -y_2 dy_1 + y_1 dy_2 = 2 dA_xy. Hence integral_0^T |B|^2 ds = -2 omega
A_xy(gamma). For the inequality, let (y_1(s), y_2(s)) be the projection, a T-periodic C^1 curve; the Wirtinger (isoperimetric)
inequality for T-periodic curves gives |oint (y_1 dy_2 - y_2 dy_1)| <= (T/(2 pi)) integral_0^T (y_1'^2 + y_2'^2) ds, with equality
iff the curve is a circle traversed at constant speed. (Proof: write z = y_1 + i y_2 = sum_k c_k e^{2 pi i k s/T}; then
oint (y_1 dy_2 - y_2 dy_1) = Im integral_0^T conj(z) z' ds = 2 pi sum_k k |c_k|^2 and integral_0^T |z'|^2 ds = (4 pi^2/T) sum_k k^2 |c_k|^2,
so |2 A_xy| <= 2 pi sum_k k^2 |c_k|^2 = (T/(2 pi)) integral |z'|^2, with equality iff c_k = 0 for every k outside {0, 1} or c_k = 0 for every k outside {0, -1}; c_0 is unrestricted.) Since
|y_perp'|^2 = B_1^2 + B_2^2 <= |B|^2,
    integral_0^T |B|^2 ds = 2 |omega| |A_xy| <= |omega| (T/(2 pi)) integral_0^T |B|^2 ds.
For a nonstationary orbit integral |B|^2 ds > 0, so T >= 2 pi/|omega|. Equality forces |B_3| = 0 and the Wirtinger equality
case. For omega = 0 the identity gives integral |B|^2 = 0, i.e. gamma is a point. QED

Remarks. (i) (a)-(c) use only H0 and the algebraic structure of (D0.1); (d) uses H1' only through the existence of a complete
flow. (ii) In (b) nothing is assumed about the stagnation set or about omega; the exponents 1+c and 2c-1 are exact, which is
the "constant exponent" rigidity used in D2. (iii) (Sharpness outside the decay class [A231].) The harmonic-gradient profile U = (-c y_1, -c y_2, 2c y_3) = grad phi,
phi = (-c(y_1^2 + y_2^2) + 2c y_3^2)/2, solves (D0.1) for every c > 0 and omega with the quadratic pressure
P = -(1-2c) phi - ((cI - omega J)y).grad phi - |grad phi|^2/2 (every harmonic gradient is an exact profile with this pressure),
but violates H1'. Its carrier is B = (-omega J y_h, 3c y_3). For omega != 0, every horizontal circle in {y_3 = 0} is a periodic
orbit of period exactly 2 pi/|omega|, and for every point with y_h != 0 the backward limit set is such a circle (y_3 decays backward while the
horizontal angle rotates uniformly). So the period bound in (d) is sharp within exact nondecaying profiles, and periodic
backward limits cannot be excluded by algebra alone; the example is irrotational and not sublinear. At omega = 0 the same
profile has B = (0, 0, 3c y_3), and the backward limit of (y_1, y_2, y_3) is the point (y_1, y_2, 0); the pressure formula
holds for every omega [A248].

#### D2. The exact Lyapunov spectrum on the vortical set

Theorem D2 (0 < c < 1/2, every omega) [A037]. Assume H0, H1'. Let mu be an ergodic phi-invariant probability measure with
compact support such that mu(Z) = 1 and mu(N) = 0. Then the Lyapunov exponents of the flow phi_s with respect to mu are
exactly
        chi_1 = 1 + c   (Oseledets direction R Omega),    chi_2 = 0   (direction R B),    chi_3 = 2c - 1   (a third direction E^s),
and Omega(a), B(a) are linearly independent for mu-almost every a. For the backward flow the exponents are -(1+c), 0, 1-2c:
for mu-almost every a the vorticity direction is the only Oseledets direction with negative exponent. On every compact K0 in
Z there is a uniform upper bound along Omega: by (F4) with s = -t, |Dpsi_t(a) Omega(a)| <=
(sup_{D'}|Omega|/inf_{K0}|Omega|)
e^{-(1+c)t} |Omega(a)| for a in K0 and t >= 0, where D' is a closed ball centred at 0, of radius at least R_0, containing K0
(psi_t(D') is contained in D' because |y| decreases along backward orbits outside D, (F5)). This is a bound along Omega only
and is not a claim of uniform hyperbolicity.
The flux area form sigma = i_Omega vol on the local quotient by vortex lines is expanded exactly by e^{(1-2c)t} (the Euclidean area of the
quotient is expanded by at least (|Omega(a)|/sup_{D'}|Omega|) e^{(1-2c)t} for a in K0 and t >= 0, with D' as above, not
by an exact law).

Proof. Step 1 (exponent of Omega). By (F4), for every a and s,
        (1/s) log( |Dphi_s(a) Omega(a)| / |Omega(a)| ) = (1+c) + (1/s)( log|Omega(phi_s a)| - log|Omega(a)| ).
On Z the function h := log|Omega| is C^1 with B.grad h = Omega.(DU - I - omega J)Omega / |Omega|^2 = n.Sn - 1 (n := Omega/|Omega|;
Omega.J Omega = 0), which is bounded on supp mu. Hence g_s(a) := h(phi_s a) - h(a) = integral_0^s (n.Sn - 1)(phi_r a) dr is a
bounded-increment cocycle, and by the Birkhoff ergodic theorem g_s(a)/s -> L := integral (n.Sn - 1) dmu for mu-a.e. a. If L != 0,
then h(phi_s a) -> +-infinity for mu-a.e. a, which is impossible because h is finite mu-a.e. (mu(Z) = 1) and h o phi_s has the
same distribution as h for every s (invariance): for every K, mu{h o phi_s < -K} = mu{h < -K} -> 0 as K -> infinity, whereas
h(phi_s a) -> -infinity a.e. would give mu{h o phi_s < -K} -> 1 as s -> infinity for each K. Hence L = 0, integral n.Sn dmu = 1,
and (1/s) log|Dphi_s(a) Omega(a)| -> 1+c as s -> +infinity for mu-a.e. a. The same argument for s -> -infinity (the cocycle has
bounded increments in both time directions and h o phi_s has the distribution of h for every real s) gives the limit 1+c as
s -> -infinity as well, so R Omega(a) is the pure Oseledets line of the exponent 1+c (forward growth alone would not exclude a
component of smaller exponent).
Step 2 (exponent of B). Dphi_s(a) B(a) = B(phi_s a). Since mu(N) = 0, log|B| is finite mu-a.e., and B.grad log|B| =
B.(DB)B/|B|^2 is bounded by sup_{supp mu} |DB|. The argument of Step 1, in both time directions, gives exponent 0 in the direction B(a), and R B(a) is the pure Oseledets
line of the exponent 0.
Step 3 (independence of Omega and B). The set {Omega x B = 0} is invariant: Dphi_s maps B(a) to B(phi_s a) and Omega(a) to a
positive multiple of Omega(phi_s a) by (F4). If Omega(a) = f(a) B(a) on an invariant set of positive mu-measure (f != 0 there,
since Omega != 0), then applying Dphi_s: f(a) B(phi_s a) = e^{(1+c)s} Omega(phi_s a) = e^{(1+c)s} f(phi_s a) B(phi_s a), so
f(phi_s a) = e^{-(1+c)s} f(a) -> 0 as s -> +infinity, while by Poincare recurrence f(phi_s a) returns to a neighbourhood of
f(a) != 0 for arbitrarily large s for mu-a.e. such a: contradiction. So Omega(a) and B(a) are independent mu-a.e.
Step 4 (third exponent). The sum of the exponents equals lim (1/s) log det Dphi_s(a) = 3c by (F1); with chi_1 = 1+c and
chi_2 = 0 on the independent directions Omega, B, the Oseledets theorem gives a third exponent chi_3 = 3c - (1+c) - 0 = 2c-1 < 0
on a complementary measurable direction E^s(a).
Step 5 (uniformity on compact sets, backward reading). For a in a compact K contained in Z, (F4) with s = -t gives
|Dpsi_t(a) Omega(a)| = e^{-(1+c)t} |Omega(psi_t a)| <= e^{-(1+c)t} sup_D |Omega|, a uniform contraction at rate 1+c once the orbit
is in D (F5); det Dpsi_t = e^{-3ct}; hence the induced map on the quotient TR^3 / R Omega(a) expands area by at least
(|Omega(a)| / sup_{D'}|Omega|) e^{(1-2c)t} for t >= 0, where D' is a closed ball centred at 0, of radius at least R_0,
containing K, so that psi_t a stays in D' (F5). The exact statement is about the flux form: by (F6), psi_t^* sigma =
e^{(1-2c)t} sigma, and sigma is basic for the
vortex-line foliation (i_Omega sigma = 0, L_Omega sigma = (div Omega) sigma = 0), so it descends to an area form on the local leaf
space of vortex lines, which the backward flow expands by exactly e^{(1-2c)t}; the Euclidean quotient area is expanded by
e^{(1-2c)t} |Omega(a)|/|Omega(psi_t a)|. QED

Remarks. (i) The theorem uses c < 1/2 only for the sign of chi_3; Steps 1-3 hold for every c > 0. (ii) "Omega is the strong
direction": for the backward flow the only contracting Oseledets direction is R Omega, with the exact rate 1+c; this is what makes
vortex lines the backward-stable curves (every point of the vortex line through a vortical point has the same backward limit set
as that point, since psi_t maps a vortex segment of Omega-time tau to one of Omega-time e^{-(1+c)t} tau, of Euclidean length at
most sup_D|Omega| e^{-(1+c)t} |tau|). (iii) For mu supported on a periodic orbit the exponents are the Floquet exponents of
Theorem D1(b), consistently. (iv) The mean stretching identity integral n.Sn dmu = 1 of Step 1 is itself a consequence of (F3)-(F4); no further use of
the momentum equation is made in this theorem.

#### D3. Backward limit sets of vortical points: points and sets of equilibria

Theorem D3 (0 < c < 1/2, every omega). Assume H0, H1'.
(a) [A058] The set W_pt := {a in Z : alpha(a) is a single point} is Lebesgue-null.
(b) [A122] If a in Z and alpha(a) is contained in N = {B = 0}, then alpha(a) is a single point. Consequently
    {a in Z : alpha(a) is contained in N} = W_pt is Lebesgue-null, whether or not the limiting zeros are vortical.
(c) [A111] (Contained in (b); independent proof.) The set of a in Z whose alpha(a) is a compact set of vortical zeros is null.

##### D3.1 Two lemmas on vortical backward limits

Lemma D3.1 (exponent transfer) [A098]. Let a in Z and K := alpha(a). Then there is an ergodic phi-invariant probability measure
mu on K whose largest Lyapunov exponent for the forward flow is >= 1 + c.
Proof. For a continuous linear cocycle over a compact invariant set K of a continuous flow, the uniform growth rate
chi_* := lim_{t -> infinity} (1/t) log sup_{x in K} |Dphi_t(x)| exists and equals the maximum over ergodic invariant probability
measures on K of their top Lyapunov exponent (Schreiber, J. Differential Equations 148 (1998) 334-350; Morris, Proc. LMS 107
(2013), Appendix A). Suppose chi_* < 1 + c and fix eps > 0 with chi_* + 3 eps < 1 + c. Choose T with sup_K |Dphi_T| <=
e^{(chi_* + eps) T}; by continuity there is a neighbourhood O of K with |Dphi_T(x)| <= e^{(chi_* + 2 eps)T} for x in O. The
backward orbit of a eventually stays in O; shift a along its orbit so that psi_t(a) in O for all t >= 0. For integer n,
Dphi_{nT}(psi_{nT} a) is the product of the n matrices Dphi_T(psi_{jT} a), j = n, ..., 1, each of norm <= e^{(chi_* + 2eps)T},
so |Dphi_{nT}(psi_{nT} a)| <= e^{(chi_* + 2 eps) nT}; as Dpsi_{nT}(a) is its inverse, |Dpsi_{nT}(a) v| >= e^{-(chi_* + 2 eps) nT}|v|
for all v. With v = Omega(a), (F4) gives |Omega(psi_{nT} a)| = e^{(1+c) nT} |Dpsi_{nT}(a) Omega(a)| >= e^{(1 + c - chi_* - 2 eps) nT}
|Omega(a)| -> infinity, contradicting the boundedness of Omega on the compact ball D (F5). Hence chi_* >= 1 + c, and the
maximizing ergodic measure, which exists by the Remark below, has top exponent >= 1 + c. QED
Remark (attainment in the maximum formula) [A2721, A2731, A2733]. Schreiber's Theorem 1 gives chi_* as a supremum over
ergodic measures, and Morris's Theorem A3 and Proposition A5 give attainment for maps (the printed proofs of his Lemmas
A1 and A6 contain two finite slips, a missing term in the Fekete bound and a block-sum endpoint one too large; both
lemmas hold with the repaired proofs, and Theorem A3 is unaffected, A2778-A2783 and 2D.4 point 49). For the flow, use
the normalized derivative flow F_t(x, v) = (phi_t(x), Dphi_t(x)v/abs(Dphi_t(x)v)) on K times the unit sphere and the
growth rate g(x, v) = v.DB(x)v. Take t_n -> infinity and (x_n, v_n) in K times the sphere with abs(Dphi_{t_n}(x_n)v_n)
equal to the supremum of abs(Dphi_{t_n}) over K. A weak limit eta of the empirical measures of the segments F_t(x_n,
v_n), 0 <= t <= t_n, is F-invariant and has integral of g equal to chi_*. An ergodic component of eta with integral of g
at least chi_* projects to an ergodic phi-invariant probability measure on K whose top exponent is at least chi_*
(Birkhoff on the lift, Oseledets on K). No invariant measure has top exponent above chi_*, by the uniform bound, so the
maximum is attained.

Lemma D3.2 (spectrum at a limiting zero) [A058]. Let a in Z with psi_t(a) -> p (so B(p) = 0). Then DB(p) has an eigenvalue with
real part >= 1 + c, hence (trace 3c) one with real part <= (2c-1)/2 < 0.
Proof. If Omega(p) != 0, (F3) at p gives DB(p) Omega(p) = (1+c) Omega(p). If Omega(p) = 0, let mu_max be the largest real part
of an eigenvalue of L := DB(p) and fix eps > 0; there is an inner product <., .>_eps with <L v, v>_eps <= (mu_max + eps)|v|_eps^2
(Lyapunov adapted norm). Since DB is continuous and psi_t(a) -> p, |DB(psi_t a) - L|_eps <= eps for t >= t_eps. The vector
w(t) := Dpsi_t(a) Omega(a) solves w' = -DB(psi_t a) w and never vanishes; for t >= t_eps, d|w|_eps^2/dt >= -2(mu_max + 2 eps)|w|_eps^2,
so |w(t)| >= C_eps e^{-(mu_max + 2 eps)t}. By (F4), |Omega(psi_t a)| = e^{(1+c)t}|w(t)| >= C_eps e^{(1 + c - mu_max - 2 eps)t}, and the
left side tends to |Omega(p)| = 0; hence mu_max >= 1 + c - 2 eps for every eps. The second claim: the three real parts sum to
tr DB(p) = 3c, one is >= 1+c, so the other two sum to <= 2c-1 and one of them is <= (2c-1)/2. QED
(Alternatively Lemma D3.2 is the case K = {p} of Lemma D3.1: the only ergodic measure on {p} is delta_p, whose exponents are
the real parts of the eigenvalues of DB(p).)

##### D3.2 The local null-graph lemma

Lemma D3.3 (local center-stable graph; the nonrotating argument, step 7.5, reproved in the accompanying artifacts section 4)
[A010, A058]. Let Y be a C^1 vector field on R^3 with Y(p) = 0 such that L := DY(p) has an eigenvalue with positive real part.
Then there is an open neighbourhood O of p such that the set T := {b : the forward Y-orbit of b stays in O for all t >= 0}
is contained in a Lipschitz graph over a linear subspace of dimension <= 2; in particular T is Lebesgue-null.
Proof. Split R^3 = E^cs + E^u into the real generalized eigenspaces of L for the eigenvalues with real part <= 0 and > 0;
dim E^u >= 1, so dim E^cs <= 2. Use the norm |z|_* := |z_cs| + |z_u| (Euclidean norms on the summands), in which both spectral
projections have norm 1. Choose beta > 0 below the smallest positive real part, eps := beta/4, eta := beta/2 and M_0 with
|e^{-tL_u}| <= M_0 e^{-beta t} and |e^{tL_cs}| <= M_0 e^{eps t} for t >= 0. Write Y(p + z) = L z + r(z) with r C^1, r(0) = 0,
Dr(0) = 0; on a small convex neighbourhood O of p (coordinates z = y - p), r has Lipschitz constant l. Let z(t), z~(t) be two
forward orbits that stay in O for all t >= 0 and w := z - z~, D_* := sup_{t >= 0} e^{-eta t}|w(t)|_* (finite, since O is
bounded). By variation of constants, the cs-component satisfies w_cs(t) = e^{tL_cs} w_cs(0) + integral_0^t e^{(t-s)L_cs}
(r(z) - r(z~))_cs ds, and the u-component, which cannot grow faster than e^{eta t} while staying bounded, satisfies the terminal
formula w_u(t) = - integral_t^infinity e^{(t-s)L_u} (r(z) - r(z~))_u ds (the boundary term at infinity vanishes because
|e^{-(s-t)L_u} w_u(s)| <= M_0 e^{-beta(s-t)} D_* e^{eta s} -> 0 as s -> infinity, as eta < beta). Hence
    e^{-eta t}|w_cs(t)| <= M_0 |w_cs(0)| + M_0 l D_* integral_0^t e^{(eps - eta)(t-s)} ds <= M_0|w_cs(0)| + M_0 l D_*/(eta - eps),
    e^{-eta t}|w_u(t)| <= M_0 l D_* integral_t^infinity e^{-(beta - eta)(s-t)} ds = M_0 l D_*/(beta - eta),
so D_* <= M_0 |w_cs(0)| + M_0 l (1/(eta - eps) + 1/(beta - eta)) D_*. For O small enough that M_0 l (1/(eta-eps) + 1/(beta-eta))
<= 1/2, this gives D_* <= 2 M_0 |w_cs(0)|, and in particular |w_u(0)| <= D_* <= 2 M_0 |w_cs(0)|: on T the projection to E^cs is
injective with Lipschitz inverse, i.e. T is contained in a Lipschitz graph over E^cs, of dimension <= 2, a Lebesgue-null set. QED

##### D3.3 Proof of Theorem D3(a) [A058]

Let N_1 := {p in N : DB(p) has an eigenvalue with real part <= (2c-1)/4}; N_1 is compact (N is compact by (F5), and the
condition is closed by continuity of the spectrum). By Lemma D3.2 every singleton backward limit of a vortical trajectory lies in
N_1. For every p in N_1 the vector field Y := -B satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma D3.3 (-DB(p) has an eigenvalue with real part >=
(1-2c)/4 > 0); let O_p be the neighbourhood it provides and T_p := {b : psi_t(b) in O_p for all t >= 0}, a null set. Choose
open O'_p with closure in O_p and extract a finite subcover O'_{p_1}, ..., O'_{p_k} of N_1. If a in W_pt then psi_t(a) -> p in
some O'_{p_i}, so there is an integer n >= 0 with psi_t(a) in O_{p_i} for all t >= n, i.e. psi_n(a) in T_{p_i}, i.e. a in
phi_n(T_{p_i}). Hence W_pt is contained in the countable union over i <= k, n >= 0 of the null sets phi_n(T_{p_i}) (phi_n is a
C^1 diffeomorphism, which maps null sets to null sets). QED
Remarks. Uncountably many zeros, arcs of zeros, and zeros that are sinks of the backward flow cause no difficulty: only the
compact set N_1 is covered, and backward sinks (which exist among irrotational zeros when omega != 0, e.g. the 1-jet
S = diag(1,-1,0), omega^2 > 1 - c^2 [A017]) lie outside N_1 and are never limits of vortical points by Lemma D3.2. For omega = 0
Lemma D3.2 reduces to lambda_max(S(p)) >= 1 at irrotational limit points (Bendixson), which is the set E in the nonrotating argument.

##### D3.4 Proof of Theorem D3(b): all-equilibrium backward limits are points [A122; the auditor's proof, reproduced]

Step 1 (spectral reduction; uses only Lemma D3.1). Let a in Z and K := alpha(a) contained in N, and suppose K is not a point. K is
compact, connected and consists of equilibria of B, so no point of K is isolated in N and det DB(q) = 0 for every q in K
(an invertible derivative would isolate the zero by the inverse function theorem). By Lemma D3.1 some ergodic invariant
probability on K has top forward exponent >= 1 + c; every ergodic probability on a set of equilibria is a point mass delta_p,
whose exponents are the real parts of the eigenvalues of DB(p). Hence there is p in K with max Re spec DB(p) >= 1 + c. The
spectrum contains 0 and has trace 3c; the two eigenvalues other than 0 sum to 3c and cannot form a complex pair (its common
real part would be 3c/2 < 1 + c). So spec DB(p) = {lambda, 0, 3c - lambda} with lambda >= 1 + c and 3c - lambda <= 2c - 1 < 0,
three distinct real numbers; rank DB(p) = 2. For the backward field Y := -B this is one negative, one zero and one positive
eigenvalue. Nothing is assumed about Omega(p).

Step 2 (an interior arc of equilibria near p; local topology). Since rank DB(p) = 2, two components of B have independent
differentials at p, and by the implicit function theorem there is a neighbourhood O of p in which the common zero set of these
two components is an embedded C^2 curve gamma through p and N intersected with O is a closed subset of gamma (possibly a proper
subset). Along gamma near p the two nonzero eigenvalues of DB stay real, simple and of opposite signs, and the third eigenvalue
is 0 at every non-isolated zero. Parametrize gamma with gamma(0) = p. If for some delta > 0, small enough that
gamma([-delta, delta]) lies in O, one of the two sides
gamma([0, delta)) or gamma((-delta, 0]) lies entirely in K, an interval of equilibria with endpoint p is found. Otherwise pick
coordinates alpha < 0 < beta with gamma(alpha), gamma(beta) not in K and a thin closed tube D around gamma([alpha, beta]), compactly
inside O, whose end faces meet gamma only at gamma(alpha), gamma(beta); since all zeros in O lie on gamma, the whole boundary of D is
disjoint from K, so K intersected with D is nonempty (it contains p), relatively open and closed in K, hence equal to K by
connectedness: K is a compact connected subset of gamma, i.e. a closed interval, and as it is not a point it contains an
interior subinterval. In either case choose q in the interior of an interval J of equilibria of gamma so close to p that the two
nonzero eigenvalues of DB(q) still have opposite signs; near q the equilibrium set is exactly an open arc of gamma.

Step 3 (two local invariant C^2 surfaces at the arc). Extend Y outside a compact neighbourhood to a complete C^2 flow without
changing it near J, fix T > 0 and let f be the time-T map of Y; J is a compact arc of fixed points of f. Along J the derivative
Df has the continuous invariant splitting E^s + E^c + E^u (E^c tangent to J, Df = identity on E^c, uniform contraction on E^s,
uniform expansion on E^u; eigenvalues distinct; an adapted norm and a large T make the bounds uniform). Apply the Main Theorem
and Corollary 1.5 of Bonatti and Crovisier (Center manifolds for partially hyperbolic sets without strong unstable connections,
J. Inst. Math. Jussieu 15 (2016); arXiv:1401.2452) to f with center bundle E^s + E^c and strong unstable bundle E^u: the
condition "no strong unstable connections" holds because distinct points of J are fixed and so never lie on a common strong
unstable leaf, and the splitting is 2-normally hyperbolic (center derivative bounded under positive iterates, unstable
derivative expanding). This gives a C^2 surface S^cs through J, locally invariant under f. The same applied to f^{-1}
(center bundle E^c + E^u) gives a C^2 locally invariant surface S^cu. Their tangent spaces meet exactly in E^c along J, so they
are transverse and their local intersection is exactly J near q. Local invariance is an equality of germs near the fixed arc
(f(S) intersected with S contains a neighbourhood of J in S, and continuity of f^{-1} near fixed points gives the other
inclusion after shrinking).

Step 4 (straightened coordinates and the finite-passage estimate). Take simultaneous C^2 coordinates (w, s, u) near q with
J = {s = u = 0}, S^cs = {u = 0}, S^cu = {s = 0}. By Hadamard's factorization the map f reads
    w_{n+1} = w_n + F(w_n, s_n, u_n),   s_{n+1} = A(w_n, s_n, u_n) s_n,   u_{n+1} = D(w_n, s_n, u_n) u_n,
with continuous A, D, F, and on a small closed chart box, for some 0 < kappa < 1 and C < infinity,
    |A| <= kappa,   |D| >= kappa^{-1},   |F| <= C(|s| + |u|)
(the factors on the arc are the stable and unstable normal eigenvalues of Df; F vanishes on the arc since its points are fixed;
only C^1 regularity of the coordinate map and bounded first derivatives of F are used). For a finite passage z_0, ..., z_n inside
the box, iterating gives |s_j| <= kappa^j |s_0|, |u_j| <= kappa^{n-j} |u_n| (the second from the backward iteration of the u-equation),
and therefore
    |w_n - w_0| <= sum_{j<n} C(|s_j| + |u_j|) <= C (1 - kappa)^{-1} (|s_0| + |u_n|).                                     (D3.1)
This endpoint estimate bounds the total center drift of a passage by the normal distances at entry and exit, independently of
its duration; a bound by (duration) x (normal size) would not suffice.

Step 5 (capture). Take an inner box Q = {|w| <= r, |s|, |u| <= d} and a larger box Q^+ compactly inside the chart, with the center
interval of Q compactly inside that of Q^+. Since f fixes the center arc, by continuity and compactness all points of Q with
|s| + |u| small enough have their f-image in Q^+. The backward orbit psi_t(a) of our vortical point has distance to K tending to 0
and K is contained in the equilibrium set; in Q^+ the equilibrium set is exactly the center arc, so at sufficiently late times every
visit of the orbit to Q^+ has |s|, |u| < eps, where eps > 0 can be taken arbitrarily small. The point q in K is also a limit of the
time-T samples z_n := psi_{nT}(a) (if psi_{t_j}(a) -> q write t_j = n_j T + tau_j, 0 <= tau_j < T; then z_{n_j} = phi_{tau_j}(psi_{t_j} a) ->
q by uniform continuity of phi on [0, T] and phi_tau(q) = q). Choose eps so small that eps < d, that f maps the normally eps-close
part of Q into Q^+, and that 2 C eps/(1 - kappa) < r/2. Take a late sample z_0 in Q with |w_0| < r/4, |s_0|, |u_0| < eps and suppose
n is the first later index with z_n not in Q. All samples z_0, ..., z_{n-1} lie in Q and z_n lies in Q^+; all are late, so their
normal coordinates are < eps, and (D3.1) applied in Q^+ gives |w_n - w_0| < r/2, hence |w_n| < 3r/4, |s_n|, |u_n| < d: z_n is in Q,
a contradiction. So all later samples stay in Q. Then the uniform expansion of u forces u_0 = 0, the stable coordinate decays
geometrically, and by (D3.1) the center increments are absolutely summable: the samples converge to a point of the arc, and by
uniform continuity of phi_tau, 0 <= tau <= T, so does the whole backward orbit. Hence alpha(a) is a point, contradicting the
assumption that K is not a point. This proves the first statement of (b); the nullity follows from (a). QED
Remark. The argument uses no Lyapunov function, no volume argument and no condition on the vorticity at the zeros; it needs
that the ENTIRE limit set consists of equilibria (a limit set containing a nonstationary orbit is outside its scope).

##### D3.5 Proof of Theorem D3(c): limits made of vortical equilibria [A111; the auditor's proof, reproduced]

Although (c) is contained in (b), its proof is different and worth recording. Let a in Z with K := alpha(a) a compact set of
vortical zeros that is not a point. Every q in K is a non-isolated zero, so det DB(q) = 0; with Omega(q) != 0, (F3) gives the
eigenvalue 1 + c on Omega(q), and the trace fixes the third eigenvalue: spec DB(q) = {1+c, 0, 2c-1}, three distinct reals, rank 2.
For delta > 0 let K_delta := {q in N : q non-isolated in N, |Omega(q)| >= delta}: compact (the derived set of N is closed and the
vorticity bound is closed). On K_delta the backward field -B has the continuous invariant splitting into the eigenlines of
-(1+c), 0, 1-2c; for a large fixed time T and f := psi_T the splitting E^cs (the first two) + E^u (the third) is dominated with E^u
uniformly expanding, and in an adapted metric these properties persist on a small neighbourhood V of K_delta (no invariance of
the extended bundles away from K_delta is needed). Suppose the basin W := {x : dist(psi_t x, K_delta) -> 0} had positive
Lebesgue measure. Restrict it to a bounded set of positive measure, then by Egorov's theorem and inner regularity choose a
compact E of positive measure on which the convergence dist(f^n x, K_delta) -> 0 is uniform; for n >= n_0, f^n(E) is contained in
V. The set S := K_delta union closure(union_{n >= n_0} f^n(E)) is compact, forward f-invariant, of positive measure, and
intersection_{m >= 0} f^m(S) = K_delta by uniform convergence. The extended splitting is dominated over the maximal invariant set
K_delta of S, and the inverse derivative on the extended E^u has norm <= some sigma < 1 on V, so f is (uniformly) nonuniformly
expanding along E^u on S. Theorem A of Alves and Pinheiro (Topological structure of (partially) hyperbolic sets with positive
volume, Trans. AMS 360 (2008); arXiv:math/0603148) then yields a nontrivial local unstable disk contained in the maximal invariant
set K_delta. But f is the identity on K_delta, so two distinct points of such a disk, whose backward iterates would have to
converge exponentially to each other, stay at constant distance: contradiction. (To meet the source's compact-manifold setting,
cut the field off outside a compact neighbourhood of S and its finite-time orbit segments and compactify to S^3; none of the
dynamics used is changed.) Hence each basin of K_{1/k}, k >= 1, is null. Finally, if alpha(a) is a nonpoint compact connected set
of vortical zeros, none of its points is isolated in N (connectedness) and min_{alpha(a)} |Omega| > 0, so alpha(a) is contained in
some K_{1/k} and a lies in its basin; the point case is (a). QED

#### D4. Positive entropy of the core

Theorem D4 (0 < c < 1/2, every omega). Assume H0, H1', and let Lambda be the compact invariant set of points with bounded
forward orbit (F5). Let F := psi_1 be the time-one map of the backward flow.
(i) [A055; synthesis CO3] If U is C^r for an integer r >= 2 and not constant, then with the compactified map F' of S^3 defined in Step 2
    below, 1 - 2c <= h_top(F|Lambda) + R(F')/r, where R(F') := lim_n (1/n) log max(1, sup |DF'^n|). In particular, if U is
    C^infinity and not constant, h_top(F|Lambda) = h_top(phi_1|Lambda) >= 1 - 2c > 0.
(ii) [A080] If U is C^2 and Omega has no zero on Lambda, then h_top(F|Lambda) >= 1 - 2c (no loss term).
Consequently a C^infinity profile satisfying H0, H1' whose backward flow has zero topological entropy on Lambda is constant
(zero under U -> 0): every smooth counterexample to the conjecture has a chaotic core, for every omega.

Proof of (i). Step 1 (a loop of nonzero circulation and its stretching). If Omega = curl U vanished identically, U would be
harmonic (div U = 0, curl U = 0) and o(|y|), hence constant by the Liouville theorem; so there is a with Omega(a) != 0. Let
gamma be the boundary of a small disk of radius eps centered at a, normal to Omega(a); by Stokes and continuity its circulation
Gamma := oint_gamma U.dl = pi eps^2 (|Omega(a)| + o(1)) is nonzero. By Theorem D1(a) read backward, oint_{psi_t gamma} U.dl =
e^{(1-2c)t} Gamma. Let D be the trapping ball of (F5) and M := sup_D |U| (M > 0, since sigma below lies in D and has
nonzero circulation). Every compact set enters
int D under psi_t after a uniform finite time, so sigma := psi_T gamma lies in int D for some T and all its backward images stay in
D; since |oint U.dl| <= M length, 
        length(psi_n sigma) >= |Gamma| e^{(1-2c)(T+n)} / M      for all integers n >= 0.                                (D4.1)
This is a length estimate for one fixed curve, not an inference from a Lyapunov exponent.
Step 2 (compactification without changing the relevant dynamics). Fix R_1 > R_0 and a smooth cutoff chi, 0 <= chi <= 1, equal to
1 on |y| <= R_1 and 0 on |y| >= 2R_1, and put B' := (cI - omega J)y + chi U. For |y| >= R_0, B'.y >= c|y|^2/2, so D is still
backward-trapping for B', B' = B on D, and the backward B'- and B-orbits of points of D coincide. For |y| >= 2R_1, B' = Ay with
A = cI - omega J; in the inversion chart z = y/|y|^2 the push-forward of Ay is (A - 2cI) z = -(cI + omega J) z, because
y.Ay = c|y|^2. Hence B' extends to a C^r vector field on S^3 = R^3 union {infinity} with a hyperbolic sink at infinity, its
flow is complete, and F' := its time -1 map is a C^r diffeomorphism of S^3 with F'^n = psi_n on D for all n >= 0.
Step 3 (all invariant mass is on Lambda or at infinity). F'(D) is contained in D; every point of R^3 enters D under some
iterate of F' (outside D, |y| decreases at rate >= c|y|/2 along the backward flow), so union_{n >= 0} F'^{-n}(D) = S^3 minus
{infinity}; and intersection_{n >= 0} F'^n(D) = Lambda (a point whose forward orbit leaves D never returns, so staying in D at
all integer times means a bounded forward orbit, and conversely). For an F'-invariant probability nu all the sets F'^{+-n}(D)
have mass nu(D), so by continuity along the two nested sequences nu(Lambda) = nu(D) = 1 - nu({infinity}): every ergodic
invariant probability is carried by Lambda or is the point mass at infinity. The variational principle (and h(F) = h(F^{-1})
for a homeomorphism) gives h_top(F') = h_top(F'|Lambda) = h_top(F|Lambda) = h_top(phi_1|Lambda).                    (D4.2)
Step 4 (Yomdin's volume-growth inequality). For a C^r diffeomorphism f of a compact manifold and a compact C^r submanifold Y
of dimension l, the exponential growth rate of the l-volume of f^n(Y) is at most h_top(f) + (l/r) log^+ Rad(Df), Rad(Df) :=
limsup_n sup|Df^n|^{1/n} (Y. Yomdin, Volume growth and entropy, Israel J. Math. 57 (1987) 285-300; M. Gromov, Entropy,
homology and semialgebraic geometry, Seminaire Bourbaki 663, Asterisque 145-146 (1987), Theorem 2.2 and sections 3.1-3.8,
stated there for the graph volume, which dominates the volume of f^n(Y) since the projection is 1-Lipschitz; checked by the auditor
against the printed source). Apply it to f = F', Y = sigma (a C^r embedded circle in int D), l = 1: by (D4.1) the left side is >=
1 - 2c, and with (D4.2) this is the claim. For C^infinity data the same F' and sigma satisfy the hypothesis for every r, so the
loss R(F')/r disappears as r -> infinity. QED (i)

Proof of (ii) [A080, reproducing the auditor's argument; it follows the characteristic-foliation idea of Arnaud and Fejoz, J. Ec.
polytech. Math. 11 (2024), Theorem 5, but uses only C^1 flow boxes on a trapping set]. By (F6), F^* sigma = e^{1-2c}
sigma, and F preserves the kernel line field R Omega of sigma where Omega != 0. Since Omega has no zero on the compact set Lambda
and the nested sets F^n(D) converge to Lambda, there is N such that Omega != 0 on a neighbourhood of K := F^N(D), a compact
forward-invariant set with intersection of F^n(K) = Lambda. Choose finitely many C^1 flow boxes of Omega covering K (coordinates
(q_1, q_2, z) with Omega = d/dz, plaques {q = const}), each with a smaller relatively compact box, with uniform constants C, eta > 0
such that two points of a smaller box lying on one plaque of the larger box can be joined inside that plaque by an arc of length
<= C times their distance, and every arc of length < eta starting in a smaller box stays in the larger box. Let S be a small C^1
embedded disk in K, contained in one smaller box, called the box of S, and transverse to Omega, oriented with sigma > 0 on it and, as a graph over the plaque coordinate q of the larger box of S, meeting each plaque of that larger box at most once (possible for S small and transverse); put
A_0 := integral_S sigma > 0; then integral_{F^n S} sigma = e^{(1-2c)n} A_0. Let L bound |DF^{-1}| on a compact neighbourhood of K that contains the larger boxes (hence every plaque arc used below) and
choose delta > 0 so small that every subset of K of diameter <= 2 delta lies in one smaller box, and 2 L C delta < eta. Let E be
the intersection of S with a Bowen ball of radius delta for the times 0, ..., n (a set of points whose first n iterates stay
delta-close to those of a fixed point). For k = 1, ..., n the box at time k is a smaller box containing F^k(E), which exists by the choice of delta; at time 0 it is the box of S, which contains E. Claim: the projection to q is injective on F^n(E). Indeed, if x_n, y_n in F^n(E) lie on one
plaque of the terminal larger box, join them by a plaque arc of length <= 2 C delta; its F^{-1}-image is an arc in a plaque
(F preserves the Omega-line field, hence plaques) of length <= 2 L C delta < eta starting in the preceding smaller box, so it
stays in the preceding larger box and its endpoints lie on one plaque there; replace it by the short plaque arc and repeat
backward n times; at time 0 both endpoints lie in S on one plaque of the larger box of S, hence coincide, since S meets each such plaque at most once. In each box sigma = g(q, z) dq_1
dq_2 with g bounded, and the q-projection is a local C^1 diffeomorphism on the transverse disk F^n(S), injective on F^n(E), so
integral_{F^n(E)} sigma <= M with M independent of n and of the Bowen ball. If r_{n+1}(K, delta) Bowen balls cover K, they cover S,
and summing the positive contributions, e^{(1-2c)n} A_0 <= M r_{n+1}(K, delta); hence h_top(F|K) >= 1 - 2c. Finally every F-invariant
probability on K gives full mass to Lambda, so h_top(F|K) = h_top(F|Lambda) by the variational principle. QED (ii)

Remarks. (i) Both proofs are kinematic in the sense that they use only the exact circulation/flux law and trapping; what they
show is that a nonconstant profile is never "simple" (under decay, nonconstant means nonzero; a constant profile
U = u != 0 is uniformly sublinear and its bounded-forward core is one point, A264): its core carries positive entropy for every omega when U is C^infinity and not constant (part (i)) or when U is C^2 and Omega has
no zero on the core (part (ii)); at finite smoothness C^r without the latter condition only the bound of part (i), with the loss
R(F')/r, is proved (for omega = 0 this is
consistent with Theorem L2 of the nonrotating argument only because that theorem forces U constant). (ii) By Ruelle's inequality and Theorem D2,
every ergodic measure on {B != 0, Omega != 0} has entropy <= 1 - 2c; a measure attaining 1 - 2c is an SRB measure for the backward
flow (Ledrappier-Young, for the field cut off and compactified to S^3 as in D4 Step 2), which is the conditional structure discussed in the final report (not part of this section).

#### D5. The trichotomy for vortical backward limit sets and the structure of case (alpha)

Notation. Reg := {B != 0, Omega != 0, B x Omega != 0} (the regular region); for delta > 0, R_delta := {y in D : |Omega| >= delta,
|B x Omega| >= delta} (compact); alpha^flat := (B x Omega)^flat, the 1-form v -> (B x Omega).v = det(B, Omega, v) = -sigma(B, v) = -(i_B sigma)(v). Backward flow psi_t; its "unstable" objects are the forward-stable
ones of phi.

##### D5.1 Exact transport of the covector B x Omega and degenerate orbits [A056 (a), (b)]

Lemma D5.1 (exact covector law; every c, omega; H0, H1'). For all x, s and v:
        (B x Omega)(phi_s x) . Dphi_s(x) v = e^{(2c-1)s} (B x Omega)(x) . v.
Proof. det(B(phi_s x), Omega(phi_s x), Dphi_s v) = det(Dphi_s B(x), e^{-(1+c)s} Dphi_s Omega(x), Dphi_s v) (flow invariance of B and
(F4)) = e^{-(1+c)s} det(Dphi_s) det(B(x), Omega(x), v) = e^{(3c - 1 - c)s} det(B, Omega, v)(x) by (F1). QED
Equivalently phi_s^*(i_B sigma) = e^{(2c-1)s} i_B sigma; under the backward flow the covector B x Omega is expanded exactly at rate
1 - 2c.

Lemma D5.2 (degenerate orbits). The sets {B = 0}, {Omega = 0}, {B x Omega = 0} are closed and invariant. If x has a bounded full
orbit with B(x) != 0, Omega(x) != 0 and Omega(x) = lambda_0 B(x), then along the orbit Omega(phi_s x) = lambda_0 e^{-(1+c)s} B(phi_s x);
hence |B(psi_t x)| <= sup|Omega| e^{-(1+c)t}/|lambda_0| -> 0 and |Omega(phi_s x)| <= |lambda_0| sup|B| e^{-(1+c)s} -> 0: the backward
limit set of x lies in {B = 0} and its forward limit set in {Omega = 0}. In particular a compact invariant set containing such a
point meets both {B = 0} and {Omega = 0}.
Proof. Invariance of the three sets follows from Dphi_s B = B o phi_s, (F4), and Lemma D5.1. The rest is (F4) applied to
Omega(x) = lambda_0 B(x) and the boundedness of B and Omega on the bounded orbit closure. QED

##### D5.2 Hyperbolicity of compact vortical invariant sets in the regular region [A056 (c)]

Lemma D5.3 (0 < c < 1/2). Let K be a compact invariant set contained in Reg (so |B|, |Omega|, |B x Omega| lie in [d, D'] on K,
d > 0). Then K is a hyperbolic set of the flow phi: TR^3|_K = E^s + R B + R Omega with E^s a continuous invariant line field,
|Dphi_s v| <= C e^{(2c-1)s}|v| for v in E^s, s >= 0, the direction Omega expanded exactly (|Dphi_s Omega(x)| = e^{(1+c)s}
|Omega(phi_s x)|), and R B neutral. For the backward flow the splitting is E^u_psi := E^s (rate 1 - 2c), R B (rate 0), and the
strong stable direction R Omega (rate 1 + c).
Proof. E^cu(x) := span(B(x), Omega(x)) is a continuous invariant 2-plane field on K (Lemma D5.2 and invariance of B, Omega); for
v = a B + b Omega, Dphi_s v = a B(phi_s x) + b e^{(1+c)s} Omega(phi_s x), and since the angle between B and Omega is bounded below
on K, |Dphi_s v| >= C^{-1}|v| for s >= 0. E^cu(x) is the kernel of the covector alpha^flat_x = (B x Omega)(x), and |alpha^flat_x(v)| is
uniformly comparable on K to the distance from v to E^cu(x); by Lemma D5.1 the induced cocycle on the quotient TR^3/E^cu contracts
exactly by e^{(2c-1)s} in the quotient norm [v] -> |alpha^flat_x(v)|, and therefore up to a factor bounded on K in the
Euclidean quotient norm. An invariant subbundle whose quotient cocycle is uniformly dominated by the cocycle on the subbundle (rate
2c - 1 < 0 against rate >= 0) has a unique continuous invariant complement with the quotient rate: the standard graph-transform
argument (Hirsch, Pugh, Shub, Invariant Manifolds, LNM 583; the cone-field criterion in Bonatti, Diaz, Viana, Dynamics beyond
uniform hyperbolicity, Appendix B), the contraction constant being the domination gap. This complement is E^s. QED
Remark. The three exponents on K are exactly {1+c, 0, 2c-1} (Theorem D2 for any ergodic measure on K): a hyperbolic set with
constant exponents, an unusual rigidity. Periodic orbits in K have the multipliers of Theorem D1(b).

##### D5.3 The trichotomy [A056 (d)]

Theorem D5.4 (0 < c < 1/2, every omega). Assume H0, H1' and Omega(a) != 0. Then at least one of the following holds:
 (alpha) alpha(a) is contained in Reg; then alpha(a) is a compact hyperbolic set as in Lemma D5.3;
 (beta)  alpha(a) contains a zero of B;
 (gamma) alpha(a) contains a point where Omega = 0.
Proof. If (alpha) fails, alpha(a) contains a point x with Omega(x) = 0 (then (gamma)) or with Omega(x) != 0 and B(x) x Omega(x) = 0;
in the latter case either B(x) = 0 (then (beta)) or x is a degenerate regular point and Lemma D5.2, applied to the orbit of x
(which lies in the compact invariant set alpha(a)), gives both (beta) and (gamma). QED
(A single point alpha(a) is a zero, hence (beta); a single periodic orbit is (alpha) or (gamma); for a in Z the point case is
Lebesgue-null by Theorem D3(a). Since {Omega = 0} is invariant (Lemma D5.2), a cycle either has Omega != 0 at every point or lies
in {Omega = 0}. For a cycle gamma of the first kind, D1(b) makes gamma a hyperbolic saddle, so {a : alpha(a) = gamma} lies in its
2-dimensional unstable manifold for phi, an injectively immersed C^1 surface, hence is null; a hyperbolic periodic orbit is the
only periodic orbit with period in some open interval around its own that lies in some neighbourhood of it (one may take a finite
union of rational balls and an interval with rational ends), so these cycles are countable and the union of the sets is null.
A cycle in {Omega = 0} is case (gamma). The point-or-cycle Liouville theorem [A020] is cited and not proved here.)

##### D5.4 Refinement of case (alpha): basins of regular basic backward attractors [synthesis CO9: A115; Lemma 12.7: A118]

Throughout D5.4, 0 < c < 1/2, H0, H1'. Let chi_tau denote the (local) flow of the vorticity field Omega (vortex lines).

Lemma D5.5 (vortex lines are complete and are contracted exactly by the backward flow; on a compact regular hyperbolic set
they are the global strong-stable curves) [CO9 Lemma 12.1; A106, A047;
completeness per as summarized in the accompanying artifacts section 5]. Under H0, H1' (c > 0, every omega) the flow chi_tau of the
C^1 field Omega is complete, although no bound on Omega at infinity is assumed, and for every a, tau and real t
        psi_t(chi_tau a) = chi_{tau e^{-(1+c)t}}(psi_t a);
if t >= 0 and the vortex segment {chi_sigma a : |sigma| <= |tau|} lies in D then
dist(psi_t chi_tau a, psi_t a) <= M_Omega |tau| e^{-(1+c)t}, M_Omega := max_D |Omega|.
Proof. Completeness: fix a compact set E of initial points; all psi_s(E), s >= 0, lie in a common compact ball D' (F5), on a
slightly larger ball the C^1 field Omega has a common local existence time delta > 0. For s >= 0 and |tau| <= delta e^{(1+c)s}
define z_s(tau) := phi_s(chi_{e^{-(1+c)s} tau}(psi_s x)), x in E. By (F4), z_s'(tau) = e^{-(1+c)s} Dphi_s Omega(chi_{...}(psi_s x)) =
Omega(z_s(tau)) and z_s(0) = x: each z_s solves the vortex-line initial value problem through x, so by uniqueness they agree on
overlapping intervals, and their domains exhaust R. The same computation with s = -t gives the conjugacy. For a compact vortex
segment choose a backward-trapping ball containing it; its images stay there and have length at most M_Omega |tau| e^{-(1+c)t}.
On a compact regular hyperbolic set the local vortex arc is therefore the local strong stable curve (local stable manifold
theorem and equal dimension), and iterating backward identifies the full strong stable curve with the complete vortex line. QED
For a hyperbolic set K in Reg, R Omega is the strong stable line of psi (Lemma D5.3), so Lemma D5.5 identifies the strong stable
leaves globally as the vortex lines.

Standing facts for a compact psi-invariant set K contained in R_delta (Lemma D5.3): K is hyperbolic for psi with splitting
E^u_psi + R B + R Omega, E^u_psi = E^s of Lemma D5.3 (psi-rate 1 - 2c). By the strong unstable manifold theorem for hyperbolic
sets of C^2 flows (Hirsch-Pugh-Shub, LNM 583; Fisher-Hasselblatt, Hyperbolic Flows, EMS 2019, chapter 6) there is eps > 0 such
that every x in K has a local strong unstable curve W^u_eps(x), a C^1 embedded arc tangent to E^u_psi(x), depending continuously
on x in the C^1 topology, contracted by psi_{-t} at a uniform exponential rate; W^u(x) := union over n of psi_n W^u_eps(psi_{-n} x),
W^u(x') = W^u(x) for x' in W^u(x); W^wu(x) := union over s of psi_s W^u(x) (weak unstable leaf, 2-dimensional). A compact
psi-invariant G contained in K is u-saturated if W^u_eps(x) is contained in G for every x in G (then W^u(x), W^wu(x) are in G).

Lemma D5.6 (closures of leaves are u-saturated) [CO9 Lemma 12.2]. If x is in K and W^wu(x) is contained in K then cl W^wu(x) is
u-saturated. Proof: if z_n in W^wu(x) converge to z, then z_n is in W^u(psi_{s_n} x) for some s_n, so W^u_eps(z_n) is contained in
W^u(psi_{s_n} x) = psi_{s_n} W^u(x), which lies in W^wu(x); by continuity of W^u_eps on K, W^u_eps(z) lies in cl W^wu(x). QED

Lemma D5.7 (u-saturated regular sets are attracting) [CO9 Lemma 12.3; independently A110]. Let G be a nonempty u-saturated compact
invariant set contained in some R_delta. Then there are an open neighbourhood O of G and constants C, T, r > 0 with
 (i) dist(psi_t z, G) <= C e^{-(1+c)t} for all z in O, t >= 0;
 (ii) with N_G := {z : dist(z, G) < r}: cl N_G is contained in O, psi_t(cl N_G) is contained in N_G for t >= T, and the intersection over
      t >= 0 of psi_t(cl N_G) equals G.
So G is an attracting set of psi with trapping neighbourhood N_G, locally maximal, and its basin Bas(G) := {z : dist(psi_t z, G) -> 0}
= union over t >= 0 of psi_{-t}(N_G) is open.
Proof. Fix x in G and a C^1 parametrization gamma_x of W^u_eps(x) with gamma_x(0) = x. The C^1 map G_x(s, r', tau) :=
chi_tau(psi_s(gamma_x(r'))) has at 0 the derivative with columns -B(x) (the s-derivative of psi_s), gamma_x'(0), Omega(x), which span R^3 (they span the three
lines of the splitting), so by the inverse function theorem G_x maps a small box diffeomorphically onto an open neighbourhood
O_x of x. For z = G_x(s, r', tau) in O_x the point w := psi_s gamma_x(r') lies in G (u-saturation and invariance) and z = chi_tau w.
Cover G by finitely many O_{x_i}, let O be their union and rho the largest box size; all vortex segments used lie in a compact set,
hence in D after enlarging R_0, and Lemma D5.5 gives (i) with C = M_Omega rho. For (ii) take r with cl N_G in O and T with
C e^{-(1+c)T} < r/2; a point of every psi_t(cl N_G) is the psi_t-image of a point of O, so by (i) it is within C e^{-(1+c)t} of G
for every t; hence the intersection is G (which it contains, G being invariant and in N_G). QED

Lemma D5.8 (minimal u-saturated sets are basic attractors) [CO9 Lemma 12.4]. Let K be a compact invariant set contained in R_delta
and G a nonempty u-saturated compact invariant subset of K. Then G contains a set A with:
 (a) A is nonempty, compact, invariant, u-saturated, and cl W^wu(x) = A for every x in A;
 (b) A is an attracting set as in Lemma D5.7, locally maximal, with no zero of B and no zero of Omega;
 (c) for open sets V_1, V_2 meeting A and every T_0 there is t >= T_0 with psi_t(V_1 cap A) cap V_2 nonempty (topological
     transitivity for arbitrarily large times); a residual set of x in A has omega_psi(x) = A;
 (d) periodic orbits are dense in A, and A is not a single orbit.
Proof. (a) The nonempty u-saturated compact invariant subsets of G, ordered by inclusion, have the finite intersection property
along chains and the intersection of a chain is again nonempty, u-saturated, compact and invariant; Zorn's lemma gives a minimal
element A; for x in A, cl W^wu(x) is contained in A and u-saturated (Lemma D5.6), hence equals A. (b) Lemma D5.7; B, Omega do not
vanish on R_delta. (c) Let y in A. By (a) there is z in W^wu(y) cap V_2, so z lies in psi_{s+n} W^u_eps(psi_{-n} y) for some s and
integer n >= 0; by continuity of W^u_eps and psi the same holds, with the same s, n, for all y' in a relatively open
neighbourhood W_y of y in A. Cover A by W_{y_1}, ..., W_{y_m}; put n_* := max n_i, s_* := max |s_i|. Take x in V_1 cap A and
delta' > 0 with W^u_{delta'}(x) contained in V_1 (it lies in A). By uniform expansion there is t_0 with W^u_eps(psi_t x) contained in
psi_t W^u_{delta'}(x) for t >= t_0. Given T_0 take t >= t_0 + n_* + s_* + T_0 and i with psi_t x in W_{y_i}; then
psi_{s_i + n_i} W^u_eps(psi_{t - n_i} x) is contained in psi_{t + s_i}(V_1 cap A) and meets V_2, with t + s_i >= T_0. The residual
statement is the Baire argument with a countable base. (d) By (c) every point of A is nonwandering for psi|A; A is a locally
maximal hyperbolic set without zeros, so the Anosov closing lemma for hyperbolic sets of flows (Fisher-Hasselblatt 2019, chapters
5-6; Katok-Hasselblatt 1995, chapter 18) gives periodic orbits in the trapping neighbourhood N_A of A (Lemma D5.7 with G = A) arbitrarily close to any nonwandering point, and they lie in A
by local maximality. A contains a 2-dimensional leaf, so it is not one orbit. QED

Lemma D5.9 (disjoint basins) [CO9 Lemma 12.5]. If A_1, A_2 are attractors as in Lemma D5.8 with Bas(A_1) cap Bas(A_2) nonempty,
then A_1 = A_2. Hence there are at most countably many such attractors.
Proof. For z in both basins, omega_psi(z) is a nonempty subset of A_1 cap A_2, so A_2 meets the open set Bas(A_1); take x in A_2
with omega_psi(x) = A_2 (Lemma D5.8(c)); its forward psi-orbit enters Bas(A_1), so A_2 = omega_psi(x) is contained in A_1; by
symmetry A_1 = A_2. Nonempty pairwise disjoint open subsets of R^3 are countably many. QED

Lemma D5.10 (positive-measure survivors produce weak unstable leaves) [A091; Alves-Pinheiro Theorem A]. Let C be a compact set
contained in R_delta, forward invariant under psi (psi_t C contained in C for t >= 0), with positive Lebesgue measure. Then the full
invariant part K_C := {x in C : psi_t x in C for all real t} contains W^wu(q) for some q in K_C.
Proof (with the supplements of as summarized in the accompanying artifacts section 6). K_C = intersection_{n >= 0} psi_{nT}(C) for any
T > 0 is a compact psi-invariant set in R_delta, hyperbolic by Lemma D5.3, with the dominated splitting E^cs := R B + R Omega (for
psi: rates 0 and -(1+c)) and E^u := E^u_psi uniformly expanding (rate 1 - 2c). First choose T so large that for f := psi_T both the
domination product and the inverse unstable norm are strictly below 1 on K_C; the continuous splitting extends to a
neighbourhood V_N of K_C with these strict estimates preserved after shrinking V_N. The nested compacts psi_{nT}(C) converge to K_C,
so C' := f^m(C) lies in V_N for m large; C' is compact, forward invariant, of positive volume, with the same full invariant part K_C,
and f is uniformly expanding along the extended E^u on every orbit in C'. The hypotheses of Theorem A of Alves and Pinheiro
(Topological structure of (partially) hyperbolic sets with positive volume, Trans. AMS 360 (2008)) are met for the C^2 map f on
C' (cut the field off outside a compact region and compactify to S^3 as in D4; the source's uniformly contracting center-stable
variants are not used): there is a nontrivial local unstable interval I contained in K_C. This does not directly give a full
unstable manifold. Choose p in the interior of I and a subsequence f^{n_j} p -> q in K_C; for each fixed m >= 0, f^{n_j - m} p -> f^{-m} q,
and by expansion along I both intrinsic endpoint distances of f^{n_j - m}(I) tend to infinity, so these images contain a
fixed-size local unstable interval about f^{n_j - m} p for large j; continuous C^1 dependence of local unstable manifolds and
closedness of K_C give W^u_loc(f^{-m} q) contained in K_C for every m >= 0, hence (applying f^m and taking the union) W^u(q)
contained in K_C, and flow saturation gives W^wu(q) contained in K_C. The point q is a forward accumulation point of images of I
and need not lie in I. QED

Theorem D5.11 (refined trichotomy) [CO9, A115]. Assume H0, H1', 0 < c < 1/2, any omega. Let V_alpha := {a : alpha(a) is contained in
Reg} (contained in Z) and let calA be the family of basic hyperbolic backward attractors A of Lemma D5.8 with A contained in Reg.
Then calA is countable, the basins Bas(A), A in calA, are pairwise disjoint open sets contained in V_alpha, and
        | V_alpha minus union_{A in calA} Bas(A) | = 0.
Consequently, for Lebesgue-almost every a with Omega(a) != 0, at least one of:
 (alpha*) a lies in the basin of some A in calA; every periodic orbit in A has multipliers exactly e^{(1+c)T}, e^{(2c-1)T}, zero
          circulation and integral_0^T |B|^2 = -2 omega A_xy (Theorem D1), so calA is empty when omega = 0;
 (beta)   alpha(a) contains a zero of B;
 (gamma)  alpha(a) contains a point where Omega = 0.
Proof. Countability and disjointness: Lemma D5.9. Bas(A) is contained in V_alpha since alpha(z) = omega_psi(z) is contained in A,
contained in Reg, for z in Bas(A). Measurability: T_{delta, m} := {x : psi_t x in R_delta for all t >= m} is closed and V_alpha is the
union over delta = 1/k and m, for positive integers k and m, of the T_{delta, m} (if alpha(a) lies in Reg then |Omega|, |B x Omega| >= 2 delta on it for some delta, and the
backward orbit, being eventually in D and converging to alpha(a), is eventually in R_delta; the converse is clear). Let V' := V_alpha minus
the union of the basins, a Borel invariant set, and suppose |V'| > 0. Then |V' cap T_{delta, m}| > 0 for some delta, m; choose a compact
E_1 in it of positive measure and put E_0 := psi_m(E_1): compact, of positive measure, contained in V', with psi_t E_0 contained in
R_delta for all t >= 0. Let C := cl(union over t >= 0 of psi_t E_0): compact, contained in R_delta, forward invariant, of positive
measure. By Lemma D5.10 its full invariant part K_C contains W^wu(q) for some q; by Lemma D5.6, G := cl W^wu(q) is a nonempty
u-saturated compact invariant subset of K_C, and Lemma D5.8 gives A in calA with A contained in C. A is contained in the closure of
the union of the psi_t E_0, so the open set Bas(A) contains psi_t e for some t >= 0 and e in E_0; basins are psi-invariant, so e lies
in Bas(A), contradicting e in V'. Hence |V'| = 0. The properties in (alpha*) are Theorem D1(b), (c), (d); the trichotomy is
Theorem D5.4 with case (alpha) refined. QED

Corollary D5.12 (shape of a basin) [CO9 Corollary 12.6]. For A in calA:
 (i) Bas(A) is the union of the complete vortex lines through the points of A;
 (ii) B, Omega and B x Omega have no zero on Bas(A);
 (iii) Bas(A) is an open invariant set of infinite volume (vol(phi_s V) = e^{3cs} vol V for invariant V excludes 0 < vol < infinity);
 (iv) vol(A) = 0.
Proof of (i). If z is in Bas(A), then psi_{t_1} z lies in the neighbourhood O of Lemma D5.7 for some t_1, so psi_{t_1} z = chi_tau w
with w in A; Lemma D5.5 with t = -t_1 gives z = phi_{t_1} chi_tau w = chi_{e^{(1+c)t_1} tau}(phi_{t_1} w) with phi_{t_1} w in A.
Conversely, for x in A and any tau, Lemma D5.5 gives dist(psi_t chi_tau x, psi_t x) -> 0, so chi_tau x is in Bas(A). (ii) The three
sets are closed and invariant (Lemma D5.2), so a point of one of them has its backward limit set inside it, while alpha(z) lies in
A, contained in Reg. (iv) vol(A) = vol(psi_t A) = e^{-3ct} vol(A). QED
(Also cited from [A158] and not proved here: both half vortex lines through every point of A leave every compact trapping region of A. Lemma D5.13 below [A118] is proved here.)

Lemma D5.13 (no regular compact invariant set contains a plaque of a span(B, Omega) leaf) [CO9 Lemma 12.7, A118]. Let L be a
compact invariant set contained in Reg. Then L contains no plaque Pi(z) := {phi_s chi_tau z : |s|, |tau| < eta}, eta > 0.
Proof. L is hyperbolic (Lemma D5.3). Suppose Pi(z) is contained in L. Every w in Pi(z) has a local stable curve W^s_eps(w) for phi
(tangent to E^s, uniform size, continuous in w, with points converging to the forward orbit of w). The map (w, r) -> (point of
W^s_eps(w) at parameter r) on Pi(z) x (-eps', eps') is continuous and injective for small eta, eps' (local product structure: distinct
points of a center-unstable plaque have disjoint local stable curves), so by invariance of domain its image is a neighbourhood of z;
every point of it has bounded forward orbit, so Lambda would have interior, contradicting |Lambda| = 0 (F5). QED
Consequence: for A in calA and a periodic point p in A, the vortex line through p (invariant under phi_T up to the rescaling
tau -> e^{(1+c)T} tau) is unbounded or its closure leaves Reg.

Remarks on D5. (i) The Euler content used is the Cauchy transport of Omega = curl U (F4), the exact covector law (Lemma D5.1), and,
for the periodic-orbit facts in (alpha*), the Bernoulli identity. (ii) Excluding case (alpha*) is a question about a single rigid
object: a transitive hyperbolic attractor A of the backward flow in Reg, with strong stable foliation given by the vortex lines,
weak stable foliation given by the leaves of the integrable plane field span(B, Omega) (on which X^flat is exact with potential
-H/(1-2c), and U^flat with potential -H/(1-2c) - c|y|^2/2 [A059]), the covector B x Omega expanded by exactly e^{(1-2c)t} on
unstable arcs, constant exponents (1-2c, 0, -(1+c)), topological entropy exactly 1 - 2c on A, and all periodic orbits retrograde
with zero circulation. The entropy statement for an individual attractor is NOT a consequence of Theorem D4 (a bound on the whole
core) plus Ruelle; its proof [A085; as summarized in the accompanying artifacts section 7] is: with alpha^flat = (B x Omega)^flat and a unit
vector e^u_x in E^u_psi(x), g(x) := |alpha^flat_x(e^u_x)| is continuous and bounded away from zero on A, and Lemma D5.1 gives the exact
unstable Jacobian J^u_t(x) = e^{(1-2c)t} g(x)/g(psi_t x), so the geometric potential q^u := -(d/dt) log J^u_t|_{t=0} integrates to
-(1-2c) against every flow-invariant probability on A; for a C^2 basic attracting flow the pressure of q^u vanishes (Bowen and
Ruelle, Invent. Math. 29 (1975), Proposition 4.4(b), stated for C^2 basic sets, in particular attractors, of flows on a compact manifold; it is applied after the field is cut off outside a compact region and compactified to S^3 as in D4 Step 2), so the variational principle gives 0 = P(q^u) = h_top(psi_1|A) - (1-2c). Such an object is kinematically realizable with a divergence-free bracket eigenfield W along its
strong stable direction, for every 0 < c < 1/2 and every omega [A242, A243, A246; item 6 of this report]; W is not curl U there,
and whether the actual coupling W = curl U allows it is the open question. The Lorenz-type singular case (beta) is kinematically realizable as well, for
2(2 - sqrt 2)/(5 - sqrt 2) < c < 1/2 (a range containing 2/5 < c < 1/2) and every omega: a transitive singular-hyperbolic
backward attractor that contains a zero of B and nonstationary orbits, with W nowhere zero near it, is the backward limit set of
Lebesgue-almost every point of a trapping genus-two handlebody [A066, A121, A252, A253; item 6 of this report]. Both
realizations are cited from the audit records; they are not proved in this section and no proof in this section uses them. So excluding
(alpha*) and (beta) requires the coupling Omega = curl U. (iii) If calA is empty, in particular when omega = 0,
Lebesgue-almost every vortical point is in case (beta) or (gamma).

#### D6. Zeros of B in nonpoint vortical backward limit sets are real saddles of Lorenz type

Theorem D6 (0 < c < 1/2, every omega) [A147, A159]. Assume H0, H1'. Let K = alpha(a) be the backward limit set of a point a,
assume K is not a single point and Omega is nowhere zero on K (so a is vortical and K is contained in Z := {Omega != 0}), and
let p in K be a zero of B. (The hypothesis that K is a backward LIMIT SET, not merely a compact invariant set, is essential:
the proof uses the late entrances of the orbit of a toward p [A232].) Then the spectrum of DB(p) is real,
        spec DB(p) = {1+c, lambda_2, lambda_3},     lambda_3 < 0 <= lambda_2,     lambda_2 + lambda_3 = 2c - 1,
with Omega(p) the eigenvector of 1+c. No connecting orbit converging to p is assumed, and no upper bound on lambda_2 is claimed.
For the backward flow the eigenvalues at p are -(1+c) (along the vortex line through p), -lambda_2 <= 0 and
-lambda_3 = lambda_2 + 1 - 2c > 0: a saddle (with a zero eigenvalue, hence not hyperbolic, when lambda_2 = 0) with the Lorenz expanding condition -lambda_3 > lambda_2, which is equivalent to
c < 1/2; the vortex line is the strongest stable direction iff lambda_2 < 1 + c.

Lemma D6.1 (regular points of a compact vortical invariant set are nondegenerate) [A130]. Let K be compact, invariant,
with |Omega| >= delta > 0 on K. If x in K, B(x) != 0 and Omega(x) = lambda_0 B(x), then applying (F4), lambda_0 B(phi_s x) =
e^{(1+c)s} Omega(phi_s x), so |Omega(phi_s x)| <= |lambda_0| sup_K |B| e^{-(1+c)s} -> 0 along an orbit that stays in K: contradiction.
Hence Omega x B != 0 at every regular point of K. In particular the vortex line through a zero p of B in K, on which
B(gamma_p(tau)) = (1+c) tau Omega(gamma_p(tau)) [A106], meets K only at p.
(The identity: by (F4), phi_s(gamma_p(tau)) is an integral curve of e^{(1+c)s} Omega through phi_s(p) = p, so it equals
gamma_p(e^{(1+c)s} tau), and differentiating in s at s = 0 gives B(gamma_p(tau)) = (1+c) tau Omega(gamma_p(tau)). The vortex
line through p is complete: the same conjugacy extends its domain from |tau| < delta to |tau| < delta e^{(1+c)s} for every s.)

Lemma D6.2 (entrance lemma) [A159]. Let Y be a C^1 vector field, p a hyperbolic zero of Y and x(t) a precompact Y-orbit whose
omega-limit set K is not a single point and meets the stable manifold W^s_Y(p) at most in p. Then p is not in K.
Proof. Choose a closed ball D_p around p so small that every forward orbit that stays in D_p for all positive times lies in the
local stable manifold (local stable manifold theorem for the hyperbolic zero p), and so that K has a point outside D_p (K is not
{p}). If p is in K, the orbit has arbitrarily late visits close to p and arbitrarily late visits outside D_p; choose t_n -> infinity
with x(t_n) -> p and, before each t_n, a visit outside D_p later than n; let s_n be the last entry time into D_p before t_n, so
x(s_n) is on the boundary of D_p, s_n -> infinity and x([s_n, t_n]) stays in D_p. A Lipschitz bound |Y(z)| <= L|z - p| on D_p gives
|x(t_n) - p| >= radius(D_p) e^{-L(t_n - s_n)}, so t_n - s_n -> infinity. Passing to a subsequence, x(s_n) -> z with z on the
boundary of D_p, z != p, and z in K (since s_n -> infinity). By continuous dependence and the diverging durations, the forward
orbit of z stays in D_p for all t >= 0, so z lies in W^s_Y(p), contradicting W^s_Y(p) intersected with K = {p}. QED

Proof of Theorem D6. At the vortical zero p, (F3) gives DB(p) Omega(p) = (1+c) Omega(p), and the two remaining eigenvalues sum
