to 3c - (1+c) = 2c - 1 < 0. Suppose both had negative real parts. Then p is a hyperbolic zero of Y := -B with a one-dimensional
stable manifold tangent to Omega(p); the vortex line through p is an invariant curve tangent to Omega(p) whose points converge to
p under the backward flow (Lemma D6.1's identity: psi_t gamma_p(tau) = gamma_p(e^{-(1+c)t} tau)), so by uniqueness of the stable
manifold it IS the local stable manifold of p for Y, and by Lemma D6.1 it meets K only at p. Lemma D6.2, applied to the backward
orbit of a (whose omega-limit set for Y is K) then excludes p from the nonsingleton limit set K: a contradiction. Hence one of the two remaining eigenvalues has nonnegative real part; since they sum to 2c - 1 < 0 they cannot
form a complex pair (equal real parts would both be negative), so they are real, lambda_3 < 0 <= lambda_2. The backward reading
and the expanding condition -lambda_3 - lambda_2 = 1 - 2c > 0 are arithmetic. QED

Remarks. (i) The hypothesis "Omega nowhere zero on K" is essential and is stated explicitly: it supplies Lemma D6.1, i.e. that
the vortex line through p meets K only at p. (ii) Consequently a zero with a complex pair or with two negative eigenvalues cannot belong to any nonsingleton backward
limit set on which Omega is nowhere zero; nothing is claimed for arbitrary compact invariant sets. (iii) The theorem does not give lambda_2 < 1 + c; exact affine profiles (e.g. omega = 1, U = (2x - y, x - 3y, z),
spectrum {c+2, c-3, c+1} [A057]) show the vortex direction can be the weaker stable one, and the degenerate case lambda_2 = 0
occurs along lines of zeros (U = diag(-c, c-1, 1) y + omega J y [A072]). These affine examples are local models only: they
are not decaying and violate H1', and the line-of-zeros example is vortical only for omega != 0 (its vorticity is 2 omega e_3). (iv) Cited consequence, proved in the audit record [A155, A248] and not in this section (the sketch below is not a proof):
let Gamma be a finite network of hyperbolic vortical zeros of B and connecting orbits inside Z.
Every backward orbit whose limit set is contained in Gamma converges to one of the nodes, and the set of such initial points is
null. So no nonsingleton Gamma is a backward limit set; a one-node network is a limit (for instance of the zero itself). Proof
sketch: the vortex-line quotient makes the backward flow a planar flow near the network, and a passage near a saddle of
Theorem D6 obeys the exact law |g'(r)| = exp((1-2c) T(r)) in the flux coordinate r, with T(r) -> infinity as r -> 0; the
expansion inequality follows by integration. The full proof is in the audit record [A155] and is not part of this section.

#### 2C.1 Statement and dependency map

##### 2C.1.1 Setting and notation

Fix 0 < c < 1/2 and omega in R. J(y1,y2,y3) = (-y2,y1,0), A = cI - omega J, R(y) = Jy. The profile equation is

    (1-c)U + [(cI - omega J)y + U].grad U + omega J U + grad P = 0,    div U = 0.     (E)

- B = Ay + U; Omega = curl U (W in the sources); d = 3c; a = 1-2c; kappa = 1+c. Then a > 0 and kappa > d.
- Phi_t is the flow of B; Psi_t = Phi_(-t) is the flow of -B; Gamma_tau is the local flow of Omega.
- alpha = (B x Omega).dy, the one-form v -> det(B, Omega, v).
- O = {Omega != 0}, Z = {Omega = 0}.
- "Uniformly sublinear" means |U(y)|/|y| -> 0 as |y| -> infinity.
- Q is a closed ball of radius R1 centered at 0, admissible in the sense of Lemma 3; K = intersection_(t>=0) Psi_t(Q).
- Leb is Lebesgue measure on R^3. For a curve, lambda is normalized arclength and J_g is the arclength Jacobian of g
  along the curve.
- The continuous-time basin of a Borel probability nu on R^3 is the set Basin(nu) of x with
  (1/T) int_0^T phi(Psi_t x) dt -> int phi dnu for every bounded continuous phi on R^3.

##### 2C.1.2 Theorem C (PROVED: A308, with A207 and A223)

Hypotheses: U is C-infinity on R^3, P is C^1, (E) holds, U is uniformly sublinear, 0 < c < 1/2, omega is arbitrary
real. Fix an admissible Q. Then there is an at most countable family {nu_i} with the following properties.

1. Each nu_i is a Borel probability supported in K, invariant and ergodic for the whole flow Psi.
2. nu_i(B != 0, Omega != 0) = 1. The Lyapunov spectrum of Psi under nu_i is (1-2c, 0, -(1+c)), all simple. The zero
   direction is R B and the stable direction is R Omega. h_(nu_i)(Psi_1) = 1-2c.
3. The conditional measures of nu_i on its full one-dimensional Pesin unstable plaques are absolutely continuous with
   respect to arclength.
4. Basin(nu_i) is Borel, has positive volume and lies in O. The basins are pairwise disjoint and their union covers
   Leb-almost every point of O. If U is nonconstant then O is nonempty and the family is nonempty.
5. (A207) On nu_i-almost every local unstable plaque the conditional density with respect to arclength is C A, where
   A(x) = |alpha_x(e^u(x))|, e^u is a unit unstable tangent, and C > 0 is a normalizing constant that may depend on
   the plaque. Equivalently the density is constant with respect to the length element |alpha| on the plaque.
6. (A223) There is a unique maximal open set D_i contained in O with Basin(nu_i) contained in D_i,
   Leb(D_i minus Basin(nu_i)) = 0 and nu_i(D_i) = 1. D_i is invariant under every Psi_t and locally saturated by the
   Omega flow. Distinct D_i are disjoint, each D_i (= D_(nu_i)) has infinite volume, and their union covers O up to a
   null set.

Not asserted (A308 section 1 and section 8): no C^2 or fixed finite-r theorem (unconditional C^2 coverage is OPEN; the
finite-r results in 2C.2.9 are CONDITIONAL); no finiteness of the family, uniqueness, uniform hyperbolicity or
classification of supports; the supports may meet {B = 0} or {Omega = 0}; no time-one ergodicity; no helicity sign;
no Euler nonexistence.

##### 2C.1.3 Theorem C' (abstract form, A308 section 1)

Let B, W be C-infinity vector fields on R^3, B complete in both time directions, with

    div B = d > 0 (constant),    [B, W] = -kappa W,    kappa > d,

and b0, R0 > 0 with B(y).y >= b0 |y|^2 for |y| >= R0. Let Psi be the flow of -B, O = {W != 0}, Q the closed ball of
any radius R1 > R0, K its core. Then conclusions 1 to 4 of Theorem C hold with spectrum (kappa-d, 0, -kappa), entropy
kappa-d, Omega replaced by W, and "U nonconstant" replaced by "W not identically zero".

Bracket convention: [X, Y] = (X.grad)Y - (Y.grad)X.

#### 2C.2 Lemmas and proofs

##### 2C.2.1 Identities, trapping, Liouville, basins

**Lemma 1 (profile identities).** Let U be C^2 with (E). Then

    (a) div B = 3c;
    (b) Omega + (B.grad)Omega + omega J Omega - (Omega.grad)U = 0;
    (c) [B, Omega] = -(1+c) Omega;
    (d) curl(B x Omega) = a Omega, hence d alpha = a i_Omega vol;
    (e) alpha(B) = alpha(Omega) = 0, L_Omega alpha = 0, L_B alpha = -a alpha, Psi_t^* alpha = exp(at) alpha;
    (f) where B x Omega != 0, ker alpha = span(B, Omega).

Proof. (a) tr A = 3c, tr J = 0, div U = 0. For (b): Ay = cy - omega R, and DR = J gives [R, U] = (R.grad)U - JU.
Hence (B.grad)U + omega JU = (U.grad)U + c(y.grad)U - omega [R, U], and (E) reads

    (1-c)U + (U.grad)U + c(y.grad)U - omega [R, U] + grad P = 0.

Take curls. curl((U.grad)U) = (U.grad)Omega - (Omega.grad)U (write (U.grad)U = grad(|U|^2/2) - U x Omega and use
div U = div Omega = 0); curl((y.grad)U) = Omega + (y.grad)Omega (differentiate y_k d_k U_j); curl [R, U] = [R, Omega],
because the flow of R is the rotation exp(tJ), curl commutes with pullback by rotations, and [R, .] is the Lie
derivative along R; curl grad P = 0 (P is C^1 and grad P = -(rest) is C^1, so curl grad P = 0 in the distributional
and classical sense). Summing,

    Omega + (U.grad)Omega - (Omega.grad)U + c(y.grad)Omega - omega [R, Omega] = 0,

which equals (b) after expanding (B.grad)Omega + omega J Omega with [R, Omega] = (R.grad)Omega - J Omega.
(c) (Omega.grad)B = A Omega + (Omega.grad)U = c Omega - omega J Omega + (Omega.grad)U, so by (b)
[B, Omega] = (B.grad)Omega - (Omega.grad)B = -Omega - c Omega.
(d) curl(B x Omega) = B div Omega - Omega div B + (Omega.grad)B - (B.grad)Omega = -3c Omega - [B, Omega]
= (1-2c) Omega. For a C^1 field V, d(V.dy) = i_(curl V) vol; alpha is C^1 since U is C^2.
(e) alpha(B) = det(B, Omega, B) = 0, alpha(Omega) = 0. Cartan: L_Omega alpha = i_Omega d alpha + d(alpha(Omega)) =
a i_Omega i_Omega vol = 0, and L_B alpha = a i_B i_Omega vol = a vol(Omega, B, .) = -a alpha. Since Psi is the flow
of -B, (d/dt) Psi_t^* alpha = Psi_t^*(L_(-B) alpha) = a Psi_t^* alpha, so Psi_t^* alpha = exp(at) alpha.
(f) alpha_x(v) = (B x Omega).v vanishes exactly on span(B, Omega) when B x Omega != 0. QED

**Lemma 2 (transport).** Let B be C^1 and complete and W be C^1 with [B, W] = -kappa W and div B = d. Then for all real t

    D Psi_t(x) W(x) = exp(-kappa t) W(Psi_t x),   D Psi_t(x) B(x) = B(Psi_t x),   det D Psi_t(x) = exp(-dt).

Consequently {W != 0}, {W = 0}, {B = 0} and {B != 0} are invariant under every Psi_t.

Proof. Put V1(s) = D Phi_s(x) W(x) and V2(s) = exp(kappa s) W(Phi_s x). V1' = DB(Phi_s x) V1. Using
(B.grad)W = (W.grad)B - kappa W, V2' = exp(kappa s)[kappa W + (B.grad)W](Phi_s x) = DB(Phi_s x) V2. Both solve the
same linear ODE with V(0) = W(x), so V1 = V2 by uniqueness. Replace s by -t. The same argument with W = B and kappa = 0
gives the second identity. Liouville's formula gives det D Phi_s = exp(int_0^s div B) = exp(ds). Invertibility of
D Psi_t gives the invariance. QED

**Lemma 3 (trapping, core, cutoff map).** Let U be C^1 and uniformly sublinear, B = Ay + U.

(a) There is R0 with B(y).y >= (c/2)|y|^2 for |y| >= R0, and B has at most linear growth; B is complete.
(b) Call Q (radius R1) admissible when R1 > R0 for an R0 as in (a); in Theorem C' admissibility is R1 > R0 for the
given R0. Then Psi_t(Q) is contained in int Q for every t > 0, and every bounded set S satisfies
Psi_t(S) contained in int Q for all t >= T_S.
(c) K is nonempty, compact, contained in int Q, and Psi_t(K) = K for all real t. Every open V containing K contains
Psi_T(Q) for some T. Moreover intersection_n Psi_(np)(Q) = K for every integer p >= 1.
(d) If U is C-infinity, there is a C-infinity diffeomorphism f of R^3, equal to the identity outside a compact set,
with f^n = Psi_n together with all derivatives on Q for n >= 0 and on K for all integers n. All derivatives of f of
positive order and D f^(-1) are bounded.
(e) There is a closed Riemannian 3-manifold (S^3) containing a neighbourhood of Q isometrically, to which f extends as a
C-infinity diffeomorphism, and on which the flow of -rho B extends.

Proof. (a) (Ay).y = c|y|^2 - omega (Jy).y = c|y|^2. Choose R0 with |U(y)| <= (c/2)|y| for |y| >= R0; then
B(y).y >= c|y|^2 - (c/2)|y|^2. Also |B(y)| <= C1(1 + |y|) for all y. B is locally Lipschitz, so solutions exist locally,
and Gronwall gives |x(t)| <= (|x(0)| + C1|t|) exp(C1|t|), which excludes blow-up in either time direction.
(b) For |Psi_t y| >= R0, (d/dt)|Psi_t y|^2 = -2 B.y <= -c|Psi_t y|^2, so (d/dt) log|Psi_t y| <= -c/2 =: -b0.
On the sphere |y| = R1 the derivative of |Psi_t y|^2 is negative. If y is in Q and Psi_t y is on the sphere for some
t > 0, with Psi_s y in Q for s in [0, t], then |Psi_s y| > R1 for s slightly less than t, a contradiction; so
Psi_t(Q) is in int Q for t > 0. If S lies in the ball of radius R, the log-derivative bound brings each point of S into
Q by time max(log(R/R1), 0)/b0, and one more unit of time puts it in Psi_1(Q), a compact subset of int Q.
(c) The sets Psi_t(Q) decrease in t (Psi_(t-s)(Q) is in Q), are compact and nonempty, so K is nonempty compact and
K is in Psi_1(Q), inside int Q. For s >= 0, Psi_s(K) = intersection_t Psi_(t+s)(Q) = K by monotonicity; apply Psi_(-s)
for negative times. If V is open and contains K, the compact sets Psi_n(Q) minus V decrease with empty intersection,
so one is empty. Monotonicity gives the statement for multiples of p.
(d) Choose a C-infinity rho with compact support, 0 <= rho <= 1, radial and nonincreasing in |y|, rho = 1 on a
neighbourhood of Q. The field -rho B is
C-infinity with compact support, so its flow is global; f is its time-one map, the identity outside supp rho. Psi
orbits starting in Q stay in Q for positive time, where the fields agree on a neighbourhood, so f^n = Psi_n with all
derivatives on Q. On K, orbits stay in K in both time directions. Boundedness: f is the identity outside a compact set.
(e) Stereographic projection identifies R^3 with S^3 minus a point. The field -rho B vanishes near infinity and extends
by zero. A metric phi g_euc + (1-phi) g_round, with phi = 1 near supp rho and phi supported in a larger ball, is
positive definite. QED

Remark. A308 does not mention (e); A216 needs a closed manifold and A257 a compact one, and A417 section 6 and
A431 section 6 state the extension explicitly. See 2C.4, point 3.

**Lemma 4 (harmonic Liouville).** If U is C^2, div U = 0, curl U = 0 on R^3 and U is uniformly sublinear, then U is
constant. Hence a nonconstant U in Theorem C has O nonempty and open, so Leb(O) > 0.

Proof. Delta U = grad div U - curl curl U = 0, so each component u = U_j is harmonic, and so is d_i u. By the mean value
property for d_i u on the ball B(x0, R) and the divergence theorem,
d_i u(x0) = |B_R|^(-1) int_(boundary B_R) u nu_i dS, so |d_i u(x0)| <= (3/R) max over the sphere of |u|. Given eps > 0
there is C_eps with |U(x)| <= C_eps + eps|x|. Then |d_i u(x0)| <= 3(C_eps + eps(|x0| + R))/R, which tends to 3 eps as
R -> infinity. Since eps is arbitrary, DU = 0. QED

**Lemma 5 (Omega-shift identity and Borel basins).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem C' (or Theorem C):

(a) There is tau0 > 0 with Gamma_tau x defined for x in Q and |tau| <= tau0, staying in a compact neighbourhood N of Q,
and for x in Q, r >= 0, |tau| <= tau0,

    Psi_r Gamma_tau x = Gamma_(tau exp(-kappa r)) Psi_r x,
    |Psi_r Gamma_tau x - Psi_r x| <= (max_N |W|) |tau| exp(-kappa r).

(b) If x is in Q and in Basin(nu), then Gamma_tau x (|tau| <= tau0) and Psi_s x (every real s) belong to Basin(nu)
(they need not lie in Q). Basin(nu) is invariant under every Psi_s.
(c) If nu is supported in Q, Basin(nu) equals the set of x for which the integer-time averages
(1/n) int_0^n phi_k(Psi_t x) dt converge to int phi_k dnu for each k, where {phi_k} is any countable family of bounded
continuous functions on R^3 whose restrictions are dense in C(Q). Such families exist, and Basin(nu) is Borel.

Proof. (a) W is C^1, so its local flow exists for a uniform time on a compact neighbourhood. Put
y(tau) = Psi_r Gamma_tau x and z(tau) = Gamma_(tau exp(-kappa r)) Psi_r x. By Lemma 2,
y'(tau) = D Psi_r W(Gamma_tau x) = exp(-kappa r) W(y(tau)), and z'(tau) = exp(-kappa r) W(z(tau)), with
y(0) = z(0) = Psi_r x. Psi_r x is in Q, so z is defined for |tau| <= tau0, and y is defined by completeness of B.
Uniqueness gives y = z, and the displacement bound integrates |z'|.
(b) Both forward orbits stay in a compact set (N, then Q after a uniform time by Lemma 3(b)). A bounded continuous phi
is uniformly continuous there, and |phi(Psi_t Gamma_tau x) - phi(Psi_t x)| -> 0 by (a), so the Cesaro averages have
the same limit. A time shift by s changes the average over [0, T] by at most 2|s| sup|phi|/T.
(c) C(Q) is separable; take a countable dense set and extend each element by Tietze's theorem to a bounded continuous
function on R^3. Every orbit is in Q after a time T_x (Lemma 3(b)). Given bounded continuous phi and eps > 0, choose
phi_k with sup_Q |phi - phi_k| <= eps; for t >= T_x the integrands differ by at most eps, and int phi dnu and
int phi_k dnu differ by at most eps, so convergence for all phi_k implies convergence for phi. Real T can be replaced
by integers n = floor(T), since the averages differ by at most 2 sup|phi|/n. Each
x -> (1/n) int_0^n phi_k(Psi_t x) dt is continuous (continuity of the flow, dominated convergence), so Basin(nu) is a
countable intersection of countable unions of countable intersections of closed sets. QED

**Lemma 6 (volume to arc, A308 section 2).** Under Theorem C' with f from Lemma 3(d), let G be a measurable subset of
O intersect int Q with Leb(G) > 0, and lambda_0 = (kappa-d)/2. There are an open box V with closure in O intersect
int Q, a coordinate vector e_i, a straight compact segment D0 contained in closure(V) parallel to e_i, and a measurable G0
contained in D0 intersect G of positive length, such that for every x in G0

    limsup_(N->infinity) N^(-1) log J_(f^N)(x) >= lambda_0,    J_(f^N)(x) = |D f^N(x) e_i|.

Proof. Let Mw = max_Q |W| and x in O intersect Q. Let s1 >= s2 >= s3 be the singular values of D Psi_t(x), t >= 0.
By Lemma 2, s3 <= |D Psi_t W(x)|/|W(x)| = exp(-kappa t)|W(Psi_t x)|/|W(x)| <= exp(-kappa t) Mw/|W(x)|, and
s1 s2 s3 = exp(-dt). Hence s1^2 >= s1 s2 >= exp((kappa-d)t)|W(x)|/Mw, i.e.

    ||D Psi_t(x)|| >= exp((kappa-d)t/2) (|W(x)|/Mw)^(1/2).

For a 3x3 matrix T and unit v, |Tv| <= sum_i |v_i||T e_i| <= sqrt(3) max_i |T e_i|. For each N some i(N) has
|D f^N(x) e_(i(N))| >= ||D f^N(x)||/sqrt(3) (here f^N = Psi_N on Q); some i occurs for infinitely many N, so x lies in
G^i = {x in G: limsup N^(-1) log|D f^N(x) e_i| >= lambda_0}. These sets are measurable (limsup of continuous
functions) and cover G, so one has positive volume. Cover the open set O intersect int Q by countably many open boxes
with rational corners and closures in it; one box V has Leb(G^i intersect V) > 0. By Fubini, for almost every
transverse coordinate the slice of G^i intersect V along e_i is measurable, and for a positive-measure set of
transverse coordinates it has positive length. Take one such line: D0 is the closure of its intersection with V,
a compact segment in closure(V), contained in O intersect int Q, and G0 is the slice. QED

The arc D0 lies in O and in int Q, and O is invariant (Lemma 2), so every forward image of D0 lies in O intersect Q.

##### 2C.2.2 The affine curve tree (A305)

Setting for Lemmas 7 to 9. r >= 2 is an integer; g: R^m -> R^m is a C^r diffeomorphism with bounded derivatives of
orders 1 to r and bounded D g^(-1); L_+ = sup||Dg||, L_- = sup||Dg^(-1)||, Mg = max(2, L_+, L_-) (A305 calls it M).
Fix 0 < eps <= 1 with eps^(j-1) sup||D^j g|| <= L_+ for 2 <= j <= r. Put eta = 1/100 and D = 50/49 = 1/(1-2 eta).
Curves are regular embedded C^r maps gamma: [-1,1] -> R^m with s = s(gamma) = sup|gamma'|. gamma is bounded if
sup|gamma^(j)| <= eta s for 2 <= j <= r, small if moreover s <= eps. An image curve is large if its maximum speed is at
least eps/3, nonlarge otherwise. (In A305 every output is small; the counted class is the nonlarge outputs. See
2C.4, point 1.)

**Lemma 7 (bounded curves).** Let gamma be bounded.
(a) (1-2 eta)s <= |gamma'(t)| <= s, so max|gamma'|/min|gamma'| <= D.
(b) If theta(u) = u0 + bu maps [-1,1] into [-1,1] with 0 < b <= 1-2 eta, then gamma o theta is bounded, and small if
gamma is small. In particular slopes b <= 1/100 preserve both properties.
(c) If alpha and beta = g^n o alpha are both bounded, the ratio |beta'|/|alpha'| (the arclength Jacobian of g^n along
alpha) has max/min at most D^2 < 2.

Proof. (a) Take t0 with |gamma'(t0)| = s. |gamma'(t) - gamma'(t0)| <= 2 sup|gamma''| <= 2 eta s.
(b) (gamma o theta)^(j) = b^j gamma^(j) o theta, so its sup is at most b^j eta s, while its maximum speed is at least
b(1-2 eta)s by (a). The ratio is at most eta b^(j-1)/(1-2 eta) <= eta, as b^(j-1) <= b <= 1-2 eta for j >= 2. The
maximum speed is at most bs <= s.
(c) max(|beta'|/|alpha'|)/min(|beta'|/|alpha'|) <= (max|beta'|/min|beta'|)(max|alpha'|/min|alpha'|) <= D^2, and
D^2 = 2500/2401 < 1.042. QED

**Lemma 8 (one step).** There are constants A_r, B_r, C_r depending only on r (not on m, g or eps) such that every small
bounded gamma has a partition of [-1,1] into finitely many closed intervals I_i, meeting only at endpoints, with affine
normalizations theta_i: [-1,1] -> I_i of slope at most 1/100, such that each g o gamma o theta_i is small and bounded,
and:
(i) every large output has length in (eps/2, 2 eps];
(ii) there are at most C_r Mg^(3/(r-1)) nonlarge outputs;
(iii) for each integer l, fewer than 16 exp(l) large intervals contain a point where floor(log J_g) = l, J_g being the
arclength Jacobian of g along gamma;
(iv) on each interval, J_g has max/min at most D^2.

Proof. Step 1 (chain rule). Let F = g o gamma. By the Faa di Bruno formula F^(r) is a sum, with a number A_r of terms
depending only on r, of terms D^j g(gamma)[gamma^(k1), ..., gamma^(kj)] with k1 + ... + kj = r, ki >= 1. Each
|gamma^(k)| <= s. For j >= 2 the term is at most sup||D^j g|| s^j <= L_+ eps^(-(j-1)) s^j <= L_+ s, using s <= eps; for
j = 1 it is at most L_+ eta s. Also |F'| >= |gamma'|/L_- >= (1-2 eta)s/L_- and |F'| <= L_+ s. Hence

    sup|F^(r)| <= A_r L_+ s,  sup|F^(r)|/min|F'| <= D A_r Mg^2,  max|F'|/min|F'| <= D Mg^2.

Step 2 (equal pieces). Fix delta_r <= 1/100 depending only on r (A305 leaves its value free; any fixed value works).
Let N = ceil((D A_r Mg^2/delta_r)^(1/(r-1))) and cut [-1,1] into N equal intervals; F_j is F composed with the affine
map of slope 1/N onto the j-th piece. With m_j = min|F_j'|, sup|F_j^(r)| = N^(-r) sup_piece|F^(r)| and
m_j = N^(-1) min_piece|F'|, so sup|F_j^(r)| <= delta_r m_j. Let P_j be the vector Taylor polynomial of F_j' at 0 of
degree r-2. The integral remainder gives sup_[-1,1] |F_j' - P_j| <= delta_r m_j/(r-1)!.
Step 3 (dyadic bands). From Step 2, 0.99 m_j <= |P_j| <= (D Mg^2 + 0.01)m_j. For each integer k with
m_j/2 <= 2^k m_j <= 4 Mg^2 m_j, cut at the real roots of the scalar polynomial |P_j|^2 - (2^k m_j)^2, of degree at most
2(r-2); an identically vanishing polynomial gives no cuts, and for r = 2 no cuts are needed (P_j is constant). There are
O(1 + log Mg) values of k, so each piece splits into O_r(1 + log Mg) closed intervals. These thresholds bracket the range
of |P_j|, so on each closed interval |P_j| stays in one band [2^k m_j, 2^(k+1) m_j], and with mn = min|P_j| there,
0.01 m_j <= mn/99 and max|F_j'|/min|F_j'| <= (2 + 1/99)/(1 - 1/99) = 199/98 < 4.
Step 4 (normalize). Rescale one such interval affinely to [-1,1], obtaining G = F o (affine). Rescaling by slope b
multiplies the r-th derivative by b^r and the first by b, so sup|G^(r)| <= delta_r min|G'| and max|G'| <= 4 min|G'|.
Step 5 (interpolation). For vector-valued G and each x in [-1,1], pick [x, x+1] or [x-1, x] inside [-1,1] and r-1
equally spaced points x_i in it. Taylor's theorem for G' at x gives G'(x_i) = sum_(k<=r-2) G^(k+1)(x) h_i^k/k! + R_i with
|R_i| <= sup|G^(r)|. The (r-1)x(r-1) Vandermonde-type matrix (h_i^k/k!) is fixed (two choices) and invertible, with
scalar entries, so by the triangle inequality

    max_(2<=j<=r) sup|G^(j)| <= B_r (sup|G'| + sup|G^(r)|),

B_r independent of the dimension; for r = 2 this is trivial. Hence sup|G^(j)| <= B_r(4 + delta_r) min|G'| <= 5 B_r min|G'|.
Step 6 (bounded pieces). Cut G into K_r equal pieces, K_r >= 100 and 5 B_r/K_r <= eta. A piece G_i has
sup|G_i^(j)|/sup|G_i'| <= K_r^(-(j-1)) 5 B_r <= eta, so it is bounded. The composed slope is at most
(1/N)(1)(1/K_r) <= 1/100. The number of these intermediate pieces is at most
N O_r(1 + log Mg) K_r <= C'_r Mg^(2/(r-1))(1 + log Mg) <= C_r Mg^(3/(r-1)), using 1 + log Mg <= c_r Mg^(1/(r-1)) for
Mg >= 2. This count is made before speed normalization.
Step 7 (speed normalization). Let v be the maximum speed of an intermediate piece. If v <= eps keep it. If v > eps cut it
into ceil(v/eps) >= 2 equal pieces, slope at most 1/2, so they are bounded by Lemma 7(b). Each has maximum speed at
most v/ceil(v/eps) <= eps and at least (1-2 eta) v/ceil(v/eps) > (1-2 eta)eps v/(v + eps) > (1-2 eta)eps/2 = 0.49 eps >
eps/3: all are large. Each uncut piece contributes at most one nonlarge output. This proves (ii).
Step 8 (lengths). A large output has minimum speed at least (1-2 eta)eps/3 by Lemma 7(a), so length >=
2(0.98)eps/3 > eps/2, and length <= 2 eps.
Step 9 (bins). Input and output are bounded, so Lemma 7(c) gives (iv). If a large interval contains a point with
floor(log J_g) = l, then J_g <= D^2 exp(l+1) on it. The inputs have disjoint interiors and total length at most
length(gamma) <= 2 eps, so the outputs of these intervals have total length at most 2 eps D^2 exp(l+1). Each has length >
eps/2, so their number is less than 4 D^2 e exp(l) < 11.4 exp(l) < 16 exp(l). QED

**Lemma 9 (iteration and compactness).** Let gamma_0 be a small bounded large curve. Applying Lemma 8 to each output
recursively gives nested finite interval partitions P^n of [-1,1] (depth-n atoms). For a depth-n atom P and
0 <= k <= n, let the time-k curve of P be g^k o gamma_0 restricted to P and affinely normalized. Then:
(a) the time-k curve of P is small and bounded, is an affine restriction of slope at most 100^(-(n-k)) of the time-k
curve of its depth-k ancestor, and has speed at most eps 100^(-(n-k)) and diameter at most 2 eps 100^(-(n-k));
(b) for 0 <= k <= n, J_(g^(n-k)) from the time-k to the time-n curve of P has max/min at most D^2;
(c) for i < n, floor(log J_g(g^i x)) takes at most two consecutive values on P (log D^2 < 1);
(d) curves gamma_k: [-1,1] -> R^m with images in a fixed compact set and sup|gamma_k^(j)| <= C for 1 <= j <= r have a
subsequence converging in C^(r-1); the limit has Lipschitz (r-1)-st derivative with constant C. Length is continuous in
C^1, so limits of large curves have length >= eps/2 and are not constant. No convergence in the C^(r-1,1) norm is
asserted.

Proof. (a) Compose the affine restrictions (each slope <= 1/100) and apply Lemma 7(b); the bounds follow from
s <= eps and length <= 2 sup|gamma'|. (b) Lemma 7(c) for the two bounded endpoint parametrizations; no factors are
multiplied over time. (c) Apply (b) between times i and i+1. (d) Arzela-Ascoli for derivatives of orders 0 to r-1
(equicontinuous because the next derivative is bounded). QED

##### 2C.2.3 Large hyperbolic times (A306)

**Lemma 10 (finite-time count).** Let D be one large initial curve of the tree of Lemma 9 with normalized arclength
lambda. Assume: image curves have length at most 2 eps and large ones at least eps/2; every parent has at most A >= 1
nonlarge children; restricted iterates between two levels have arclength distortion at most 2; on each depth-j atom
the labels l_i(x) = floor(log J_g(g^i x)), 0 <= i < j, oscillate by at most one; the l_i take at most q integer values
and are at most L. Let 0 < h < alpha <= L with h > log A, theta = (alpha-h)/(L-h), 0 < beta < theta. A time j is
hyperbolic for x if sum_(i=s)^(j-1) l_i(x) >= h(j-s) for all 0 <= s < j. Let G_n(x) count hyperbolic times j <= n
whose depth-j image is large. Then

    lambda{ x : sum_(i<n) l_i(x) >= alpha n, G_n(x) < beta n } <= 2 exp(n[log(32q) - (h - log A)(theta - beta)]),

and if j is hyperbolic for x, then J_(g^(j-s)) >= exp((h-1)(j-s)) at every point of the depth-j atom of x, s < j.

Proof. Records. Fix a word l_0, ..., l_(n-1) with sum >= alpha n and put S_j = sum_(i<j)(l_i - h), S_0 = 0. If S_j > S_i
for all i < j then S_j - S_s > 0 for s < j, so j is hyperbolic. A new record exceeds the previous maximum by at most
S_j - S_(j-1) <= L - h, and the maximum rises from 0 to at least S_n >= (alpha - h)n, so there are at least theta n
records.

Colors. Fix also a color word u_1, ..., u_n (large or nonlarge for the depth-j atom), u_0 = large, and let E be the set
of points realizing both words; its hyperbolic set H depends only on the l-word. Each maximal run of nonlarge times is
preceded by a large time s. If the run contains hyperbolic times, retain (s, t] with t the last hyperbolic time in the
run. The retained intervals are disjoint and their total length T is at least the number of hyperbolic nonlarge times.

Fractions. Let R_j be the supremum, over depth-j atoms P meeting E, of length(g^j(E intersect P))/length(g^j P). Then
R_0 = lambda(E) and R_n <= 1.
(i) For s < t, R_s <= 2 R_t: for a depth-s atom P, the fraction of g^s P occupied by g^s(E intersect P) is the sum over
depth-t descendants Q meeting E of [length(g^s Q)/length(g^s P)] times the fraction of g^s Q occupied by
g^s(E intersect Q); by distortion at most 2 the latter is at most 2 R_t, and the weights sum to at most one.
(ii) For a retained (s, t]: each relevant depth-s image is large; all intermediate colors are nonlarge, so P has at
most A^(t-s) depth-t descendants meeting E. Each such Q contains a point of E for which t is hyperbolic, so
J_(g^(t-s)) >= exp(h(t-s)) there, hence >= exp(h(t-s))/2 on all of Q. Therefore
length(g^s(E intersect Q)) <= 2 exp(-h(t-s)) length(g^t(E intersect Q)) <= 2 exp(-h(t-s)) R_t (2 eps), and dividing by
length(g^s P) >= eps/2 and summing over Q:

    R_s <= 8 (A exp(-h))^(t-s) R_t.

Chain. Apply (ii) on the k <= n retained intervals and (i) on the at most k+1 gaps:
lambda(E) <= 8^k 2^(k+1) (A exp(-h))^T <= 2 (16)^n exp(-(h - log A)T). For a bad word T >= (theta - beta)n. There are
at most q^n l-words and 2^n color words; summing gives the bound.

Whole atom. On a depth-j atom l_i(y) >= l_i(x) - 1 for i < j, and log J_g >= floor(log J_g); sum from s to j-1. QED

Remark. A306 writes "weights sum to one" in (i); they sum to at most one when only descendants meeting E are kept
(A394 says "at most one"). A306 also displays length(g^s Q) <= 2 exp(-h(t-s)) length(g^t Q) and states the constant 8;
the route above reaches 8 directly; combining the displayed length bound with (i) gives 16, which only changes the
constant 32 in log(32q) to 64. 2C.4, point 6.

**Lemma 11 (time selection for the smooth map).** Let f be as in Lemma 3(d) (any C-infinity diffeomorphism of R^m with
bounded derivatives of positive order and bounded D f^(-1)), Mf = max(2, ||Df||_infinity, ||Df^(-1)||_infinity), and
let a straight arc contain a measurable F of positive length with limsup_N N^(-1) log J_(f^N) >= lambda_0 > 0 on F. Then
there are r >= 3, p >= 1, eps > 0, beta > 0 and a straight subarc carrying positive F-measure, with the tree of
Lemma 9 for g = f^p, such that for every measurable F' contained in F (on that subarc) with lambda(F') > 0 and
infinitely many n there are E_n contained in F' with lambda(E_n) >= 1/(2n^2) and every x in E_n has at least beta n
large hyperbolic times (threshold h > 1) up to n. The parameters do not depend on F'.

Proof. Write zeta < zeta' for the two rates that A306 calls chi < chi' (the letter chi is reserved below for the
positive exponent). Choose 0 < zeta < zeta' < lambda_0; note lambda_0 <= log Mf since J_(f^N) <= ||Df||^N. Choose r >= 3
with 3 log Mf/(r-1) < zeta/2. For g = f^p, Mg <= Mf^p, so Lemma 8 gives A = C_r Mg^(3/(r-1)) with
log A <= log C_r + 3p log Mf/(r-1) < log C_r + p zeta/2. Take

    h = p zeta + 2,  alpha = p zeta' - 1,  L = p log Mf,  theta_0 = (zeta' - zeta)/(2 log Mf),  beta = theta_0/2,
    q = 2 ceil(p log Mf) + 3.

The labels lie in [-ceil(p log Mf), p log Mf] (J_g >= Mf^(-p)), so there are at most q values and l_i <= L. For p large:
alpha > h iff p(zeta' - zeta) > 3; alpha <= L since zeta' < log Mf; L > h; h > 1; h - log A >= p zeta/2 + 2 - log C_r > 0;
and theta = (p(zeta'-zeta) - 3)/(p log Mf - p zeta - 2) >= (p(zeta'-zeta) - 3)/(p log Mf) >= theta_0 as soon as
p(zeta' - zeta) >= 6. Since T >= (theta - beta)n >= (theta_0 - beta)n for bad words, Lemma 10 holds with theta_0 in
place of theta. The quantity (h - log A)(theta_0 - beta) - log(32q) grows linearly in p; fix p with it > 1, so the bad
set has measure at most 2 exp(-n).

Only now choose eps for the derivatives of this g as in 2C.2.2, decreasing it if necessary so that 2 eps is less than the
length of the straight arc. Cover the interior of the straight arc by countably many
subarcs of length 2 eps; one carries positive F-measure. Parametrize it at speed eps on [-1,1]: it is small, bounded
(higher derivatives vanish) and large. Use the tree of Lemma 9 on it.

For N = np + j, 0 <= j < p, |log J_(f^N) - log J_(f^(np))| <= p log Mf, so limsup_n n^(-1) log J_(g^n) >= p lambda_0 >
p zeta' on F. Given F', let F_n = {x in F': J_(g^n)(x) >= exp(n p zeta')}; each x in F' is in infinitely many F_n. If
lambda(F_n) < 1/n^2 for all large n, the first Borel-Cantelli lemma gives lambda(limsup F_n) = 0, contradicting
lambda(F') > 0. So infinitely many n have lambda(F_n) >= 1/n^2. On F_n, sum_(i<n) l_i >= log J_(g^n) - n >= alpha n
(chain rule along the tree curve). Remove the bad set: E_n = F_n minus bad has measure >= 1/n^2 - 2 exp(-n) >=
1/(2n^2) for large n. QED

##### 2C.2.4 The entropy lemma (A257)

**Lemma 12.** Let D be a compact embedded C^1 curve with normalized arclength lambda in a compact Riemannian manifold M,
g a C^1 diffeomorphism, P^ell nested finite interval partitions of D (modulo null boundaries). For measurable E_n with
m_n = lambda(E_n) > 0 let eta_n = lambda|E_n / m_n, L_n = log(1/m_n) = o(n), and integers N_n -> infinity with
N_n/n -> 0 and N_n L_n/n -> 0. For each n and 0 <= ell < n select whole atoms P of P^ell; parametrize g^ell(P) by
gamma_(ell,P) on a fixed interval I, all in a fixed compact C^1 class C, with (g^ell)_*(lambda|P/lambda(P)) <= D0
lambda_gamma (normalized image arclength), and diam(g^ell Q) <= eps_N -> 0 for every descendant Q in P^(ell+N) of a
selected P. Let rho_(n,ell,P) be the pullback to I of (g^ell)_*(eta_n|P/eta_n(P)),
p_n = (1/n) sum_(selected) eta_n(P) delta_(gamma,rho), p a limit along a subsequence, q its curve marginal, and theta
the image of p under (gamma, rho) -> delta_gamma x gamma_* rho. Then on C_+ = {length(gamma) > 0},
theta << q(dgamma) lambda_gamma(dx), and for q-almost every gamma in C_+ the conditional theta_gamma is absolutely
continuous with respect to lambda_gamma.

Proof. Fix n, write eta = eta_n, N = N_n, H_ell = sum_(P in P^ell) eta(P) log(eta(P)/lambda(P)). Jensen gives
H_ell >= 0, and eta <= lambda/m_n gives H_ell <= L_n. For a parent P at level ell let p_Q = eta(Q)/eta(P),
q_Q = lambda(Q)/lambda(P) over its level-(ell+N) descendants; fix K > 1, call Q bad if p_Q > K q_Q, and let
b_P = sum_bad p_Q, d_P = sum_bad q_Q <= b_P/K. The log-sum inequality on the two groups gives
KL(p||q) >= b_P log(b_P/d_P) + (1-b_P) log((1-b_P)/(1-d_P)) >= b_P log K + (1-b_P)log(1-b_P) >= b_P log K - log 2
(x log x >= -1/e). The chain rule H_(ell+N) - H_ell = sum_P eta(P) KL(p_P||q_P), summed over ell < n-N, telescopes
along the N residue classes mod N to at most N L_n. Hence

    (1/n) sum_(ell<n-N) sum_P eta(P) b_P <= [N L_n/n + log 2]/log K.                          (1)

Let rho^K be rho restricted to good children (a subprobability), keep the weight eta(P)/n even if rho^K = 0, and drop
ell >= n-N. The resulting pcheck_n^K and its joint image thetacheck_n^K satisfy 0 <= thetacheck_n^K <= theta_n and
mass(theta_n - thetacheck_n^K) <= N/n + [N L_n/n + log 2]/log K (2); the curve marginal changes only by the dropped
times, mass <= N/n. For nonnegative Lipschitz h on M, pick x_Q in g^ell(Q); h oscillates by at most eps_N Lip(h) on
g^ell(Q), p_Q <= K q_Q on good Q, and sum_Q q_Q h(x_Q) <= int h d((g^ell)_*(lambda|P/lambda(P))) + eps_N Lip(h), so

    int h d(gamma_* rho^K) <= K D0 int h dlambda_gamma + (K+1) eps_N Lip(h).                  (3)

Take a common subsequence for K = exp(j), j >= 1 (diagonal argument; C and the spaces of subprobabilities on I are
compact). Evaluation of continuous joint tests at (gamma, gamma(t)) is continuous, so 0 <= thetacheck^K <= theta and
mass(theta - thetacheck^K) <= log 2/log K (4); the curve marginal of pcheck^K is q. On C_+, gamma -> lambda_gamma is
weakly continuous (numerator int . |gamma'| dt, denominator locally bounded below). For h in a countable family of
nonnegative Lipschitz functions dense in the nonnegative continuous functions and delta = 1/k, the set
{(gamma, rho): gamma in C_+, int h d(gamma_* rho) > K D0 int h dlambda_gamma + delta} is open and, by (3), has
pcheck_n^K-measure zero once (K+1) eps_N Lip(h) < delta; by the portmanteau theorem it is pcheck^K-null. Hence
gamma_* rho^K <= K D0 lambda_gamma for pcheck^K-almost every pair over C_+, and integrating with curve marginal q,
thetacheck^K restricted to C_+ is at most K D0 q(dgamma) lambda_gamma(dx). If A is null for that reference measure,
theta(A) <= log 2/log K by (4), for every K = exp(j). Conditional form (the "standard disintegration" of A257, made
explicit here): let f = dtheta/d(q x lambda_gamma) on C_+ (Radon-Nikodym, both measures finite). Since the curve
marginal of theta is q, int f(gamma, x) lambda_gamma(dx) = 1 for q-almost every gamma, so f(gamma, .) lambda_gamma is a
disintegration of theta over q; by q-almost-everywhere uniqueness of disintegrations (X6) theta_gamma =
f(gamma, .) lambda_gamma. For a bounded increasing family of joint measures with this property, each member is
absolutely continuous with respect to (limiting curve marginal) x lambda_gamma, because its curve marginal is dominated
by the limit. A set that is null for that measure is null for every member, and so also for the increasing limit. QED

Remark. Lemma 12 does not exclude constant limit curves: with g = identity, dyadic partitions and E_n = D, all
hypotheses hold and the limit curves are constant (A257 section 4). Noncollapse is supplied separately (Lemma 13(c)).

##### 2C.2.5 The incoming-curve measure (A307)

Setting for Lemmas 13 to 15. f is as in Lemma 11, Qc is a compact set with f(Qc) contained in Qc (in the application
Qc = Q, so A307's K is our Q), D0 is a straight compact arc in Qc, and G0 contained in D0 has positive length with
limsup N^(-1) log J_(f^N) >= lambda_0 > 0. Fix r, p, eps, beta, the subarc D (normalized arclength lambda,
G = G0 intersect D of positive length) and its tree, as in Lemma 11, with g = f^p.

**Lemma 13 (original density, selection, noncollapse).**
(a) There is a compact E contained in G with lambda(E) > 0 such that the fraction length(P^ell(x) intersect G)/
length(P^ell(x)) tends to 1 uniformly on E, P^ell(x) being the depth-ell atom containing x.
(b) For a window M >= 0 and 0 <= ell < n, select an entire depth-ell atom P if it contains y in E_n (Lemma 11 applied
to F' = E) whose depth-(ell+i) atom is good for some 0 <= i <= M with ell + i <= n, where an atom is good if its image is
large and it contains a point for which that depth is a hyperbolic time (a witness). Discard eta_n-null parents. With
eta_n = lambda|E_n/m_n, gamma_(ell,P) the normalized image curve on [-1,1] and rho_(n,ell,P) as in Lemma 12, let
p_n^M = (1/n) sum eta_n(P) delta_(gamma,rho), theta_n^M its joint image and mu_n^M the x-marginal. Then the masses are
in [beta - 1/n, 1] and increase with M; along a common diagonal subsequence for all M there are limits p^M, theta^M,
mu^M, increasing in M.
(c) With L_M = max(1, ||Dg||_infinity^M) and v_M = eps/(2 L_M), every selected image curve has length >= v_M, and
q^M-almost every limit curve is regular and embedded with maximum speed >= v_M/2 and minimum speed >=
(1-2 eta)v_M/2.

Proof. (a) Atoms have lengths tending uniformly to zero. For an interval I containing x, the complement fraction of G
in I is at most twice that in the centered interval of length 2 length(I), so the Lebesgue density theorem gives
fractions -> 1 at almost every x in G. Remove partition endpoints (countable). Egorov's theorem and inner regularity
give E. (b) For window 0, every point of E_n has at least beta n good depths up to n, and each good depth j >= 1 is
counted through its parent at ell = j; only the time n can be omitted, so the mass is at least beta - 1/n. Enlarging M
adds terms with unchanged weights, curves and conditionals. All curves lie in Qc and satisfy the uniform C^r bounds of
Lemma 9, so their closure is compact in C^(r-1), hence a compact C^1 class; weak compactness and a diagonal subsequence
give the limits, and positivity of differences gives monotonicity. (c) A selected P has a good descendant Q at depth
ell + i, i <= M: eps/2 <= length(g^(ell+i)Q) <= L_M length(g^ell Q) <= L_M length(g^ell P). Length is C^1-continuous.
Bounded curves have max speed s and |gamma'(t) - gamma'(t')| <= 2 eta s, which passes to C^1 limits; with length >= v_M
this gives s >= v_M/2 and minimum speed >= (1-2 eta)v_M/2. Projection on a maximal-speed tangent is strictly
increasing, so the limit is embedded. QED

**Lemma 14 (absolute continuity and invariance).** theta^M << q^M(dgamma) lambda_gamma(dx) for every M. The increasing
limits p, theta, mu, q (M -> infinity) have mass in [beta, 1], q is carried by nonconstant curves, and
theta << q(dgamma) lambda_gamma(dx). mu is g-invariant, nonzero and supported in intersection_n g^n(Qc).

Proof. Apply the proof of Lemma 12 for fixed M directly in R^m, with interval [-1,1] in place of [0,1]; all curves
involved lie in the compact set Qc and their parametrizations form a compact C^1 class, which is what that proof uses (in
the Euler application the compact manifold of Lemma 3(e) is also available): the
partitions are the tree partitions of D, the selected sets are whole atoms, L_n = log(1/m_n) <= log 2 + 2 log n,
N_n = floor(sqrt(n)), D0 = 2 (the pushforward of normalized original arclength on P is at most twice normalized image
arclength by Lemma 9(b)), eps_N = 2 eps 100^(-N) (Lemma 9(a)), C the compact C^1 class of Lemma 13(b), and C_+
contains q^M-almost every curve by Lemma 13(c). The increasing-family clause of Lemma 12 gives the statement for theta.
Invariance: if a depth-ell parent, ell >= 1, is selected for window M, its depth-(ell-1) ancestor is selected for
window M+1 (same witness, one more step ahead). This applies to every sampled point of the parent. Hence for
nonnegative continuous phi, int phi d(g_* mu_n^(M+1)) >= int phi dmu_n^M - ||phi||_infinity/n, the missing term being
ell = 0. Let n -> infinity along the subsequence, then M -> infinity: g_* mu >= mu, and equal finite masses give
g_* mu = mu. Supports: every curve at time ell is in g^ell(Qc). QED

**Lemma 15 (original approximants, backward bounds, components).**
(a) For every M and every gamma in the support of q^M there are depth-ell_j atoms P_j, ell_j -> infinity, each meeting E,
whose normalized image curves gamma_j = g^(ell_j)(P_j) converge to gamma in C^1, with lengths in [v_M, 2 eps],
distortion of g^(ell_j) on P_j at most D^2 < 2, and length(P_j intersect G)/length(P_j) -> 1.
(b) For all k >= 0, diam(g^(-k) gamma) <= 2 eps 100^(-k), ||(g^(-k) gamma)'||_infinity <= eps 100^(-k), and
||D g^(-k)(gamma(t)) gamma'(t)/|gamma'(t)|| <= [2 eps/((1-2 eta)v_M)] 100^(-k). All limit curves and their negative
iterates lie in intersection_n g^n(Qc).
(c) If Y is a Borel set with mu(Y) > 0, then mu^M(Y) > 0 for some M, every mu-full set is mu^M-full, and there is a
curve in supp q^M carrying a positive-arclength compact set of points of Y that are two-sided Birkhoff generic and
Oseledets regular (for a countable test family fixed in advance), and lie in one uniform Pesin block.
(d) Generic points on one incoming curve have the same g-ergodic component, and disintegrating by the component label
preserves incoming absolute continuity.

Proof. (a) For fixed L, times ell < L contribute mass at most L/n. Each shrinking C^1 neighbourhood of gamma in supp q^M
has positive limiting mass, so by the portmanteau theorem late finite measures give it mass from arbitrarily large ell;
pick a positive-weight parent there. Lengths: Lemma 13(c) and Lemma 9(a). Distortion: Lemma 9(b). Every parent meets
E_n contained in E, and Lemma 13(a) gives the density uniformly on E. (b) For ell_j >= k, g^(-k) gamma_j is a
restriction of the depth-(ell_j - k) curve with extra slope at most 100^(-k), so Lemma 9(a) applies; composition with
g^(-k) preserves C^1 convergence on compacts. The last bound divides by the minimum speed (1-2 eta)v_M/2. Finite-time
images lie in g^n(Qc). (c) mu^M increases to mu (monotone convergence). Generic regular points have full mu-measure, hence full
mu^M-measure, and countably many Pesin blocks cover them; choose a block and a subset Y' of Y of generic regular points in
it with mu^M(Y') > 0. Since theta^M << q^M x lambda_gamma (Lemma 14) and the x-marginal of theta^M is mu^M, the set of
(gamma, x) with x in Y' has positive q^M x lambda_gamma measure. So some gamma in supp q^M has lambda_gamma(Y') > 0, and
inner regularity gives a compact subset of positive arclength. (d) For x, y on one incoming curve,
d(g^(-k)x, g^(-k)y) <= 2 eps 100^(-k); a continuous test is uniformly continuous on the compact set, so backward Cesaro
limits agree when they exist; a countable dense family of tests identifies the ergodic component at two-sided generic
points (X4). For the disintegration write theta(dgamma dx) = sigma_gamma(dx) q'(dgamma) with q' << q and
sigma_gamma << lambda_gamma (Lemma 14), so mu = int sigma_gamma q'(dgamma); the component label c(x) is measurable on
the two-sided generic points, it is sigma_gamma-almost surely constant on q'-almost every curve by what was just shown,
with a value c_gamma that is measurable in gamma (countably many continuous tests), and disintegrating q' over c_gamma
gives mu_eta = int sigma_gamma q'_eta(dgamma) for almost every component eta. QED

At a two-sided Oseledets-regular point the tangent of an incoming curve lies in the sum of the Oseledets spaces with
exponents >= log 100, by (b). A307 states regularity C^(r-1,1) for one r >= 3 and asserts nothing on unstable
dimension, physicality, vortical localization or coverage.

##### 2C.2.6 Capture geometry, irrotational plaques, curve measures (A299, A201, A216)

**Lemma 16 (tangency, A299 lemma 1).** Let L be an injectively immersed C^1 one-manifold in R^3 with second countable
domain, gamma: I -> R^3 C^1 on a compact interval, E a measurable subset of I with gamma(E) contained in L. Then
gamma'(s) is tangent to L at gamma(s) for almost every s in E.

Proof. Cover the domain by countably many compact coordinate arcs with embedded images L_j; E_j = {s in E: gamma(s) in
L_j} is measurable. Almost every s in E is a density point of some E_j in which it lies (density theorem, countable
union of null sets). Then s_n -> s with s_n in E_j distinct; secant limits of the embedded compact arc L_j at gamma(s)
lie in its tangent line, and the C^1 expansion of gamma puts gamma'(s) there (trivially if gamma'(s) = 0). Injectivity
makes the leaf tangent well defined. QED

**Lemma 17 (transverse persistence, A299 lemma 2).** Let F be C^1 near (0,0) in R^2 with values in R^3, sigma a C^1
regular arc with sigma(0) = F(0,0), and d1 F(0,0), d2 F(0,0), sigma'(0) independent. If continuous F_n -> F uniformly
near (0,0), then for large n the image of F_n meets any prescribed open subarc of sigma around sigma(0).

Proof. G(s,t,v) = F(s,t) - sigma(v) has invertible derivative A0 at 0. On a small closed ball of radius r,
|A0^(-1)G(z) - z| <= r/4; for large n, |A0^(-1)(G_n - G)| <= r/4 there, G_n = F_n - sigma. Then
z -> z - A0^(-1)G_n(z) maps the r-ball into the r/2-ball; Brouwer gives G_n(z_n) = 0. Small r puts v in the subarc. QED

**Lemma 18 (fraction in a product set, A299 lemma 3).** Let H be a C^1 diffeomorphism from an open box (s,t,tau) onto an
open set, gamma(s) = H(s,0,0), T a compact positive-length subset of int I, and E a measurable set containing
H(T x J x L) for open intervals J, L around 0. If C^1 curves gamma_n: I -> R^3 converge uniformly to gamma, then after
shrinking I around a density point of T (and replacing T by a compact positive-length T1), gamma_n carries image
arclength at least length(T1)/L1 in E for large n, L1 the Lipschitz constant of the first coordinate pi of H^(-1) on a
small ball. If the gamma_n are restrictions of full curves of length <= L0, a fraction
delta = length(T1)/(L1 L0) of the full length lies in E. If the full curves are g^(ell_n)(P_n) with arclength Jacobian
max/min <= D' on P_n and E is g-invariant, then length(P_n intersect E) >= (delta/D') length(P_n); if moreover
length(P_n intersect F0)/length(P_n) -> 1, then P_n intersect F0 intersect E has positive length for large n.

Proof. pi o gamma_n -> s uniformly, so its endpoint values bracket T1 and the other two coordinates stay in J x L; the
intermediate value theorem gives pi(gamma_n(A_n)) = T1 for A_n = {s: pi(gamma_n(s)) in T1}, compact, with
gamma_n(A_n) in E. So length(T1) <= L1 H^1(gamma_n(A_n)) <= L1 int_(A_n)|gamma_n'| (multiplicity allowed). Pullback:
length(Q_n) >= length(g^(ell_n)Q_n)/j_max >= delta length(g^(ell_n)P_n)/j_max >= (delta/D')length(P_n), where Q_n is the
part mapped into E, equal to P_n intersect E by invariance. The F0-complement has relative length -> 0. QED

**Lemma 19 (irrotational stable plaques, A201).** Let Bp be a complete C^2 vector field on R^3 (the carrier), Fp the
time-one map of the flow Theta of -Bp, Wt a C^1 field with the real-time transport law
Wt(Theta_t x) = exp(kp t) D Theta_t(x) Wt(x) for all real t (equivalently [Bp, Wt] = -kp Wt), kp > 0; in particular
Wt(Fp^n x) = exp(kp n) D Fp^n(x) Wt(x) for integers n. (A481: the integer law alone gives only integer-time invariance
of {Wt = 0}; the Euler application in Lemma 23 has the bracket identity.)
Let q be a two-sided Oseledets-regular point of an Fp-invariant probability with compact support, with three simple
exponents chi_q > 0, 0, -lambda < 0 at q, Wt(Fp^n q) = 0 for all integers n, and suppose a compact neighbourhood of the
support contains the forward iterates of small local stable plaques. Then Wt vanishes on the global strong stable curve
W^s(q) and on its flow translates.

Proof. Let q_n = Fp^n q. Oseledets and Pesin theory at q (X1, X2) give, for small eps > 0, linear maps L_n from an
adapted R^3 onto the tangent space at q_n with ||L_n|| <= C, ||L_n^(-1)|| <= C_eps exp(eps n), and the conorm (least
singular value) m(A_n) >= exp(-lambda - eps) for A_n = L_(n+1)^(-1) DFp(q_n) L_n; and for a in a small local stable
plaque, |a_n - q_n| <= C_(a,eps) exp((-lambda + eps)n). The norm is the two-sided Lyapunov norm: on each Oseledets line
sum the norms of all iterates with weights exp(-lambda_i k - eps|k|), orthogonal sum over the lines; the one-step bounds
follow by shifting the sum, and comparison with the Euclidean norm is tempered. DFp is Lipschitz on a compact
neighbourhood of both orbits (Fp is C^2), so with Atilde_n = L_(n+1)^(-1) DFp(a_n) L_n,
||Atilde_n - A_n|| <= C exp((-lambda + 2 eps)n). Take 2 eps < lambda; for large n this is below
exp(-lambda - eps) - exp(-lambda - 2 eps), and the conorm is 1-Lipschitz, so m(Atilde_n) >= exp(-lambda - 2 eps).
Multiplying and converting with L_n, |DFp^n(a)v| >= c exp((-lambda - 3 eps)n)|v|. Wt is C^1 and Wt(q_n) = 0, so
|Wt(a_n)| <= C|a_n - q_n| <= C exp((-lambda + eps)n). Transport gives |Wt(a_n)| = exp(kp n)|DFp^n(a)Wt(a)| >=
c exp((kp - lambda - 3 eps)n)|Wt(a)|, hence |Wt(a)| <= C exp((-kp + 4 eps)n); take 4 eps < kp and n -> infinity. Every
point of W^s(q) enters a local plaque under iteration, and transport is invertible. The real-time law makes
{Wt = 0} invariant under every Theta_t, since D Theta_t is invertible; this gives the flow translates. QED

Remarks. A201 states this for an ergodic measure with mu(Wt = 0) = 1; its proof fixes one regular q and uses only the
Lyapunov data at q, which is how it is used in Lemma 23 (2C.4, point 10). A201's hypothesis that the zero direction
is the flow direction is not used in this argument. A201 says the Blumenthal-Young Lemma 2.8 and Theorem 3.1 are not
cited for the full conorm bound; the Lyapunov norm construction above is the argument. A201's positive-volume corollary
(via Blumenthal-Young Theorem A) is not needed here.

**Lemma 20 (curve measure to SRB, A216).** Let X be C^2 on a closed Riemannian 3-manifold, flow Theta, F = Theta_1, mu an
ergodic F-invariant probability on a compact invariant set Kc, div X = -d near Kc (d > 0 constant), and mu a measurable
mixture of probabilities mu_gamma, each absolutely continuous with respect to arclength on a compact regular embedded C^1
curve gamma with gamma contained in W^u(x) for almost every gamma and mu_gamma-almost every regular x. Then mu has simple
spectrum (chi, 0, -d-chi), chi > 0, its conditionals on full Pesin unstable plaques are absolutely continuous, and
h_mu(F) = chi.

Proof. Nonatomic mixture, so mu is not a point mass; if mu(X = 0) = 1 then F = identity mu-a.e. and ergodicity forces a
point mass; so X != 0 a.e. At a two-sided regular point DF^n X = X o F^n is bounded for all integers n, so the
two-sided growth rates of X vanish and X lies in E^0 (X1: the forward rate of v is the largest exponent among its
nonzero Oseledets components, the backward rate minus the smallest). A nondegenerate incoming curve in W^u gives a
positive exponent; the sum of exponents is -d; so the spectrum is (chi, 0, -d-chi). Null sets: let xi be a measurable
partition subordinate to W^u (X2) whose atoms are plaques of finite positive leaf length, with a measurable normalized
leaf-volume kernel s -> lambda_s (a partition built in Pesin boxes has these properties), A measurable with zero leaf arclength in xi(x) for mu-a.e. x, G a full-measure set
where this holds and xi(x) contains a leaf neighbourhood of x. For an incoming gamma with mu_gamma(G) = 1 and a regular
base point x0 with gamma in W^u(x0), all unstable leaves through gamma are one leaf L (exponential backward
equivalence). Cover gamma intersect G by intrinsically open segments I_x in xi(x); second countability of L gives a
countable subcover; on compact leaf charts the immersion is Lipschitz, so each A intersect I_x has zero ambient H^1
measure, which on the embedded gamma is arclength; so mu_gamma(A) = 0 and mu(A) = 0. This null-set property is
equivalent to absolute continuity of the conditionals on xi. Let q be the quotient measure of mu on xi, mu_s its
conditionals and lambda_s normalized arclength on xi(s). Put rho_s = mu_s + lambda_s and m = int rho_s dq, and let f and
g be the Radon-Nikodym densities with respect to m of mu and of int lambda_s dq (both are at most m). Both f m and g m
disintegrate over q with conditionals f rho_s and g rho_s, so uniqueness of disintegration gives mu_s = f rho_s and
lambda_s = g rho_s for q-almost every s. The set N = {g = 0} has lambda_s(N) = 0 for q-almost every s, that is zero leaf
arclength in xi(x) for mu-almost every x, so mu(N) = 0 by the null-set property, and mu_s = (f/g) lambda_s for q-almost
every s. Entropy: absolute continuity on unstable manifolds gives the lower bound h_mu(F) >= int sum lambda_i^+ = chi
([LS]; this is the direction of LY Part I Theorem A that LY attribute to Sinai; X3), and Ruelle's inequality
h_mu(F) <= int sum lambda_i^+ (X3) gives equality, h_mu(F) = chi. QED

On the compactification of Lemma 3(e), rho is as in Lemma 3(d): radial and nonincreasing in |y|, with rho = 1 on a
neighbourhood of Q.
On {rho > 0} outside int Q, including the collar where rho = 1, B.y > 0, so |y| strictly decreases along orbits of
-rho B, and rho is bounded below along each such orbit. Each such orbit therefore enters int Q and never returns, so
no invariant probability charges that set. The set {rho = 0}, with the added point, consists of fixed points with all
exponents zero. Hence an ergodic measure with a
positive exponent lies in Q, hence in K (A216, dependencies paragraph).

##### 2C.2.7 Assembly: proof of Theorem C' (A308 sections 2 to 7)

Standing assumptions: those of Theorem C'; Q, K, f, rho as in Lemma 3(b)-(e) (whose proofs use only completeness,
the radial inequality of Lemma 3(a) and smoothness, so they apply verbatim; the proof of Lemma 3(a) also uses linear
growth, which Theorem C' replaces by assumed completeness); G is a measurable subset of O intersect int Q with Leb(G) > 0.

**Lemma 21 (curve output).** There are p >= 1, g = f^p (equal to Psi_p on Q), a straight arc D contained in
O intersect int Q, F = G0 intersect D of positive length (G0 from Lemma 6), and a g-invariant probability m supported in
K, with an incoming representation theta << q(dgamma) lambda_gamma(dx) and finite-window parts theta^M, m^M as in
Lemmas 13 to 15. Every curve in supp q^M has original approximants g^(ell_j)(P_j), P_j a depth-ell_j atom of the tree
of D meeting E (a compact subset of F), ell_j -> infinity, converging in C^1, with image lengths in [v_M, 2 eps],
distortion < 2 and length(P_j intersect F)/length(P_j) -> 1. All limit curves and their negative g-iterates lie in K.

Proof. Lemma 6 gives D0, G0 with lambda_0 = (kappa-d)/2 > 0. Apply Lemma 11 and Lemmas 13 to 15 with Qc = Q; normalize
mu to m. intersection_n g^n(Q) = intersection_n Psi_(np)(Q) = K by Lemma 3(c). The level of P_j is ell_j, the clause
supplied in A308 section 2. QED

**Lemma 22 (regular components).** m(B = 0) = 0. At m-almost every point the exponents of g are p chi, 0, -p(d+chi)
(simple, chi > 0 depending on the point), B spans E^0, and each incoming curve through a regular point lies in the
global unstable manifold W^u(x) = {y: limsup_n n^(-1) log d(g^(-n)y, g^(-n)x) < 0}. For m-almost every g-ergodic
component mu: mu has absolutely continuous conditionals on full unstable plaques and h_mu(g) = p chi.

Proof. Two distinct points of {B = 0} on one incoming curve are fixed by g^(-k), yet the curve's g^(-k)-image has
diameter at most 2 eps 100^(-k) (Lemma 15(b)); so each curve meets {B = 0} in at most one point, an arclength-null set,
and theta << q x lambda_gamma gives m(B = 0) = 0 (A216 gives a second route, Lemma 20). E^0: as in Lemma 20, since
Dg^n B = B o g^n is bounded on K for all integers n. Positive exponent: Lemma 15(b) gives backward contraction at rate >=
log 100 of the incoming tangent. det Dg^n = exp(-pdn) on K. So exactly the stated three simple exponents. Unstable
manifold: points of an incoming curve approach the regular orbit at backward rate >= log 100 (Lemma 15(b)), so they lie
in W^u(x) as defined (the definition used in LY Part I; Pesin's theorem, X2, makes it an injectively immersed C^1
curve tangent to E^u). By Lemma 15(d), almost every ergodic component is a mixture of incoming curve measures; apply
Lemma 20 to it with X = -p rho B on the compactification (F = g near K, div X = -pd near K). QED

**Lemma 23 (no irrotational mass).** m(Z) = 0.

Proof. Suppose m(Z) > 0. Z is closed and invariant (Lemma 2). Apply Lemma 15(c) to Y = Z intersect {B != 0}
intersect (regular set): there is a finite-M curve gamma in supp q^M carrying a positive-length compact set of regular
generic points in Z, all in one ergodic component. By Lemma 16 (with L = W^u, Lemma 22) choose such x = gamma(s0) at
which gamma'(s0) spans E^u(x). Apply Lemma 19 with carrier Bp = pB, Fp = Psi_p = g on Q, kp = p kappa
(Lemma 2 gives W(Psi_(pt) x) = exp(p kappa t) D Psi_(pt) W(x)), Wt = W: W(g^n x) = 0 for all n (Z invariant), the
spectrum at x is as in Lemma 22, and forward orbits of a bounded neighbourhood stay bounded (Lemma 3(b)). So a small
strong stable plaque sigma through x lies in Z. Let F(s,t) = Psi_t(gamma(s)) and F_j(s,t) = Psi_t(gamma_j(s)) for the
approximants of Lemma 21, on a small rectangle around (s0, 0) (t of both signs; B is complete). The columns of F at
(s0, 0) are gamma'(s0) in E^u and -B(x) in E^0, and sigma'(0) is in E^s: independent. F_j -> F uniformly by continuous
dependence on initial data on compacts. Lemma 17 gives, for large j, a point Psi_t(gamma_j(s)) in sigma, contained in Z.
But gamma_j lies in g^(ell_j)(D), contained in O, and O is invariant (Lemma 2). Contradiction. QED

**Lemma 24 (flow average, spectrum, entropy).** Let mu be a g-ergodic component as in Lemma 22 with mu(O) = 1 (m-almost
every component, by Lemma 23), and nu = (1/p) int_0^p (Psi_s)_* mu ds. Then nu is supported in K, invariant and ergodic
for the whole flow, nu(B != 0, W != 0) = 1, its spectrum is (kappa - d, 0, -kappa) with stable direction R W and zero
direction R B, h_nu(Psi_1) = kappa - d (so chi = kappa - d), its unstable conditionals are absolutely continuous, and
every mu-generic point x (for the tests phibar_k below) is in Basin(nu).

Proof. (Psi_u)_* nu is the average of the p-periodic family (Psi_(s+u))_* mu, hence equals nu. A flow-invariant Borel set
A is g-invariant, so mu(A) is 0 or 1, and (Psi_s)_* mu(A) = mu(Psi_(-s)A) = mu(A); so nu(A) = mu(A). The sets
{B != 0} and {W != 0} are invariant (Lemma 2). Spectrum: for mu-almost every regular x with W(x) != 0,
|Dg^n W(x)| = exp(-p kappa n)|W(g^n x)| (Lemma 2), the numerator is at most max_K |W|, and by Poincare recurrence to
{|W| >= |W(x)|/2} it is at least |W(x)|/2 along a subsequence; the Oseledets limit exists, so it equals -p kappa. The only
negative exponent is -p(d + chi), so chi = kappa - d and W(x) is in E^s (independent of E^0 = R B). Each (Psi_s)_* mu is
the image of mu under the conjugacy Psi_s, which commutes with g and has bounded derivative and inverse on K, so it has
the same spectrum and entropy p chi. Entropy is affine over this integral mixture (X5, applied to the measurable
kernel s -> (Psi_s)_* mu of g-invariant probabilities, A2493-A2494; no ergodic decomposition is used), so
h_nu(g) = p chi, and since p is a positive integer and g = (Psi_1)^p on K, the iterate law h_nu(T^p) = p h_nu(T)
(X5, A2477, A2494) gives h_nu(Psi_1) = chi = kappa - d. Then h_nu(Psi_1) equals the positive exponent, so LY Part I
Theorem A ("if" direction, proved in Part I; X3) gives absolutely continuous unstable conditionals for nu (A216 also
allows transporting the conditional representations). Genericity: with phibar(x) = (1/p) int_0^p phi(Psi_s x) ds,
(1/(np)) int_0^(np) phi(Psi_t x) dt = (1/n) sum_(k<n) phibar(g^k x) -> int phibar dmu = int phi dnu, for x generic
for the countable family {phibar_k}; the phibar_k must be included in the test family fixed in Lemma 15(c) (section
4, point 8). Integer times suffice by Lemma 5(c). QED

**Lemma 25 (product set).** Let nu be a Borel probability supported in K, invariant for the flow, with
nu(B != 0, W != 0) = 1 and E^u, E^0 = R B, E^s = R W at regular points. Let gamma be a C^1 arc in int Q (a local unstable
plaque, or a limit curve from Lemma 21) and T a positive-length set of parameters s such that gamma(s) is regular, in
Basin(nu), and gamma'(s) spans E^u(gamma(s)). Then Basin(nu) has positive volume; precisely, at a density point s0 of
T with s0 in T, H(s,t,tau) = Gamma_tau(Psi_t gamma(s)) is a C^1 diffeomorphism from a box around (s0,0,0) onto an open set, and
H(T' x (-delta, delta)^2) is contained in Basin(nu) for a compact positive-length T' in T.

Proof. The columns of DH at (s0,0,0) are gamma'(s0), -B and W at gamma(s0): independent. The inverse function theorem
gives the box. Since gamma(s0) is in int Q, shrinking the arc and the box keeps Psi_t gamma(s) in Q for t of both
signs (A481; alternatively enlarge Q to another admissible ball, since the basin is flow invariant independently of
Q, and every application through K has the interior condition). Psi_t gamma(s) is in Basin(nu) (Lemma 5(b)); Lemma 5(a), 5(b) give Gamma_tau Psi_t gamma(s) in
Basin(nu) for |tau| <= tau0. Change of variables: Leb(H(T' x box)) = int |det DH| > 0. QED

**Lemma 26 (capture in the original set).** In the setting of Lemma 21 there is a component mu as in Lemma 24, with
flow average nu, such that G intersect Basin(nu) is nonempty (indeed it contains a positive-length subset of D). This
existential form is what Lemma 27 uses; a statement for every preassigned component would need the selection below to be
repeated after disintegrating the finite-window measures over the component label.

Proof. By Lemma 15(c), applied to an m-full Borel set Y of two-sided generic regular points whose g-ergodic component
satisfies Lemma 22 and has mu(O) = 1 (one exists by Lemmas 22 and 23, since the component label is measurable, Lemma
15(d)), and Lemma 22 there is a finite-M curve gamma in supp q^M with a compact positive-length set of
mu-generic regular points (mu as in Lemma 24, chosen so that the component label is constant on it, Lemma 15(d)),
tangent to E^u (Lemma 16). Lemma 25 gives the product set. Lemma 18 with E = Basin(nu) (g-invariant by Lemma 5(b)),
the approximants gamma_j of Lemma 21 (uniform convergence, full lengths <= 2 eps, distortion D' < 2), and F0 = F gives
a positive-length subset of P_j intersect F intersect Basin(nu) for large j; F is contained in G. QED

**Lemma 27 (countable coverage; proof of Theorem C').** Let N be the class of Borel probabilities on K, invariant and
ergodic for the whole flow, with nu(B != 0, W != 0) = 1, simple spectrum (kappa - d, 0, -kappa) and absolutely
continuous unstable conditionals. Every nu in N has nu(Basin(nu)) = 1 (Birkhoff's theorem for the flow applied to the
countable family of Lemma 5(c)) and a positive-volume basin: by absolute continuity some local unstable plaque (a C^1
arc near K, inside Q) carries a positive-length set of regular nu-generic points, and Lemma 25 applies, since its
hypotheses E^s = R W and E^0 = R B hold for every nu in N. The stable direction is R W: as in Lemma 24, the exponent of
W at a regular vortical point is -kappa. As in Lemma 20, D Psi_t B = B o Psi_t is bounded on K, so B spans E^0, and
absolute continuity with Ruelle's inequality gives h_nu(Psi_1) = kappa - d ([LS], X3). Distinct members have disjoint
basins (a common point gives int phi dnu1 = int phi dnu2 for every bounded continuous phi), which are Borel by Lemma
5(c); a family of pairwise disjoint Borel sets of positive volume is countable (each meets some ball B(0,k) in volume >
1/j, and only finitely many disjoint sets can do so for fixed k, j). So N is countable. Each basin lies in O: if x is in
Z, its orbit stays in Z, so the time averages of min(1, |W|) vanish, while int min(1, |W|) dnu > 0. Let U_N be the union
of the basins (Borel, flow invariant). If Leb(O minus U_N) > 0, then since every orbit enters int Q and both sets are
invariant, O minus U_N is contained in the union over n of Psi_(-n)((O minus U_N) intersect int Q); the maps Psi_(-n)
preserve null sets, so G = (O minus U_N) intersect int Q has positive volume. Lemmas 21 to 26 produce nu in N (Lemma 24)
and a point of G in Basin(nu), contradicting the definition of G. If W is not identically zero, O is open and nonempty,
so Leb(O) > 0 and N is nonempty. QED

##### 2C.2.8 Densities, essential domains, proof of Theorem C (A207, A223, A308 section 8)

**Lemma 28 (alpha densities, A207).** Let B be C^2, W C^1 near a compact invariant set, complete carrier flow, with
F = Psi_1 extended to the closed manifold of Lemma 3(e) (as in Lemma 20, so that the LY results apply), alpha a
C^1 one-form with alpha(B) = alpha(W) = 0, Psi_t^* alpha = exp(at) alpha, L_W alpha = 0, a > 0. Let mu be an invariant
probability for F = Psi_1 with simple spectrum (+, 0, -), absolutely continuous unstable conditionals, and
E^s + E^0 = span(W, B) = ker alpha almost everywhere. Then on almost every local unstable plaque the conditional density
is C A, A(x) = |alpha_x(e^u(x))|, with C depending on the plaque. A C^1 map following W orbits preserves alpha; one
following Psi-time s(p) multiplies alpha by exp(a s(p)), one following Phi-time s(p) by exp(-a s(p)).

Proof. A > 0 at regular points (alpha is nonzero on E^u since ker alpha = E^s + E^0). Covariance gives the unstable
Jacobian J^u F(x) = exp(a) A(x)/A(Fx). The conditional density formula of LY Part I (X3: Section 6.1 and
Corollary 6.1.4, printed page 534; Corollary 6.2 for the nonergodic case) gives, for y, z on one local unstable plaque,
rho(y)/rho(z) = lim_N prod_(n=1)^N J^u F(F^(-n)z)/J^u F(F^(-n)y), which telescopes to
[A(y)/A(z)][A(F^(-N)z)/A(F^(-N)y)]. Fix a countable family of compact Pesin blocks with A bounded below, uniform local
unstable size and uniform C^1 control of unstable tangents; almost every regular y lies in one of them and, by Poincare
recurrence, returns to it backward infinitely often. Take such a y and its block (the density identity is an
almost-everywhere statement about conditional measures, with one normalizing constant for each plaque). Along backward returns of y to the
block, F^(-N)z is exponentially close to F^(-N)y on the same local unstable graph, the tangent directions converge, and
alpha is C^1, so the last ratio tends to 1; the product has a full limit, equal to A(y)/A(z). Holonomies: for
h(p) = Gamma_(s(p))p, Dh adds W ds, annihilated by alpha, and Gamma_s^* alpha = alpha (L_W alpha = 0); for
h(p) = Psi_(s(p))p the extra term is -B ds, also annihilated, giving exp(a s(p)) alpha. QED

**Lemma 29 (essential domains, A223).** Let B be complete C^2, W C^1, [B, W] = -kappa W (kappa > 0), every forward Psi
orbit bounded, and nu a compactly supported flow-ergodic probability with nu(O) = 1, simple spectrum, stable direction
R W, center R B, and unstable conditionals equivalent to arclength with strictly positive densities. Then there is a
unique maximal open D_nu contained in O with Basin(nu) contained in D_nu, Leb(D_nu minus Basin(nu)) = 0, nu(D_nu) = 1,
invariant under every Psi_t and locally saturated by the W flow. Distinct such nu have disjoint D_nu. If div B = d > 0,
each nonempty D_nu has infinite volume.

Proof. Basin(nu) is in O (the min(1,|W|) argument of Lemma 27). At a nu-typical regular point x on a local unstable
plaque gamma, positive densities make the set T of generic regular points of full arclength in a small open subarc.
H(s,t,tau) = Gamma_tau(Psi_t gamma(s)) is a C^1 diffeomorphism from a small box onto an open V contained in O (Lemma
25); H(T x rectangle) is in Basin(nu) by Lemma 5 (with the bounded-orbit hypothesis supplying the compact set), and
its complement in V is null by Fubini and change of variables. D_nu is the union of all open V contained in O with
Leb(V minus Basin(nu)) = 0; a countable subcover (second countability) shows Leb(D_nu minus Basin(nu)) = 0, and
nu(D_nu) = 1 by the construction at almost every x. Diffeomorphisms preserve null sets and Basin(nu), O are
invariant, so Psi_t D_nu = D_nu; local W invariance follows from the shift identity of Lemma 5(a), (b), used
pointwise: for y in O, also outside Q, the closure of the forward orbit of y is compact by the bounded-orbit
hypothesis, so the W flow has a uniform existence time tau_y on a compact neighbourhood of it, and the proof of Lemma
5(a) gives d(Psi_r Gamma_s y, Psi_r y) <= C_y abs(s) exp(-kappa r) for abs(s) <= tau_y; hence membership in Basin(nu)
is locally constant, and so constant, along every W segment (no bound uniform over a neighbourhood of y is used; that
stronger trapping holds in the Euler application, Lemma 3(b), but is not assumed here). For y in Basin(nu) choose
continuous compactly supported phi >= 0 inside D_nu with int phi dnu > 0; its time average along y is positive, so
Psi_t y is in D_nu for some t, and invariance gives y in D_nu. Two overlapping domains would give a nonempty open set
where both disjoint basins have full volume. Finally Leb(D_nu) = Leb(Phi_t D_nu) = exp(dt) Leb(D_nu) and Leb(D_nu) >
0. QED

**Proof of Theorem C.** U is C-infinity, so B and Omega are. Lemma 3(a) gives completeness and the radial inequality
with b0 = c/2; Lemma 1 gives div B = 3c = d > 0 and [B, Omega] = -(1+c) Omega; kappa = 1+c > 3c because c < 1/2. Theorem
C' (Lemma 27) gives items 1 to 4, with spectrum (1-2c, 0, -(1+c)) and entropy 1-2c; Lemma 4 gives nonemptiness for
nonconstant U. Item 5: Lemma 1(e), (f) give the alpha hypotheses of Lemma 28 (alpha is C-infinity), and at nu_i-almost
every point B and Omega are nonzero and independent (they span E^0 and E^s), so span(B, Omega) = ker alpha =
E^s + E^0. Item 6: Lemma 29 applies (bounded forward orbits by Lemma 3(b); the densities of item 5 are strictly positive on
almost every plaque xi(x) by LY Corollary 6.1.4, with Corollary 6.2 for the nonergodic case, as in 2D Lemma 11(b);
item 5 alone gives positivity only at regular points), and the union
of the D_i contains the union of the basins. QED

##### 2C.2.9 Finite regularity (CONDITIONAL, hypothesis of type H6: A416-A417, A430-A431)

Fix an integer r >= 2; U is C^r, P is C^1, (E) holds, U is uniformly sublinear, 0 < c < 1/2, omega real; Psi, Q, K as
before. For each nonempty connected component E of O put Q_E = Q intersect closure(E), K_E = K intersect closure(E),
Z_E = K_E intersect ({B = 0} union {Omega = 0}), M_n(E) = max(1, max_(Q_E) ||D Psi_n||),
Lambda_E = lim_n n^(-1) log M_n(E), and Gamma_E = the maximum of the largest backward Lyapunov exponent over
whole-flow-ergodic probabilities on Z_E (Gamma_E = -infinity if Z_E is empty).

**Theorem C_r (componentwise form).**
(A) (PROVED: A430; no extra hypothesis.) Q_E is nonempty, compact, forward invariant; K_E is nonempty, compact and
whole-flow invariant; Lambda_E = lim = inf_n n^(-1) log M_n(E) exists, is independent of the admissible radius and of an
equivalent norm, equals the rate on K_E, and Lambda_E >= a; Gamma_E is attained when Z_E is nonempty (Gamma_E = -infinity if Z_E
is empty, A481), and Lambda_E = max(a, Gamma_E).
(B) (A431, CONDITIONAL on the growth bound.) If Gamma_E < r(1-2c) for every component E (equivalently Lambda_E < ra for
every E; equivalently, for each E separately, log M_(N_E)(E) < r a N_E for some N_E >= 1), then conclusions 1 to 6 of
Theorem C hold for this C^r profile. No common gap below ra across components is assumed; the supremum over E may equal
ra while each condition holds (a logical possibility, not a constructed Euler profile).
(C) (Special case: A398-A399, A416-A417.) Put Lambda_core = lim_n n^(-1) log max(1, max_Q ||D Psi_n||), and let
Gamma_Z be defined as Gamma_E but on Z_K = K intersect ({B = 0} union {Omega = 0}) (not the set Z of 1.1). If
Omega is not identically zero, then Lambda_core = max(a, Gamma_Z) (A399, which assumes this; for U = 0,
Lambda_core = 0 < a). Lambda_core < ra, equivalently (when Omega is not identically zero) Gamma_Z < r(1-2c),
implies the hypothesis of (B) (A431 section 7). If Omega is identically zero, the coverage statement is vacuous.
At r = 2: coverage holds if Gamma_E < 2(1-2c) for every E, in particular if Gamma_Z < 2(1-2c).

Status: (B) and (C) are CONDITIONAL (report label), on a bound of type H6. Whether decay implies the bound at
r = 2 is OPEN (A456; A431 section 7). Unconditional C^2 coverage is OPEN.

Proof outline.
1. Part (A) (A430 sections 2 to 4). Components of O are open, countable and Psi-invariant (Lemma 2, continuity of
orbits), with Psi_t(Q_E) = Psi_t(Q) intersect closure(E). Submultiplicativity M_(m+n)(E) <= M_m(E) M_n(E) gives the
limit; a fixed entry time T compares radii; the core reduction M_(T+qN+s)(E) <= C_(T,N)(M_N(K_E) + eps)^q uses no
convexity. Lower bound: exp(an)|alpha(x)| <= A_E ||D Psi_n(x)|| by Lemma 1(e), with alpha(x) != 0 at some point of E
(d alpha != 0 there). Attainment: on a compact invariant F, the projective flow on F x RP^2 with
q(x,[v]) = v.sym DX(x) v/abs(v)^2, X = -B, gives log(abs(D Psi_t(x) v)/abs(v)) = int_0^t q(Psi_s x, [D Psi_s(x) v]) ds; a limit of maximizing orbit averages, ergodic
decomposition, Birkhoff and Oseledets give a maximizing ergodic measure. An ergodic measure on K_E not carried by Z_E
has exponents 0 (B) and -kappa (Omega), by recurrence to {|B| >= 1/j, |Omega| >= 1/j}, and a from the determinant.
2. Partition (A416 sections 1 to 4, from A393 section 3). For g with ||Dg|| <= M on a neighbourhood of the curve and
eps^(j-1)||D^j g|| <= M, A393 (stopped before speed normalization) gives, per tangent bin
E_k = {exp(k) <= rho < exp(k+1)}, rho = |(g o gamma)'|/|gamma'|, at most m_k <= C_r N_k intervals, N_k = (M exp(-k))^(1/(r-1)),
with a0 exp(k) <= rho <= b0 exp(k), a0 = 0.97/D, b0 = De + 0.03 (log(b0/a0) < 2). Cut at all endpoints to get a
global partition; charge each atom to its left endpoint: n_k <= 1 + 2 sum_(|j-k|<=2) m_j <= C'_r N_k (using
exp(k) <= M). Halve each atom. An affine restriction of slope b <= 1 of its bounded intermediate curve H has
derivative-to-speed ratios at most eta D b^(j-1) for 2 <= j <= r (because min|H'| >= sup|H'|/D). Halving makes
b <= 1/2, so the ratios are at most eta D/2 < eta and every half is bounded (A416 section 4). Only then normalize speed: a half of maximum speed t > eps is
cut into ceil(t/eps) equal pieces with speeds in [t/(D ceil(t/eps)), eps], and t/(D ceil(t/eps)) > eps/(2D) > eps/3, so
they are all large and each half has at most one nonlarge child. Nonlarge children meeting E_l number at most
2 sum_(|k-l|<=2) n_k <= C''_r (M exp(-l))^(1/(r-1)) (this is A416 (1)); distortion D^2 < 2; large lengths in
[eps/2, 2 eps].
3. Times (A394 with A416 section 5). With gamma_* = (rh - log M)/(r-1) - log C''_r: R_s <= 2 R_t across gaps and
R_s <= 8 exp(-gamma_*(t-s)) R_t across retained runs (count C''_r^k exp((k log M - sum l_i)/(r-1)) times expansion
exp(-hk)), so the bad set is at most 2 exp(n[log(32q) - gamma_*(theta - beta)]).
4. Parameters (A417 section 7, A431 section 5), in this order: Lambda_E < L0 < L < ra and L/r < zeta < zeta' < a; p
large with max_(Q_E)||D Psi_p|| <= exp(p L0) < M = exp(pL); g = Psi_p; an open neighbourhood V_p of Q_E with
||Dg|| < M; a smaller one bounding D^j g, j <= r; only then eps. Labels: q = O(p) from
||(D Psi_p)^(-1)|| <= exp(p Lminus), Lminus = max(0, max_Q lambda_max(cI + sym DU)). h = p zeta + 2, target
p zeta' - 3 (A431; A417 uses p zeta' - 1, 2C.4, point 7), gamma_* = p(r zeta - L)/(r-1) + 2r/(r-1) - log C''_r,
linear in p; the target is below the largest label, since p zeta' - 3 < pa <= p Lambda_E < pL.
5. Localization to Q_E (A431 section 5). A393 needs derivative bounds only on a neighbourhood of each curve; V_p is
such a neighbourhood for all curves in Q_E at once, and need be neither invariant nor convex. Alternatively, the
Taylor step of A393 is for F = g o gamma along the curve parameter, with derivatives of g evaluated only at gamma(t)
and never along a spatial chord. Hence convexity of Q is not needed (A417 section 7 says "convex forward-invariant Q";
2C.4, point 7). Every forward image of the arc stays in E intersect Q and children are affine restrictions.
6. Arc (A431 section 5). Remove the zero set of alpha in E, which is null: d alpha = a i_Omega vol != 0 on E (Lemma 1(d)), so at a zero of
alpha some coefficient of alpha has nonzero gradient and the zero set lies locally in a C^1 hypersurface; exp(an)|alpha(x)| <= A ||D Psi_n(x)|| gives upper
operator exponent >= a; then the sqrt(3) pigeonhole and Fubini in a box with closure in E intersect int Q. The bound
a matters: step 4 needs a tangent exponent above zeta', and zeta' > L/r > Lambda_E/r; the bound a/2 of Lemma 6 would
only allow L < ra/2. Multiples of p keep the upper tangent exponent.
7. C^2 endpoint (A416 section 6). Uniform second derivatives give C^1 compactness at r = 2; limits have Lipschitz
derivative; a fixed window gives positive minimum speed and a narrow tangent cone, so incoming limits are embedded
C^(1,1) arcs (hence C^(1+theta), 0 < theta < 1); carrier strips are C^(1,1) because B is C^2. A201 needs a C^2 carrier
and C^1 Omega; A216 a regular embedded C^1 arc in W^u; A299 C^1 maps and uniform convergence; A307 and A257 C^1
compactness. Psi_p is C^2, as LY and Pesin theory require. The closed-manifold extension is made after the Euclidean
geometry.
8. Capture and countability (A431 section 6). Limit curves lie in Q_E and may meet its boundary; supports lie in K_E,
inside int Q; stable plaques and product boxes may leave Q_E, using coarse C^2 bounds on Q. Lemmas 21 to 27 then run in
each E; the exceptional null sets over countably many E have null union, with no common gap. Lemmas 28, 29 give items
5, 6.

Remarks. (i) A432 (CONDITIONAL): if also U -> 0, 2/5 <= c < 1/2 and U.Omega has one sign on each essential domain
(signs may differ), then U = 0; this is A422 with its growth condition replaced by that of (B) (Section 2D).
(ii) A415: exact affine rotating Euler solutions, for every omega, have arbitrarily large backward top exponent at a
vortical equilibrium; they are unbounded, not sublinear, have no absorbing core and are not helicity-free. So no local
Euler identity alone bounds Gamma_Z; a bound using the global hypotheses is not refuted.
(iii) A418 (CONFIRMED at the explicitly repaired scope): a greedy partition gives a second proof of the step 2 count,
hence of (B) and (C) under their hypotheses, with "small outputs" read as "nonlarge outputs" (for g = K I and
