gamma(t) = eps t e1 there are at least K small outputs, all with one label, while the bound is independent of K).
(iv) A454 (CONDITIONAL): lambda_min(sym DU) > -(c + ra) on each compact Z_E implies Gamma_E < ra; A455: a cutoff example
has Gamma_Z > 2a, but it satisfies Euler only near its core and every K_E is empty, so it tests neither (B) nor the
conjecture; A456: decay alone does not yet give the bound (OPEN).

#### 2C.3 External theorems (cited, not proved)

The auditor checked the parallel-source statements of X1-X3 against the sources at the compact C^2 scope used here:
the nonergodic two-sided splitting, the stable and unstable manifolds and the real-time interpolation (A2475), and the
entropy bounds and the orientation of the unstable density product (A2476). The two steps of X5 were proved instead of
compared with a source: the integer iterate law (A2477) and the affinity step (A2478, and for an arbitrary measurable
kernel the literature audit LIT303, A2491-A2495). The auditor also separated checked parallel sources from unread originals (A2479).
This certifies no unread original and no whole paper (A2480, A2496 OPEN).

X1 (cited). Oseledets multiplicative ergodic theorem, two-sided invertible form, with the nonergodic version
(exponents and splitting measurable and invariant) and the continuous-time form for cocycles bounded with their
inverses over unit times. V. I. Oseledec, "A multiplicative ergodic theorem. Lyapunov characteristic numbers for
dynamical systems", Trans. Moscow Math. Soc. 19 (1968), 197-231 (original not read). Checked parallel source: D. Ruelle,
"Ergodic theory of differentiable dynamical systems", Publ. Math. IHES 50 (1979), 27-58, Theorem 3.1 with Section 3.2
and Corollary 3.3 (two-sided, no ergodicity hypothesis; read by the literature audit). For a measure invariant under one time map, the
real-time limits at a regular point follow from the integer-time ones because D Psi_s and its inverse are bounded for 0
<= s <= 1; Ruelle's continuous-time Appendix B assumes invariance under the whole flow and is not used for such
measures. Used in Lemmas 15, 19, 20, 22, 24, 27, 28 and 2C.2.9.

X2 (cited). Pesin theory for C^(1+alpha) (here C^2) diffeomorphisms of compact manifolds: local stable and unstable
manifolds at regular points, Pesin blocks with uniform sizes and C^1 control, global unstable manifolds as injectively
immersed C^1 manifolds tangent to E^u and characterized by exponential backward approach, measurable partitions
subordinate to W^u. Ya. B. Pesin, "Families of invariant manifolds corresponding to nonzero characteristic exponents",
Math. USSR Izvestija 10 (1976; listed as 1978 by LY), 1261-1305; Ya. B. Pesin, "Characteristic Lyapunov exponents and smooth
ergodic theory", Russian Math. Surveys 32:4 (1977), 55-114; A. Fathi, M. Herman, J.-C. Yoccoz, "A proof of Pesin's
stable manifold theorem", Geometric Dynamics, Springer LNM 1007 (1983), 177-215; subordinate
partitions: LY Part I, Section 3 (Lemma 3.1.1; also [LS], Proposition 3.1). The three originals above were not read;
checked parallel sources (read by the literature audit): Ruelle 1979 (as in X1), Section 6, Theorems 6.1 and 6.3 and Remark 6.4(b)
(local and global stable manifolds of C^(1,theta) maps, applied to the inverse map for W^u); LY Part I, Section 2
(Lyapunov charts) and Lemma 4.2.2 (Lipschitz control of the tangent field with a chart-dependent constant, hence uniform
on a Pesin block, not on the whole regular set); [LS], Proposition 3.3 (blocks with uniform local leaf size). Used in
Lemmas 19, 20, 22, 27, 28, 29.

X3 (cited). F. Ledrappier and L.-S. Young, "The metric entropy of diffeomorphisms. Part I: Characterization of measures
satisfying Pesin's entropy formula", Ann. of Math. (2) 122 (1985), no. 3, 509-539. Theorem A (1.5), p. 513: for a C^2
diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold and an invariant Borel probability, absolutely continuous conditionals
on unstable manifolds hold if and only if h = int sum lambda_i^+ dim E_i. LY state "We prove the 'if' part of Theorem A
in Part I"; the converse is attributed there to Sinai and stated to be proved in precise form in F. Ledrappier and J.-M. Strelcyn ([LS]), "A proof of the estimation from below in
Pesin's entropy formula", Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 2 (1982), 203-219 (see also R. Mane, "A proof of Pesin's
formula", Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 1 (1981), 95-102). Corollary 6.1.4 (p. 534): density formula for ergodic m
satisfying Pesin's formula; Corollary 6.2: the nonergodic case. D. Ruelle, "An inequality for the entropy of
differentiable maps", Bol. Soc. Brasil. Mat. 9 (1978), 83-87: h_mu(f) <= int sum lambda_i^+ dim E_i for a C^1 map of a
compact manifold. Used: Lemma 20 ([LS] for the lower bound, Ruelle for the upper bound), Lemma 24 ("if" part),
Lemma 27 ([LS] and Ruelle, as in Lemma 20), Lemma 28 (Corollaries 6.1.4 and 6.2), the proof of Theorem C item 6
(Corollary 6.1.4).

X4 (cited). Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem for maps and flows (G. D. Birkhoff, "Proof of the ergodic theorem",
Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. USA 17 (1931), 656-660); ergodic decomposition of invariant Borel probabilities on compact
metric spaces, with components identified by limits of a countable dense family of tests (V. A. Rohlin, "On the
fundamental ideas of measure theory", AMS Transl. (1) 10 (1962), 1-52). Used in Lemmas 15, 22, 24, 27 and 2C.2.9.

X5 (cited, two steps proved). Entropy: invariance under measurable conjugacy (cited); integral affinity,
h_(int mu_s dlambda(s))(T) = int h_(mu_s)(T) dlambda(s), including the value +infinity, for every measurable kernel
s -> mu_s of T-invariant probabilities on standard Borel spaces, with no ergodicity of the mu_s and no ergodic
decomposition, which is what Lemma 24 uses (not only finite convex affinity); and the iterate law
h_nu(T^p) = p h_nu(T) for a positive integer p (with B the join of T^(-i)A, 0 <= i < p, the n-fold T^p join of B is
the pn-fold T join of A, so h(T^p, B) = p h(T, A), while h(T^p, A) <= p h(T, A); no ergodicity, invertibility or
finite entropy is needed, A2477). The affinity step is the literature audit LIT303
(as summarized in the accompanying artifacts; independent proof
the accompanying artifacts): on the product probability the lifted finite parameter
partitions are invariant, conditioning on them lowers the block entropy by at most their own entropy, which does
not depend on the block length, two infima are interchanged, and one common increasing sequence of finite Borel
partitions generating the sigma algebra gives the full identity by monotone convergence (A2491-A2495; wording
as suggested in A2530). An earlier proof for kernels of ergodic probabilities is in
the accompanying artifacts, Sections 4-5 (A2478). So the
unread sources once cited for it (K. Jacobs; P. Walters, An Introduction to Ergodic Theory, GTM 79, Springer 1982,
Theorems 8.1 and 8.4) are not needed, and neither is Abramov's formula, of which the iterate law is the integer case
(L. M. Abramov, "On the entropy of a flow", Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR 128 (1959), 873-875). Used in Lemma 24.

X6 (cited). Existence and almost-everywhere uniqueness of disintegrations of finite Borel measures on compact metric
(Polish) spaces over a measurable map into a standard Borel space, or along a countably generated measurable partition,
modulo null sets (Rohlin 1962, as in X4; original not read). Used in Lemmas 12, 15, 20, 22.

Elementary facts used (cited, not proved): Lebesgue density theorem; Egorov's theorem; inner regularity;
Fubini-Tonelli; Tietze extension; separability of C(Q); Arzela-Ascoli; weak compactness of finite measures on compact
metric spaces and the portmanteau theorem; Radon-Nikodym; monotone and dominated convergence; second countability of
R^3; first Borel-Cantelli lemma; Poincare recurrence; Brouwer fixed point theorem; inverse function theorem; change of
variables; Gronwall's inequality; uniqueness for Lipschitz ODEs; Liouville's formula for det of the derivative of a
flow; Cartan's formula; mean value property of harmonic functions; Faa di Bruno formula; Taylor's formula with integral
remainder; invertibility of the Vandermonde matrix at distinct nodes; Jensen and log-sum inequalities; stereographic
projection.

### 2D. The helicity-sign Liouville theorem (item 1c(ii)-(iii))

Verification record. This reconstruction of the audited sources named in each lemma was recorded at 2026-11-04T03:26Z
and checked line by line at 03:34Z (see 2D.4). Every result in it carries
its own audit verdict (A309, A317-A319, A326-A328, A422, A430-A432). The repaired 988-line text was audited as a
text: CONFIRMED as a repaired proof-chain and source-attribution audit (A479, 05:02Z), with one minor published-text
qualification (Lemma 11(a) at Oseledets regular points), applied at 05:20Z. Inside 2D, a reference such as 2D.1.2 or "point n" is to this subsection and its list in 2D.4, and a reference
such as "A278 section 7" is to a section of the corresponding proof in the accompanying artifacts. Notation differs from
2A in the places listed in 2D.1.1: q = U.B; beta = 5 - 2/c, which 2A calls alpha; Gamma is the vortex flow.

Labels follow the summary of this report: PROVED means independently CONFIRMED by the auditor, with no hypothesis
beyond the problem class; CONDITIONAL means CONFIRMED in the same way under an extra hypothesis that is stated. Verdict numbers A0xx-A4xx refer to the audit record in the accompanying artifacts, which also contains the cited proofs for A430-A432.
The six precision items of the synthesis as summarized in the accompanying artifacts are marked P1-P6 where they are used.
Everything below is a reconstruction of audited sources; where this section supplies a step that the sources leave
implicit, this is said in the text and repeated in 2D.4.

#### 2D.1 Statement

##### 2D.1.1 Setting and notation

Fix c > 0 and omega in R. J(y1,y2,y3) = (-y2,y1,0), A = cI - omega J. The profile equation is

    (1-c)U + [(cI - omega J)y + U].grad U + omega J U + grad P = 0,    div U = 0,    U -> 0 at infinity.     (E)

"Decaying" means sup_{|y| >= R} |U(y)| -> 0 as R -> infinity. Notation:

- B = Ay + U, div B = 3c = d; Omega = curl U; a = 1-2c; kappa = 1+c; beta = 5 - 2/c (section 2A calls this
  exponent alpha). For 2/5 <= c < 1/2: 0 <= beta < 1, a > 0 and kappa > d.
- M = sup|U|; |.| is the Euclidean norm, ||.|| the operator norm; ||A|| = (c^2 + omega^2)^(1/2).
- Phi_t is the flow of B, Psi_t = Phi_(-t) is the flow of -B (the backward carrier), Gamma_s is the flow of Omega
  (complete by Lemma 3).
- O = {Omega != 0}, Z = {Omega = 0}, D_Z = int Z.
- h = U.Omega (helicity density), q = U.B. (section 2A uses q for |U|^2/2; here |U|^2/2 is always written out.)
- H = P + |U|^2/2 + (Ay).U; p_inf is the constant of Lemma 7; P0 = P - p_inf; H0 = H - p_inf.
- F = B x Omega and the one-form alpha = F.dy.
- E(R) = int_{|y|<R} |U|^2 dy; B_R = {|y| < R}; Leb is Lebesgue measure.
- For a Borel probability nu: Bas(nu) is the set of x with (1/T) int_0^T phi(Psi_t x) dt -> int phi dnu as
  T -> infinity for every bounded continuous phi (continuous-time basin); Bas^-(nu) is the same with Phi_t.

Identities (Lemma 2): aU + grad H0 = B x Omega; B.grad H0 = -a q; Omega.grad H0 = -a h; [B,Omega] = -kappa Omega;
Phi_t Gamma_s = Gamma_(s exp(kappa t)) Phi_t (Lemma 3).

##### 2D.1.2 Growth quantities (A398, A399, A430)

A closed ball Q = closure(B_(R_Q)) with R_Q > 0 is admissible if B(y).y >= b|y|^2 for |y| >= R_Q and some b > 0;
then B.y > 0 on and outside its boundary, as A398 requires. By Lemma 1(d) every R_Q >= 2M/c is admissible with b = c/2. Put
K = intersection_{t>=0} Psi_t(Q) and

    M_n = max(1, max_{y in Q} ||D Psi_n(y)||),    Lambda_core = lim_{n->infinity} n^-1 log M_n.

A398 (CONFIRMED): the limit exists, equals inf_n n^-1 log M_n, is independent of the admissible ball and of the norm,
and Lambda_core >= a when Omega is not identically 0. A399 (CONFIRMED; assumes Omega not identically 0):
Lambda_core = max(a, Gamma_Z), where Gamma_Z is the attained maximum of the top Lyapunov exponent of Psi over
full-flow-ergodic invariant probabilities on K cap ({B = 0} cup {Omega = 0}), with value -infinity if that set is
empty; every full-flow-ergodic invariant probability on K that is not concentrated on {B = 0} cup {Omega = 0}
(it then gives this closed invariant set zero mass) has spectrum (a, 0, -kappa).

Componentwise form (A430, CONFIRMED; U in C^r for an integer r >= 2, uniformly sublinear, 0 < c < 1/2, every omega). For each
nonempty connected component E of O put Q_E = Q cap closure(E), K_E = K cap closure(E),
Z_E = K_E cap ({B = 0} cup {Omega = 0}), M_n(E) = max(1, max_{Q_E} ||D Psi_n||), and
Lambda_E = lim_n n^-1 log M_n(E) = inf_n n^-1 log M_n(E). Let Gamma_E be the attained maximum of the largest
Lyapunov exponent of the backward flow Psi over full-flow-ergodic invariant probabilities supported on Z_E
(-infinity if Z_E is empty). Then Lambda_E = max(a, Gamma_E), independent of the admissible ball and the norm.

The two growth hypotheses are

    (C)  r(1-2c) > Lambda_core                                     (global form, A417, A422),
    (G)  Gamma_E < r(1-2c) for every connected component E of O   (componentwise form, A431, A432).

Facts used about them.
- (G) is equivalent to Lambda_E < r a for every E, and to: for each E there is an integer N_E >= 1 with
  log M_(N_E)(E) < r a N_E (A430-A431). No gap below r a uniform over components is assumed.
- (C) implies (G) (A432, section 7 of its proof). Directly: Q_E is a subset of Q, so M_n(E) <= M_n, hence
  Gamma_E <= max(a, Gamma_E) = Lambda_E <= Lambda_core < r a.
- When O is nonempty, (C) is equivalent to Gamma_Z < r a (A399). At r = 2, (C) reads a <= Lambda_core < 2a and (G)
  reads Gamma_E < 2a for every E. Both include point masses and measures of entropy zero.
- Neither (C) nor (G) is known to follow from decay; local Euler identities cannot give (C) (A415; see also A423),
  and A431 records that its sufficient condition "is additional and not automatic at C2".
- If O is empty, (G) is vacuous.

##### 2D.1.3 Main theorem

**Theorem L (CONDITIONAL on (G), a hypothesis of type H6, and on the helicity sign; A422 for the global form (C), A432 for the componentwise
form (G); both CONFIRMED in the auditor's ledger (the accompanying artifacts) as conditional theorems).** Let 2/5 <= c < 1/2, let omega be any
finite real number and let r >= 2 be an integer. Let U in C^r(R^3;R^3) and P in C^1(R^3) solve (E), with U decaying.
Assume (G). Let F be the family of compactly supported full-flow-ergodic vortical SRB probabilities supplied by A431
(by A417 if (C) holds), and for nu in F let D_nu be its invariant open essential basin domain (A223, Lemma 13). If,
for each nu in F, h >= 0 on D_nu or h <= 0 on D_nu (the sign may depend on nu), then U = 0.

In particular U = 0 if h >= 0 everywhere or h <= 0 everywhere; h = 0 everywhere is included. No Dini strain decay,
finite energy, axisymmetry, Fourier restriction, mixing, density of O, or nonsingular uniformly hyperbolic support is
assumed. After coverage the proof uses only U in C^2 and P in C^1.

Special case. Under (C) (equivalently Gamma_Z < r(1-2c) when O is nonempty), (G) holds and Theorem L is A422.

Equivalent form (Corollary L.1). Every nonzero decaying C^r profile in this range satisfying (G) has at least one
nu in F such that h takes both strict signs on D_nu, each on a nonempty open (hence positive-volume) subset; such a
nu gives full mass to {B != 0, Omega != 0}, has spectrum (1-2c, 0, -1-c) and entropy 1-2c, and its topological
support may meet either zero set. This is a conditional Liouville theorem and a necessary sign-changing-basin
condition; it does not exclude the sign-changing case and does not prove the main conjecture.

##### 2D.1.4 The C-infinity theorem

**Theorem L-infinity (CONDITIONAL on the helicity sign; proof complete, CONFIRMED A309).** The conclusion of Theorem L holds for U in C-infinity, P in C^1, decaying,
2/5 <= c < 1/2 and every omega, with F the family of Theorem C (A308) and no growth hypothesis.

It is the case of Theorem L where r is large: for C-infinity U, Lambda_core is finite, so some integer r satisfies
(C) (A422 section 6). 2D.2.21 also gives the direct proof from Proposition L0 and Theorem C, which is how A309
argues.

##### 2D.1.5 The coverage input and Proposition L0

**(CI) (coverage input).** F is an at most countable family of Borel probability measures on R^3 such that for each
nu in F:
- (CI-1) supp nu is compact; nu is invariant under Psi_t for every real t and ergodic for the flow (every Borel set
  invariant under all Psi_t has measure 0 or 1);
- (CI-2) nu({B != 0, Omega != 0}) = 1;
- (CI-3) the Lyapunov exponents of Psi_1 with respect to nu are a, 0, -kappa (each simple), and h_nu(Psi_1) = a;
- (CI-4) nu has absolutely continuous conditional measures on unstable manifolds of Psi_1 (implied by (CI-3); see
  Lemma 11(b); listed because the sources list it);

and moreover

- (CI-5) Leb(O minus union_{nu in F} Bas(nu)) = 0.

**Proposition L0 (CONDITIONAL on (CI); A278 with A283; the last sentence of A327).** Let 2/5 <= c < 1/2, omega
real, U in C^2, P in C^1, (E), U decaying, and let F satisfy (CI). If h has one sign on each D_nu, nu in F, then
U = 0.

The packaging of A278 (CONFIRMED with given vortical SRB properties, positive density, zero helicity on each basin
and separate coverage) and A283 (CONFIRMED for C^2 uniformly sublinear profiles, 0 < c < 1/2) as one proposition
is added in this section; A327's last sentence states the corresponding levelwise deduction "at C2 with a separately given
family of vortical SRB basins covering the vortical region" as a conditional conclusion.

Remark (weaker energy premise; CONDITIONAL on (CI) and the sign, as Proposition L0; CONFIRMED A3015 as a conditional
theorem; the accompanying artifacts, an independent reconstruction of the step
after coverage). Proposition L0 holds for every 0 < c < 1/2 and every finite omega with "U decaying" replaced by "U
bounded and E(R) = o(R) as R -> infinity", with Bas(nu) and D_nu as above. In the review the pressure is the
canonical one up to an additive constant, and the Bernoulli function less that constant has square integral o(R^3)
over B_R (section 4 of the review, as A3027 reads A3015); sublinear-volume recurrence of the vortex flow gives zero
helicity on each signed domain; and the product boxes, the transported Cesaro limit, the zero extension and the
positive stress test give U = 0. A decaying profile is bounded and satisfies Hb, so for 2/5 <= c < 1/2 Theorem 1
(section 2A) gives E(R) = o(R) (U in L^2 at c = 2/5, and E(R) = O(R^beta) with beta = 5 - 2/c < 1 for
2/5 < c < 1/2); hence the remark contains Proposition L0 (this deduction is the synthesis's and is checked in
A3027). Conversely, a bounded U with E(R) = o(R) satisfies Hb, since the integral of abs(U(Rx))^2 over abs(x) < L is
R^-3 E(LR) = o(R^-2); so for 0 < c < 1/2 the premise of the remark is equivalent to Hb, and for 0 < c < 2/5 Theorem
1(i) gives U = 0 without (CI). The remark thus replaces decay by Hb in Proposition L0 and adds content only for
2/5 <= c < 1/2 (integral-estimate analysis A109, as summarized in the accompanying artifacts; CONFIRMED A3026, for solutions of the profile equation and
not for arbitrary bounded functions). The positive-density theorem of Ledrappier and Young enters exactly as audited
in A2948-A2949. The comparisons of integral-estimate analysis (A108) and of the literature audit
(as summarized in the accompanying artifacts) are CONFIRMED with their diagnostic limits
(A3016): integral-estimate analysis's diagnostic script has thirteen symbolic calculations and one finite exact sample, sets no failing
exit code and is not a premise. The coverage, spectrum, entropy and sign hypotheses are assumed, not derived, and no
unconditional conclusion follows (A3017 OPEN).

##### 2D.1.6 Coverage theorems used as inputs (cited here; proved in 2C)

Names. Below, "Theorem C" is the abstract form, which 2C calls Theorem C' (2C.1.3), with its Euler application
(2C Theorem C); "Theorem C_r" (A417) is part (C) of 2C's Theorem C_r and "Theorem C_E" (A431) is its part (B). The
hypothesis labels (C) and (G) of 2D are not the part labels of 2C's Theorem C_r. In this report's labels, A417 and
A431 are CONDITIONAL on (C) and (G) respectively. 2C's Basin(nu) is 2D's Bas(nu), and 2C's D_i is D_(nu_i). Every
ball admissible in the sense of 2C Lemma 3 is admissible in the sense of 2D.1.2; K and the rates do not depend on the
choice (for nested admissible balls the cores coincide, A398, A430).

- **Theorem C (A308, CONFIRMED).** Let B, W be complete C-infinity fields on R^3 with div B = d > 0 constant,
  [B,W] = -kappa W, kappa > d, and B(y).y >= b0|y|^2 outside a ball. Then almost every point of {W != 0} belongs to
  the continuous-time basin of one of countably many probabilities, each ergodic for the full flow and supported in
  K, giving full mass to {B != 0, W != 0}, with spectrum (kappa-d, 0, -kappa), entropy kappa-d for Psi_1 and
  absolutely continuous full unstable conditionals; the basins have positive volume, lie in {W != 0} and cover
  almost every point of it; the family is nonempty if W is not identically 0. Euler application: nonconstant
  C-infinity uniformly sublinear profiles, 0 < c < 1/2, every omega, spectrum (1-2c, 0, -1-c). A308 asserts no C^2
  existence theorem. Source: the accompanying artifacts.
- **Theorem C_r (A417, CONFIRMED; uses A398-A399).** For integer r >= 2, U in C^r uniformly sublinear,
  0 < c < 1/2, any omega, (C) implies the conclusion of Theorem C (the "A308 class"), with A207/A223 giving the
  domains; supports may meet the zero sets. Source: the accompanying artifacts,
  sections 6-8.
- **Theorem C_E (A431, CONFIRMED as a conditional theorem; uses A430).** At the A430 hypotheses, (G) gives "exactly
  the A417 coverage package, spectrum (a,0,-kappa), entropy a, positive unstable densities and A223 essential basin
  domains"; the families of the countably many components are combined; supports lie in K_E subset int Q and may
  meet both zero sets. Source: the accompanying artifacts, sections 5-6.
- **Theorem C_strain (A312, CONFIRMED).** For an integer r >= 3, 0 < c < 1/2, U in C^r uniformly sublinear,
  Y = -rho(cy + U), where rho is a smooth radial cutoff equal to 1 on a neighborhood of an admissible ball
  Q = {abs(y) <= R1}, positive for abs(y) < R2 and 0 for abs(y) >= R2, with (cy + U).y >= b0 abs(y)^2 for abs(y) >= R1
  (so omega J y + Y = -B near Q), L = sup ||sym DY||, the condition (r-1)a > 3L gives the A308-type
  conclusion with A207/A223 domains. Source: the accompanying artifacts.

Each of these supplies a family F with (CI) for the profiles in its class (sections 2.20-2.21, 2.23).

##### 2D.1.7 Scope corrections A317-A319

- A317 (CONFIRMED at that exact regularity scope): for fixed omega and c in the OPEN interval (2/5, 1/2), in the class
  of decaying C-infinity profiles, and in the A312-restricted finite-r class, nonexistence (N) is equivalent to the
  absence (S) of an essential basin with both strict signs of h (Corollary L.2). The statement concerns at least one
  basin, not every basin, and not regular hyperbolic supports.
- A318 (REFUTED as a statement of task scope): C-infinity is not the posed class; the task starts from U in C^2.
  Replacement: for C-infinity profiles the remaining issue is a sign-changing essential basin; for the C^2 baseline
  both the coverage step and the unrestricted nonexistence problem remain open. Theorem L adds the C^2 profiles that
  satisfy (G); without (G) the C^2 coverage step is open.
- A319 (OPEN for the almost-every-line assertion): A283 does not give nonmonotonicity of H on almost every vortex
  line of a sign-changing basin. The safe statement is Corollary L.3.

concerns the family and uses (CI-5) (A2675). Lemmas 15-17 are the global step. Lemma 18 is the abstract crossing lemma
used only for Corollary L.4.

#### 2D.2 Lemmas and proofs

Standing assumptions unless stated otherwise: 0 < c < 1/2, omega real, U in C^2, P in C^1, (E), U decaying (so U is
bounded, M < infinity, and uniformly sublinear).

##### Lemma 1 (carrier flow). Source: A277 section 3, A048, A422 section 4.

(a) B is C^r if U is C^r, |B(y)| <= ||A|| |y| + M, and Phi, Psi are complete C^1 flows.
(b) For t >= 0 and all y:
    |Phi_t y| <= e^(ct)(|y| + M/c),   |Phi_t y| >= e^(ct)(|y| - M/c) + M/c,
    |Psi_t y| <= e^(-ct)|y| + (1 - e^(-ct)) M/c <= max(|y|, M/c).
(c) det D Phi_t = e^(3ct), det D Psi_t = e^(-3ct).
(d) B(y).y >= (c/2)|y|^2 for |y| >= 2M/c.
(e) Every closed ball of radius R_Q >= M/c is forward invariant under Psi.
(f) Every compact set invariant under all Phi_t lies in {|y| <= M/c}. If Q is admissible with R_Q >= 2M/c, then K is
    compact, invariant under all Psi_t, and every compact invariant set (in particular supp nu for nu as in (CI-1))
    lies in K.
(g) grad P = -(1-c)U - (DU)B - omega JU is C^(r-1), so P is C^r, H and H0 are C^2, Omega is C^(r-1), in particular
    C^1.

Proof. (a) B is locally Lipschitz with linear growth, so solutions exist for all times (external theorem X1).
(b) z(t) = Phi_t y solves z' = Az + U(z), so z(t) = e^(At) y + int_0^t e^(A(t-s)) U(z(s)) ds. Since cI and J commute,
e^(At) = e^(ct) e^(-omega t J) and e^(-omega t J) is a rotation about the y3-axis, of norm 1. Hence
|z(t)| <= e^(ct)|y| + M(e^(ct) - 1)/c <= e^(ct)(|y| + M/c) and |z(t)| >= e^(ct)|y| - M(e^(ct) - 1)/c. For Psi,
z' = -Az - U(z) gives |Psi_t y| <= e^(-ct)|y| + M(1 - e^(-ct))/c, a convex combination of |y| and M/c.
(c) Liouville's formula (X1) with div B = 3c.
(d) (Ay).y = c|y|^2 - omega (Jy).y = c|y|^2, so B.y >= c|y|^2 - M|y| >= (c/2)|y|^2 when |y| >= 2M/c.
(e) From (b).
(f) Let K' be compact and invariant, contained in B_(R'). For x in K' and t >= 0, x = Psi_t(Phi_t x) with Phi_t x in
K', so |x| <= e^(-ct) R' + M/c by (b); let t -> infinity. For K: Psi_t Q is a subset of Q by (e), so the sets
Psi_t Q decrease in t, K is compact, and Psi_s K = intersection_{t >= s} Psi_t Q = K for s >= 0 (Psi_s is a
bijection); applying Psi_(-s) gives the case s < 0. A compact invariant K' lies in closure(B_(M/c)), a subset of Q,
and K' = Psi_t K' is a subset of Psi_t Q for all t >= 0, so K' is a subset of K. The support of an invariant
probability under a flow of homeomorphisms is invariant.
(g) Solve (E) for grad P; (B.grad)U = (DU)B with (DU)_ij = d_j U_i. The right side is C^(r-1) since U, B are C^r.
H = P + |U|^2/2 + (Ay).U is then C^r, in particular C^2. []

##### Lemma 2 (identities). Source: A199, A277 section 1, A422 section 3, P6.

(a) (Lamb form) aU + grad H = B x Omega, hence the same with H0.
(b) B.grad H0 = -a q and Omega.grad H0 = -a h.
(c) [B, Omega] := (B.grad)Omega - (Omega.grad)B = -kappa Omega.
(d) (Cauchy) D Phi_t(x) Omega(x) = e^(kappa t) Omega(Phi_t x) and D Phi_t(x) B(x) = B(Phi_t x) for all real t;
    equivalently D Psi_t(x) Omega(x) = e^(-kappa t) Omega(Psi_t x). O and Z are invariant under Phi and Psi.
(e) (alpha law) (D Psi_t(x))^T F(Psi_t x) = e^(at) F(x); alpha(B) = alpha(Omega) = 0.
(f) H0 = P0 - |U|^2/2 + U.B.

Proof. (a) For any v, ((DU) - (DU)^T)v = Omega x v (check the first component:
(d_2U_1 - d_1U_2)v_2 + (d_3U_1 - d_1U_3)v_3 = Omega_2 v_3 - Omega_3 v_2). So (DU)B = (DU)^T B + Omega x B. Further
(DU)^T U = grad(|U|^2/2), and grad((Ay).U) = A^T U + (DU)^T(Ay) with A^T = cI + omega J. Hence
(DU)B = grad(|U|^2/2 + (Ay).U) - cU - omega JU + Omega x B. Substituting in (E):
(1-2c)U + grad H + Omega x B = 0, which is (a). grad H0 = grad H.
(b) Dot (a) with B and with Omega; B.(B x Omega) = Omega.(B x Omega) = 0.
(c) H0 is C^2, so curl grad H0 = 0 and curl of (a) gives a Omega = curl(B x Omega). For C^1 fields,
curl(B x Omega) = B div Omega - Omega div B + (Omega.grad)B - (B.grad)Omega, with div Omega = 0 and div B = 3c. So
(B.grad)Omega - (Omega.grad)B = -(3c + a)Omega = -kappa Omega.
(d) Fix x. v(t) = D Phi_t(x) Omega(x) solves v' = DB(Phi_t x) v, v(0) = Omega(x) (X1). For
w(t) = e^(kappa t) Omega(Phi_t x), w' = kappa w + e^(kappa t)[(B.grad)Omega](Phi_t x)
= kappa w + e^(kappa t)[DB Omega - kappa Omega](Phi_t x) = DB(Phi_t x) w by (c), and w(0) = Omega(x). The linear
equation has continuous coefficients, so v = w for all real t. This uses only B and Omega in C^1. The identity for B
holds because Phi is the flow of B. Invertibility of D Phi_t gives invariance of O and Z.
(e) For an invertible matrix L, (Lv) x (Lw) = det(L) L^(-T)(v x w). With L = D Psi_t(x), (d) and Lemma 1(c):
F(Psi_t x) = (LB(x)) x (e^(kappa t) L Omega(x)) = e^(kappa t) e^(-3ct) L^(-T) F(x). So L^T F(Psi_t x) = e^(at) F(x)
because kappa - 3c = a. F is orthogonal to B and Omega.
(f) (Ay).U = (B - U).U. []

##### Lemma 3 (complete vortex flow). Source: A048, A283, A309 section 3, A422 section 3.

For rho >= 0 put m_rho = 1 + max_{|z| <= rho+1} |Omega(z)| and delta_rho = 1/m_rho; for x put
rho_x = max(|x|, M/c).
(a) Omega is complete; its flow Gamma satisfies Phi_t Gamma_s = Gamma_(s exp(kappa t)) Phi_t for all real s, t.
(b) For compact K', rho' = max(max_{K'}|x|, M/c), delta = delta_(rho') and C_(K') = rho' + 1 + M/c:
    sup_{x in K'} |Gamma_s x| <= C_(K') (1 + |s|/delta)^theta,   theta = c/(1+c).
(c) If r >= 0 and |tau| e^(-kappa r) <= delta_(rho_y), then |Psi_r Gamma_tau y - Psi_r y| <= (m_(rho_y) - 1)|tau| e^(-kappa r).
(d) det D Gamma_s = 1, and each Gamma_s is a C^1 diffeomorphism fixing every point of Z; Gamma_s(O) = O.

Proof. Omega is C^1 (Lemma 1(g)). For |x| <= rho the local solution of z' = Omega(z), z(0) = x, exists for
|s| <= delta_rho and stays in B_(rho+1), since its speed is at most m_rho - 1 there and delta_rho (m_rho - 1) < 1;
call it Gamma^loc_s x. Local conjugacy: for |z| <= rho, real tau and |sigma| <= delta_rho, the curve
u -> Phi_tau(Gamma^loc_(u e^(-kappa tau)) z), defined for |u| <= |sigma| e^(kappa tau), has derivative
e^(-kappa tau) D Phi_tau Omega(Gamma^loc_(u e^(-kappa tau)) z) = Omega(Phi_tau Gamma^loc_(u e^(-kappa tau)) z) by
Lemma 2(d), so it is the integral curve of Omega through Phi_tau z.
Definition: given x and s, choose T >= 0 with |s| e^(-kappa T) <= delta_(rho_x); |Psi_T x| <= rho_x by Lemma 1(b).
Put Gamma_s x = Phi_T Gamma^loc_(s e^(-kappa T)) Psi_T x. For T' > T, apply the local conjugacy with
z = Psi_(T') x, tau = T' - T, u = s e^(-kappa T): Phi_(T'-T) Gamma^loc_(s e^(-kappa T')) Psi_(T') x is the integral
curve of Omega through Psi_T x at time s e^(-kappa T), which by uniqueness is Gamma^loc_(s e^(-kappa T)) Psi_T x
(|s| e^(-kappa T) <= delta_(rho_x)). Applying Phi_T shows that the definition does not depend on T. The same
computation shows that s -> Gamma_s x is an integral curve of Omega defined for all s, so Omega is complete and Gamma
is its flow. For the conjugacy, s -> Phi_t Gamma_(s e^(-kappa t)) x has derivative e^(-kappa t) D Phi_t Omega =
Omega(Phi_t Gamma_(s e^(-kappa t)) x), so it equals Gamma_s Phi_t x by uniqueness, for all real t.
(b) Take T = kappa^-1 log(1 + |s|/delta); then |s| e^(-kappa T) = |s|/(1 + |s|/delta) <= delta. The inner point
w = Gamma^loc_(s e^(-kappa T)) Psi_T x lies in B_(rho'+1), so |Gamma_s x| = |Phi_T w| <= e^(cT)(rho' + 1 + M/c)
= C_(K')(1 + |s|/delta)^(c/kappa) by Lemma 1(b).
(c) By (a) with t = -r, Psi_r Gamma_tau y = Gamma_(tau e^(-kappa r)) Psi_r y, and |Psi_r y| <= rho_y. Under the
stated bound the vortex segment is a local one in B_(rho_y + 1), traversed at speed at most m_(rho_y) - 1.
(d) div Omega = 0 and Liouville's formula (X1). Points of Z are equilibria of Omega; Gamma_s is a bijection, so it
maps Z onto Z and O onto O. []

##### Lemma 4 (recurrence of the vortex flow; P1). Source: A049, A283, A422 section 3.

There is a Borel set R of full Lebesgue measure such that for every x in R, every eps > 0 and every integer N != 0,
there are infinitely many j >= 1 with |Gamma_(jN) x - x| < eps. In particular x returns within eps at arbitrarily
large positive times (N >= 1) and at arbitrarily large negative times (N <= -1).

Proof. Fix N != 0 and a bounded open ball W with rational center and radius. Let
W'_N = {x in W : Gamma_(jN) x not in W for all j >= 1}, a Borel set. The sets Gamma_(kN) W'_N, k >= 0, are pairwise
disjoint: if Gamma_(kN) x = Gamma_(lN) x' with x, x' in W'_N and k < l, then x = Gamma_((l-k)N) x' lies in W,
contradicting x' in W'_N. Each has volume Leb(W'_N) by Lemma 3(d). By Lemma 3(b) with K' = closure(W), for
0 <= k <= n they all lie in a ball of radius C_(K')(1 + n|N|/delta)^theta. Hence

    (n+1) Leb(W'_N) <= (4 pi/3) C_(K')^3 (1 + n|N|/delta)^(3 theta).

Since 3 theta = 3c/(1+c) < 1 exactly when c < 1/2, dividing by n+1 and letting n -> infinity gives Leb(W'_N) = 0.
Let X(W,N) be the set of x in W with only finitely many j >= 1 such that Gamma_(jN) x is in W. For such x let j0 be
the largest such j (j0 = 0 if there is none); then Gamma_(j0 N) x is in W'_N. So X(W,N) is contained in the
countable union over j0 >= 0 of Gamma_(-j0 N)(W'_N), which is null. X(W,N) is Borel. Let R be the complement of the
union of X(W,N) over all rational balls W and all N != 0. Given x in R, eps and N, choose a rational ball W with x in
W, contained in B(x, eps); x is not in X(W,N). []

This is P1: the wandering-set argument is applied to Gamma_N for every N >= 1 and to Gamma_(-N), each volume
preserving with the same polynomial confinement, so returns occur in N Z_+ for every N. No bounded vortex lines or
finite total volume are used.

##### Lemma 5 (one sign gives zero helicity). Source: A283, A422 section 3.

Let D be open with Gamma_s(D) = D for all real s. If h >= 0 on D, or h <= 0 on D, then h = 0 on D.

Proof. Suppose h >= 0 on D and h(x0) > 0 for some x0 in D. For z in D put f_z(t) = H(Gamma_t z); by Lemma 2(b),
f_z'(t) = -a h(Gamma_t z) <= 0 since Gamma_t z is in D, so f_z is nonincreasing on R. The map (t, z) ->
h(Gamma_t z) is continuous (X1), so there are t0 > 0 and an open ball V0 containing x0, contained in D, with
h(Gamma_t z) >= h(x0)/2 for z in V0 and 0 <= t <= t0. Put eta = a t0 h(x0)/2 > 0; then f_z(t) <= f_z(0) - eta for
z in V0 and t >= t0. Shrink V0 to an open ball V containing x0 with |H(z) - H(x0)| < eta/4 on V. V has positive
volume, so it contains a point x of R (Lemma 4). Choose eps with B(x, eps) contained in V and, by Lemma 4 with N = 1,
an integer j >= t0 with Gamma_j x in B(x, eps). Then |H(Gamma_j x) - H(x)| < eta/2, while
H(Gamma_j x) = f_x(j) <= H(x) - eta. Contradiction. For h <= 0 replace H by -H, for which Omega.grad(-H) = -a(-h). []

##### Lemma 6 (both signs along recurrent vortex lines). Source: A283; used only in Corollary L.3.

If x is in R and h(x) != 0, then for every T > 0 there are t1, t2 > T and t3, t4 < -T with
h(Gamma_(t1) x) > 0 > h(Gamma_(t2) x) and h(Gamma_(t3) x) > 0 > h(Gamma_(t4) x). In particular H is not monotone
along the vortex line of x.

Proof. Suppose h(x) > 0 (otherwise replace (H, h) by (-H, -h)). By continuity choose an open ball V around x,
delta > 0 and m > 0 with h(Gamma_s z) >= m for z in V and 0 <= s <= delta. Put eta = a m delta and choose an open ball
V' around x, contained in V, with |H - H(x)| < eta/4 on V'. Let f(t) = H(Gamma_t x). By Lemma 4 there is an integer
n > T with Gamma_n x in V'; then h(Gamma_(n+s) x) >= m > 0 for s in [0, delta], and
f(n + delta) <= f(n) - eta < f(0) - 3eta/4. By Lemma 4 again there is an integer n' > n + delta with Gamma_(n') x in
V', so f(n') > f(0) - eta/4 > f(n + delta). The mean value theorem gives t in (n + delta, n') with f'(t) > 0, that
is h(Gamma_t x) < 0. For negative times apply the same argument to the flow Gamma'_t = Gamma_(-t) of -Omega with
H' = -H: then d/dt H'(Gamma'_t x) = -a h(Gamma'_t x), and Lemma 4 with N <= -1 supplies the returns. []

##### Lemma 7 (canonical Bernoulli function and its mean decay). Source: A277 section 2, A031, A040, section 2A.

Assume U in C^1, P in C^1, (E), U decaying, 2/5 <= c < 1/2. Then:
(a) E(R) <= C_E R^beta for R >= 1, where C_E = ||U||_2^2 if c = 2/5 (U is in L^2 by 2A Theorem A(ii)) and
    C_E = 2^beta (L + C_A/2) if 2/5 < c < 1/2, with L and C_A the limit and the constant of (2.1.1).
(b) S(rho) := int_{|z| >= rho} |U(z)|^2 |z|^-3 dz <= C_S rho^(beta-3) for rho >= 1/2, C_S = 2^beta C_E/(1 - 2^(beta-3)).
(c) There is a constant p_inf such that P0 = P - p_inf satisfies int_{B_R} P0^2 <= C_P R^beta for R >= 1, with
    C_P = 2^(1+beta) M^2 C_E + 2^(2 beta + 1) C_S^2/(3 pi).
(d) H0 = H - p_inf satisfies int_{B_R} H0^2 <= C_H R^(beta+2) for R >= 1, with
    C_H = 3[C_P + M^2 C_E/4 + (c^2 + omega^2) C_E], and (1/|B_R|) int_{B_R} H0^2 <= (3 C_H/(4 pi)) R^(beta-1) -> 0.
(e) If k is a constant with (1/|B_R|) int_{B_R} (H0 + k)^2 -> 0, then k = 0. In particular, if H0 is constant then
    H0 = 0, and p_inf is the unique constant for which the normalized quadratic mean of H - p_inf tends to 0.

Proof. U decaying implies Hb (section 2A, 2.0), and H0(C^1) holds.
(a) If c = 2/5, Theorem A(ii) gives U in L^2, so E(R) <= ||U||_2^2 and beta = 0. If 2/5 < c < 1/2, (2.1.1) gives
E(R) <= (L + C_A R^-1) R^beta <= (L + C_A/2) R^beta for R >= 2; for 1 <= R <= 2, E(R) <= E(2) <= (L + C_A/2) 2^beta
<= 2^beta (L + C_A/2) R^beta. (This is the bound E(R) <= C R^beta of A040 and 2A Sharpness (a).)
(b) Split into shells 2^k rho <= |z| < 2^(k+1) rho, k >= 0. Since 2^(k+1) rho >= 1, each contributes at most
(2^k rho)^-3 C_E (2^(k+1) rho)^beta = 2^beta C_E rho^(beta-3) 2^(k(beta-3)); sum the geometric series (beta < 3).
(c) Write F_ij = U_i U_j and |K_ij(w)u_i u_j| <= |u|^2/(2 pi |w|^3) (2A, proof of (2.3.4)). For R > 0 (the range
of 2A Lemma 2.3) put N_R = sum_ij T_ij(F_ij 1_{|z| < 4R}) (in L^2), Far_R(x) = int_{|z| >= 4R} sum_ij K_ij(x - z)
F_ij(z) dz for |x| < 2R, and c_R = int_{|z| >= 4R} sum_ij K_ij(-z) F_ij(z) dz. For |x| < 2R and |z| >= 4R,
|x - z| >= |z|/2, so both integrands are bounded by (4/pi)|U(z)|^2|z|^-3, and the integrals converge absolutely
because S(rho) < infinity for every rho > 0 (by (b) if rho >= 1/2; if rho < 1/2, the shell rho <= |z| < 1/2 adds at
most M^2 4 pi log(1/(2 rho))). Hence 2A's Pi_3 = Far_R - c_R, Pi_1 + Pi_2 = N_R, and Lemma 2.3 gives
P = (p_R - c_R) + N_R + Far_R a.e. on B_(2R).
Consistency: for R' > R, N_(R') - N_R = sum_ij T_ij(F_ij 1_{4R <= |z| < 4R'}) is T_ij applied to a bounded compactly
supported function whose support has distance >= 2R from B_(2R); by (F1) it equals
int_{4R <= |z| < 4R'} sum K_ij(x - z) F_ij dz = Far_R(x) - Far_(R')(x) on B_(2R). So N_(R') + Far_(R') = N_R + Far_R
a.e. on B_(2R), and comparing the two decompositions on B_(2R) gives p_(R') - c_(R') = p_R - c_R. Define p_inf as
this common value (it does not depend on R > 0); then P0 = N_R + Far_R a.e. on B_(2R) for every R > 0, and in
particular P0 = N_(R/2) + Far_(R/2) a.e. on B_R.
Bound on B_R, R >= 1: by Plancherel and Cauchy-Schwarz as in the proof of (2.3.3),
||N_(R/2)||_2^2 <= int_{|z| < 2R} |U|^4 <= M^2 E(2R) <= 2^beta M^2 C_E R^beta. For |x| < R and |z| >= 2R,
|x - z| >= |z|/2, so |Far_(R/2)(x)| <= (4/pi) S(2R) <= (4/pi) C_S (2R)^(beta-3). Hence
int_{B_R} P0^2 <= 2||N_(R/2)||_2^2 + 2(4 pi R^3/3)(16/pi^2) C_S^2 (2R)^(2beta-6)
= 2^(1+beta) M^2 C_E R^beta + (2^(2beta+1)/(3 pi)) C_S^2 R^(2beta-3) <= C_P R^beta, since 2beta - 3 < beta and R >= 1.
(d) H0 = P0 + |U|^2/2 + (Ay).U, |Ay| <= (c^2 + omega^2)^(1/2)|y| (|Ay|^2 = c^2|y|^2 + omega^2(y1^2 + y2^2)), so
int_{B_R} H0^2 <= 3[C_P R^beta + (M^2/4) E(R) + (c^2 + omega^2) R^2 E(R)] <= C_H R^(beta+2) for R >= 1. Divide by
|B_R| = 4 pi R^3/3; beta < 1.
(e) By the triangle inequality in the normalized L^2(B_R) norm, |k| <= ||H0 + k|| + ||H0|| -> 0. []

##### Lemma 8 (transported decay). Source: A277 section 3, A278 section 3.

Under the hypotheses of Lemma 7, for every bounded measurable set Q' contained in B_(R') with R' >= 1 and every
t >= 0,

    int_{Q'} H0(Phi_t y)^2 dy <= C_(Q') e^(-2at),   C_(Q') = C_H (R' + M/c)^(beta+2),

and (1/T) int_0^T int_{Q'} H0(Phi_t y)^2 dy dt <= C_(Q')/(2aT).

Proof. Substitute z = Phi_t y, dy = e^(-3ct) dz (Lemma 1(c)); Phi_t(Q') is contained in B_(rho_t) with
rho_t = e^(ct)(R' + M/c) >= 1 (Lemma 1(b)). By Lemma 7(d) the integral is at most
e^(-3ct) C_H rho_t^(beta+2) = C_(Q') e^(c(beta-1)t), and c(beta - 1) = 4c - 2 = -2a. Integrate in t. []

##### Lemma 9 (basins). Source: A223, A278 sections 4-5; parts (d) and (f) are written out in this section.

Let nu be a Borel probability with (CI-1). Then:
(a) Psi_r(Bas(nu)) = Bas(nu) and Phi_r(Bas^-(nu)) = Bas^-(nu) for all real r.
(b) Bas(nu) is a subset of O if nu(O) > 0.
(c) Gamma_tau(Bas(nu)) = Bas(nu) for all real tau.
(d) Bas(nu) and Bas^-(nu) are Borel sets.
(e) Distinct probabilities have disjoint basins.
(f) nu(Bas(nu)) = nu(Bas^-(nu)) = 1.
(g) G^+ = supp nu cap Bas(nu) and G^- = supp nu cap Bas^-(nu) are Borel with nu-measure 1.

Proof. Write A_T phi(x) = (1/T) int_0^T phi(Psi_t x) dt.
(a) A_T phi(Psi_r x) - A_T phi(x) = (1/T)[int_T^(T+r) - int_0^r] phi(Psi_t x) dt, of absolute value at most
2|r| ||phi||_inf / T. The same for Phi.
(b) phi = min(1, |Omega|) is bounded continuous with int phi dnu > 0. If Omega(x) = 0 then Omega(Psi_t x) = 0 for all
t (Lemma 2(d)) and A_T phi(x) = 0, so x is not in Bas(nu).
(c) Let y be in Bas(nu), tau real, y' = Gamma_tau y. For r >= r1, where |tau| e^(-kappa r1) <= delta_(rho_y), Lemma 3(c)
gives |Psi_r y' - Psi_r y| <= (m_(rho_y) - 1)|tau| e^(-kappa r). Both forward orbits lie in B_(rho*) with
rho* = max(rho_y, rho_(y')) (Lemma 1(b)). A bounded continuous phi is uniformly continuous on closure(B_(rho*+1)), so
phi(Psi_r y') - phi(Psi_r y) -> 0 as r -> infinity, and the Cesaro averages have the same limit. So y' is in
Bas(nu); apply this with -tau for equality.
(d) Fix continuous cutoffs chi_n with 0 <= chi_n <= 1, chi_n = 1 on closure(B_n) and chi_n = 0 outside B_(2n), and
let p_k enumerate the polynomials with rational coefficients. The functions chi_n p_k and chi_n form a countable
family (f_j) that is uniformly dense in C_0(R^3): for f in C_0 and eps > 0 choose n with |f| < eps outside B_n and k
with |f - p_k| < eps on closure(B_(2n)) (X10); then |f - chi_n p_k| < 2 eps everywhere. Let E be the set of x with
A_T f_j(x) -> int f_j dnu for every j. For T >= 1 and N = floor(T), |A_T f_j - A_N f_j| <= 2||f_j||_inf / N, and
x -> A_N f_j(x) is continuous (joint continuity of the flow, X1), so E is a countable intersection of Borel sets.
At x in E the convergence holds for every f in C_0, by uniform density. Take n >= M/c, so chi_n = 1 on supp nu
(Lemma 1(f)) and A_T chi_n(x) -> 1. For bounded continuous phi, phi chi_n is in C_0, int phi chi_n dnu = int phi dnu
and |A_T phi(x) - A_T(phi chi_n)(x)| <= ||phi||_inf (1 - A_T chi_n(x)) -> 0. Hence E = Bas(nu), which is Borel. No
bound on the orbit of x was used, so the same argument applied to Phi shows that Bas^-(nu) is Borel. (Repaired
2026-11-03 04:46Z after the auditor audit as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, section 2. The earlier proof used the
forward boundedness of Psi orbits and asserted the same proof for Bas^-(nu); that step fails, because forward Phi
orbits outside supp nu can leave every fixed ball.)
(e) If x is in both basins, int phi dnu = int phi dnu' for all bounded continuous phi, so nu = nu' (X10).
(f) Fix bounded continuous phi and put g(x) = int_0^1 phi(Psi_t x) dt, bounded continuous. Then
A_N phi(x) = (1/N) sum_{n=0}^{N-1} g(Psi_n x). Psi_1 preserves nu, so Birkhoff's theorem (X6) gives a nu-a.e. limit
g* with int g* dnu = int g dnu = int phi dnu (invariance of nu and Fubini). Let phi*(x) = limsup_N A_N phi(x), a
Borel function; by (a) and the integer reduction, phi* is invariant under every Psi_r. Ergodicity of the flow makes
each sublevel set of phi* of measure 0 or 1, so phi* is nu-a.e. a constant; it equals g* a.e., so the constant is
int phi dnu. Thus A_T phi(x) -> int phi dnu for nu-a.e. x. Apply this to the countable family (f_j) of (d); since the set E of (d)
equals Bas(nu), nu(Bas(nu)) = 1. The same for Phi, for which nu is also invariant and ergodic.
(g) supp nu is closed and has full measure. []

##### Lemma 10 (Oseledets directions). Source: A199, A223, A399.

Let nu satisfy (CI-1)-(CI-3). There is a Borel set Reg with nu(Reg) = 1 such that for x in Reg there is a splitting
R^3 = E^u(x) + E^0(x) + E^s(x) into lines with exponents a, 0, -kappa, the two-sided limit property of X7 holds, and

    E^s(x) = R Omega(x),   E^0(x) = R B(x),   F(x) != 0,   alpha_x(e) != 0 for every nonzero e in E^u(x).

Proof. Apply X7 to Psi_1 on the compact invariant set supp nu (D Psi_1 and its inverse are bounded there); intersect
the regular set with the full-measure set {B != 0, Omega != 0} of (CI-2). Write v = v_u + v_0 + v_s. By Lemma 2(d),
|D Psi_n(x) Omega(x)| = e^(-kappa n)|Omega(Psi_n x)| <= e^(-kappa n) max_{supp nu}|Omega|, so the forward limit
lim_{n->+infinity} n^-1 log|D Psi_n Omega(x)| is at most -kappa. By X7 it equals the largest exponent among the
nonzero components; hence only v_s is nonzero, and Omega(x) is in E^s(x). Next D Psi_n(x) B(x) = B(Psi_n x) is
bounded by C = max_{supp nu}|B| for all integers n. The forward limit is at most 0, so v_u = 0. For n -> -infinity,
n^-1 log|B(Psi_n x)| >= n^-1 log C -> 0 (division by negative n reverses the inequality), and by X7 this limit is the
smallest exponent among the nonzero components, so v_s = 0. Hence B(x) is in E^0(x). Simple spectrum makes each
subspace a line. B(x), Omega(x) are nonzero and lie in different Oseledets lines, so they are independent and
F(x) = B(x) x Omega(x) != 0. Since F(x) is orthogonal to span(B(x), Omega(x)) = E^0(x) + E^s(x) and E^u(x) is not in
that plane, alpha_x(e) = F(x).e != 0 for nonzero e in E^u(x). []

##### Lemma 11 (unstable conditionals). Source: Ledrappier-Young Part I (X9); A207 for part (c).

Let nu satisfy (CI-1)-(CI-3) and let Q be admissible with R_Q =: R1 >= 2M/c + 1.
(a) (Compact model.) There are a C^r diffeomorphism f of S^3 and a smooth Riemannian metric g on S^3 such that g is
    Euclidean on B_(R1+3) (identifying R^3 with S^3 minus a point), f = Psi_1 on B_(R1+1), f^-1 = Phi_1 on a
    neighborhood of K, and for Oseledets regular x in K the unstable manifold W^u_f(x) is contained in K and
    coincides with the unstable manifold of Psi_1. (At nonregular points only the set of exponentially backward
    asymptotic points is meant; no smooth manifold is asserted there, A479.)
(b) nu is f-invariant with exponents a, 0, -kappa and h_nu(f) = a. Hence nu has absolutely continuous conditional
    measures on unstable manifolds (this gives (CI-4)), and there is a measurable partition xi subordinate to W^u such
    that, for nu-a.e. x: xi(x) is contained in W^u(x), which is a C^1 curve tangent to E^u(x) at x; xi(x) contains an
    open neighborhood of x in W^u(x); and the conditional measure nu_x on xi(x) has a density rho_x with respect to
    arclength lambda_x that is strictly positive and finite on xi(x), with lambda_x(xi(x)) < infinity. In particular
    nu_x and lambda_x restricted to xi(x) are equivalent.
(c) (A207) Moreover rho_x = C_x ell on xi(x), where ell(w) = |alpha_w(e^u(w))| and e^u(w) is a unit tangent to the
    leaf at w; ell > 0 on xi(x).

Only (b) is used later; (c) is recorded because A422 cites A207 for the positive densities.

Proof. (a) Choose R1 < R2 < R3 with R2 = R1 + 1, R3 = R1 + 2 and a smooth radial cutoff rho_c with rho_c = 1 on
B_(R2) and rho_c = 0 outside B_(R3). X = -rho_c B is C^r with compact support, so it extends by 0 to a C^r field on
S^3 = R^3 cup {infinity} (stereographic chart); let theta_t be its flow and f = theta_1. Let g = chi g_Euc +
(1 - chi) g_round with chi smooth, chi = 1 on B_(R3+1), chi = 0 outside B_(R3+2): a convex combination of positive
definite forms, smooth on S^3. For |x| < R2, Lemma 1(b) keeps Psi_t x in B_(max(|x|, M/c)), a subset of B_(R2), for
t in [0, 1], where X = -B; so theta_t x = Psi_t x there and f = Psi_1 on B_(R2). K lies in closure(B_(M/c))
(Lemma 1(f)) and Phi_t K = K, so by continuity Phi_t x stays in B_(R2) for t in [0, 1] and x in a neighborhood of K;
there theta_(-t) x = Phi_t x and f^-1 = Phi_1.
The set {|y| >= R1} is forward invariant under theta_(-t), t >= 0 (the flow of rho_c B): on it
d/dt |y|^2 = 2 rho_c B.y >= 0 by Lemma 1(d) (R1 >= 2M/c), with strict inequality at |y| = R1 where rho_c = 1; if a
solution starting in {|y| >= R1} had |y| < R1 at some time, at the last earlier time with |y| = R1 the derivative of
|y|^2 would be positive, a contradiction. Now let x be in K and y in W^u_f(x), so d(f^-n y, f^-n x) -> 0. Since
dist(K, {|y| >= R1}) >= R1 - M/c >= 1, there is n0 with |f^-n y| < R1 for n >= n0. If |theta_(-t) y| >= R1 for some
t >= 0, forward invariance gives |theta_(-m) y| >= R1 for all integers m >= t, which is false for large m. So
theta_(-t) y is in Q for all t >= 0; on Q, theta_(-t) = Phi_t, so Phi_t y is in Q for all t >= 0, that is y is in
Psi_t(Q) for all t >= 0, and y is in K. Conversely, let y be in the unstable set of Psi_1 at x. Then Phi_n y
approaches Phi_n x, which stays in the compact set K, so sup over n >= 0 of |Phi_n(y)| is finite; by the upper bound
of Lemma 1(b) on [0, 1] the whole forward Phi orbit of y is bounded, and the lower bound of Lemma 1(b) at the point
Phi_s(y), namely |Phi_(t+s)(y)| >= e^(ct)(|Phi_s(y)| - M/c) + M/c for t >= 0, gives |Phi_s(y)| <= M/c for every
s >= 0. So Phi_s y is in Q for all s >= 0, and y is in K (A2673). On K, f = Psi_1 and f^-1 = Phi_1, so the unstable
manifolds of f and of Psi_1 at x coincide.
(b) supp nu lies in K (Lemma 1(f)) where f = Psi_1, so nu is f-invariant; Df^n = D Psi_n along orbits in K for all
integers n, and g is Euclidean near K, so the exponents agree; f and Psi_1 coincide on the invariant set K of full
measure, so h_nu(f) = h_nu(Psi_1) = a = the sum of the positive exponents. f is C^2 on a compact manifold. LY
Theorem A (1.5) (the "if" direction, proved in Part I; no ergodicity is required) gives absolutely continuous
conditionals on unstable manifolds (Definition 1.4.2). LY Lemma 3.1.1 gives measurable partitions subordinate to
W^u (Definition 1.4.1: xi(x) is contained in W^u(x) and contains an open neighborhood of x in W^u(x), for a.e. x).
LY Corollary 6.1.4 (with Corollary 6.2 for the nonergodic case) gives, for nu-a.e. x, a density rho strictly positive on
xi(x) with rho(y)/rho(z) = prod_{i>=1} J^u(f^-i z)/J^u(f^-i y); Lemma 6.1.1 gives that the product is bounded away from
0 and infinity on xi(x), so lambda_x(xi(x)) is finite, since nu_x is a probability and its density with respect to
lambda_x is bounded below on xi(x). W^u(x) is one-dimensional (one positive exponent) and is a
C^1 immersed curve tangent to E^u(x) (X8). It lies in K, where g is Euclidean, so lambda_x is arclength.
(c) For w on a leaf put ell(w) = |alpha_w(e^u(w))|. Lemma 2(e) with t = 1 gives alpha_(fw)(Df(w)v) = e^a alpha_w(v),
and Df(w)e^u(w) = +-J^u(w) e^u(fw), so

    J^u(w) ell(fw) = e^a ell(w).

Iterating along the backward orbit, with P_N(z) = prod_{n=1}^N J^u(f^-n z) > 0, gives without division
ell(z) P_N(z) = e^(aN) ell(f^-N z). For y, z in xi(x), y regular (ell(y) > 0 by Lemma 10),

    ell(z) P_N(z)/P_N(y) = ell(y) ell(f^-N z)/ell(f^-N y).

Fix k with nu(A_k) > 0 for a compact Pesin block A_k (X8) on which ell >= 1/k and local unstable curves have uniform
size and uniform C^1 control of their tangents. For nu-a.e. y in A_k, Poincare recurrence for f^-1 (X6) gives
infinitely many N with f^-N y in A_k. Along these N, f^-N z lies on the local unstable curve of f^-N y at distance
tending to 0 exponentially, so the leaf tangents at f^-N z and f^-N y converge and, alpha being C^1, the last ratio
tends to 1. The left side converges to ell(z) rho(y)/rho(z) by (b). Hence rho(z) = (rho(y)/ell(y)) ell(z) and
ell(z) > 0. Letting k -> infinity covers nu-a.e. y. []

##### Lemma 12 (product box; P4). Source: A223, A278 section 5, A422 section 4.

Let nu satisfy (CI-1)-(CI-3). Let G be a Borel subset of G^+ cap G^- cap Reg cap {B != 0, Omega != 0} cap supp nu
with nu(G) = 1 (Lemmas 9(g), 10). For nu-a.e. x0 there are: an arclength-parametrized C^1 arc
gamma: (-s0, s0) -> xi(x0) with gamma(0) = x0 and gamma'(0) in E^u(x0); a Borel set T of full measure in (-s0, s0)
with gamma(T) contained in G; and an open box Rect = (-s1, s1) x (-r1, r1) x (-tau1, tau1) such that

    Theta(s, r, tau) = Gamma_tau Psi_r gamma(s)

is a C^1 diffeomorphism of Rect onto an open set V containing x0, with V contained in O, closure(V) compact,
j1 <= |det D Theta| <= j2 on Rect for constants 0 < j1 <= j2. Moreover the whole arc gamma lies in supp nu (P4), the
set E = Theta((T cap (-s1, s1)) x (-r1, r1) x (-tau1, tau1)) is Borel, E is a subset of Bas(nu), and
Leb(V minus E) = 0.

Proof. By disintegration (X10), nu(G) = int nu_x(G) dnu(x) = 1, so nu_x(G) = 1 for nu-a.e. x. Take such an x0 in G
at which Lemma 11(b) holds. Since nu_(x0) is equivalent to arclength on xi(x0), arclength-a.e. point of xi(x0) is
in G. xi(x0) contains an open subarc of W^u(x0) around x0; parametrize it by arclength as gamma, and let
T = gamma^-1(G), Borel of full measure in (-s0, s0).
P4: T is dense in (-s0, s0), gamma(T) lies in supp nu, supp nu is closed and gamma is continuous, so every point of
the arc lies in supp nu. (For s in T this is already part of the definition of G; P4 gives the bound
|H0(gamma(s))| <= max_{supp nu}|H0| for every s.)
Theta is C^1 (Gamma and Psi are C^1 flows, Lemma 1, Lemma 3). Its partial derivatives at 0 are gamma'(0) in E^u(x0),
-B(x0) in E^0(x0), Omega(x0) in E^s(x0) (Lemma 10), which are independent; so det D Theta(0) =: Delta != 0. By the
inverse function theorem (X2) and continuity of det D Theta, there is a box on which Theta is a C^1 diffeomorphism
onto an open neighborhood of x0 with |Delta|/2 <= |det D Theta| <= 2|Delta|; shrink it so that the image V lies in O
(open, contains x0) and has compact closure. E is the image of a Borel set under a homeomorphism, hence Borel. By the
change of variables formula (X2), Leb(V minus E) <= j2 Leb(((-s1, s1) minus T) x (-r1, r1) x (-tau1, tau1)) = 0. For
s in T, gamma(s) is in Bas(nu) (G is a subset of G^+), and Bas(nu) is invariant under Psi_r and Gamma_tau
(Lemma 9(a),(c)); so E is a subset of Bas(nu). []

##### Lemma 13 (essential basin domains; P2). Source: A223; global vortex invariance from A278 section 4 and A422 section 3.

Let nu satisfy (CI-1)-(CI-3) and define D_nu as the union of all open sets V contained in O with
Leb(V minus Bas(nu)) = 0. Then:
(i) D_nu is open and Leb(D_nu minus Bas(nu)) = 0;
(ii) nu(D_nu) = 1;
(iii) g(D_nu) = D_nu for every C^1 diffeomorphism g of R^3 with g(O) = O and g(Bas(nu)) = Bas(nu); in particular
     Psi_t(D_nu) = Phi_t(D_nu) = D_nu and Gamma_s(D_nu) = D_nu for all real t, s;
(iv) Bas(nu) is a subset of D_nu;
(v) if nu != nu' both satisfy (CI-1)-(CI-3), D_nu and D_nu' are disjoint;
(vi) if F satisfies (CI), Leb(O minus union_{nu in F} D_nu) = 0;
(vii) (remark) each nonempty D_nu has infinite volume.

Proof. (i) Union of open sets. By the Lindelof property (X10) D_nu is a countable union of such V_i, and
Leb(D_nu minus Bas) <= sum Leb(V_i minus Bas) = 0 (Bas is Borel by Lemma 9(d)).
(ii) For nu-a.e. x0, the set V of Lemma 12 is open, lies in O and has Leb(V minus Bas) <= Leb(V minus E) = 0, so V is
a subset of D_nu and x0 is in D_nu.
(iii) (P2) For V in the defining family, g(V) is open, lies in O, and g(V) minus Bas = g(V minus Bas) is null because
a C^1 diffeomorphism maps null sets to null sets (X2). So g(D_nu) is a subset of D_nu; the same for g^-1 gives
equality. Psi_t and Phi_t preserve O (Lemma 2(d)) and Bas (Lemma 9(a)); Gamma_s preserves O (Lemma 3(d)) and Bas
(Lemma 9(c), which rests on the exact conjugacy and the bound C|tau| e^(-kappa r) of Lemma 3(c)); all are C^1
diffeomorphisms.
(iv) By (ii) and inner regularity (X10) there is a compact K'' contained in D_nu with nu(K'') > 0. By Urysohn (X10)
there is a continuous phi with values in [0, 1], phi = 1 on K'', and compact support in D_nu; int phi dnu > 0. For x in
Bas(nu), A_T phi(x) -> int phi dnu > 0, so Psi_t x is in D_nu for some t >= 0, and x = Phi_t(Psi_t x) is in D_nu by
(iii).
(v) An overlap would be a nonempty open set W with Leb(W minus Bas(nu)) = Leb(W minus Bas(nu')) = 0 and Leb(W) > 0, so
Bas(nu) cap Bas(nu') would have positive volume, contrary to Lemma 9(e).
(vi) By (iv), O minus union D_nu is a subset of O minus union Bas(nu), null by (CI-5).
(vii) Leb(D_nu) = Leb(Phi_t D_nu) = e^(3ct) Leb(D_nu) for all t, and Leb(D_nu) > 0 for nonempty open D_nu. []

A223 itself states Psi-invariance and local saturation by the vortex flow; the invariance under every Gamma_s in
(iii) is the P2 argument from the definition.

##### Lemma 14 (zero Bernoulli value on a helicity-free domain; P3). Source: A278 sections 5-6, A422 section 4.

Assume the hypotheses of Lemma 7, U in C^2, and let nu satisfy (CI-1)-(CI-3). If h = 0 on D_nu, then H0 = 0 on D_nu.

Proof. Step 1. By Lemma 2(b), Omega.grad H0 = 0 on D_nu. For z in D_nu, Gamma_s z is in D_nu for all s
(Lemma 13(iii)), so s -> H0(Gamma_s z) has zero derivative and H0 is constant on each Gamma orbit in D_nu.
Step 2 (identity (9); P3). Take x0, gamma, T, Rect, Theta, V, E from Lemma 12 and write T1 = T cap (-s1, s1). For
y = Theta(s, r, tau) with s in T1 and every real t,

    H0(Phi_t y) = H0(Phi_(t-r) gamma(s)).                                                        (9)

Indeed, by Lemma 3(a), Phi_t y = Phi_t Gamma_tau Psi_r gamma(s) = Gamma_(tau exp(kappa t)) Phi_(t-r) gamma(s). The
point gamma(s) is forward generic, so it lies in Bas(nu), a subset of D_nu (Lemma 13(iv)); Phi_(t-r) gamma(s) is in
D_nu by carrier invariance (Lemma 13(iii)); and Step 1 applies on the Gamma-invariant set D_nu.
Step 3 (bound). gamma(s) is in supp nu, which is invariant, so |H0(Phi_t y)| <= h_max = max_{supp nu}|H0| < infinity.
Step 4 (time averages). Let chi be continuous with values in [0, 1], compact support and chi = 1 on supp nu, and
phi = chi H0^2 (bounded continuous). Put m = int H0^2 dnu = int phi dnu. Since gamma(s) is in Bas^-(nu) (G is a
subset of G^-), (1/T) int_0^T phi(Phi_u gamma(s)) du -> m; the shift by -r changes this average by at most
2|r| ||phi||_inf / T. Hence, by (9), A^-_T(y) := (1/T) int_0^T H0(Phi_t y)^2 dt -> m for every y in E.
Step 5. 0 <= A^-_T <= h_max^2 on E and Leb(E) <= Leb(V) < infinity, so by dominated convergence
int_E A^-_T dy -> m Leb(E). By Tonelli and Lemma 8 with Q' = V (contained in a ball B_(R') with R' >= 1),
int_E A^-_T dy <= (1/T) int_0^T int_V H0(Phi_t y)^2 dy dt <= C_V/(2aT) -> 0. As Leb(E) = Leb(V) > 0, m = 0.
Step 6. H0 = 0 nu-a.e.; if H0(x) != 0 at a point x of supp nu, H0 != 0 on an open neighborhood of x, which has
positive nu-measure. So H0 = 0 on supp nu.
Step 7. By (9) and Step 6 (Phi_(t-r) gamma(s) lies in the invariant set supp nu), H0(Phi_t y) = 0 for y in E and all
real t. E is dense in V (V open, Leb(V minus E) = 0), so
by continuity H0 = 0 on Phi_t(V) for every t. The set E0 = union_t Phi_t(V) is open, invariant under Phi, and H0 = 0
on E0.
Step 8. x0 is in V cap supp nu. By Urysohn choose a continuous phi0 with values in [0, 1], phi0(x0) = 1 and compact
support in V; then int phi0 dnu > 0. For x in Bas(nu), A_T phi0(x) -> int phi0 dnu > 0, so Psi_t x is in V for some
t >= 0 and x = Phi_t(Psi_t x) is in E0. Thus H0 = 0 on Bas(nu).
Step 9. Leb(D_nu minus Bas(nu)) = 0 (Lemma 13(i)), so Bas(nu) cap D_nu is dense in the open set D_nu, and H0 = 0 on
D_nu by continuity. []

No integration by parts against a measure singular in the vortex direction is used, and only one box is needed.

##### Lemma 15 (zero extension across the irrotational interior; P5). Source: A266 with the A256 argument, A278 section 7, A422 section 5.

Let U in C^1 with div U = 0, Omega = curl U, O = {Omega != 0} nonempty, and suppose U = 0 on the boundary of O. Then
U = 0 on Z.

Proof. Let D_Z = int Z. (P5) Every boundary point p of D_Z lies in the boundary of O: p is in closure(D_Z), a subset
of the closed set Z, so p is not in O; p is not interior to Z, so every neighborhood of p meets the complement of Z,
which is O; hence p is in closure(O) minus O. The same argument shows that Z minus D_Z is contained in the boundary of
O. So U = 0 on the boundary of D_Z and on Z minus D_Z.
Let V be U on D_Z and 0 on the complement of D_Z. Fix a ball B_rho and L = max_{closure(B_rho)} ||DU||. Claim: V is
L-Lipschitz on B_rho. If x is in D_Z and y is not, the segment from x to y has a first point p not in D_Z, and p is in
the boundary of D_Z (it is a limit of segment points in D_Z); so |V(x) - V(y)| = |U(x) - U(p)| <= L|x - p| <= L|x - y|
by the mean value inequality on the segment, which lies in the convex ball. If x, y are in D_Z and the segment stays
in D_Z, |U(x) - U(y)| <= L|x - y|; otherwise, with p the first point from x and p' the first point from y not in D_Z,
|V(x) - V(y)| <= L|x - p| + L|y - p'| <= L|x - y|. If neither is in D_Z the difference is 0.
By Rademacher (X3), V is in W^(1,infinity)_loc and its weak derivative equals its a.e. derivative. On D_Z it is DU. On
the zero set of V the a.e. derivative of a Lipschitz function is 0 (X3; at a Lebesgue density point x of {V = 0} where
V is differentiable with DV(x) = L' != 0, V(x + h) = L'h + o(|h|) would be nonzero on a cone of directions occupying a
fixed fraction of small balls, contradicting density 1). The boundary of D_Z may have positive volume; this argument
covers it. Hence DV = 1_(D_Z) DU a.e., so div V = 1_(D_Z) div U = 0 and curl V = 1_(D_Z) Omega = 0 a.e., and therefore
in D'. Then Delta V = grad div V - curl curl V = 0 in D'. By Weyl's lemma (X5), V is a smooth harmonic, hence real
analytic, field on the connected set R^3; it vanishes on the nonempty open set O (disjoint from D_Z), so V = 0. Thus
U = 0 on D_Z, and U = 0 on Z. []

##### Lemma 16 (localization). Source: A278 section 7, A422 section 5.

Assume U in C^2, P in C^1, (E), U decaying, 2/5 <= c < 1/2.
(a) If O is empty, then U = 0.
(b) If D_* is an open subset of O with Leb(O minus D_*) = 0 and H0 = 0 on D_*, then H0 = 0 on R^3, q = U.B = 0 and
    P0 = |U|^2/2 on R^3.

Proof. (a) curl U = 0 and div U = 0 give Delta U = grad div U - curl curl U = 0 (U in C^2). Each component is a bounded
harmonic function, hence constant (X5), and U decays, so U = 0.
(b) A full-measure subset of an open set is dense in it, so H0 = 0 on O by continuity, grad H0 = 0 on O, and by
continuity of grad H0, grad H0 = 0 on closure(O). If O is empty, (a) applies and H0 is constant by Lemma 2(a), so
H0 = 0 by Lemma 7(e). Otherwise, at a boundary point p of O, Omega(p) = 0 (O is open), so Lemma 2(a) gives
aU(p) = B(p) x Omega(p) - grad H0(p) = 0. Lemma 15 gives U = 0 on Z. On Z, grad H0 = B x Omega - aU = 0. So
grad H0 = 0 on R^3, H0 is constant, and H0 = 0 by Lemma 7(e). Dotting Lemma 2(a) with B gives aU.B = -B.grad H0 = 0.
By Lemma 2(f), P0 = H0 + |U|^2/2 - U.B = |U|^2/2. []

##### Lemma 17 (positive stress; P6). Source: A278 section 7, A422 section 5, A040.

Assume U in C^2, P in C^1, (E), U decaying, 2/5 <= c < 1/2, and P0 = |U|^2/2 on R^3. Then U = 0.

Proof. P is C^2 (Lemma 1(g)). (P6) Take the divergence of (E). The term (1-c) div U vanishes. With d_i B_j = A_ji +
d_i U_j, div((B.grad)U) = d_i(B_j d_j U_i) = A_ji d_j U_i + d_i U_j d_j U_i + B_j d_j div U, and
A_ji d_j U_i = c div U - omega J_ji d_j U_i = -omega J_ji d_j U_i. Further div(omega JU) = omega J_ji d_j U_i. The two
rotation terms cancel exactly, for every omega. Since div U = 0, d_i d_j(U_i U_j) = d_i(U_j d_j U_i) = d_i U_j d_j U_i.
Hence Delta P0 + d_i d_j(U_i U_j) = 0 pointwise, and with P0 = |U|^2/2,

    Delta(|U|^2/2) + d_i d_j(U_i U_j) = 0.

Let chi be smooth, 0 <= chi <= 1, chi = 1 on B_1, chi = 0 outside B_2; chi_R(y) = chi(y/R); psi(y) = (1 + |y|^2)^(1/2).
Test against chi_R psi and integrate by parts twice:

    int [U_i U_j d_i d_j(chi_R psi) + (|U|^2/2) Delta(chi_R psi)] dy = 0.

Expand d_i d_j(chi_R psi) = chi_R d_i d_j psi + d_i chi_R d_j psi + d_j chi_R d_i psi + psi d_i d_j chi_R and
Delta(chi_R psi) = chi_R Delta psi + 2 grad chi_R.grad psi + psi Delta chi_R. The terms containing derivatives of
chi_R are supported in R <= |y| <= 2R, where, for R >= 1, |grad psi| <= 1, psi <= (1 + 4R^2)^(1/2) <= 3R,
|grad chi_R| <= ||grad chi||_inf/R, ||D^2 chi_R|| <= ||D^2 chi||_inf/R^2, |Delta chi_R| <= ||Delta chi||_inf/R^2. Their
total is at most C_chi R^-1 E(2R) with C_chi = 3||grad chi||_inf + 3||D^2 chi||_inf + 2||Delta chi||_inf, and by
Lemma 7(a), C_chi R^-1 E(2R) <= C_chi C_E 2^beta R^(beta-1) -> 0. This uses only E(R) <= C R^beta with beta < 1.
The remaining integrand is chi_R[U^T D^2 psi U + (|U|^2/2) Delta psi], with

    D^2 psi = ((1 + |y|^2) I - y y^T)/psi^3 >= psi^-3 I,    Delta psi = (2|y|^2 + 3)/psi^3,

so it is at least chi_R |U|^2/psi^3 >= 0. For fixed rho and R >= max(rho, 1),
int_{B_rho} |U|^2 psi^-3 dy <= C_chi C_E 2^beta R^(beta-1). Let R -> infinity: U = 0 on B_rho for every rho. []

##### Lemma 18 (same-level crossing). Source: A326 (CONFIRMED); used only in Corollary L.4.

Let Gamma be a complete C^1 flow on R^3 preserving Lebesgue measure, such that almost every point returns arbitrarily
close to itself at arbitrarily large positive integer times. Let D be open with Gamma_t(D) contained in D for t >= 0,
H in C^1(D), h continuous on D, a > 0, and d/dt H(Gamma_t x) = -a h(Gamma_t x) for x in D, t >= 0. If h is nonzero
somewhere in D, there are a nonempty open interval I and a point x in D such that for every b in I there are times
s_b, t_b >= 0 with H(Gamma_(s_b) x) = H(Gamma_(t_b) x) = b, h(Gamma_(s_b) x) > 0 and h(Gamma_(t_b) x) < 0.

Proof. Replacing (H, h) by (-H, -h) if needed, {h > 0} is a nonempty open subset of D, of positive volume; choose a
recurrent x in it. Let f(t) = H(Gamma_t x), so f' = -a h(Gamma_t x). Choose delta > 0 with h(Gamma_t x) > 0 on
[0, delta]; f is strictly decreasing there. Choose ell < u in (f(delta), f(0)). By recurrence and continuity of H at
x there is an integer N > delta with f(N) > u. Let t_u = min{t in [delta, N] : f(t) = u} (exists by the intermediate
value theorem; the set is closed) and t_ell = max{t in [delta, t_u] : f(t) = ell} (f(delta) < ell < u = f(t_u)). Then
ell < f(t) < u on (t_ell, t_u): a value <= ell there would give, by the intermediate value theorem on [t, t_u], a
later time with f = ell, contradicting the choice of t_ell; a value >= u would give, on [delta, t], an earlier time
with f = u, contradicting the choice of t_u. The mean value theorem gives t* in (t_ell, t_u) with
f'(t*) = (u - ell)/(t_u - t_ell) > 0, so h(Gamma_(t*) x) < 0, and f(t*) lies in (ell, u), a subset of
(f(delta), f(0)). There is a unique s* in (0, delta) with f(s*) = f(t*), and h(Gamma_(s*) x) > 0. Since f'(s*) < 0 and
f'(t*) > 0, the one-variable inverse function theorem gives open intervals J_s around s* and J_t around t* on which f
is a C^1 diffeomorphism onto open intervals containing f(t*), with h(Gamma_t x) > 0 on J_s and < 0 on J_t (shrink by
continuity). Put I = f(J_s) cap f(J_t). All points used lie in D by forward invariance. []

##### 2D.2.19 Proof of Proposition L0

Let F satisfy (CI). If O is empty, U = 0 by Lemma 16(a). Otherwise fix nu in F. By Lemma 13(iii), D_nu is open and
Gamma-invariant, so the one-sign hypothesis and Lemma 5 (with Lemma 4, which needs c < 1/2) give h = 0 on D_nu.
Lemma 14 gives H0 = 0 on D_nu. Put D_* = union_{nu in F} D_nu, open, contained in O, with Leb(O minus D_*) = 0 by
Lemma 13(vi). Lemma 16(b) gives P0 = |U|^2/2, and Lemma 17 gives U = 0. Only U in C^2 and P in C^1 were used (P in
C^2 follows from (E)). []

##### 2D.2.20 Proof of Theorem L

r >= 2, so U is C^2. Decay implies uniform sublinearity, so the A430 hypotheses hold (C^r, r >= 2, uniformly
sublinear, 0 < c < 1/2, every omega). Under (G), A431 supplies at most countably many compactly supported
whole-flow-ergodic vortical SRB probabilities (giving (CI-1), (CI-2) and (CI-4)) with spectrum (a, 0, -kappa) and
entropy a for Psi_1 ((CI-3)), whose continuous-time basins contain almost every point of O ((CI-5)). So F satisfies
(CI), and Proposition L0 gives U = 0. If (C) holds, (G) holds (2D.1.2), and A417 also supplies such a family
directly. The growth hypothesis enters only through (CI); this is the observation of A432 (proof section 7) and A422
section 2, and the synthesis review (P1-P6) found no other use. []

##### 2D.2.21 Proof of Theorem L-infinity

Route 1 (A309). Let U be C-infinity, decaying. If U is constant, U = 0. Otherwise check the hypotheses of Theorem C
for B and W = Omega: both are C-infinity and complete (Lemmas 1(a), 3(a)); div B = 3c = d > 0; [B, Omega] =
-kappa Omega (Lemma 2(c)); kappa = 1 + c > 3c since c < 1/2; B(y).y >= (c/2)|y|^2 for |y| >= 2M/c (Lemma 1(d)), so
b0 = c/2 and R0 = 2M/c. Theorem C gives a family with (CI): spectrum (kappa - d, 0, -kappa) = (a, 0, -kappa), entropy
kappa - d = a (if Omega is identically 0 the family is empty and (CI-5) holds because O is empty). Proposition L0 applies.
Route 2 (A422 section 6). Lambda_core is finite (A398), so some integer r >= 2 has r a > Lambda_core; (C) holds and
Theorem L applies with the A417 family. (See point 39 of 2D.4 on comparing the two families.) []

##### 2D.2.22 Corollaries

**Corollary L.1 (contrapositive; A422 section 6, A432).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem L except the sign condition,
if U != 0 there is nu in F such that {h > 0} cap D_nu and {h < 0} cap D_nu are both nonempty; they are open, hence of
positive volume, and removing the null set D_nu minus Bas(nu) leaves positive-volume sets of basin points of both
signs. The same holds in the class of Theorem L-infinity with the A308 family.
Proof. If no such nu existed, h, being continuous, would have one sign on each D_nu (if h took both strict signs on
D_nu we would be in the stated case), and Theorem L would give U = 0. []
No claim is made that every essential basin has both signs, and nothing is inferred about the values of h on supp nu.

**Corollary L.2 (A317 equivalence, CONFIRMED at this scope).** Fix omega and c in (2/5, 1/2). Let C_inf be the class of
pairs (U, P) with U in C-infinity, P in C^1, (E), U decaying. Consider
(N) every profile in C_inf has U = 0;
(S) no profile in C_inf has an essential basin D_i (from A308 and A207/A223) on which h takes both strict signs.
Then (N) and (S) are equivalent. The same holds for the quantitatively restricted finite-r class of A312 (U in C^r,
integer r >= 3, (r-1)a > 3L, P in C^1, decaying).
Proof. If (N) holds, O is empty for every profile and there are no vortical essential basins. If (S) holds, each D_i
of a given profile carries at most one strict sign of h, so h >= 0 or h <= 0 on D_i, and Theorem L-infinity (or
Remark L_A312 (2D.2.23) for the A312 class) gives U = 0. []
By A318 this equivalence does not extend the conclusion to the C^2 baseline. The equivalence for the classes defined
by (C) or (G) is not recorded in the sources and is not stated here.

**Corollary L.3 (A319 safe statement; Lemmas 4 and 6).** Let D_nu be an essential basin domain as in Lemma 13. Almost
every point of D_nu is recurrent under the vortex flow in the sense of Lemma 4 (under the time-one map in
particular). Each recurrent point with h != 0 lies on a vortex line along which H is not monotone, with both signs of h
at arbitrarily large positive and negative vortex times; such points exist in every nonempty open strict-sign region
of D_nu. Thus nonmonotone vortex lines occur on a Gamma-invariant set containing the Borel set
R cap {h != 0} cap D_nu. This set has positive volume if h is not identically zero on D_nu; without that premise it
can be empty.
Proof. Lemma 4 and Lemma 6; R has full volume and {h != 0} cap D_nu is open, hence of positive volume when nonempty.
(Qualified 2026-11-03 04:46Z after the auditor audit, section 7 item 1; the earlier text called the set positive-volume
without the premise.) []
Not asserted (A319 OPEN): nonmonotonicity on almost every vortex line of a sign-changing basin. A positive-volume family
of vortex lines with h identically 0 is not excluded; ergodicity of the carrier SRB measure is not ergodicity of the
vortex flow.

**Corollary L.4 (A327, levelwise criterion, CONFIRMED at these scopes).** Let 2/5 <= c < 1/2 and omega be real, and let
(U, P) be in one of: (i) the class of Theorem L-infinity, with the A308 family; (ii) U in C^r decaying under the A312
condition, with the A312 family; (iii) U in C^2, P in C^1, decaying, with a separately given family F satisfying
(CI) (conditional conclusion). Assume that for each nu and each real b, h has at most one strict sign on
D_nu cap {H = b} (the sign may depend on nu and b). Then U = 0.
Proof. Lemma 4 supplies the recurrence hypothesis of Lemma 18; D_nu is open and Gamma-invariant (Lemma 13(iii)); H is
C^1 and d/dt H(Gamma_t x) = -a h(Gamma_t x) (Lemma 2(b)). If h were nonzero somewhere in D_nu, Lemma 18 would give a
level b attained with both strict signs of h in D_nu. So h = 0 on every D_nu, and the proof of Proposition L0 from
Lemma 14 on gives U = 0. The premise uses H only through its level sets, so it is unchanged by adding a constant to P. []
The proof gives more: a nonzero profile in these classes has an essential basin and a nonempty open interval of
Bernoulli values each attained with both helicity signs along one recurrent vortex orbit in that basin (from Lemma 18
at a recurrent point of D_nu where h is nonzero, not from the levelwise statement alone; A2674). This is not asserted
for every basin or every value, and gives no C^2 coverage theorem.

**Corollary L.5 (A328, CONFIRMED; proof omitted).** For U in C^2, P in C^1 solving the two equations of (E), without
the decay condition, with U(y) = o(|y|) uniformly,
0 < c < 1/2 and every omega, for every measurable set E' invariant under all Gamma times and every Borel set I of reals,

    int_{E' cap {H in I}} h_plus = int_{E' cap {H in I}} h_minus   in [0, infinity].

Both sides are finite and equal, or both infinite. The proof (A049 conservativity, return towers for measurable
coboundaries, a Lipschitz primitive of the band indicator) is in the accompanying artifacts,
sections 4-5. It is not used in the proofs above.

##### 2D.2.23 Remark L_A312 (finite regularity under a strain bound)

For an integer r >= 3, 2/5 <= c < 1/2, U in C^r decaying, P in C^1 and (r-1)a > 3L as in Theorem C_strain, A312 supplies a family
with (CI), and Proposition L0 gives the conclusion of Theorem L for its domains. This is the "quantitatively restricted
finite-r class" of A317 and the A312 clause of A327; Appendix B.1 item 1c labels it CONDITIONAL on the strain bound.
Nonconstant profiles force L >= 1 + c (A312), so this is a demanding extra condition. A373's sharpened strain
condition is not used here.

#### 2D.3 External theorems (cited, not proved)

- X1 (ODE). For a C^k field (k >= 1) on R^3: local existence and uniqueness, C^k dependence on initial data, joint
  continuity of (t, x) -> flow, global existence under |X(y)| <= C(1 + |y|) (Gronwall), the variational equation
  d/dt D phi_t = DX(phi_t) D phi_t, and Liouville's formula det D phi_t(x) = exp(int_0^t div X(phi_s x) ds).
  Reference: P. Hartman, Ordinary Differential Equations, chapters II and V.
- X2 (calculus). Inverse function theorem for C^1 maps; change of variables for C^1 diffeomorphisms; a C^1
  diffeomorphism maps Lebesgue null sets to null sets; mean value inequality; one-variable inverse function theorem.
- X3 (Lipschitz functions). Rademacher's theorem; a locally Lipschitz function is in W^(1,infinity)_loc with weak
  gradient equal to the a.e. gradient; the gradient of a Lipschitz function vanishes a.e. on its zero set. Reference:
  L. C. Evans and R. F. Gariepy, Measure Theory and Fine Properties of Functions, sections 3.1-3.2 and 4.2 (exact
  theorem numbers not checked).
- X4. Lebesgue density theorem.
- X5 (harmonic functions). Weyl's lemma (a harmonic distribution is a smooth harmonic function); harmonic functions are
  real analytic; an analytic function vanishing on a nonempty open subset of a connected open set vanishes; bounded
  harmonic functions on R^n are constant (Liouville).
- X6 (ergodic theory). Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem for a measure-preserving map and bounded functions (a.e.
  convergence to an invariant function with the same integral); Poincare recurrence.
- X7 (two-sided Oseledets theorem). For an invertible measurable cocycle over an invertible map preserving a
  probability, with log^+||A^(+-1)|| integrable: on a full-measure set of regular points there is an invariant
  splitting into Oseledets subspaces E_i with exponents lambda_i such that, for v = sum v_i,
  lim_{n->+infinity} n^-1 log|A^n v| = max{lambda_i : v_i != 0} and lim_{n->-infinity} n^-1 log|A^n v| =
  min{lambda_i : v_i != 0}. References: V. I. Oseledets, Trans. Moscow Math. Soc. 19 (1968); D. Ruelle, Publ. Math.
  IHES 50 (1979); L. Barreira and Ya. Pesin, Nonuniform Hyperbolicity (exact theorem numbers not checked).
- X8 (Pesin theory). For a C^2 diffeomorphism of a compact manifold and an invariant probability: at regular points
  with positive exponents the global unstable manifold W^u(x) = {y : limsup n^-1 log d(f^-n x, f^-n y) < 0} is an
  immersed C^1 submanifold tangent to the sum of the positive Oseledets subspaces; Pesin blocks are compact sets of
  measure arbitrarily close to 1 on which local unstable manifolds have uniform size and uniformly continuous tangent
  fields. References: Barreira-Pesin (as above; not read); D. Ruelle, "Ergodic theory of differentiable dynamical
  systems", Publ. Math. IHES 50 (1979), 27-58, Section 6, Theorems 6.1 and 6.3 (local and global stable manifolds;
  applied to f^-1 for W^u); Ledrappier-Young Part I, section 2 (Lemma 2.3.1, a Lyapunov chart estimate) and section 4
  (Lemma 4.2.2).
- X9 (Ledrappier-Young). F. Ledrappier and L.-S. Young, The metric entropy of diffeomorphisms. Part I, Ann. of Math.
  122 (1985), 509-539: Definition 1.4.1 (partitions subordinate to W^u), Definition 1.4.2 (absolutely continuous
  conditional measures on unstable manifolds), Theorem A (1.5) (for a C^2 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian
  manifold and an invariant Borel probability m, absolute continuity on unstable manifolds holds iff
  h_m(f) = int sum lambda_i^+ dim E_i dm; the "if" part is proved in Part I), Lemma 3.1.1 (existence of increasing
  measurable partitions subordinate to W^u), Lemma 6.1.1, Corollary 6.1.4 (ergodic case: the density is strictly
  positive on xi(x) and rho(y)/rho(x) = prod_{i>=1} J^u(f^-i x)/J^u(f^-i y)), Corollary 6.2 (6.1.4 holds without
  ergodicity). Numbers taken from the literature audit text copy of the paper.
- X10 (measure theory and topology). Stone-Weierstrass (polynomials with rational coefficients are dense in
  C(closed ball)); Urysohn's lemma in metric spaces; inner regularity of finite Borel measures on R^3; a finite Borel
  measure on a metric space is determined by the integrals of bounded continuous functions; second countability and
  the Lindelof property of R^3; disintegration of a probability along a countably generated measurable partition of a
  compact metric or Euclidean space, modulo null sets (Rokhlin); Tonelli,
  Fubini, dominated convergence; Plancherel.
- Inputs proved elsewhere in the campaign and cited: Theorem C (A308), Theorem C_r (A417 with A398-A399), Theorem C_E
  (A431 with A430), Theorem C_strain (A312) (2D.1.6); the items of section 2A listed in 2D.1.9.

## 3. Assumptions and regularity

### 3.1 Hypotheses theorem by theorem

The target class of the task is: (E) on all of R^3, div U = 0, U smooth and U(y) -> 0 as abs(y) -> infinity,
2/5 < c < 1/2, omega real. The baseline of this report is U in C^2, P in C^1 (H0) with U -> 0 (H1). The table lists
exactly what each theorem of section 1 uses. "None" in the last column means that the theorem uses no hypothesis
beyond regularity, decay and the stated range.
