Remarks.
- Theorems 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 assume no decay rate for U and no finite energy; their other hypotheses remain as stated.
  The L^s forms of Theorem 8(i) keep their integrability assumptions (U in L^s, and P - p0 in L^(s/2) for s > 3/2),
  which for s = 2 include finite energy, U in L^2 (A3261). The symmetry conditions of Corollary 2.1 (axisymmetry) and
  Theorem 7(a) (axisymmetry of the leading tail only), and all other extra hypotheses in the table, remain explicit.
- No theorem assumes a normalization of the pressure. Under Hb the pressure gradient is the canonical one (Lemma 2.2,
  A031), and for C^2 profiles with U -> 0 the pressure itself is the canonical pressure plus a constant, with no bound
  on DU (A500).
- In Theorem 7 the bound DU = O(abs(y)^(1/2)) is equivalent, for decaying profiles in the target range, to the natural
  bounds abs(U) <= C(1+abs(y))^(-(1-c)/c) and abs(DU) <= C(1+abs(y))^(-1/c) (A498 with A476-A477, A492). It is not
  known to follow from U -> 0 (section 6).
- C-infinity versus C^2. Theorems 4 and 5 need C-infinity. The profile equation gives no local regularity gain: for
  every c, omega and every C^2 function f of one variable, U = (-cx - omega y, omega x + (c-1)y + f(x), z) with
  P = (d/2)(x^2+y^2) - omega(1-2c)xy + 2 omega F(x) - z^2, F' = f, d = c(1-c) + omega^2, is an exact (nondecaying)
  profile, and with f(x) = (1 - 2 omega)x + max(x,0)^s, 2 < s < 3, U is C^2 but not C^3 (A377). So the C-infinity
  results do not settle the C^2 class (A318). At C^2 the coverage step holds under the growth condition (G) of
  Theorem L, which is not known to follow from decay.

### 3.2 How decay and regularity enter

- Decay enters through two weak consequences: Hb (energy law and pressure normalization) and uniform sublinearity
  U = o(abs(y)) (completeness of the carrier flow and compactness of the absorbing core, A006). Theorems 1 and 8 use
  only Hb, Theorems 2 and 4 only uniform sublinearity; Theorems 3, 5, 6 and 7 use U -> 0 as stated.
- C^2 is used so that Omega = curl U is C^1 and the vorticity transport [B, Omega] = -(1+c)Omega holds classically.
- C-infinity is used in Theorem 4 (curve-tree constants of every order), hence in Theorem 5, and in Theorem 3(f)
  (Yomdin's theorem, A055).
- The derivative bound of Theorem 7 is used for the leading far-field tail V (its existence, homogeneity and the tail
  equations).

The two subsections below are the detailed record of the hypothesis labels (with the physical meaning of the
derivative-decay hypotheses) and of how they enter, carried over from the earlier record.

### 3.3 The target class and the labels for extra hypotheses (detailed record)

The conjecture concerns pairs (U, P) solving the profile equation of section 0 on all of R^3, with div U = 0 and
U(y) -> 0 as abs(y) -> infinity, for 2/5 < c < 1/2 and arbitrary real omega. The prompt asks for smooth profiles. Our
baseline is weaker: U in C^2 and P in C^1 (H0), with the decay condition (H1). A result proved under H0 and H1, or
under weaker hypotheses, is called unconditional here. A result that needs C-infinity is unconditional within the
smooth class (A308) and is recorded with that regularity. It does not settle the C^2 baseline that the prompt starts
from, so the C^2 question is kept open alongside it (A318). Every other hypothesis is extra, and is labelled:

- H1': U = o(abs(y)) uniformly (sublinear growth).
- Hb: U is bounded and U(R .) -> 0 in D' as R -> infinity. This is implied by H1 for continuous U.
- H2: a decay rate for U.
- H3: decay of the strain or the gradient, for instance the Dini condition (D): int_1^infinity sup_{abs(y) >= r} abs(grad U) dr/r < infinity.
  Physical scope of (D) (integral-estimate analysis C34, PROVED, A475; pure scaling, any C^1 profile, any 0 < c < 1 and omega). For
  x_* != 0, call the blow-up Lipschitz-singular at (x_*, T) if grad u is unbounded on N x [T - tau, T) for every
  neighbourhood N of x_* and every tau > 0. Call it type-I-singular at (x_*, T) if (T-t) abs(grad u(x,t)) does not
  tend to 0 as (x,t) -> (x_*, T) jointly with t < T. Both singular sets are invariant under x -> e^(sigma A) x. So
  each is empty or contains a whole twisted ray {e^(sigma A) x_*: sigma real}, a curve from 0 to infinity that
  meets every sphere about 0 once. There is no Lipschitz-singular point away from 0 if and only if
  abs(DU(y)) <= C(1 + abs(y))^(-1/c), and this implies (D). In turn (D) implies DU -> 0, which holds if and only if
  there is no type-I-singular point away from 0. So the hypothesis (D) holds for every rotating self-similar
  blow-up whose spatial gradient is bounded near (x_*, T) for every x_* != 0. If (D) fails, the spatial gradient
  is unbounded near (x_*, T) at every point x_* of at least one twisted ray. Scaling alone gives no converse:
  the auditor gives a smooth divergence-free field, not an Euler profile, that satisfies (D) and is Lipschitz-singular
  on whole rays. (Wording from the synthesis review as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, 04:51Z.)
  Strain gap (integral-estimate analysis C35, PROVED, A476-A477): let U be a bounded C^2 profile with P in C^1, 0 < c < 1, any omega, and
  Lambda = limsup_{abs(y) -> infinity} lambda_max(sym DU(y)). The conditions DU -> 0, Lambda < 1, Lambda = 0, (D), and
  DU = O(abs(y)^(-eps)) for some eps > 0 are equivalent, and Lambda and limsup abs(DU) each lie in {0} union [1, infinity]
  (A476). Under Hb and 1/3 < c < 1, hence for every decaying profile in the target range, they are also equivalent to
  abs(DU(y)) <= C(1+abs(y))^(-1/c) (A477, using A210). So every result below labelled H3 (Dini) holds under DU -> 0, or
  under Lambda < 1. Neither is derived from U -> 0: for a decaying profile that fails them, the limsup of the largest
  strain eigenvalue at infinity is at least 1 + c/2 (A506, section 6; A2746). Constants depend on the profile,
  including a C^2 norm on a compact annulus.
  In physical terms, with the strain gap (A476): for a smooth rotating self-similar blow-up with U -> 0, the
  profile satisfies (D) if and only if (T-t) abs(grad u(x,t)) -> 0 as (x,t) -> (x_*, T) jointly, for every
  x_* != 0. Equivalently, (T-t) times the supremum of abs(grad u(., t)) over abs(x) >= rho tends to 0, for one
  rho > 0. The results conditional on (D) then apply, each under its remaining hypotheses (C^2 regularity, the
  range of c, and the pressure normalization where it is used). This condition at a single point x_*, or as a
  limit in t at each fixed x, is not known to suffice. The points x_* != 0 where it fails are exactly those at
  which (T-t) lambda_max(sym grad u) has joint limsup at least 1, and if there is one, they contain a whole
  twisted ray. Under Hb and 1/3 < c < 1 this set is empty exactly when the Lipschitz-singular set is (A477); the
  two sets are not shown to be equal. Whether U -> 0 forces (D) remains open (section 6). For bounded U and DU the
  pressure gradient and DU Ay are bounded and the orbit-direction derivative decays like 1/abs(y) (A485); full
  bounded DU then forces DU = O(log abs(y)/abs(y)), hence DU -> 0 and (D) (A492, the literature audit LIT120 and integral-estimate analysis C39).
  Under U -> 0, DU = O(abs(y)^(1/2)) suffices (A498, the literature audit LIT125).
- H4: integrability (L^p, Lorentz or weighted norms, finite energy).
- H5: pressure normalization. In the target class this is not an extra hypothesis: under Hb, grad P is the canonical
  pressure gradient (Lemma 2.2, A031), and for C^2 profiles with U -> 0 the scalar P is the canonical pressure plus a
  constant, with no bound on DU (A500). H5 is listed for results stated in larger classes.
- H6: a dynamical hypothesis on the flow of B.
- H7: symmetry.
- H8: smallness.
- H9: other (analyticity, extra equations, external premises).
  H1-H9 name categories of hypotheses, not exact classes. A row of tables A-C whose class column reads only "H9; H3" means helicity-free U
  (U.curl U = 0) with the natural bounds of Theorem 7 (for decaying U equivalently DU = O(abs(y)^(1/2))), together with the local, nodal or
  density premises stated in the row (A1280).

### 3.4 How the target hypotheses enter (detailed record)

Decay is used in only two weakened forms.

(a) Hb, in the energy law (item 1a, section 2A) and in the pressure. For bounded U with distributionally vanishing
dilates, P is determined up to an additive constant (canonical normalization, A031). So H5 is never an extra
hypothesis.

(b) H1', in the dynamical results (item 1b, section 2B). It makes the flow Phi_s of B complete, and it makes the set
Lambda of bounded forward orbits a compact null global backward attractor (trapping, A006).

The trapping and attractor results of item 1b use decay only through H1' (A006), and several parts of Theorem 3 need
only H1'; Theorem 3 as stated assumes U -> 0 (section 3.1). This is why kinematic models with compactly supported U
are meaningful tests of the dynamical arguments (items 6 and 9).

Regularity:
- The energy law needs only C^1. It also has a weak form, for U bounded with zero or nonnegative energy defect
  (A176, A177).
- The dynamical results of item 1b need C^2, so that Omega is C^1 and the Cauchy transport of Omega holds
  classically. Theorem 2 and Corollary 2.1 need only C^1; Theorem 4 needs C-infinity.
- The entropy bound h_top >= 1-2c on Lambda uses C-infinity (Yomdin's theorem, A055), or C^2 together with Omega
  nowhere zero on Lambda (A080).
- The SRB dichotomy of item 8 uses C-infinity and an external premise.
- Basin coverage (item 1c(i)) uses C-infinity (A308), or C^r for an integer r >= 2 together with condition (G) of
  Theorem L (section 1): for each component E of O, every ergodic probability of the backward carrier flow carried by
  Z_E = K cap closure(E) cap ({B = 0} cup {Omega = 0}) has top Lyapunov exponent below r(1-2c) (A416-A417, A422,
  A432). After coverage, the Liouville step of item 1c(ii) uses only U in C^2 and P in C^1 (A422). So the
  reduction of the conjecture to the sign-changing basin question holds at C^2 for every profile satisfying (G)
  with r = 2; for the other C^2 profiles the coverage step is open.
- The profile equation alone gives no local regularity gain. For every c, every omega and every C^2 function f of
  one variable, U = (-cx - omega y, omega x + (c-1)y + f(x), z) with P = (d/2)(x^2+y^2) - omega(1-2c)xy +
  2 omega F(x) - z^2, F' = f, d = c(1-c) + omega^2, is an exact profile on R^3 with B = (0, -(1-2c)y + f(x), (1+c)z)
  and Omega = (0, 0, 2 omega + f'(x)). With f(x) = (1 - 2 omega)x + max(x,0)^p, 2 < p < 3, U is C^2 but not C^3,
  also at points where B x Omega != 0. It does not decay, so any gain of regularity for decaying profiles must use
  decay (the second-model review, section 2; checked symbolically by the accompanying artifacts; CONFIRMED A377,
  which also checks that the unnormalized section operator proposed there to bootstrap regularity fixes Omega and is
  not a contraction). No bootstrap within the decaying class is refuted by this example.

No result of items 1a-1b restricts omega, except the nonrotating Liouville theorem (Theorem 2, A010), which assumes
omega = 0; Corollary 2.1 extends its conclusion to every omega under axisymmetry. Where omega = 0 and omega != 0
behave differently, both cases are stated:
- the formal Lyapunov classification (A081, A167);
- the harmonic example in D1 Remark (iii) (A248);
- the nonrotating Liouville theorem (A010), which is the omega = 0 case and is not available for omega != 0.

## 4. Does the theorem hold for every omega?

PROVED: Theorems 1 and 4, and Theorem 3 apart from its CONDITIONAL parts (i), (o) and (p) and the C^2 form of (f),
hold for every real omega, with no smallness of omega; the constant in Theorem 1(iii)
does not depend on omega, and for 0 < c < 2/5 Theorem 1(i) gives U = 0 for every omega. CONDITIONAL: Theorems 5-8
hold for every omega under their hypotheses. PROVED: for omega = 0 and 0 < c < 1/2 every uniformly sublinear profile
is constant and every decaying one is zero (Theorem 2). For omega != 0 and 2/5 <= c < 1/2 the main conjecture is
UNRESOLVED.

How omega enters (details and verdicts in Appendix B.4):
- Loss of the Lyapunov function. The omega = 0 proof (Theorem 2) uses a strict Lyapunov function of the jet; for
  omega != 0 the same function H_0 satisfies V.grad H_0 = -(1-2c)abs(V)^2 - V.T with T = omega[JU - (Jy).grad U],
  and -V.T has no sign (A3061). For omega != 0, every C^1 function of the velocity jet of order at most five and the
  pressure value that is nonincreasing along B at every nonstagnating admissible jet of one order higher is constant
  on the closure of the nonstagnating admissible jets (A044, A081, A100, A434, A489, A493; PROVED at the stated jet
  scopes). Order six and higher is UNRESOLVED. This is an obstruction to one proof method, not a restriction on
  profiles.
- Omega-blindness. Identities obtained by pairing (E) with rotation-equivariant densities and axisymmetric weights
  (energy, helicity, enstrophy, angular momentum) reproduce the omega = 0 identities exactly (A043), so they cannot
  separate omega != 0 from omega = 0. Identities that keep omega exist (A382), but none with a usable sign is known.
- Rigidity. For 0 < c < 1/2 a nonzero C^2 decaying profile solves (E) for at most one omega, and the linearization at
  U = 0 has no nonzero decaying solution for any c > 0 and omega (A046). This is not a spectral gap: the roots of the
  scalar transport symbol lie on one critical line for every omega (A077, with the scope of A384).
- Periodic orbits. Every nonconstant periodic carrier orbit needs omega != 0 and has period at least
  2 pi/abs(omega) (A030). The flat periodic witness (W2) of Theorem 6 therefore exists only for omega != 0.
- Far field. In the twisted gauge omega leaves the linear transport part of the tail equation and stays in the
  divergence constraint, the pressure and the quadratic term; the divergence-free twisted homogeneous fields of
  leading order (candidate leading tails, not shown to be tails of profiles) are in bijection with smooth tangential
  data on S^2 for c != 1/3 (A075, A077; scope as in A383); no nonlinear extension of such data is asserted. If omega != 0 and the tail has this form uniformly, the blow-up-time
  profile is discretely self-similar (A079, CONDITIONAL).
- Perturbative and endpoint results. For c in a compact subinterval of (0, 1/2) and a global C^(1,beta) bound, for some
  0 < beta < 1, there is an epsilon > 0, not computed and depending on these bounds, such that
  abs(omega) sup abs(d_theta U)/(1+abs(y)) <= epsilon forces U = 0 under decay, where d_theta U = (Jy).grad U - JU is
  the rotational defect, zero exactly for axisymmetric U (A093, A102; CONDITIONAL on the smallness). At c = 2/5 a
  globally bounded gradient forces U = 0 for every omega (A103; CONDITIONAL on the gradient bound, section 8; it is
  not a theorem of section 1).

## 5. Are non-axisymmetric profiles genuinely covered?

Yes for every theorem of section 1 except Corollary 2.1, which concerns axisymmetric profiles; each has its own label.
None of Theorems 1 and 3-6 assumes a symmetry of U (Theorems 1 and 4 and the unmarked parts of Theorem 3 are PROVED,
Theorems 5 and 6 CONDITIONAL on their helicity hypotheses), and Theorems 7 and 8 assume none except in criterion 7(a),
which concerns the leading tail only. Profiles axisymmetric about the rotation axis, (Jy).grad U = JU, are constant
for every omega and 0 < c < 1/2 under U = o(abs(y)), and zero if decaying (Corollary 2.1, CONDITIONAL on this
symmetry): the rotation terms cancel and Theorem 2 applies. An axisymmetric pressure, (Jy).grad P = 0, gives
U_theta = 0, where U_theta = U.(Jy)/abs(Jy) is the azimuthal component (A034), and with U uniformly sublinear it gives
U = b e_z, zero if decaying, for every omega and 0 < c < 1/2, with no symmetry of U (Theorem AP, CONDITIONAL on this
symmetry of P; A3029; U, P in C^1 suffice, the literature audit LIT364, A3047). Symmetry of P on one ball abs(y) < R with
B.y >= delta abs(y)^2 outside it suffices, for a decaying profile any R > sup abs(U)/c (the literature audit LIT360, A3033), and so
does axisymmetry of the pressure source q = tr((DU)^2) on R^3, which under E(R) = o(R^3) is equivalent to that of P
(the literature audit LIT361, A3040-A3041). Whether decay forces an axisymmetric pressure, on R^3 or on such a ball, is UNRESOLVED
(A3031, A3035, A3043, A3049). The main conjecture for non-axisymmetric profiles is UNRESOLVED.

Restrictions on a hypothetical non-axisymmetric profile (PROVED; they restrict, they do not exclude; Appendix B.5):
- Angular support rule (A073). With S the set of integers m for which the m-th angular Fourier coefficient U_m of the
  cylindrical components (U_r, U_theta, U_z) is not identically zero, the mode forcing is not a gradient
  for m in S, so S is contained in S + S; this excludes S = {L, -L} and every S contained in L(2Z + 1).
- Odd symmetry classes are empty (A074): if sigma in O(3) commutes with J and sigma U(sigma^(-1) y) = -U(y), then
  U = 0 (for example even fields).
- Angular mean (A032, A034, A078): the mean solves the omega-free axisymmetric system with Reynolds forcing; its
  control without axisymmetry is UNRESOLVED.
- Pressure symmetry (Theorem AP, A3029-A3030, A3033, A3040-A3042): the pressure of a nonzero decaying profile is not
  axisymmetric about the rotation axis, so some angular Fourier mode P_m with m != 0 is not identically zero; the
  pressure source q = tr((DU)^2) has exactly the same nonzero modes, q_m = 0 if and only if P_m = 0 (A3042); and
  (Jy).U is not identically zero on abs(y) < R for any R > sup abs(U)/c (A3033).
- Finite angular spectra (A137, A180, A214): the top mode solves a complex steady Euler system; for omega != 0 a
  critical top-mode tail is never irrotational; no mode is forced to vanish.
- In the helicity-free class with DU = O(abs(y)^(1/2)), Theorem 7(b)-(d) excludes non-axisymmetric profiles under
  tail conditions that do not refer to symmetry. Non-axisymmetric local tail germs with all local tail equations
  exist (A590, A599); whether one extends to a global tail with the canonical pressure is not known.

## 6. Is U -> 0 alone sufficient?

As a decay hypothesis, yes for Theorems 1-6 (Theorems 1, 2 and 4 and the unmarked parts of Theorem 3 PROVED;
Theorems 5 and 6 CONDITIONAL on their helicity hypotheses): they assume no decay rate, no derivative decay and no finite energy; U -> 0 implies Hb and uniform sublinearity, which is all that Theorems 1, 2 and 4 use.
Whether U -> 0, without a helicity condition, forces U = 0 is the main conjecture (UNRESOLVED). Whether U -> 0 forces
derivative decay is UNRESOLVED; it would supply the derivative bound of Theorem 7 for every helicity-free profile,
which would still need one of the tail conditions (a)-(g).

What is known about derivative decay (details in Appendix B.6; a result that adds a hypothesis beyond the problem
class, such as a growth, smallness or misalignment bound, is CONDITIONAL on it, the others are PROVED; the
countertests concern other classes of fields):
- Equivalences (A476-A477). For a decaying C^2 profile with 2/5 < c < 1/2 and every omega, the Dini condition, DU -> 0,
  limsup lambda_max(sym DU) < 1 at infinity, DU = O(abs(y)^(-eps)) for some eps > 0, and the natural rate
  abs(DU) <= C(1+abs(y))^(-1/c) are equivalent. If they fail, limsup lambda_max(sym DU) >= 1 + c/2 (A506).
- Physical meaning (A475-A477). For the blow-up u(x, t) of section 0.1, these conditions hold if and only if
  (T-t) abs(grad u(x, t)) -> 0 as (x, t) -> (x_*, T) jointly, for every x_* != 0. If they fail, they fail on a whole
  twisted ray.
- Growth thresholds. Bounded DU forces DU -> 0 (A492). U -> 0 together with DU = O(abs(y)^(1/2)) forces DU -> 0 (A498);
  faster velocity decay allows faster gradient growth (A507, A757-A759). So a decaying profile without derivative
  decay has limsup abs(DU)/abs(y)^(1/2) = infinity, and item 6 for Theorem 7 reduces to whether U -> 0 forces
  DU = O(abs(y)^(1/2)).
- Small far-field vorticity (integral-estimate analysis C49, A1068-A1074; integral-estimate analysis C50, A1171-A1177). For bounded C^2 profiles, every omega
  and 0 < c < 1, with no derivative bound: abs(curl U) <= W0 outside a ball gives DU = O(abs(y)^(gamma/c)) for every
  gamma > c_K W0, where c_K = (6/pi) int_0^(pi/2) sin^2 t E(sin t) dt = 1.7796..., E the complete elliptic integral
  of the second kind (c_K < 1.77963978 by an interval certificate, A1172; the first version had 2 W0, A1071); and
  limsup abs(curl U) < c/(2 c_K), about 0.281 c, gives DU -> 0 and abs(curl U) + abs(DU) = O(1/abs(y)) (A1174-A1175;
  the first version had c/4, A1072). The transverse block (integral-estimate analysis C51, A1223-A1226, A1228-A1229) improves this: for
  decaying U with abs(U) <= C(1+abs(y))^(-sigma), for a velocity-decay exponent 0 <= sigma <= 3/2 (not the
  a = 1 - 2c of section 0.2), bounded exterior vorticity and log(2 + [curl U]_{beta, B(y, abs(y)/4)}) <= K abs(y)^s
  for large abs(y), with [.]_beta the Holder seminorm, some beta in (0, 1) and 0 <= s < min(1+sigma, 1/c), give
  bounded DU (CONDITIONAL on these bounds), and bounded exterior vorticity alone gives grad P -> 0
  (A1228). With the certified angular trial of the R2 addendum to C50 (3/2 <= D_1 < 1.720646, A1231-A1234),
  limsup abs(curl U) < Gamma_sigma/1.720646, Gamma_sigma = min(c(1+sigma), 1), gives DU -> 0 and the confirmed rates
  (A1235): the threshold is c/1.720646, about 0.581 c, under bare decay and 1/1.720646 > 0.58117 under the
  natural velocity tail with 2/5 < c < 1/2. So a decaying profile without derivative decay has
  limsup abs(curl U) >= c/1.720646, and the case curl U -> 0 with DU not -> 0 is empty (A1074). Nothing is known
  at or above the threshold (A1076, A1179, A1230); its optimal value is open (A1236), and the R2 route cannot
  give more than Gamma_sigma/D_1, and D_1 > 1.66925 (integral-estimate analysis C53, A1376-A1380; a limit of the method, not a new
  threshold; the exact D_1 is not known, A1381 OPEN). Under bounded exterior vorticity and
  abs(U) <= C(1+abs(y))^(-sigma), 0 <= sigma <= 3/2, polynomial growth DU = O(abs(y)^delta) with
  delta < min(1+sigma, 1/c)
  already gives DU bounded, DU -> 0 and DU = O(1/abs(y)) (integral-estimate analysis C52, A1353-A1354, A1359); under bare decay with
  bounded exterior vorticity the transverse block of DU tends to zero in every finite L^s norm on unit balls, for
  0 < c < 1 and every omega, which is not pointwise decay (A1357-A1358); a one-scale growth barrier is open (A1360),
  and an every-scale growth alternative for actual profiles is open as well (A1388-A1394: a conditional repair is
  sound, A1391, but the needed estimate is not proved, and scalar tests show the surviving estimates do not suffice,
  A1392-A1393).
- Vorticity size without helicity (Theorem 8; CONDITIONAL). U -> 0 together with sup abs(curl U) < sqrt(3)(1 - 3c/2)
  for 0 < c < 2/3, or sup abs(curl U)^2 <= t* = (15 sqrt(7) - 20)/42 for 0 < c <= 1/2 (sqrt(t*) is about 0.684632, so sup abs(curl U) <= 0.68463 suffices; integral-estimate analysis C57, A1584-A1586; for 0 < c <= c_k the larger constants T_k of Corollary NW.2 suffice, from 0.894 for c <= 0.41 to 0.707 for c <= 0.49, A1635; the sharp threshold T*(c) of that method gives the brackets 0.982 for c <= 0.41 to 0.772 for c <= 1/2, so sup abs(curl U) <= 0.772 suffices for every 0 < c <= 1/2, integral-estimate analysis C58, A1720-A1725; the closed endpoint T*(c) and an explicit margin of no practical size above it also suffice, integral-estimate analysis C59-C60, A1782-A1789, A1886-A1890), or with int (1 + abs(y)^2)^(1/c - 3/2) abs(curl U)^2 < infinity for 2/5 < c < 1, gives U = 0 for
  every omega (A1531 with A1433-A1435; integral-estimate analysis C55, A1525). The weighted-enstrophy condition sits just beyond the far field of a
  nonzero profile: a homogeneous tail with nonzero vorticity has abs(curl U) of order abs(y)^(-1/c), for which the
  weighted integral diverges logarithmically, and every nonzero profile in the class of Theorem 8(b) (U, P in C^1, U bounded, Hb, 2/5 < c < 1) has
  normalized shell norms of curl U whose
  limsup is bounded below in terms of its energy constant (A1526). U -> 0 alone is not known to give any of these conditions
  (A1436, A1529 OPEN). Parts (a)-(c) of Theorem 8 were rechecked independently (A3036-A3037); none of their conditions
  is known to follow from bare decay (A3038 OPEN; A3068).
- Sign of the pressure source (Theorem 8(d)-(h), the literature audit LIT362, LIT366, LIT367 and LIT369, A3044-A3045, A3056-A3057,
  A3063-A3064, A3072-A3073, A3075-A3076; CONDITIONAL). For 0 < c < 2/3 and every omega, a bounded profile with
  U(R.) -> 0 in D' whose source q = tr((DU)^2) = abs(sym DU)^2 - abs(curl U)^2/2 has one sign is zero, and so is a
  uniformly decaying profile, 0 < c < 1, whose q has a nonzero period or returns to itself in D' along translations
  tending to infinity. A nonzero profile in the target range therefore has q of both strict signs. For 0 < c < 1/2 it
  suffices that the means Q(r) of q over the spheres abs(y) = r have one sign, so a nonzero profile has Q, and the
  means q_0 of q over the circles about the rotation axis, of both strict signs (Theorem 8(e), A3056-A3057). That
  statement is kinematic: a C^1 divergence-free field with E(R) = o(R) and one sign of Q is zero; the C^1 shear
  U = (0, 0, g(x1, x2)) of Theorem 8(e), with Q = 0 and E(R) = (2pi/5)R + O(R^(-1)), shows that o(R) cannot be
  replaced by O(R) there. For 2/5 < c < 1/2 it suffices that K(r) = int_0^r s G(s) ds, with G(r) the integral of q
  over the ball abs(y) < r, is bounded below at large radii, for instance that G >= 0, or that the mean of the
  pressure over the sphere abs(y) = r is nonincreasing, at all large radii; a nonzero profile has
  liminf K = -infinity, G < 0 and a pressure mean with positive derivative at arbitrarily large radii, and K(r) is
  below a negative multiple of R^(5-2/c) on a subset of [R, 2R] whose measure is at least a fixed fraction of R, for
  every large R (Theorem 8(f), the literature audit LIT367, A3063-A3064). For 0 < c < 1/2 it also suffices that, about one center a,
  the means of q over the spheres abs(y - a) = r be nonpositive for all large r; so a nonzero profile has, about every
  center, positive means at arbitrarily large radii and a negative mean below a positive one, and q is not compactly
  supported (Theorem 8(g), the literature audit LIT369, A3072-A3073). For 2/5 < c < 1/2 it suffices that int abs(y)^2 max(q, 0) be
  finite (Theorem 8(h), the literature audit LIT366, A3075-A3076). Both rest on kinematic theorems for C^1 divergence-free fields
  with E(R) = o(R), and for such fields decay and E(R) = o(R) do not make that moment finite (A3077). No sign,
  lower-bound or moment condition is derived from decay for profiles (A3046, A3058, A3065, A3074, A3077 OPEN).
- Sign of the work (Theorem 8(i), the literature audit LIT371 and spectral analysis, A3079-A3080, A3106; CONDITIONAL). Written as a forced Euler
  equation (U.grad)U + grad P = Phi, (E) has the work
  w = U.Phi = U.grad(P + abs(U)^2/2) = -(1 - c)abs(U)^2 - (Ay).grad(abs(U)^2/2). For 0 < c < 1/2 and every omega, a
  bounded profile with U(R.) -> 0 in D' whose work has one sign is zero, so a nonzero profile in the target range has
  points of both strict signs of w. The integral of w over the ball abs(y) < r is the energy flux of (2.2.2), and the
  proof uses the rate C/R of Theorem 1(iii), without differentiating the remainder. In that class a nonzero profile
  also has spheres abs(y) = r on which the mean of w is negative and spheres on which it is positive (A3106). For
  0 < c < 1 and every omega, w >= 0 everywhere alone forces U = 0, and so does a nonnegative mean of w over every
  sphere abs(y) = r, since that mean is -c r^(1-k)(r^k ebar)' with k = 2(1 - c)/c and ebar the spherical mean of
  abs(U)^2/2 (spectral analysis, A3106); one sign of w forces U = 0 when U is in L^s, 1 <= s <= 3/2, or U is in L^s and P - p0 in
  L^(s/2) for a finite s > 3/2, with no decay hypothesis; this rests on an extension, proved in LIT371, of Theorem 1.1
  of D. Chae, Liouville-type theorems for the forced Euler equations and the Navier-Stokes equations,
  arXiv:1306.5839v1, 2013. The constant profile U = a != 0 has one-signed work w = -(1 - c)abs(a)^2 but fails Hb and
  every finite L^s condition; thus one-signed work and uniform sublinearity alone do not imply U = 0. No sign of w,
  and no occurrence of both signs at arbitrarily large radii, is derived from decay (A3081, A3107 OPEN).
- Source returns of positive density and radii of negative cumulative source (Theorem 8(j)-(k), the literature audit LIT368 and
  LIT370, A3084-A3085, A3087-A3088; CONDITIONAL for the returns). For 0 < c < 1/2 and every omega, a bounded profile
  with U(R.) -> 0 in D' whose source q returns to itself in D' along the translations by na, n in a set of positive
  upper density, for one a != 0, is zero; the uniform decay needed for the return criterion of Theorem 8(d) is not
  used, since the statement is kinematic for C^1 divergence-free fields with E(R) = o(R). A smooth divergence-free
  field with bounded derivatives, E(R) = O(R^(log 3/log 10)), U(R.) -> 0 in D' and no uniform decay returns exactly on
  every compact set along the translations by 10^k e3, so E(R) = o(R) does not replace uniform decay for sparse
  returns in a kinematic argument; this field solves (E) for no c and omega, and whether sparse returns are excluded
  for profiles is not known (A3086 OPEN). For 2/5 < c < 1/2 the energy law gives, for every lambda > 1 and
  0 < kappa < 1 - (5 - 2/c), a fixed positive proportion, in logarithmic and in Lebesgue measure, of radii in
  [R, lambda R] at which K(r) <= -kappa E(r), for every large R. A smooth uniformly decaying divergence-free field
  with the same energy law has K(10^n) -> +infinity, so the energy law alone gives no eventual sign or limit of K;
  this field solves (E) for no c and omega, and such a statement for profiles is not known (A3089 OPEN).
- No finite velocity norm from the energy law (the literature audit LIT372 and LIT375, A3090-A3091, A3101-A3102; after Theorem 1).
  For 2/5 < c < 1/2, the data that Theorem 1 gives a decaying profile, a bounded field with U -> 0 uniformly and
  E(R) = L R^(5-2/c) + o(R^(4-2/c)), together with a smooth Poisson pressure, are compatible with
  int abs(U)^p = infinity and an infinite weak L^p quasinorm for every finite p > 0, by a smooth divergence-free
  control with unbounded DU that solves (E) for no c and omega. So no L^p or weak L^p hypothesis, for any finite p,
  follows from these data alone; with a bounded gradient outside a ball the energy law gives U in L^p for
  p > (17c - 6)/(2 - 4c) (A3091). More generally, a local Holder seminorm of exponent nu in (0, 1] on the balls B_2(y)
  that grows at most like (1 + abs(y))^kappa, 0 <= kappa < nu(1 - alpha)/3, alpha = 5 - 2/c, gives
  abs(U) <= C(1 + abs(y))^(-sigma), sigma = [nu(1 - alpha) - 3kappa]/(2nu + 3), and U in weak L^(p_V) and in every
  L^p with p > p_V, p_V = 2 + alpha/sigma, with no divergence condition; smooth divergence-free controls with the same
  data and a smooth Poisson pressure lie in no L^p with p <= p_V, in no weak L^p with p < p_V and in no L^(p_V, q)
  with q finite, and solve (E) for no c and omega (the literature audit LIT375, A3101-A3102). For C^2 profiles with
  DU = o(abs(y)^(1/2)) the natural rate gives more: abs(U) <= C(1 + abs(y))^(-(1-c)/c), so U lies in weak L^(3c/(1-c))
  and in every L^p with p > 3c/(1-c), while U in L^(3c/(1-c), q) for one finite q gives U = 0 (A3102; corollaries of
  Theorem 1). Whether every bounded Hb or decaying profile lies in some finite L^p space is not known (A3092, A3103
  OPEN).
- The critical positive-source weight (Theorem 8(l), the literature audit LIT373, LIT374, LIT376 and LIT377, A3094-A3095,
  A3098-A3099, A3118, A3121; CONDITIONAL). For 2/5 < c < 1/2 and every omega, a bounded profile with U(R.) -> 0 in D'
  is zero if, about one center a, int (1 + abs(y - a))^(2/c-3) max(q, 0) is finite, or int_1^infinity r^(2/c-1)
  max(Q_a(r), 0) dr is finite, with Q_a(r) = int_{S^2} q(a + r theta) dtheta, equivalently a finite weighted decrease
  4pi int_1^infinity r^(2/c-3) max(-(r^2 Pbar_a')', 0) dr of the spherical means Pbar_a of the pressure, or the same
  weighted integral of abs(DU)^2 is finite. The weight 2/c - 3 lies in (1, 2), so this contains the moment criterion
  of Theorem 8(h). The underlying statement is kinematic: for a C^1 divergence-free field with E(R)/(L R^beta) -> 1,
  L > 0, 0 < beta < 1, the moment int_{abs(y) < R} abs(y)^2 max(q, 0) is at least c_beta L R^beta for all large R and
  the moment with the weight abs(y)^(2-beta) grows at least like log R, with liminf of its ratio to log R at least
  beta(2 - beta)(1 - beta)L, about every center, a coefficient that cannot be raised in this kinematic class, nor for
  the radial form int_1^R r^(4-beta) max(Q_a(r), 0) dr (the literature audit LIT377 and LIT376, A3118, A3121); a smooth uniformly
  decaying swirl with E(R) = L R^beta for R >= 2, which solves (E) for no c and omega, shows that the power 2 - beta
  cannot be lowered. The natural rate abs(DU) <= C(1 + abs(y))^(-1/c) decides neither convergence nor divergence of
  the derivative form (A3096), and finiteness of these moments for profiles is not known (A3097, A3100, A3120,
  A3124 OPEN).
- The critical gradient weight (Theorem 3(n) and Theorem 8(m), the literature audit LIT378, A3125-A3126; the lower bound PROVED, the
  criterion CONDITIONAL). For 2/5 < c < 1/2 and every omega, a nonzero bounded profile with U(R.) -> 0 in D' has
  limsup_{abs(y) -> infinity} abs(y)^(1/c) abs(DU(y)) >= ((5 - 2/c)H L/(4pi))^(1/2) > 0, with abs(DU) the Frobenius
  norm, L the energy constant of Theorem 1 and H = (1 - 1/c)^2((3 - 1/c)^2 + 4)/((3 - 1/c)^2 + 2) the sharp constant
  of the Hardy-Leray inequality for solenoidal fields at gamma = 1/c - 3/2 (Hamamoto, arXiv:2305.12177v1); so
  DU = o(abs(y)^(-1/c)) gives U = 0. The underlying statement is kinematic: with the energy law,
  int_{1 < abs(y - a) < R} abs(y - a)^(2-beta) abs(DU)^2 >= beta H_beta L log R - C_a about every center, the
  coefficient beta H_beta is larger than the coefficient beta(2 - beta)(1 - beta) of the positive-source moment, and
  it is attained by one smooth uniformly decaying field with E(R) = L R^beta for R >= 2 that solves (E) for no c and
  omega. The limit superior bound is strict, by the rigidity of the Hardy endpoint (Theorem 8(o), the literature audit LIT382,
  A3149-A3150), and it holds with H replaced by H + (5 - 2/c)/10000 (the literature audit LIT385, A3179); under the energy law alone
  the larger endpoint value D_* of Theorem 8(o) is not a lower bound, since a smooth kinematic field that fails (E)
  has an amplitude strictly between D_H and D_* there, D_H being the bound with H before the explicit improvement
  (the literature audit LIT384, A3157-A3158, A3232; A3151, A3159 OPEN). If moreover the negative part of q has a vanishing
  logarithmic moment, for instance q >= 0 outside a compact set, the bound holds with H replaced by H + zeta, an
  explicit zeta > (5 - 2/c)/10000, and near the Hardy value the three source moments are within an explicit
  O(delta^(1/2)) of their endpoint values (Theorem 8(p), the literature audit LIT386, A3161-A3162; A3163 OPEN); for C^1
  divergence-free fields with the energy law and this premise the best such zeta lies between that value and
  2 beta k(2 - k)/((k^2 + 2)(k + 1)), with k = 3 - 1/c, the value of a degree-one field of Theorem 8(o) that fails (E)
  (A3176; A3178 OPEN); the spherical source moment can exceed its endpoint value by an amount of order delta at
  gradient excess delta for fields with the energy law alone, whose negative source need not vanish (the literature audit LIT390,
  A3181-A3182; A3183 OPEN), and at a finite gradient rate H_beta + delta the negative spherical source moment is at
  most delta/(2 - beta) in the same logarithmic sense, which improves the constants 4, 16/13 and C_beta of the earlier
  bounds, C_beta = max(1, c_1(beta)) of Theorem 8(p) being the least constant of the modal comparison at fixed beta,
  and the coefficient 1/(2 - beta) cannot be decreased in a bound required to hold for every admissible gradient
  excess delta, as an explicit family of smooth decaying fields that are not profiles shows when delta tends to 0,
  while optimality at a fixed positive delta is not known (the literature audit LIT391, A3186; the literature audit LIT393, A3194-A3195;
  the literature audit LIT394, A3203-A3204; the literature audit LIT396, A3215-A3216; the literature audit LIT397, A3223-A3224; A3187, A3196, A3205, A3217,
  A3225 OPEN; A3227); under the budget H_beta + delta the spherical source J_a is stable to order delta, with
  deviations of order delta of both signs, while the pointwise source parts I_a and N_a are stable only to order
  delta^(1/2) (the literature audit LIT389, A3188-A3189; A3190 OPEN). Under the C^2 premises of A3102 the natural rate
  abs(DU) <= C(1 + abs(y))^(-1/c) makes this limit superior finite; whether the decay of U controls DU, and optimality
  for profiles, are not known (A3127 OPEN).
- The source-gradient tradeoff (Theorem 3(o) and Theorem 8(n), the literature audit LIT379, A3132-A3133; PROVED as stated, the
  profile consequence CONDITIONAL on a gradient bound). For 2/5 < c < 1/2 and every omega, if a nonzero profile has a
  finite limit superior of G_a(R)/log R, with G_a the critical gradient moment of Theorem 8(m), then its critical
  positive-source moments have liminf of their quotient by log R strictly above (5 - 2/c)(2/c - 3)(2/c - 4)L, by the
  explicit amount m beta^2 L d_beta(M - t^2) of Theorem 8(n); the limit superior is finite when U is C^2 and
  DU = o(abs(y)^(1/2)) (A3102). A source quotient tending to (5 - 2/c)(2/c - 3)(2/c - 4)L along a sequence forces
  G_a(R)/log R -> infinity along it, and one smooth kinematic field that solves (E) for no c and omega attains that
  value with G_a(R)/log R -> infinity (the literature audit LIT380, A3139-A3140). At each finite gradient rate M the least possible
  surplus of the spherical form over C^1 divergence-free fields with the energy law is m beta^2 L d_opt(M), with the
  envelope d_opt of Theorem 8(n), attained by kinematic fields that fail (E) (the literature audit LIT383, A3152; it improves the
  earlier root of the literature audit LIT381, A3146-A3147). Every pair of a finite gradient rate M and a tangential fraction
  between the lower and upper envelopes is attained exactly by such fields, and for each ell0 >= 2 the logarithmic
  energy share of angular degrees at least ell0 is at most min(1, (M - H_beta)/(M_ell0 - H_beta)), a sharp bound
  (the literature audit LIT388, A3173). Whether the decay of U gives a finite gradient rate, and optimality for profiles, are not
  known (A3135, A3141, A3148, A3155, A3175 OPEN).
- The pressure needs no derivative bound: for C^2 profiles with U -> 0, P is the canonical pressure plus a constant
  (A500).
- A misalignment criterion (integral-estimate analysis C48, A902-A907, A943-A945; A909, A946 OPEN). For decaying C^2 profiles, every omega,
the strain at a
  far point in the vorticity direction is bounded by a local misalignment integral D_rho of curl U (defined in Appendix B.6) plus o(1) (A902-A903).
  If the C^beta seminorm of curl U on B(y, 3), for some 0 < beta < 1, grows at most polynomially in abs(y) and the
  average of D_rho along every backward carrier segment from a far vortical point to a fixed sphere is at most 1 + c/2 - epsilon, then DU -> 0, with the natural rates for c > 1/3
  (A904). Conversely, vorticity growth abs(curl U(z_n)) >= delta abs(z_n)^(1/2) forces that average along the segments
  from
  z_n to be at least 1 + c/2 - o(1) (A905); under the same Holder growth, a failure of DU -> 0 gives far vortical points
  whose segment averages are at least 1 + c/2 - o(1) (A943, the contrapositive of A904). Neither the Holder growth
  nor the misalignment bound is derived from decay (A909, A946 OPEN).
- Obstructions to a proof (countertests, not profiles): a smooth divergence-free field with U -> 0, exact Newtonian
  pressure and vanishing momentum residual keeps a fixed strain along an outgoing orbit (A505); local harmonic exact
  profiles with linear or exponential strain along an outgoing axis (A582); blow-up limits at a gradient concentration
  can be a shear or a strain that satisfy every derived limit equation (A682-A688, A689 OPEN for method completeness; integral-estimate analysis as summarized in the accompanying artifacts); smooth
  steady Euler fields with U -> 0 and arbitrarily large gradients exist (A690). Kinematic decay of the canonical
  pressure does not bound gradients either (A760-A761), and neither does a small momentum residual: smooth,
  rapidly decaying, divergence-free, helicity-free swirl tubes with their exact canonical pressure have residual
  O(eps (1+abs(y))^(-4)) uniformly in c and omega, with DU and grad P in L^3 and superpolynomial peaks of both
  (A806-A809, the literature audit LIT180); the residual has unbounded curl, so this says nothing against exact profiles.
- Bounded profiles. Every bounded C^1 profile is a shift of a profile satisfying Hb plus a constant, and for
  0 < c < 2/5 boundedness alone forces U constant (Corollary A.5, A406-A407).

## 7. Status of the main nonexistence conjecture

UNRESOLVED. No proof and no counterexample was found for any c in (2/5, 1/2) and any omega != 0 (A009 OPEN). The
problem has been reduced as follows; each reduction is CONFIRMED at the stated scope (CONDITIONAL where that scope adds
a hypothesis, such as zero helicity in (R3)), and the open problem at the end of each is what remains open on that route.

(R1) Smooth profiles. For C-infinity decaying profiles, fixed omega and c in (2/5, 1/2), nonexistence is equivalent to
the statement that no essential basin domain D_i (Theorem 4) carries U.curl U of both strict signs (Corollary 5.1,
A317). A nonzero smooth profile has a basin and a Bernoulli level on which the helicity takes both strict signs
(Corollary 5.2, A326-A327), and on every vortex-invariant set the positive and negative parts of the helicity have
equal integrals over every Bernoulli band (A328). Almost every vortex line either has U.curl U identically zero or
sees both strict signs arbitrarily far in both directions (A348); for real-analytic profiles the first kind is null
(A349). Closing from a sign holds for a whole gauge family (integral-estimate analysis C47, A852-A859; as summarized in the accompanying artifacts): for
lambda != 0 and f in C^3 with bounded gradient, Omega.(U + lambda y + grad f) = 0 outside a compact set forces U = 0
already at C^2 with no helicity or derivative premise (A853), and one sign of Omega.(U + lambda y + grad f) on every
essential basin forces U = 0 in the C-infinity class (A854); mirror-symmetric profiles have Omega = 0 on the mirror
plane and their essential basins come in reflected pairs (A856-A857). So the bottleneck is deriving a sign. Open:
exclude a sign-changing essential basin. What blocks it: reduced models in which the pressure is not the physical one
satisfy the specified reduced scalar identities at their recorded scopes (B27, A331-A338 at the scopes of A333-A334;
integral-estimate analysis C42, A524-A529 at the scopes of A528-A529; A372). Those identities alone do not decide the sign. A proof needs a
further property that the models fail, which could be a consequence of the pressure or momentum equations (A2745;
A2742 and A2743 REFUTED the earlier wording).

(R2) C^2 profiles. At C^2, one sign of the helicity everywhere already forces U.curl U = 0 identically (A328). The
coverage step of Theorem 4 holds at C^2 under the growth condition (G) of Theorem L (A398-A399, A416-A417,
A430-A432), and then one sign of the helicity on each basin gives U = 0. Open: (G) is not known to follow from decay,
and local identities cannot give it (A415, A423, A447: exact nondecaying profiles violate it).

(R3) Helicity-free C^2 profiles. A nonzero helicity-free decaying profile must contain one of the witnesses (W1v),
(W1i), (W2) of Theorem 6 (A571). None is excluded; by Remark 6.1, (W1v) and (W2) both end in a heteroclinic connection
inside one Bernoulli level to an irrotational carrier equilibrium of the same covector rate, or in an escaping orbit
over a zero of the tail (A831 OPEN). For 2/5 < c < 1/2, under the natural bounds and C^1_loc convergence to the
tail, if the tail is of class C^2 near the scattering direction of an escaping lower-window (W2) trace, that
direction is a finite-jet T0 point (dynamical analysis B59-B61, A1734-A1735; B66, A2457-A2460), and at the equality rate it
lies in the interior of {k = 0} (dynamical analysis B67, A2516).

Under DU = O(abs(y)^(1/2)) the profile also has a leading twisted homogeneous tail V, and Theorem 7 excludes it under
any of seven tail conditions. The current form of this route (CO43, CO45, CO46, LIT195, LIT196): a nonzero profile in
this class forces a critical concentration of vorticity flux near the nodal set of k = (Ax).V on the unit sphere,
int_{abs(K) < tau} abs(G) dA >= C tau (A730), at a closed set Sigma, which lies in the closure of the critical
vortical nodes (points with grad k = 0 and curl V != 0) union the flat zeros of V in the support of curl V (CO46,
A914). Every vortical zero of k is an interior point of {k = 0} (regular nodes A897, noninterior critical nodes A963;
Remark 7.1), and the boundary of the interior of {k = 0} consists of flat zeros of V in supp curl V (A973). So a
nonzero profile has (N2) a flat zero of V in supp G, or (N3) k = 0 on all of R^3 minus 0 (A974). Branch (N3) without
flat zeros is empty: V then has a zero of nonnegative index (Poincare-Hopf) at which curl V is a nonzero multiple of Ax
(CO47, A999-A1002), and every vortical zero of V of an actual profile is a saddle, of index -1 (LIT199,
A1018-A1021).

In branch (N3), two-sided bounds r_- abs(S) <= abs(V)^2 <= r_+ abs(S) (0 < r_- <= r_+) on the whole unit sphere give
V = 0, across arbitrary zeros of S and for every omega (the literature audit LIT264, A1822-A1826, at the natural tail regularity by
LIT267, A1847-A1851); with the rank relation on {S != 0} in place of k = 0 the same bounds force k = 0 by a zero-flux
argument (LIT268, A1866-A1871), and tail vanishing gives U = 0 (Theorem 7(g), LIT269, A1873-A1878); the upper bound on
the whole sphere with a lower bound near the common zero set {V = S = 0} suffices, at the natural tail regularity
(CO67, LIT278, A1950-A1954, A1974-A1977; A2020-A2026); these bounds are not derived from the profile (A1827, A1879,
A2027). Without the rank relation a nonzero profile with the global two-sided comparison has an open spiral sector of
exact irrotational flow with a noncritical contact on supp curl V (Theorem 7(g), LIT271-LIT272, A1904-A1908,
A1915-A1918); for 1/3 < c < 1/2 such a sector with P2 + abs(V)^2/2 = 0 cannot be matched in a C^3 tail (LIT275,
LIT277, A1956-A1959, A1967-A1972), planar sectors with any remainder P2 + abs(V)^2/2 are excluded in a global C^4 tail
with the upper comparison (LIT280, A1995-A1998), exact nonplanar sectors with a nonzero remainder and rank defect
vanishing through order four exist for 1/3 < c < 1/2 and every omega (LIT279, LIT281, A1989-A1993, A2028-A2033; their
rank order is exactly five, and at an axial point with the normalization and scalar homogeneities of Theorem 7(g)
order-five vanishing is excluded for every transverse Hessian, LIT282-LIT284, A2049-A2053, A2055-A2060, A2093-A2097),
and a general sector is not excluded (A1909, A1919, A1938, A1960, A1973, A1994, A1999, A2034, A2054, A2061, A2098).

In fact a nonzero profile has a point of T0, a flat zero of V in supp curl V at which also S = P2 = 0 (LIT201, A1057).
Local tails with open regions where k = 0 exist for every omega (A840, A875-A876, A899-A900, A947-A951; those of
A875 and A899 satisfy all local necessary tail equations), and none is known to be the tail of a whole-space
profile. At a flat zero of V in supp curl V, vortical components with k != 0 that are dense in a punctured
neighbourhood and carry power laws S = D_j abs(k)^q with bounded constants D_j are excluded (A697), and so is finite
local nodal complexity in the dense case (A835); accumulating irrotational regions and unbounded constants are not.

(R4) What every exclusion must use. The open dynamical cases are realized kinematically: a regular hyperbolic
backward attractor (case (alpha*), A242-A246) and a singular-hyperbolic attractor containing a carrier zero (case
(beta), A252-A253) occur for smooth carrier fields B = Ay + U with U decaying, and transported fields W != curl U with all the
kinematic identities. So these cases cannot be excluded by the kinematic identities alone; an exclusion must use a
property these models lack, such as W = curl U or the pressure equation. No kinematic model of case (gamma) is known;
several natural constructions of one fail for kinematic reasons (A2265-A2269), but the case itself is not excluded
(A2270 OPEN). The details of cases (alpha*), (beta), (gamma), the regular and singular attractor results and the
irrotational SRB branch are in Appendix B.7.

Method limit, not a nonexistence result (integral-estimate analysis C53, A1376-A1380): 1.66925 < D_1 < 1.720646, so the R2 route cannot
lift the vorticity threshold above Gamma_sigma/D_1 < 0.599072 Gamma_sigma (Gamma_sigma = min(c(1+sigma), 1), with
sigma the velocity-decay exponent of section 6); the exact value of D_1 is not known (A1381 OPEN).

The natural critical tail abs(curl U) comparable to abs(y)^(-1/c) is not covered by the integrability criteria
(A169).

## 9. Credible counterexample

No counterexample was obtained in this work; its existence is UNRESOLVED. No candidate found solves (E) on all of R^3
with div U = 0 and U -> 0. The explicit fields found during the run are recorded
because each one shows that a particular package of necessary conditions cannot decide the problem. Each line below
is PROVED at the stated scope (verdict given) unless marked; full descriptions are in Appendix B.9 and B.6-B.7, and
for the last four lines in Appendix A.
