under a fixed time-L map of the flow. A continuous function invariant under that map whose shell means vanish is
zero, because an invariant open set on which it exceeds eps has positive density in fixed-ratio shells at infinity,
and Theorem A makes the shell means of abs(U.B) tend to 0 when c < 1/2. Hence H is constant on every such basin on
which U.Omega = 0, or, by LIT60, has one sign; mixing is not needed. With almost-everywhere coverage of the vortical
set by regular basins and decay, U = 0 (LIT55). So within case (alpha*) the remaining gaps are sign-changing
helicity on a basin and coverage by regular basins (A308 gives coverage by SRB basins whose supports need not be
regular attractors). dynamical analysis B26 proves the regular-basin statement by a different route (A310); its quoted energy input
for merely bounded profiles is false as stated (A311: a constant profile), and B26 assumes decay, which suffices.
Its revision B26-v2 adds a periodic-observable rigidity statement and an orbit-segment mean-square bound (A313,
CONFIRMED at C^2, decay, every omega). Its normalization sentence is wrong: the reduced and original Bernoulli functions
differ by c(1-2c)abs(y)^2/2, not c abs(y)^2/2, and the quadratic term is not negligible (A314, REFUTED for that
sentence only). Its remark that a single constant-roof regular basin must carry nonzero helicity is OPEN (A315):
constant H on one basin gives U = 0 only together with global coverage.
Helicity-free singular attractors (dynamical analysis B28-B29, A365-A366). For C^2 profiles, every omega and c != 1/2, a vortical
zero of B (B = 0, Omega != 0) never lies in the closure of an open set on which H is constant (Lemma Z, A365; no decay
is used). For decaying C^2 profiles, 0 < c < 1/2 and every omega, a compact transitive singular-hyperbolic attractor
of the backward carrier that contains a zero of B, with Omega != 0 on it, hyperbolic zeros and a dominated
sectionally expanding splitting (for example lambda_2 < 1+c at every zero, A134), cannot have a basin on which
U.Omega = 0 (Theorem HF-beta, A366; the inputs from Araujo-Pacifico-Pujals-Viana 2009, Theorems B-C, and
Araujo-Souza-Trindade 2018, Proposition 2.10 and Remark 2.11, were rechecked by the auditor; the argument needs only the
finite periodic stable family of the latter, not the physical measure of the former, A397). One such basin already gives
the contradiction; no coverage or energy argument is used. On the helicity-free side only non-dominated singular
attractors (a zero with lambda_2 >= 1+c or lambda_2 = 0) and case (gamma) remain; the sign-changing side is P1.
Helicity-free nonflat irrotational measures (the auditor A442, A444, A445, A449; item 1c and table A). In the same
helicity-free C^2 class, the nonflat irrotational ergodic probabilities whose exponent 1+c exceeds the C^2 coverage
threshold do not exist (A467, the auditor from the literature audit LIT103-LIT104): the velocity would be a transported covector with
rate -(1+c) or 1+4c, the rate 1+4c and all periodic orbits are excluded (A445, A449), the support contains no zero of U
(A464), and such a support is periodic (A465-A466). With A432 this leaves two obstacles to a C^2 helicity-free
Liouville theorem: carrier equilibria and the flat stratum D Omega = 0 (A446, A467). The flat stratum is now
reduced to periodic orbits (A470-A471, the literature audit LIT105-LIT106): a compact ergodic flat probability with B != 0 almost
everywhere and support in closure{Omega != 0}
(automatic for probabilities on Z_E, A484) has U.B = 0 on its support, a
constant covector rate rho and backward spectrum (0, -rho, rho - 3c), and an aperiodic one has top exponent 0. So a
decaying helicity-free C^2 profile with 2/5 <= c < 1/2 vanishes if, for every component E of {Omega != 0}, the set
Z_E of A430 carries neither a carrier equilibrium atom (necessarily at a point with U != 0, A478) with backward top
exponent at least 2(1-2c) nor a flat periodic
orbit with rho <= -2(1-2c) or rho >= 2 - c (CONDITIONAL, A432, A471). Neither witness type is excluded; A473 and A474
(item 1c) restrict both. For flat
periodic orbits an exact irrotational family shows that the known identities on the orbit of order at most two (the
flat law, Hess H = -aM and the differentiated momentum equation) do not bound rho; this does not show that every
restriction from vortical accumulation has been found (synthesis check as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, audited later, A2329-A2335; A2336 OPEN).
Renormalized Bernoulli coefficient (the literature audit LIT61-LIT63, CONDITIONAL theorems at this scope, A287, A288, A292, A293;
decaying C^2 profiles, 2/5 <= c < 1/2, every omega; no Dini, helicity or basin assumption). With the canonical
pressure of A277, the future integral of the Bernoulli equation converges absolutely almost everywhere, and
K = lim e^((1-2c)t) H0(Phi_t y) exists on an invariant full-measure set, with K o Phi_s = e^(-(1-2c)s) K and K in
L^p_loc for 1 <= p < 2(1-c)/(1-2c). A covariant scalar of this kind that lies in L^p_loc for some p >= 3c/(1-2c)
vanishes; the guaranteed range falls short of this threshold exactly when c > 2/5, and even K = 0 does not yet give
U = 0. Exponential L^2 decay of a transported scalar does not by itself give a pointwise endpoint (A289, a scalar
counterexample). Under the Dini hypothesis (D) the coefficient is computed exactly (integral-estimate analysis C28, A295-A296; synthesis
CO23, as summarized in the accompanying artifacts section 24, A300, an independent cross-check): K = (AS).V(S) off the null core, where S is
the scattering map and V the twisted homogeneous tail of Theorem T; the limit holds at every escaping point; and K
is in L^p_loc exactly for p < 3c/(1-2c), unless the angular scalar k(z) = (Az).V(z) vanishes identically. So under
(D) this route is equivalent to the linear tail identity k = 0, that is (1-2c)V = (Az) x curl V. The tail equation
does not imply this identity, and it does not exclude it either: for every omega there are nonzero formal
divergence-free twisted homogeneous tails with k = 0 and V.curl V = 0 (A297; an algebraic countertest, singular at
0, not an Euler profile). Smooth scalar models that satisfy the Bernoulli transport law but not the velocity and
pressure identities can have K singular and nonzero, or K = 0 with H nonzero (the literature audit LIT64, A298).
Invariant-set identities (integral-estimate analysis C28, H.1-H.3, A302; full Dini hypotheses, 2/5 < c < 1/2, every omega). The helicity
density h = U.Omega is in L^1, and int_E h dy = 0 for every measurable set E invariant under the whole vortex flow.
For every measurable set D invariant under the carrier flow and every finite p > 3c/(1-2c),
(1-2c) p int_D abs(H0)^(p-2) H0 U.B dy = 3c int_D abs(H0)^p dy. So under (D) the helicity cancels on every essential
basin of item 1c; this is an integral cancellation and gives no pointwise sign. Also under (D), K is locally
essentially bounded if and only if the tail scalar k vanishes (A303). A local limitation (A304): for every
0 < c < 1/2 and omega != 0 there are affine exact profiles (unbounded) with a vortical equilibrium having two positive
backward exponents, so a bracket or curl argument alone cannot remove such equilibria from the older entropy route;
the elementary construction behind A308 does not need that step.

### B.9 Credible counterexample (historical section 9)

None. Kinematic models satisfy the specific packages stated for them but are not Euler profiles: a smooth
decaying field with the LIT15 frozen-vorticity properties (A051), and the decoupled bracket pairs of item 6 (A066,
A121; with a transitive singular attractor, A252-A253). An exact local Euler solution (singular on the axis, not decaying) has a vortical saddle periodic
orbit with zero circulation and the forced exponents (synthesis Example 13.3, A144), so the periodic-orbit
constraints are locally consistent. A smooth decaying non-profile satisfies the exact energy, vertical angular momentum and helicity
balances on every centered ball of radius R >= 1, Dini strain decay and zero total helicity (LIT29, A145; one
coefficient corrected by A146): this integral package alone cannot decide the conjecture. The smooth decoupled
model of item 6 has the exact critical weak vorticity tail, and its Biot-Savart reconstruction is a smooth decaying
field with actual curl and the natural energy tail, but it changes the carrier and leaves a residual, so it is not a
profile (LIT36, A179); every nonzero amplitude of that particular reconstruction has a nonzero Euler residual
(LIT39, A195). This is not extended to other bracket constructions. The harmonic polynomials of CO18 and LIT47 (A225, A237; every c > 0 and every omega != 0 for LIT47) with their
Bernoulli pressure are global smooth Euler profiles with a saddle horseshoe that do not decay (U = grad phi grows
polynomially); a cutoff keeps the horseshoe and decays, but is then not a profile (A226). The regular kinematic
model of item 6 (A243) realizes case (alpha*) with W different from curl U, and the Biot-Savart reconstruction of its
W fails the Euler equation at every nonzero amplitude when 2/5 < c < 1/2 (LIT49, A244-A245). The same holds for the singular-hyperbolic parameter variant of item 6 (case (beta)): for
2/5 < c < 1/2 and every omega no nonzero multiple of its Biot-Savart reconstruction is an Euler profile (LIT54, A262;
this construction only).

### B.10 Next mathematical step (historical section 10)

State of the problem: every open case requires the coupling W = curl U, combined with the profile equation beyond
the kinematic identities. The reasons:
- Case (alpha*) is realized kinematically: there is a decaying bracket pair with a transitive regular attractor
  (item 6; A242-A246).
- Case (beta) is realized kinematically for 2(2 - sqrt 2)/(5 - sqrt 2) < c < 1/2, a range containing the target range:
  a parameter variant of CO6 has a singular-hyperbolic backward attractor, containing a zero of B, that is the backward
  limit of almost every point of a trapping handlebody (item 6; A252, A253).
- Irrotational horseshoes occur in exact, nondecaying profiles (A225, A237).

So the next step is an argument that is Euler-coupled and global. It should be tested first on case (alpha*).

1. Recommended: transfer the LIT49 mechanism from a fixed W to an actual profile. LIT49 (A244-A245) excludes the
   Biot-Savart reconstruction of the regular model as follows:
   - The difference D of the two carriers commutes with W, so D x W = grad F with F a decaying first integral of W.
   - A nonzero F has a level torus that traps the backward flow.
   - The orbit map to the trapping boundary turns its compact boundary leaf into a periodic W orbit, and the bracket
     scaling forbids periodic W orbits.

   For an actual profile there is only one carrier, so the step that produces F is missing. The form of the
   coupling on a trapping knot exterior N of the attractor is known exactly (spectral analysis C24, A249; item 7): if curl U = W
   on N, the pressure is single-valued if and only if the period of (1-2c)U.dy - alpha, alpha = (B x W).dy, on a
   meridian of N vanishes. The question is whether this period condition, together with the Biot-Savart law
   U = BS(W) on R^3 and the far-field structure below, produces a decaying first integral of W or a trapping torus.

   Inputs not yet combined with the period condition:
   - The Bernoulli relation Omega.grad H = -(1-2c) U.Omega. H is a vortex-line first integral exactly where the
     helicity density vanishes. If H is constant on R^3 and U is uniformly sublinear, then U = 0 (LIT51, A256). On a
     regular basin with one-signed helicity, H is constant without mixing (CO22, A290-A291; item 8), so within
     (alpha*) the problem is reduced to basins on which U.Omega changes sign, together with coverage by regular
     basins. In the C-infinity class coverage by SRB basins is PROVED, so for C-infinity decaying profiles the
     conjecture reduces to sign-changing helicity on some essential basin (item 1c, A309, A317). The same holds for
     C^r profiles with Gamma_Z < r(1-2c), or Gamma_E < r(1-2c) for every vortical component E (CONDITIONAL, A417,
     A422, A430-A432). At the C^2 baseline without that bound the
     coverage step is open (A318).
   - The renormalized Bernoulli coefficient (item 8): under (D), K = (AS).V(S), and the integrability route to K = 0
     is equivalent to the tail identity (Az).V = 0, which the tail theory alone does not decide (A296, A297, A300).
   - The far-field decomposition U = V + W_r (integral-estimate analysis C23, C24; A250, A251). Here V is the exact twisted homogeneous
     tail and W_r is a finite-energy remainder, whose energy (5c-2) norm(W_r)_2^2 = 2N is fixed by the strictly
     positive alignment N of U (x) U with the strain of the tail.

   Since N > 0 whenever U != 0 (A250, under the Dini condition), a bound N <= 0 derived from the geometry of the
   basin of an attractor would exclude (alpha*) under that condition. The identity (5c-2) norm(W_r)_2^2 = 2N is
   obtained by testing the equation against W_r itself, so such a bound needs a second expression for N independent
   of that test; it is equivalent to the exclusion, not a weaker target. In local form (integral-estimate analysis C27, A275),
   N_D = ((5c-2)/2) int_D abs(W_r)^2 - b_D for an open set D, where b_D is the outward flux of
   J = (Ay) abs(W_r)^2/2 + (abs(U)^2/2 + P) W_r. A basin bound N_D <= 0 therefore requires the basin to export J-flux,
   while in total the vortical set absorbs J-flux, since div J = ((5c-2)/2) abs(W_r)^2 on the irrotational set.
   (A275 qualifications: W_r is bounded only away from 0, and an ordinary surface flux on an unbounded D needs separate
   convergence.) For every invariant open D, with S the scattering map, the weighted pressure work
   int_{D, abs(S) < r} abs(S)^(-(5c-2)/c) U.grad P dy tends to -(c/2) int_{sigma_D} abs(V)^2 dA as r -> infinity, where
   sigma_D is the trace of S(D) on the unit sphere and V is the tail (integral-estimate analysis the accompanying artifacts B.9, A276, under the Dini and
   scattering assumptions; the integral converges absolutely under the full Dini assumptions for 2/5 < c < 1/2,
   A282). This localizes energy to invariant sets with no boundary term; it gives no sign for N_D.
   Basin geometry: the basin has positive density at infinity (A092), and almost every vortex line of the basin
   crosses the attractor infinitely often in both directions (A154); almost every such line also returns arbitrarily close to its
   starting point at both ends (integral-estimate analysis C26, Theorem V(d), A274; V.6 uses Omega = curl U), so a basin argument cannot use one-way escape
   of vortex lines to infinity.

2. Case (beta). It is realized kinematically (A252, A253), so it has the same status as (alpha*) and is the second
   test case for item 1. The setting is the genus-two trapping handlebody H of item 6: H_1(H) has rank two, so the
   A249 pressure condition consists of two periods, and the zero of B in the attractor is subject to the local
   constraints of item 7 (real saddle spectrum, A147, A159; null basins of finite vortical networks, A155). Case
   (gamma) has no kinematic model yet; its irrotational part is item 5.

3. Local versus global. It is open whether an exact local profile with omega != 0 can carry a compact vortical
   hyperbolic set of positive entropy, in particular an attractor. At omega = 0 the Lyapunov identity C2 excludes local
   recurrence: every recurrent point is an equilibrium, and every invariant probability on a compact invariant set lives
   on {B = 0}. (Compact invariant sets can still contain heteroclinic orbits: for U = grad(-x^3/3 + x y^2) the segment from
   0 to (c, 0, 0) is invariant.) An the second-model review (as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, collected 23:10Z; its explicit formulas checked
   by the synthesis in the accompanying artifacts; audited later at the scopes below, A2363-A2364 and
   A2366-A2370, while A2365 REFUTED the premise of the question that at omega = 0 every compact invariant set consists
   of equilibria, which the parenthesis above corrects, and A2371 is OPEN) found neither a construction nor an
   obstruction, and identified why the natural local constructions fail:
   - a compact invariant set on which B and Omega do not vanish is automatically uniformly hyperbolic, with rate
     e^(-(1+c)t) along Omega and e^((1-2c)t) transversally for the backward flow, and the skew return maps of CO13
     admit an abstract horseshoe, so the rates and the return-map algebra give no obstruction;
   - on a product neighbourhood with constant vorticity Omega = q e, q != 0, the bracket forces (e.grad)B = (1+c)e, so
     the flow is a planar flow with an affine fibre equation and has no horseshoe; harmonic-gradient perturbations of the
     local saddle solution of item 9 (A144) keep this reduction;
   - for omega != 0 (at omega = 0 the saddle circle of that solution consists of equilibria, A2368), a small
     perturbation cannot create a horseshoe in a thin tube around that saddle orbit (hyperbolic isolation), and
     a perturbed irrotational horseshoe stays irrotational on every continued periodic orbit whose monodromy lacks the
     multiplier e^((1+c)T) (vorticity transport would make e^((1+c)T) a multiplier).
   The cylindrical family U = (-r/2 + C/r) e_r + (kappa r + D/r) e_theta + z e_z satisfies the bracket for all C, D, but it
   has a single-valued pressure on an annular neighbourhood only when 2 kappa C + (1-2c) D = 0: an explicit instance of
   the A249 period condition. A local construction would show that every obstruction must use the far field. A local
   obstruction would exclude (alpha*) and (beta) directly.

4. Basin coverage (the literature audit LIT41; PROVED in the C-infinity class, A305-A308; CONDITIONAL for C^r profiles on the
   strain bound (r-1)(1-2c) > 3L, A312, sharpened to (r-1)(1-2c) > L_+ + L_- in A373, or on Gamma_Z < r(1-2c),
   A416-A417). History: the literal derivative seminorm of the source does not give the needed C^1
   bounds (A259), and a step of its measure construction is false as stated (A260). The team replaced the external
   construction by an elementary one: an affine curve tree, a geometric-time selection and an original-curve measure
   construction (the literature audit LIT65-LIT67, A305-A307). The capture deduction (A299) was reviewed by the synthesis
   (as summarized in the accompanying artifacts), whose one necessary correction (the parent levels must tend to infinity) is supplied by
   A307, and was then confirmed (A308). Consequence: item 1c(ii). What remains of this item: coverage for C^2
   profiles, and coverage by regular attractors (the SRB supports may meet {B = 0} or {Omega = 0}). For C^2 the
   question is now sharper. The derivative growth rate of the backward flow on its absorbing core is
   Lambda_core = max(1-2c, Gamma_Z) when Omega is not identically zero (for U = 0, Lambda_core = 0 < 1-2c, A484),
   where Gamma_Z is the largest Lyapunov exponent of ergodic probabilities on the carrier or vorticity zero set of the
   core, and the maximum is attained when that set is nonempty, with Gamma_Z = -infinity otherwise (A398-A399). Coverage at C^r follows from
   Gamma_Z < r(1-2c) for every integer r >= 2 (CONDITIONAL on this bound, A416-A417), and from the weaker componentwise
   bounds Gamma_E < r(1-2c) (A430-A431). The concrete C^2
   question is therefore: does decay force every ergodic probability on {B = 0} or {Omega = 0} to have largest exponent
   below 2(1-2c)? At an equilibrium p of B with Omega(p) != 0 the eigenvalues of -DB(p) are -(1+c) (eigenvector
   Omega(p)) and two numbers whose real parts sum to 1-2c; for the point mass at p the condition says that the
   smaller of these two real parts exceeds -(1-2c). Nothing proved so far gives this, and the first jet does not:
   the admissible first jets at a vortical carrier zero (tr DU(p) = 0 and DB(p)Omega(p) = (1+c)Omega(p), with
   Omega(p) = curl of the linear part) allow any transverse pair with real-part sum -(1-2c). For example, c = 0.45,
   omega = 0, Omega(p) = e3, DB(p) = [[-0.05, 0.5, 0], [1.5, -0.05, 0], [0, 0, 1.45]] is admissible, and the top
   eigenvalue of -DB(p) is 0.916, far above 2(1-2c) = 0.2 (synthesis check; first jets only, not a profile).
   Exact solutions confirm this beyond the first jet: the affine profiles U = Ny of A415 (LIT84) solve the full
   equation, for every omega, and have a vortical equilibrium of arbitrarily large exponent; they do not decay. So a
   bound on Gamma_Z must use decay or another global property. A violation needs large compressive strain on the
   carrier of the measure: along Psi, d/dt abs(v)^2 = -2 v.(cI + sym DU)v and sym DU is traceless, so every ergodic
   probability nu has largest backward exponent at most -c + int (-lambda_min(sym DU)) dnu, and an exponent at least
   2(1-2c) requires int (-lambda_min(sym DU)) dnu >= 2 - 3c (integral-estimate analysis Note A9 item 2; spectral analysis C32;
   A454, CONFIRMED). So lambda_min(sym DU) > -(2 - 3c) on each compact Z_E gives Gamma_E < 2(1-2c) and C^2
   coverage (A454). Decay does not bound sup abs(DU), so this is a necessary condition for a violation,
   not a bound. At carrier equilibria with Omega = 0 and D Omega != 0 large exponents are realized by exact entire
   quadratic profiles for every omega (the literature audit LIT96, A447); these do not decay. The two stress tests of spectral analysis C32
   (A455) do not change this: a smooth cutoff of a fast core satisfies the equation only near the core, and its
   vorticity vanishes near K, so it tests Gamma_Z but no Gamma_E; an exact decaying multipole with a carrier
   equilibrium of any exponent is singular at the origin. Whether decay gives the bound is OPEN (A456). In the global helicity-free class the
   nonflat irrotational probabilities with exponent 1+c do not exist (A467; item 1c and table A: the covector law
   A444, the exclusions A445 and A449 of the rate 1+4c and of periodic orbits, no zero of U on the support A464, and
   periodicity of such a support A465-A466, from the literature audit LIT103-LIT104); so in that class the C^2 test can fail only at
   carrier equilibria or on the flat stratum D Omega = 0.
   On the flat stratum, a compact ergodic flat probability in that class with B != 0 almost everywhere (A490) whose
   support lies in closure{Omega != 0}
   (automatic on Z_E, A484) has U.B = 0 on its support (A470), a
   constant covector rate rho and backward spectrum (0, -rho, rho - 3c), and top exponent 0 when it is aperiodic
   (A471, the literature audit LIT105-LIT106). So carrier equilibria and periodic flat orbits with rho <= -2(1-2c) or rho >= 2 - c
   are the only places where the C^2 test can fail in that class (A471). For such a periodic orbit, Omega vanishes on
   the local unstable cylinder and is tangent to the stable one; when rho <= -2(1-2c) every nearby Bernoulli loop on
   the stable cylinder carries a zero of Omega (A014); every loop on a nearby Bernoulli annulus has zero circulation,
   so the Kelvin step of A449 gives nothing; and an exact irrotational family shows that the known identities on the
   orbit of order at most two do not bound rho, although not every restriction from vortical accumulation is known
   to have been found (synthesis checks as summarized in the accompanying artifacts and as summarized in the accompanying artifacts,
   audited later, A2329-A2335; A2336 OPEN). Carrier-equilibrium witnesses have U != 0 (A478). For vortical equilibria the exact threshold is
   -2(1-2c) < rho < 1-2c (A468), and rho >= 1-2c is impossible (A496), so only rho <= -2(1-2c) remains. These two are the concrete next targets.

5. Branch (I). An irrotational SRB measure with Omega flat on its support and Leb{Omega = 0} > 0. Exact profiles with
   an irrotational SRB measure and a positive-volume basin exist for every omega != 0 (LIT50, A255), but they are
   unbounded. So a local obstruction specific to irrotational SRB measures does not exist (this answers the question
   left open in A227), and an exclusion of branch (I) must use decay or sublinearity. LIT51 (A256) is a tool of this
   kind. It localizes to the vortical set under sublinearity and to almost-everywhere covers by constant-H open
   sets under decay (LIT55, LIT56, A265-A266); localization to a single nondense basin is open.

Quantities already checked and found not to discriminate, so not worth repeating (each is satisfied by the regular
kinematic model or by a smooth decaying non-profile):
- the Omega flux through surfaces bounded by compact boundary leaves;
- zero circulation on a single periodic orbit;
- the unstable-current identities (A217);
- scalar moment identities on invariant measures (A104; whether their list of test vectors is complete is OPEN, A105);
- the centred-ball energy, angular momentum and helicity package (A145);
- periodic multiplier ratios (A164).
The full Kelvin law for the actual U along every material closed curve is not in this list: it is equivalent to the
profile momentum equation with a single-valued pressure (A284), so no non-profile satisfies it (A285 corrects an
earlier version of this list). Whether zero circulation on all periodic orbits can hold on a regular attracting
kinematic model is OPEN (spectral analysis C27).

Since A309 (00:30Z, hour 6.4) the C-infinity problem is one question (A317): can U.Omega change sign on an
invariant open essential basin D of a vortical SRB measure of a C-infinity decaying profile? At the C^2 baseline the
coverage step and the unrestricted problem both remain open (A318). On such a basin D almost every point is recurrent
for the vortex flow, and H0 is not monotone along the vortex line through each recurrent point with U.Omega != 0
(A283); these lines fill a positive-volume vortex-invariant subset of D. Whether almost every vortex line of D has
this property is OPEN (A319): a positive-volume family of lines on which U.Omega vanishes identically is not
excluded. A348 shows this is the only exception (every other line sees both strict signs arbitrarily far in both
directions), and A349 removes it for real-analytic profiles. A326 adds that some open interval of Bernoulli values is attained with both signs along one recurrent
vortex orbit, and A328 that on every vortex-invariant set the positive and negative parts of U.Omega have equal
integrals over every Bernoulli band. Both follow from Omega.grad H = -(1-2c)U.Omega alone, and the reduced scalar
countertest LIT71 (A329) satisfies them. Under (D), int_D U.Omega dy = 0 (A302). The synthesis's lean for the
hour-16 choice is this question as the primary target, with the Euler-coupled routes of item 1 as the second.

What the known estimates give on a sign-changing basin. This paragraph is exploration: the synthesis's
as summarized in the accompanying artifacts section 25 and the second-model review as summarized in the accompanying artifacts, whose formulas were checked by
the accompanying artifacts (exact evaluation at rational points). The auditor checked the four result
proofs of that consultation in A367-A371 at the scopes stated below; the comparisons in (2) are threshold
calculations, not theorems.
(1) The Bernoulli mean decay used in A309 is the ball bound int_(abs(y)<R) H0^2 <= C R^(7-2/c) after the change of
variables under Phi_t. On a fixed ball it is weaker than the trivial volume bound e^(-3ct) once c > 2/7, so it
constrains only the far part of Phi_t Q. Under (D) the canonical H0 is O((1+abs(y))^(-a/c)), and raising the power
does not help: the means of abs(H0)^p over Phi_t Q saturate at the volume rate e^(-3ct) (A371). Along the vortex line through a support point z it says that a times the
helicity integral from z to the far part of the line is close to H0(z) in mean square. This is consistent, not
contradictory.
(2) Assume, as an extra hypothesis, that the measure obtained by spreading nu along short vortex segments has a
bounded density. Then the nu-averaged time a vortex line spends in a bounded set up to vortex time T is
O(T^((1-2c)/(1+c))) (A370; without the density hypothesis the smear is only L^1, and the matching averaged lower
bound needs in addition an attractor carrying nu and a positive lower bound for the density near it). Comparing this with the energy bound for abs(U)^2 would give a contradiction only for c < 2/5,
the range already covered by Theorem A; with H0^2 in place of abs(U)^2 the range is c < 2/7. So averaging arguments
of this kind stop at the lower end of the target interval. dynamical analysis's pointwise form of this occupation estimate is
OPEN (A334), and conservativity and ergodicity alone give no polynomial occupation lower rate (the abstract tower
LIT70, A325). The auditor's averaged occupation estimate and SRB-to-vortex transfer are CONFIRMED (A374-A375, after the
synthesis review as summarized in the accompanying artifacts and a literature review): nu-typical vortex semiorbits are
unbounded and recurrent, and if supp nu is compact and avoids both {B = 0} and {Omega = 0}, every fixed smear has
bounded density, so the bounds above hold for such nu without (D); for such supports the smear also has a positive
lower density near supp nu, the support attracts, and the averaged occupation bounds are two-sided (A388, the literature audit
LIT75). Whether the A308 measures have such supports is not known, and no pointwise occupation rate or pointwise
vanishing of H0 follows.
(3) Exact examples. (a) A local exact profile, singular on an axis and not decaying, with a periodic orbit of
backward spectrum (1-2c, 0, -(1+c)) and helicity of both signs near it; its stable set has zero volume. (b) A
twisted-homogeneous tail field that solves the linear tail equation and whose helicity is proportional to
cos(theta)^3, for every omega (A369). dynamical analysis found the example (a) independently; it is CONFIRMED by direct computation in A335 and, in a shifted form with h != 0 on the periodic circle, in A368, where
e^((1-2c)T) and e^(-(1+c)T) are the backward multipliers. So neither the local Lamb structure nor the tail equation forces a sign of the helicity.
(4) Holding B and Omega fixed, the substitution (H0, U) -> (H0 + F, U - grad F/(1-2c)) preserves the Lamb identity
and curl U = Omega for every C^2 function F, and preserves the coarse far-field bounds when F has compact support. It
breaks only div U = 0 and B = Ay + U among the equations; it does not preserve the refined energy law, since the
energy changes by the positive constant (1-2c)^(-2) int abs(grad F)^2 while E(R) = L R^beta + O(R^(beta-1)) with
0 < beta < 1 (A372). So the Lamb identity, curl U = Omega and the coarse far-field bounds alone do not decide P1; a
proof needs a further property that this substitution breaks, such as incompressibility, the self-consistency of the
carrier in the near field or the refined energy law (A2745; A2742 REFUTED the earlier wording).
dynamical analysis as summarized in the accompanying artifacts makes the same
point for the
scalar identities; the audit (A322) requires the coefficient R = H - U.B = P - abs(U)^2/2 to be transformed as well, to
R + F + B.grad F/(1-2c), so the physical pressure is not retained. The audited model B27 (dynamical analysis; A331-A338) makes this
concrete. A prescribed regular carrier, the Biot-Savart velocity of its transported vorticity, a decaying Lamb
potential, the subcritical energy bound and both helicity signs on the regular basin coexist for 2/5 < c < 1/2 and
every omega (A331). The model is not an Euler profile: the momentum residual (U_1 - v) x W is nonzero (A332), the
Lamb-derived pressure violates the pressure Poisson equation with a positive spherical defect (A337, LIT72), and no
nonzero multiple of its velocity is a profile for any pressure (A338). So the reduced scalar system with an
independent coefficient R, the Biot-Savart law and the energy bound do not decide P1 at the scopes of A333-A334; a
proof needs a further property that the model fails, which could be a consequence of the physical pressure equation or
of the momentum equation itself (A2745; A2742 REFUTED the earlier wording). B27 does not satisfy every scalar
identity of the campaign: the full-profile second-order identity on its invariant measure fails (A2743 REFUTED the
claim that B27 satisfies every scalar identity). This does not show that every scalar method
fails (A333). integral-estimate analysis C42 makes the scalar obstruction precise (A524-A529). For every measurable vortex-invariant set E the
helicity density has zero integral against every bounded function measurable for the sigma-algebra generated by the
vortex-invariant subsets of E and by H, so the conditional expectation of sgn(U.Omega) vanishes where it is defined
(A524, CONFIRMED at the natural-tail scope; no pointwise cancellation and no sign follow). On a fixed vortical
background, replacing H by an arbitrary compactly supported C^2 function preserves the reduced scalar system and gives
both helicity signs near any vortical point (A525); the pressure boundary formulas hold on arbitrary measurable sets
(A526); the explicit reduced sign-changing tails and energy models are confirmed at their reduced, singular or
nondecaying scopes (A527), with exact pole values -3 and 5 replacing the printed extrema (A528). Whether such tests
exhaust all arguments for P1 is OPEN (A529); a correlation inequality equivalent to U.Omega = 0, if proved
independently, would still be useful.

## Appendix C. Accompanying artifacts

The accompanying artifacts contain:

- Reproduction instructions: the problem statement, references, exact commands and pass criteria for the supplied checks.
- Literature review: statements of References A to C, the Liouville theorems of Chae and related results, with their assumptions and applicability to rotating profiles.
- Preprint audits: independent examinations of the Liu preprint.
- Exact identities: derivations of the profile, pressure, vorticity, Bernoulli, circulation and Fourier equations.
- Proof attempts: successful and unsuccessful arguments, with the steps at which unsuccessful arguments fail.
- Counterexample audits: explicit examples, candidate counterexamples and tests of proposed inequalities.
- Proof obstructions: the unresolved mathematical obstacles.
- Audit record: numbered verdicts A001-A3270 cited throughout this report.
- Check scripts: Python 3 scripts using sympy, with checksums, covering symbolic identities, exact-arithmetic tests and numerical diagnostics.
- Written proofs and reviews: 928 documents, located through the cited verdicts in the audit record.
